Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 12:58:58 GMT

"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that – he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead – both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.

She teased the new prime minister over his informal style – he "seems like a nice guy…I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.

"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.

But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.

Firstly, on the domestic front – his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options – which criminals to free first.

Secondly, on the international front – after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again.

Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.

He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?

It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.

And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".

What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.

Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.

Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?

And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?

Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?

Given the intended long term home of No 10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032, this is a live question.

And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.

Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all – that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".

It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one – where is your mandate for doing this?

The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.

It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.

His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.

Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.

Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."

Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.

His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.

In other words, whether he is popular enough.

Let's see.

Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 10:40:05 GMT

Klopp's first game in charge will be against the Netherlands on 24 September

Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.

The former Liverpool manager was appointed on a four-year deal on Friday to replace Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned this month after Germany's shock World Cup defeat by Paraguay in the last 32.

But the 59-year-old issued a warning to the media as he held his first news conference as Germany's head coach.

"If you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace then I'll be gone, I'll just turn away," Klopp said.

"I know there are other countries where national team coaches are treated even worse.

"I'm not doing this job for myself, I'm doing it for you. I'm taking this job even though I've seen how you've treated Julian Nagelsmann and Thomas Tuchel.

"I love this job but I am always ready to call it quits if need be."

Both Nagelsmann and England boss Tuchel came under media scrutiny after their exits from the World Cup, with Tuchel criticised for his defensive tactics and substitutions as the Three Lions let slip a 1-0 lead in their semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Klopp's appointment was widely expected for weeks and his contract will see him through to the 2030 World Cup, co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

"Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team," he added.

"This is the pinnacle, the absolutely high point of my footballing career as coach. I will give everything I have got."

They became best friends - then discovered they were brother and sister

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 09:52:26 GMT

Dave Green and Andrea Urmston found they instantly hit it off when their paths crossed while working in separate roles at Manchester Airport.

The two strangers got on so well they could complete each other's sentences - which made sense when they discovered the truth.

Dave was Andrea's biological brother, but had been adopted by another family when he was a baby.

"I was shaking, I was just shaking and my heart was pounding," Andrea told the BBC. "I'd finally found him. It's unbelievable."

In 2005, Dave was managing the bus station at the airport and Andrea serviced the vending machines.

Over the next two years they became firm friends, texting and phoning each other when they were not at work.

One day during a phone call, Dave told Andrea something he had never mentioned before. He was adopted and his birth name was Stuart Proudlove.

"I kind of froze and didn't speak for a minute," said Andrea.

Her maiden name was Proudlove and she had a brother who was adopted before she was born.

"It's not a very popular name and it had to be him. Other than family, I had never heard that surname anywhere else," she added.

She immediately rang her mother, Susan, to check her long-lost brother's birth date. They matched: 24 March 1966. She called Dave straight back.

"I said 'it's got to be you, it's got to be you', and I said 'I need to see you', and so I went to pick him up," Andrea said.

As they were driving to their mother's house, Dave realised where he was. They were driving along the bus route he used to cover before becoming a manager.

His old route had taken him right past his mother's house, and the school that Andrea had attended.

He had been within touching distance of his birth family without realising.

Susan said finally meeting Dave was a surreal moment.

"There were lots of tears. Then we just all hugged," said Andrea.

"I couldn't believe that I'd got my brother and my mum together, it was amazing."

Andrea's mother had told her that she had a brother when she was younger.

She told her he had been given up for adoption and had gone to a lovely lady who could not have children of her own.

"I immediately wanted to go and call him so we could play," Andrea said.

Susan said she had tried to find her son with the help of the Salvation Army, but had not got anywhere.

"I asked if we could go and get him back," Andrea said. "She did explain that it didn't work that way, so I promised her that I would find him for her one day."

Now they were finally being reunited.

"She had wanted that since being as young as I can remember," Andrea added.

"So yeah, I gave her that. I promised her that."

On the mantlepiece in Susan's home was a picture of Dave as a baby.

It had been sent by his adopted parents to his birth mother days after his adoption.

The same photograph had also been displayed in his adopted parents' house.

Dave had known since he was 10 that he was adopted, because his adoptive parents had shown him the paperwork.

But he said he had a very happy childhood, and had never harboured any desire to track down his birth mother.

"I didn't feel like I had to go searching or have any unanswered questions," he added.

For all three, finding each other has been a life-changing experience.

"I went from having really not a lot of positivity in my life at the time, to finding out that my best friend was my sister," Dave said.

"I'd found my birth mum being able to sort of make her truly happy. And I'd found a family really that I never really knew existed."

Their mother died recently, but both said they were glad she got to be reunited with her son.

"She was so desperate to find you to make sure you'd had a really good life," Andrea said.

For Andrea, the reunion was bittersweet. She had longed to find her brother for years.

"My mum and dad, they separated unfortunately and so I went through a lot of hard times knowing [Dave] was out there but I didn't know [where]."

The pair said they were now making the most of the time they have together after moving in with each other in Kidsgrove, Staffordshire.

Finding each other was, they said, their "lottery win".

Heatwave anxiety can make you feel 'incredibly helpless' - here's how to manage it

BBC News Fri, 24 Jul 2026 00:05:55 GMT

At the peak of the June heatwave, the warmest June on record in England, all Tavia Watts could think about was how hot it was in her two- and five-year-old's bedroom - above 30C in some cases.

"During the heatwave, I've got a high level of anxiety all the time and I'm pretty much useless," she told the BBC. "I've had to leave bedtime when my husband reads [my kids] stories to have a little cry and to calm down, because it's just too hot in their room and I'm afraid for them."

Feeling "incredibly helpless", the 36-year-old posted a short reel to her hundreds of followers on Instagram, in which she voiced her inner anxieties. To her surprise, it got more than 18,000 likes and 1,700 reposts.

In the video Tavia, a stay-at-home mum living in Cheltenham, says the heat "feels like the world is literally ending", she's "terrified for [her] children's lives", and that she "wants to scream at the people not taking this seriously".

Watts is not alone. A 2022 study from the University of Bath estimates that about 4.6% of people in the UK have climate anxiety, which is recognised as a form of mental distress by professional bodies and the NHS. Young people and women are among the groups most at risk, according to a study published in 2025.

"Anticipatory anxiety", related to heatwaves in particular, has become more common, say psychologists Dr Caroline Hickman from the University of Bath and Dr Emma Lawrance from the University of Oxford.

"Once people have been through a traumatic event like a flood or a heatwave, they anticipate the next one," Hickman, who offers therapy to individuals experiencing climate anxiety, told the BBC.

In the UK, "now we're getting the repeat, repeat, repeat [heatwaves]. It triggers that sense that 'I can't be safe in the world, and the world can't be trusted'," she added.

In June's heatwave, Hickman said she "had people saying they're going to kill themselves, I've had people saying they're going to terminate pregnancies, I've had people saying that they want to sell their houses and move somewhere cooler".

Watts said that her video "clearly struck a chord with people" - including therapists posting comments about coping mechanisms - and that she wanted to help others deal with climate anxiety.

"It can go one of two ways. You can either just fall into doomism and think, 'What is the point?'" she said.

"Or you can try to do something. I sign petitions during a heatwave; I organise climate community events; I run a free children's clothes swap shop. During the last heatwave, I finally became vegetarian, because then I can tell my kids at least I tried."

Lizzie Ellen was "terrified" when she first learned about climate change in school, but at the time felt like it was "quite far off".

Now, the scorching temperatures of recent weeks have left the 38-year-old from west London "obsessively" reading about the heatwave and constantly checking her weather app.

Ellen, who gave birth to her first child a few months ago, told the BBC she had felt both isolated and worried about keeping her baby cool.

"With the baby, I've been staying indoors more, keeping on top of checking the temperature… so there's that isolation," she said.

"Then there's the future, which is really scary to be honest - thinking about how the heat we experienced back in June could become a daily reality within a very short time, [my baby's] lifetime… and that's pretty miserable, staying indoors all day in the dark."

Some have made major life changes in response to their climate concerns.

Ecologist Dr Francis Windram told the BBC that he had moved from Ascot, near London, to Lancaster in the north-west of England, specifically because of the cooler climate.

He still bought a portable air conditioning unit in spring as a precaution, and is concerned about his grandparents and his father living further south in Hertfordshire.

"We're looking at 35C-plus heat in houses that were not designed for it, with people who are not as able to regulate their temperature, and can't necessarily afford to just fit an AC," Windram said.

Lawrance had some recommendations on how to cope with climate anxiety:

Talk to others: There's often "a huge perception gap between how concerned people are about climate change, and how much they think other people care", said Lawrance - meaning you might wrongly assume that you're in the minority, or even that you're alone.

"Make space to be kind to yourself, to tend to those emotions and know that it's coming from a place of care for the world," she added.

Find a community: Lawrance recommended finding a strong social network who care about the same things, and taking positive action together.

Whether it's planting a garden in your school or putting solar panels on the roof of your business, action can not only help you channel your anxiety into something positive, but can help alleviate the symptoms of anxiety too.

Lawrance cited the Climate Psychology Alliance in the UK for further support, as well as groups like the Resilience Project, the Climate Cares Centre, and the Climate Majority Project.

Keep yourself cool: Your physical health also affects your mental health, and being hot can also make your anxiety and mood worse, Lawrance said - so she recommended making sure to keep yourself physically cool in extreme heat.

"Having a cool shower, putting a cold washer on your neck, making sure you're hydrated - all of those things will help physiologically as well," she said. "There's a lot we can do - we're not powerless."

Advertisement

El Niño happens when easterly winds weaken in the tropics, allowing water they’ve pushed into the Western Pacific Warm Pool to wash back towards the eastern Pacific. Rainfall shifts eastward, weakening easterly winds further in a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Although it’s a natural cycle, it delivers a jolt of heat on top of 1.4°C of global warming, setting off extreme weather around the world, according to Berkeley Earth.

Already, this El Niño is revving up faster than any previous event. Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific have reached 2.1°C above average, vastly outpacing the 1.6°C increase seen at this time of year during the 1997-98 El Niño, the previous record-holder for speedy development.

Within a few months, the huge swathe of warm water across the Pacific will heat up the rest of the world. Global temperatures in 2027 are likely to reach 1.7°C above the pre-industrial average, smashing the record set in 2024, when temperatures were 1.5°C above the average. The El Niño is coming on so fast that there’s even a chance 2026 will break that global temperature record first, as some have predicted.

As a result, the 20-year temperature average will likely exceed 1.5°C by 2029, failing the goal set by the Paris Agreement, said Robert Rohde at Berkeley Earth in the briefing.

Different regions will see different extreme weather. The 1997-98 super El Niño caused flooding on the Yangtze that killed more than 3000 people.

The north-eastern US tends to face drier conditions during El Niño, while the southern US gets wetter, which can unleash mudslides in places like California. Australia tends to dry out, raising the threat of bushfires like those seen during the “Black Summer” of 2018-19.

India, southern and central Africa and parts of Central and South America all face drought risks, which could push up the price of commodities like rice, coffee and chocolate even in less-exposed countries like the UK.

How extreme heat affects the body – and the best ways to cope

“We might get lucky and have smaller reduction in rainfall in Africa or India, but generally… the damages scale with the strength of the El Niño,” said Hausfather.

Strong El Niño events also cause harm to ecosystems, such as widespread coral bleaching, which is expected this year as well.

While some research suggests El Niño events are getting stronger, other studies disagree. What is clear is that the impacts will get worse as global warming accelerates.

“It’s something we need to start preparing for today and make sure we have systems in place to deal with drought conditions,” said Hausfather.

Graph theory is the study of networks made up of nodes, or vertices. The Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture can be thought of as a logistical challenge: imagine shipments from a warehouse to multiple locations can be split into much smaller deliveries that can be sent on different routes. The conjecture states that this scenario can be converted into another where shipments cannot be split, and that the total cost of shipping will not increase.

Chris Bowman-Scargill at the University of York, UK, says there’s a running joke in mathematics that every conjecture in graph theory is false, just as the Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture has now been proved to be.

“In fields like number theory or algebra, patterns that hold for small rank [simple situations] often hold for a long time,” says Bownman-Scargill. “Whereas in graph theory, structural behaviour can shift dramatically once you add just one or two vertices… which is how these conjectures continue to be made. You can see how people miss these things.”

AI has made rapid advances in mathematics in recent months. In May, an OpenAI model cracked a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős, causing a stir in mathematical circles. Earlier this week, an AI found a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, which had stood for nearly a century. “AI is really good, and at least at some mathematical tasks, already superhuman,” says Saha. “There is a fair bit of low-hanging fruit out there. Some conjectures can now be proved or disproved by AI with very little human input; the main challenge is simply pointing the system in the right direction. On the other hand, I don’t think AI is yet at a place where it can build the theory needed to prove some of the deepest open conjectures people care about.”

But there are signs that AI is here to stay and will become a vital tool for mathematicians. Alexander Yong at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign says AI’s growing role in mathematics will empower researchers to discard dead ends and instead push in promising directions.

“Counterexamples to old conjectures are never quite as impressive as finding a sequence of interlocking arguments that constitute a proof,” says Yong. “However, I’d expect that AI will soon prove many conjectures by a combination of their inherent superhuman energy in knowing the literature and trying many things at a prompt. Those conjectures that survive AI scrutiny will be the genuine goals for human innovation.”

A parasitic fungus that grows on caterpillars has been turned into a dress designed to be able to repair itself if damaged.

In the video game and TV series The Last of Us, Cordyceps fungi evolve to infect humans and turn them into zombies, but in reality they are harmless to humans.

How our ancestors used mushrooms to change the course of human history

Using the fungus Cordyceps militaris as a base, Ke Li at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and her colleagues created a living textile that can be “programmed” with different properties using various microbial components.

Advertisement

It feels denser and less fibrous than cotton, says Li, and is closer to a soft, non-woven sheet or a flexible leather-like material.

“After washing and processing, the material does not have a strong mushroom-like smell,” she says. “A slight biological or fermentation-related odour may be detectable in freshly prepared samples, but this can be greatly reduced through cleaning, drying and post-treatment.”

Free newsletter

The fungus is made up of thin filaments known as hyphae. Li and her colleagues first grew the fungus as small, spherical pellets in liquid culture, then washed them and placed them into moulds where they formed a sheet.

To prevent the resulting textile from becoming brittle, it was soaked in glycerol, which acts as a “plasticiser”, making the naturally rigid fungal structure softer and more flexible.

“We do not use a conventional fabric, polymer mesh or other external supporting scaffold,” says Li. “The Cordyceps militaris mycelial pellets themselves serve as the structural building blocks, and their intertwined hyphae form a continuous, self-supporting sheet.”

To add colour to the material, the team introduced yeast cells that were engineered to produce orange, blue and purple pigments. “These cells can be applied to the fungal textile so that the colour is generated biologically, rather than through conventional synthetic dyes,” says Li.

The researchers also showed they could change the properties of the textile by adding other fungi, for example making it clean itself by repelling water droplets. For UV protection, they added Aspergillus niger, a mould that commonly grows on fruit and vegetables. This forms a dark layer on the surface of the material containing melanin pigment, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

How our ancestors invented clothing and transformed it into fashion

If the textile is damaged, then fresh, wet fungal pellets can be applied to the area that needs repair and the fungus simply grows over the breach.

Under dry conditions, most biological activity is greatly reduced, and the cells may remain inactive or dormant, says Li.

But under humid conditions with nutrients present, some cells can become active again. This latent biological capacity is what enables functions such as regrowth and repair, and also means that the material is readily biodegradable, showing near-complete visible degradation in soil after just over 40 days.

Li and her colleagues created a dress out of their fungal material, but so far no one has worn it. “We’ve treated it as a rather precious display piece, and it was made in a small size,” she says. “Perhaps next time we should find a few petite and adventurous volunteers to try it on and see how it looks in motion.”

Justin Beardsley at the University of Sydney, Australia, says the biodegradability of the dress is amazing compared with what we currently have in terms of getting rid of waste from fast fashion.

But that is also a drawback because you don’t really want to be wearing something that is too easily biodegradable, as “it’ll break down while you’re wearing it”, he says.

As the textile is alive, Beardsley envisages one day being able to change its qualities in real time. “If there was some way that you can make it water-repellent for a while, becoming less breathable during rain, that would be fantastic, and then you can revert to the more breathable, less water-repellent version afterward,” he says.

Earth is heating up faster than at any time in its history

New Scientist July 24, 2026

As Europe bakes in what could be its hottest and driest summer on record, the rapid transformation of our climate is harder than ever to ignore. But how much hotter will it get, and what will that mean for life on Earth?

To get a picture of our future, we can either use computer models or look to episodes of rapid climate change in the geological record. While models are invaluable in terms of tracking where our world may be heading, peering back into deep time provides unrivalled information about cause and effect; about how the climate has changed in the past and what the consequences were. There is no guesswork involved, as the evidence is all laid out for us in the sediments and rocks, in the ice sheets and in the remains of ancient life.

Europe’s heatwave is the hottest and most humid ever

Looking back in time also helps us to put human-caused global heating in context by making comparisons with past episodes of rapid temperature increase, and when we do this, the news isn’t good. It isn’t so much the degree of heat that is the issue – our world has been much hotter than it is today for much of its 4.6-billion-year history – but the speed of change.

Advertisement

Perhaps barring the immediate aftermath of the dinosaur-obliterating asteroid impact 66 million years ago, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels have never risen as quickly as they have in the last couple of centuries. Even worse, nowhere in the geological record is there evidence for the average temperature of our world climbing as quickly as it is now. This means 10 times faster than during the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, which marked extreme hothouse conditions 56 million years ago, and at least 20 times faster than at the end of the last glacial period.

Judicious analysis of past climates also permits us to recognise potential analogues for where our world is heading in the decades and centuries to come. Over the last 50 million years or so, the planet’s climate has followed a broadly cooling trend, which we are now rapidly rewinding – a process, if you like, of prehistorification. Deciding how far back we will end up is still within our gift, but it is a given that our grandchildren will grow up in a climate different to any experienced during the tenure of human civilisation.

Free newsletter

Modelling studies suggest that if – and it’s still a big if – emissions peak by 2040 and then fall quickly, we will rewind the climate clock 3 million years and bequeath to our descendants a Late Pliocene climate. Then, atmospheric CO2 levels were much lower than today, at 330 to 400 parts per million (ppm), but the temperature was between 2.5ºC and 4ºC above the pre-industrial average, and sea level 15 to 25 metres higher. Pliocene conditions could start to appear in the continental heartlands as soon as the 2030s and spread out from there.

If we fail to rein in emissions fast enough, or if natural feedback effects drive more heating than expected, then a further rewinding of the climate clock back to the Miocene becomes more likely; to a time 15 million to 17 million years ago, when CO2 concentrations, at 400 to 600 ppm, were a bit lower to moderately higher than they are today. At 6ºC to 8ºC above the 1800s, however, the temperature was far higher than expected for such CO2 levels, suggesting the involvement of other heating factors that we don’t yet fully understand. Sea level was maybe 50 metres higher than it is today.

Collapse of AMOC ocean current may already be locked in

But this may not be the end of it. The current high rate of heating documented by satellite observations and borne out by Earth’s rapidly escalating energy imbalance implies that rewinding the climate clock back fully 50 million years remains within the bounds of possibility, eventually reprising the blistering heat of the early Eocene hothouse. Such conditions would make most of our world uninhabitable for humans, and severely test the capacity of our species to prevail.

As the Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam observed almost 1000 years ago: “When I want to understand what is happening today, or try to decide what will happen tomorrow, I look back.” They are words that serve us well as we contemplate our future climate, and that we ignore at our peril.

Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London. His book, The Fate of the World: A history and future of the climate crisis, is published by HarperNorth.

But fasting can also involve eating no, or very little, food for a single, continuous stretch of time, which is sometimes done for religious reasons.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Focusing on this type of fasting, Steve Horvath at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues recruited 32 volunteers with no known health conditions, who consumed just 200 to 250 calories a day in the form of fruit juice, vegetable broths and honey for 12 days. “This is not something to try at home,” says Horvath. “It was a medically supervised inpatient programme at a specialist clinic, with clinical monitoring throughout.”

Advertisement

These calories were consumed in three windows: 7am to 9am, 11.30am to 1pm and 6.30pm to 8pm. This put the participants – who were aged between 25 and 72 – in a fasting metabolic state, says team member Robin Mesnage at King’s College London, which occurs when the body shifts from burning energy from food to energy stored in the body.

The team used 12 different epigenetic clocks to estimate and track the volunteers’ biological ages over the course of the study. These mostly work by looking at patterns of chemical tags on DNA, which change in predictable ways with age, but can also be altered by our lifestyle, such as how much we exercise.

Free newsletter

The clocks varied in their responses to the fast. Some ticked upwards to an older age, suggesting that the extreme fast put negative stress on the body. But one clock, which was built to detect changes in body mass index, went down.

Incongruous results are a known issue between different epigenetic clocks. But one finding was fairly consistent: the participants who were generally deemed to have a young biological age, relative to their chronological age, at the start of the study lost more weight than those who were biologically older.

The researchers weren’t expecting this result, according to Hovarth. “Honestly, we don’t know the mechanism,” he says. But he thinks the most likely explanation is that biologically younger people have better metabolic adaptability, which means they can swiftly switch from using food for energy to stored fat when calories are scarce.

This is plausible, because biologically younger people tend to have more efficient mitochondria, which leads to faster switching to fat burning, says Paulina Correa-Burrows at the University of Chile.

A clinical trial to reverse age-related vision conditions using stem cell treatment could finally deliver on the promise of a major discovery in ageing and regeneration made 20 years ago, says columnist Graham Lawton

Biologically younger people may also have better pathways for sensing nutrients in cells, which could also enable more efficient switching between fuel sources to burn fat. But Correa-Burrows cautions that the group of volunteers was small, so the results are inconclusive.

Horvath now wants to see investigations into whether biologically younger people also lose more weight under less restrictive diets. “A 12-day medically supervised fast is not a long-term diet and it isn’t meant to be one,” he says.

In the meantime, a healthy lifestyle can help lower our biological age. “The habits with the strongest evidence for healthy epigenetic aging are the familiar ones: do not smoke, [do] physical exercise, keep a healthy body weight and maintain good relationships,” says Hovarth.

Do not change your diet without first speaking to a doctor.

10 of the best pictures of solar eclipses throughout history

New Scientist July 24, 2026

A total eclipse occurs somewhere in the world about once every 18 months on average, and that has been the case for all of human history. For millennia, humans have been documenting their views as the moon moved between Earth and the sun, blocking out the sun’s light and revealing its swirling outer layers.

The earliest confirmed written record of a solar eclipse comes from the 13th century BC, when scribes in China wrote that the sun had been “eaten”. Scientific and religious texts continued to document eclipses up until the present day, and researchers now use these texts to study both how eclipses have changed in the intervening centuries and how human views of them have evolved throughout time. This particular petroglyph, carved into stone by the early Pueblo people in New Mexico, is thought to represent a total solar eclipse that occurred on 11 July 1097. The swirls around its perimeter bear a resemblance to the corona of the sun, which is only visible when the moon hides the rest of the solar disc.

More recent art depicts religious and scientific figures observing eclipses directly. This watercolour from the late 17th century shows a group of French missionaries observing a solar eclipse with King Narai of Siam and his court in April 1688. They can be seen using the projection method to avoid looking directly at the sun: the light passes through a telescope and projects the shape of the eclipse on a screen beneath it. This technique is still commonly used today, with pinhole cameras or even just the gaps between shadows cast by leaves on the ground.

Advertisement

Scientific sketches of eclipses proliferated as science became more of a formal, professionalised pursuit. This drawing, by astronomer José Joaquín de Ferrer, depicts an eclipse that occurred over New York on 16 June 1806. Watching this event led de Ferrer to give the outermost layer of the sun, the corona, its name. He was among the first people reported to have hypothesised that the corona must be part of the sun, not the moon, because of its incredible size – it can stretch to as much as 20 times the width of the main disc of the sun, as he sketched here.

The first photograph of a total solar eclipse with enough detail on the corona to be scientifically useful was taken on 28 July 1851 by Julius Berkowski at the Royal Observatory in Königsberg, Prussia. With help from the astronomers at the observatory, he attached a small telescope to a device called a heliometer, a specialised instrument for measuring the sun. This daguerreotype was an 84-second exposure taken through the telescope. Not only is the corona visible, but several eruptions can be seen blasting from the sides of the sun over the edge of the moon.

After Berkowski’s image, the ability to take photographs of eclipses became more widespread around the world. These images were taken by William and Frederick Langenheim on 26 May 1854 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Without access to the scientific tools Berkowski used to magnify the light from the eclipse, they were forced to use small cameras to create these miniature daguerreotypes, the largest of which is just 7.2 centimetres tall and the smallest less than half that size.

The total solar eclipse that swept over parts of Africa and South America on 29 May 1919 proved to be one of the most important eclipses ever observed. This image comes from the expedition that astronomer Arthur Eddington made to the African island of Principe. He and his team photographed several stars located close to the sun to compare their apparent positions in the sky before and then during the eclipse. In this image, the stars are marked with horizontal lines. The comparison proved that the gravity of the sun bent the light coming from those stars, providing some of the first evidence for Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity and creating a new understanding of the workings of the universe.

Eclipses became popular photographic targets for scientists and non-scientific photographers alike. This image, taken by Frederick Goetz on 24 January 1925, shows an effect called the diamond ring, or Baily’s beads. This effect occurs just at the beginning and end of totality, when the edge of the moon is nearly, but not quite, covering the entire disc of the sun. Ridges and craters on the moon’s surface let through only a few rays of sunlight, creating the glare that earned Goetz’s inscription of “Signs and Wonders”.

Modern images of solar eclipses, such as this one taken in California on 11 July 1991, display the corona in much more detail than has ever been achievable before. Past observations revealed an astonishing mystery: the corona is about 300 times hotter than the sun’s surface. Eclipses provide prime opportunities to try to figure out how and why it gets so hot, plus research how we might be able to predict solar activity someday to mitigate its potential effects on satellites, astronauts and even electrical grids on Earth.

The sun itself is, of course, not the only thing that researchers study during eclipses. As seen in this image taken in Chile on 2 July 2019, during a total solar eclipse the sky darkens almost completely. Temperatures drop precipitously. Birdsong ceases almost entirely. Through studying how animals react, researchers try to decipher what they may be feeling and thinking, and how they perceive the unexpected darkness.

When viewing an eclipse from the ground, it can be hard to imagine the scale of it. These images of an 8 April 2024 eclipse, taken by NASA’s Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR) satellite, show that handily. The dark spot moving across the planet in these pictures is the shadow of the moon. People standing within that spot witness totality, and those along the edges see only partial eclipses.

Our ability to image and understand these phenomena has come a long way since petroglyphs in stone walls – imagine what we’ll be able to see in another few thousand years.

The researchers found that the only areas with specialised neurons were those in dedicated sensory cortices, such as the primary visual cortex. Instead, the neurons in most areas of the brain responded to various aspects of the task. For instance, those outside of the visual cortex also seemed to be involved in processing the image, as well as deciding which side of the screen it was on and generating the movement to turn the wheel. “The important thing to stress is that there are specialised neurons [such as place cells],” says Fusi. But these are not the norm, he adds.

Free newsletter

The researchers also found that most neurons didn’t respond in the same way to the same stimulus. For example, the somatomotor areas, which are regions associated with planning movements, responded strongly to licks and whisker movements. Other areas still responded, but not as strongly. This suggests that while specialism exists, individual neurons generally aren’t myopically focused on one type of information.

“The problem is if you’re arguing there’s no [specialisation], somebody can always say: ‘You just needed [to study] a few more neurons [to uncover it],’” says Ben Hayden at Baylor College of Medicine in Texas. “This [study] is a giant smack in the face saying: ‘Fine, we got 14,000 neurons and we still didn’t find it [for the most part].’”

Having a collection of neurons that respond to the same stimulus in slightly different ways may maximise the amount of information the brain can process. This may mean that these generalised neurons contribute to a plethora of tasks, including memory, cognition, decision-making and perception.

Around a third of people are able to almost fully rebuild their brains after a stroke and uncovering why is pointing the way to better treatments for everyone

The researchers point out that the mice’s task wasn’t particularly complex. A complicated, multidimensional set of tasks could shed light on when individual neurons focus their responses on one aspect of such tasks versus another, says Fusi.

He and his team are now collaborating with researchers who study non-human primates and patients who are conscious during open brain surgeries, such as those treating epilepsy, to see if the findings in mice apply to people.

With all these projects, Fusi hopes to shift the emphasis from looking at the role of individual neurons to patterns of activity across many cells in the brain. “It’s very difficult to draw conclusions by looking at one neuron at the time,” he says. “Instead, we [should] look at all the neurons together. That’s the perspective of the brain because each neuron in the brain doesn’t [get input from] one single [other] neuron. Each neuron in the brain looks at 10,000 other neurons that are connected on its dendritic tree.”

Nature DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10668-4

We now know how a black hole can be flung across the universe

New Scientist July 24, 2026

Two supermassive black holes smashing together can create another supermassive black hole that recoils at such high speeds that it launches out of its galaxy. Though this would only happen in rare instances, it provides an explanation for the recent possible sighting of such a runaway black hole.

In 2023, researchers noticed a thin, line-like shape in an image that the Hubble Space Telescope took of a patch of space about 7.5 billion light years from Earth. Based on further analysis, including images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and studying the line’s light, Pieter van Dokkum at Yale University and his colleagues concluded that the line was a consequences of a never-before-seen cosmic event – a supermassive black hole flying out of a galaxy at supersonic speeds and leaving a chain of young stars in its wake.

Not everyone agrees with this analysis, but Tousif Islam at the University of California, Santa Barbara and his colleagues have now uncovered what it would take for a supermassive black hole to behave this way.

Advertisement

This physicist is hunting for the biggest black hole in the universe

Informed by observations and large-scale simulations of the universe, the team built a mathematical model that could take the idea and properties of a runaway black hole (RBH) and reveal its origin story. “It’s similar to fossil analysis, we are working backwards to see what the past looked like,” says team member Digvijay Wadekar at the University of Texas at Austin.

The team found that an RBH like the one posited by van Dokkum and his colleagues would have had two parent supermassive black holes, where one was spinning quickly and was six times more massive than the other. These would have violently merged about 70 million years ago, creating a recoiling RBH.

“When we do simulations of binary black hole mergers… almost every time there is a recoil kick, but in most of the cases the recoil kick is much smaller,” says Islam. The team estimated that a large enough recoil to match the proposed RBH could happen in fewer than 10 per cent of black hole mergers.

“As a mathematical exercise, it’s very interesting, because the physical mechanism to produce a runaway supermassive black hole is there. Now, the chances that this happens in reality are very low,” says Jorge Sánchez Almeida at the Institute of Astrophysics of the Canary Islands in Spain.

Since 2023, he and his colleagues have argued for a less exotic interpretation of the original images. According to their analysis, the line represents a galaxy, full of star-forming regions, viewed edge-on.

Free newsletter

Analysing light from these regions is subtle and it can easily be mistaken for a consequence of a fast-moving RBH, says Sánchez Almeida. He says that several other measurements are consistent with the edge-on galaxy interpretation, including the relationship between the mass of the stars and their rotational velocity, which fits the Tully-Fisher relation, a known fingerprint of a disc-shaped galaxy.

The team, however, stands by the RBH view. “There are competing explanations and this seems like the least unfavourable, or you can call it most favourable,” says Wadekar. Islam says that he learned about the RBH when his university hosted a conference about black holes, and it was speaking with astronomers there that convinced him that its existence and past were compelling to study.

This debate could be resolved by future observations. Sánchez Almeida says that the JWST already has the capability to image this region of space further and definitively identify the edge-on galaxy. The team wants to use its model to predict gravitational waves that the merger of RBH’s parents would have produced, which could be detected by near-term instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), says Islam.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

New Scientist July 24, 2026

I’m a big fan of the New Scientist podcast Change Your Mind, on which my erstwhile colleagues Cat de Lange and Helen Thomson discuss “all the brain health advice you really need to know”. One recent episode is well worth a listen if you’re interested in keeping your brain healthy. Cat and Helen invited JoAnn Manson, who is head of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Massachusetts, to the podcast to discuss her research on multivitamin supplements and brain health. She described how she and her colleagues found that people over 60 who take a daily multivitamin show significantly slower cognitive decline and age-related memory loss over two to three years.

The only four skincare ingredients that have been proven to work

For me, that was a marmalade dropper. On the issue of supplements, I’m a hardened sceptic. Based on a New Scientist feature I edited many years ago, as well as a recent update by another ex-colleague, Alison George, my informed opinion is that very few supplements work and some are positively harmful. I make an exception for vitamin D because I live too far north to make enough on my own from the feeble winter sunshine. But once the clocks have gone forward, I stop taking it. I would also take folic acid if I were female and trying for a baby (I’m neither), long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids if I didn’t eat oily fish weekly and vitamin B12 if I were a vegan. But as for the rest, I don’t waste my money.

For people who are willing to shell out for supplements, there are myriad opportunities. One of the thriving markets is in anti-ageing. Although very few if any have been scientifically validated, I’m slightly less sceptical. A few years ago, I took an anti-ageing supplement called alpha-ketoglutarate for six months for a story I was doing. I had my biological age measured before and after, and it went down. But that is hardly solid data of the sort you get from a clinical trial.

Advertisement

Of that, there is plenty, and it doesn’t cast anti-ageing supplements in a good light. I found a gold mine of information in an academic book published earlier this year called Supplements and Drugs for Healthy Longevity. Under the guidance of the eminent biogerontologist Suresh Rattan at Aarhus University in Denmark, an expert panel rated the evidence for more than 250 compounds with supposed anti-ageing effects. These ranged from vitamins and minerals to plant extracts, traditional medicines, probiotics and hormone supplements, plus some much-hyped compounds I often hear bigged up in anti-ageing circles: NAD+, coenzyme Q10, spermidine and D&Q, or dasatinib and quercetin. Interestingly, they didn’t look at the evidence for alpha-ketoglutarate.

Suffice to say that none of them met the highest standard of evidence, which Rattan defines as “solid, reproducible and trustworthy”. A few reached a secondary level, but, on the whole, the authors recommend obtaining these compounds from food. “At present using one or more nutritional and other supplements… is mostly an act of faith and hope”, rather than being based on strong scientific evidence-based data, the book concludes.

Suddenly feeling old? Evidence now suggests that rather than a long, steady decline, we dramatically age around three specific times in our lives. Might it be possible to stay younger for longer?

But it also says that more research is needed. So, I had a look at Manson’s. Her results come from a clinical trial she and her colleagues ran between 2015 and 2023 called COSMOS (Cocoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study). The trial recruited more than 21,000 people aged over 60 and gave one group of them a daily multivitamin plus cocoa extract, which contains flavonoid compounds thought to be beneficial for some age-related conditions. Other groups received just a multivitamin, just cocoa extract or nothing. The principal goal of the trial was to test whether the multivitamin/cocoa cocktail would reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer. It didn’t, but the researchers still found nuggets of useful information in the data.

One of these was the effect on brain health, as discussed on the podcast. Another, which was published earlier this year, looked at the effect on ageing in general. A subgroup of 958 participants had their biological age measured at the start of the trial and then again two years later. Those who received the daily multivitamin aged, on average, more slowly than those who did not (the cocoa extract had no effect). The effect was relatively modest – a month or two over the two years – but over the course of longer periods that could really add up.

Free newsletter

Another study adds weight to the idea that supplements can slow down ageing. Last year, a team including researchers at the University of Zurich in Switzerland published a study on omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in people aged 70 to 91. The traditional verdict on these supplements has been that they aren’t worth taking unless your diet is deficient in the main sources of omega-3, which are oily fish, flaxseed, chia seeds and walnuts. The Zurich research challenges that. Over the course of three years, the people who took the supplement aged biologically three months less, on average, than those who took a placebo. Adding vitamin D and strength training increased the benefit to four months.

So, have I changed my mind about supplements? Not yet. Both studies rely on biological age measurements, which are notoriously unreliable. Neither found any meaningful change in the health of their participants, and slowing down biological ageing doesn’t necessarily correspond to what really matters: an increase in healthspan. It is also possible, Manson told the podcast, that the participants in her study were deficient in one or more vitamins, and the multivitamin supplement merely corrected for that.

But it’s a start. As Daniel Belsky and Calen Ryan at Columbia University in New York wrote in response to the multivitamin study, “Evidence that simple multi-vitamin supplementation can slow aging, even slightly, would have substantial implications, including for public health guidelines.” We’re not quite there yet, but if and when we are, I’m heading to the pharmacy.

A severe thunderstorm warning has been issued for Wellington.

MetService said its weather radar detected severe thunderstorms near the city and Wellington Airport at 9.07am.

“These severe thunderstorms are moving towards the eastnortheast.

“These thunderstorms are expected to be accompanied by torrential rain.”

MetService said torrential rain can cause surface and/or flash flooding about streams, gullies and urban areas, and make driving conditions extremely hazardous.

The National Emergency Management Agency advises people should:

- Take shelter, preferably indoors away from windows;

- Avoid sheltering under trees, if outside;

- Get back to land, if outdoors on the water;

- Move cars under cover or away from trees;

- Secure any loose objects around your property;

- Check that drains and gutters are clear;

- Be ready to slow down or stop, if driving.

The warning is due to be updated or lifted by 10.07am.

Taumarunui and surrounding areas have been hit by torrential downpours overnight, some right when a ‘severe’ 5.9 magnitude earthquake hit.

The combination of a large quake and heavy rain has caused slips to come down, some closing roads, with geotechnical assessments being carried out this morning.

MetService said Taumaranui recorded 48mm of rain in the past 24 hours.

Nearby National Park, south of Taumarunui, saw 73mm over 24 hours, peaking at around 10mm an hour.

MetService said showers moving in from the west were markedly heavier around coastal areas overnight, as warmer seas fuelled the downpours.

That led Taharoa, near Kawhia just south of Raglan, to have the biggest overnight falls, recording 24.5mm of rain in a single hour.

MetService said across the country the weather is looking “pretty grunty” this weekend, with sharp winds, localised downpours and scattered thunderstorms possible.

Overnight, west coast regions near Raglan had some of the heaviest falls and storms, while National Park saw 73mm over 24 hours.

Bitter winds are expected to see temperatures plummet into single digits, while forecasters are warning hail and heavier showers could fall in multiple areas across the North Island

West of Taupō and into the Bay of Plenty could experience the heaviest falls.

Snow is also tipped to fall as low as 800m on the Desert Rd plateau, with a road snowfall warning in place.

In its latest video update, NIWA says the upper half of the North Island is expected to cop harsh winds.

“The winds, they’re going to be howling, a pretty grunty south westerly for coastal areas of Northland, Auckland and down through the Waikato and a similar story for those southerlies developing about the Wellington region.”

A strong wind watch is in place for Auckland and Great Barrier Island until 7pm, with drivers being warned that strong, sudden winds could close the Auckland Harbour Bridge intermittently today.

New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA) said it expected wind gusts of up to 75-85 km/h between 4am and 11am, before ramping up to speeds of 90-100 km/h until 10pm.

“With the potential for sudden and high wind gusts, traffic control measures may be implemented on the bridge including the possibility of short closure periods,” NZTA said.

NIWA said isolated downpours could not be ruled out anywhere in the North Island or upper South Island.

Heavy rain is on the cards for central parts of the North Island including in the Tararua Range, Taihape, Taupō as well as Christchurch through Kaikōura and Marlborough.

Snow levels are expected to be just a “couple of centimetres” in Otago including on Milford Rd and Crown Range Pass and north through Lindis Pass.

Eight MetService orange road snowfall warnings are in place across the South Island, while one is in force for the North Island’s Desert Rd, with 1 to 2 centimetres possible down to around 800 metres.

Meanwhile 6-metre-high swells are forecast for the northwestern coastal areas.

5.9 magnitude quake strikes Manawatū region, more than 20,000 people report feeling ‘severe’ shaking

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

An earthquake has struck south of Taumarunui in the Manawatū-Whanganui region with tens of thousands of people reporting feeling the shake. Photo / Geonet

A 5.9 magnitude earthquake has struck Manawatū-Whanganui in the early hours of this morning.

The quake hit 5km south of Taumarunui at 4.51am, at a depth of 9km.

Nearly 23,000 people have reported feeling the shaking, marked as ‘severe’ on Geonet, from as far north as Auckland to the top of the South Island - with a few people even reporting feeling it in Dunedin.

Minor slips have been reported on roads in the region and drivers have been urged to drive with caution.

Emergency services and roading crews are “currently assessing the situation”.

A series of aftershocks have been reported after a 5.9 magnitude earthquake struck Manawatū-Whanganui before 5am.

GeoNet has recorded 10 aftershocks south of Taumarunui following the initial quake.

The most recent was recorded at 9.16am, 10 km south of Taumarunui.

The aftershock was magnitude 2.2 and at a depth of 10km.

The strongest aftershock recorded at 5.21am was magnitude 3.7 at a depth of 6km.

A series of aftershocks have been reported after a 5.9 magnitude earthquake struck Manawatū-Whanganui in the early hours of this morning.

Manawatū-Whanganui Civil Defence Emergency Management Public Information Manager Jono Galuszka told the Herald aftershocks could cause additional damage as well as raise anxiety.

“The advice around earthquakes remains the same: if you feel an earthquake, no matter how strong it is, drop, cover, hold,” Galuszka said.

He said if you’re in bed, the best thing you can do is put your pillow over your head and stay in bed.

Manawatū-Whanganui Civil Defence Emergency Management Public Information Manager Jono Galuszka said crews have been assessing damage from the quake this morning.

He said Ruapehu District Council and Fire and Emergency New Zealand have been inspecting minor property damage such as broken windows.

Galuszka said he understood no major damage was reported.

He said they have also not received any reports of damage to three waters infrastructure at this stage.

“All the reservoirs are all good, and everything seems to be working."

Galuszka said KiwiRail told them the Marton to Hamilton and Whanganui to New Plymouth train lines were currently closed for inspection, but they were hoping to have those lines open again at about 11.30am.

Manawatū-Whanganui Civil Defence Emergency Management Public Information Manager Jono Galuszka told the Herald State Highway 43 and State Highway 3 were currently closed.

“State Highway 4 is still open, although apparently there’s some small slips along the route, so just take care,” he advised.

Galuszka said they had not heard much regarding local roads being affected, but urged residents to report any problems to the Ruapehu District Council.

“If people are travelling through the area, if they have to, it would be great if they could stick to state highways as the detours rather than using those local roads, until we get a better idea of what they’re like.”

Some North Islanders awoke to a blaring alarm from their Android phone before they even felt the ground shake this morning.

On social media, some people said their phones alerted them before they felt the effects of the quake.

Others said the alert arrived as the shaking began or shortly afterwards.

Civil Defence Manawatū Whanganui said it had been asked lots of questions about why some people got an alert on their cellphone before/during the Taumarunui earthquake, and others didn’t.

“Android cell phones have a function called the Android Earthquake Alerts System. Android phones have a built-in accelerometer which picks up vibrations,” it wrote.

If the Android phone senses movements which feel like an earthquake, it would send a signal to Google’s servers, which then do cross-checks from nearby phones.

Civil Defence said this helps to confirm if the vibrations from that phone and others nearby are actually caused by an earthquake, rather than just a few people dropping their phones at the same time.

New Plymouth resident Nikita Phillips was travelling through Awakino Gorge with her partner and daughter when the road started disappearing ahead of them early this morning.

"We went into survival mode, it was so scary.

"My partner looked out the window and said 'f*** babe, the cliff is coming down'.

"Then a road worker come running towards us screaming and waving his hands and said 'you need to f***en go! Hurry, go go!'"

Awakino Gorge at State Highway 3 is closed between Mōkau and Piopio due to the slip.

Phillips told the Herald her and her family had a "narrow" escape as debris from a cliff-slip began engulfing the road ahead of them.

She praises the roading contractor who she says "contributed massively" to her family's safety.

"I have massive appreciation for his mahi. I don't think people realise how dangerous the roads around the gorge can be.

"People are quick to attack road closures but this proves how important they are."

She said they're home safe and while she didn't feel the earthquake, there had been light rain throughout the morning.

One woman described her horror on social media.

"It was a violent earthquake, wouldn't of wanted to of gone on much more before it started smashing things. Been over 30 aftershocks already some as shallow as 3km deep."

One person said they were on Mt Ruapehu when the quake hit.

"I was on Mt Ruapehu and it felt like the whole mountain shook. Snowing outside and was just waiting for an eruption!"

NZTA is warning of the possibility of slips and debris on both SH4 and SH43.

An Auckland bus driver who dreamed up a sophisticated long-running fare scam that cheated his employer out of $243,000 has blamed his poor decision-making on mental health issues caused by passenger assaults.

Epsom resident Loganathan Manikum Pillay, 67, asked a judge for mercy last week as he appeared in Auckland District Court for sentencing.

He’s now a pensioner who drives an Uber part-time to make ends meet, but he’d be willing to pay $25,000 upfront out of his KiwiSaver and $2000 per month thereafter to slowly reimburse Ritchies, his lawyer said, arguing for 70% in sentence reductions so that his client could have a non-custodial outcome.

But Judge Kevin Glubb, during his last day on the bench before his own retirement, described the proposed repayment offer as “unrealistic” and “simply beyond belief” – especially given Pillay had already squandered all of the stolen fares at SkyCity Casino.

The judge instead ordered a prison sentence, declining to require reparation.

If Pillay wanted, after prison, to clear his conscience by contacting Ritchies and volunteering payments, he should “by all means” do so, the judge suggested. But he didn’t see it as a strong basis for substantially reducing the retiree’s punishment.

Pillay, who had been a bus and taxi driver for most of his career, was hired as a casual worker by Ritches in 2024 to operate one of four buses on the company’s Skydrive route.

For a $20 adult fare, the buses haul passengers directly between SkyCity in the city centre and Auckland Airport. Customers can book tickets online, pay cash or use an Eftpos machine as they embark.

In February last year, Pillay purchased his own Eftpos machine. He registered it under the name “Skydrive”, but all payments went to his own bank account. The scheme worked so well that he repeated it more than 11,500 times over eight months.

He was finally caught after a customer contacted Ritchies about an overcharge and staff were unable to find any record of the transaction. The customer provided a receipt with the terminal number, which after an internal investigation was traced back to the defendant.

When approached, “the defendant stated that he knew this was in relation to him pocketing some money whilst working for the bus company”, the agreed summary of facts states.

During last week’s hearing, Pillay’s lawyer emphasised that his client was remorseful despite a pre-sentencing report questioning his attitude towards the theft.

“He says there was a mental change and he wasn’t himself,” lawyer Lincoln Burns explained, noting that Pillay had an otherwise clean record. “This fractured personality that he didn’t recognise is the one that expressed itself.”

The lawyer pointed out that his client has not gotten rich off the scam, explaining: “The fares that should have ended up in the pockets of Skydrive shareholders have instead ended up in the pockets of SkyCity shareholders.”

Judge Glubb noted that Pillay told a pre-sentence report writer that he doesn’t have a gambling problem. But the defendant has received therapy for a workplace injury that caused trauma and reports that he is getting back to the person he used to be, the judge added.

Pillay faced a sentence of up to seven years’ imprisonment after pleading guilty to a representative charge of obtaining by deception.

The defence sought a 39-month starting point followed by discounts of 10% for his apology letter to Ritchies and willingness to participate in a meeting with the company; 20% for his remorse and offer to pay reparations; 10% for previous good character; 25% for his guilty plea; and 5% for his background which included growing up in difficult circumstances in South Africa and suffering assaults while working in public transport.

The judge instead ordered a higher starting point of 42 months, suggested by police, followed by 35% in combined discounts for his guilty plea, previously clean record and offer to pay reparations.

It resulted in a sentence of two years and three months’ imprisonment, just above the two-year threshold at which judges can consider replacing a prison term with a non-custodial alternative.

It took significant planning and pre-mediation to commit such a large theft, Judge Glubb said, adding that Pillay breached the trust of his employer “in a gross manner”.

“None of that does you any credit.”

Craig Kapitan is an Auckland-based journalist covering courts and justice. He joined the Herald in 2021 and has reported on courts since 2002 in three newsrooms in the US and New Zealand.

Why former Labour MP Michael Wood thinks Mt Roskill voters should trust him again

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

Former Transport Minister and Labour MP Michael Wood resigned from Cabinet following a scandal in 2023, after the Herald revealed his failure to sell Auckland Airport shares despite repeatedly being told to do so. He tells senior writer Derek Cheng why he believes the Mount Roskill electorate should give him another chance.

You live in Mount Roskill and former Labour MP Michael Wood knocks on your door. You tell him his repeated failure to sell his Auckland Airport shares when he was Transport Minister, after being told to do so a dozen times, crossed a line. You’ll never vote for him.

“I certainly understand and respect the fact that you made that decision last election,” Wood says after the Herald puts this role-playing scenario to him.

“For me, that period of 2023 was the absolute worst period of my life. It’s pretty clear that I made a mistake in not selling those shares.”

He adds, for context but not as an excuse, that he hadn’t touched the shares since buying them as a 19-year-old.

“I started the process of selling them several times but didn’t get it done. That was my responsibility.”

The Herald, still in role-playing mode, tells him it doesn’t seem credible to have started the process many times only to leave it hanging.

“Look, that is what happened,” Wood replies.

“There were multiple points during that period where I contacted the people who managed these matters for me and asked that process to be sorted. Every time, there was a hitch or some issue, an FIN [Faster Identification Number, which identifies shareholders] I didn’t have because I wasn’t regularly engaged in these issues, or there was someone else we needed to get to sign some papers.

“And in the midst of working 90 hours a week as a senior minister, that was always something I put to one side and didn’t get back to. It wasn’t that I was ignoring the issue totally. It wasn’t that I wasn’t aware of it. It wasn’t that I was thumbing my nose at anyone. It was just an important but small job that I didn’t do, and should have done.”

He also wants to know the local issues for you, and how you think he can resolve them.

“At every moment over the last 13 years that I’ve been in elected roles in Mount Roskill up until that point, I put every hour of the day working for you and trying to serve this community. That’s what I want to do again.

“I do believe I’m the best person who can represent you and make a difference on the things that actually matter to you. So, I’ll leave the choice to you.”

Wood’s inability to sell those shares was one of the catalysts for Labour’s inexorable slide in the polls in mid-2023.

Labour had already lost then-Cabinet Ministers Stuart Nash, for divulging Cabinet discussions to his donors, and Meka Whaitiri, who defected to Te Pāti Māori, but party insiders say the real hit in their internal polling came with the Wood scandal.

The subtext was that the rules didn’t apply to him, or by association to Labour. It reeked of arrogance.

Wood had started 2023 on the rise, with many ministerial portfolios under his wing and several significant policy wins.

When Dame Jacinda Ardern stepped away from politics, his name was in the mix as a possible successor, though ultimately he decided not to formally raise his hand.

It was a steep fall from potential Labour Party leader and Prime Minister to resigning from Cabinet five months later, following the disclosure of more shareholding interests he had somehow been previously unaware of.

Wood was still hopeful the Mount Roskill faithful would send him back to Parliament, but the electorate rejected him loudly and clearly. His 14,000-strong majority in 2020 flipped to a 1564-vote defeat in 2023 to National’s Carlos Cheung.

“The year and a half afterwards were the very darkest of my life,” Wood recalls.

“I thought back to many people I’ve met over the years, often middle-aged blokes who’d had a career setback, lost their job, been made redundant, their business folded or marriage collapsed, who were stuck and unable to move forward.

“Certainly, for a while, that was me.”

He has since worked for the union E tū, gaining some media prominence in the fight against TVNZ cuts in 2024.

While contemplating whether to attempt a political comeback, he took a solo three-week trip last year to the mountains of Italy for a 500km pilgrimage.

“Partly, going on that walk was about moving on from that period, clearing my head and working out what the direction was for me. There is just something about being out there by yourself, in the elements, with everything on your back, focused on getting through that day.”

He had chosen the St Francis walk, roughly from Florence to Rome, because the Catholic saint who gave away his wealth and served the poor and dispossessed has always inspired him.

The pilgrimage didn’t lead to a reinvention, but renewed what had been a key part of his ethos for decades, “a bit of a hunger, a need, to serve”.

“I also realised that what I enjoyed about politics, and missed, was the fight to win good changes on something that is wrong or unjust or needs fixing. I get a lot of satisfaction out of doing that.”

The trip also helped him move on from the lows of 2023.

“You can blame others, you can be bitter, you can say this was unfair, or people got me wrong about this. You can keep relitigating all of that stuff in your own mind, but it doesn’t take you anywhere.

“So I was just clear at the end of that, that I still wanted to refocus on public service in Mount Roskill.”

He has shunned the party list so he must win the electorate to return to Parliament. He has some regional party support as well as from senior MPs including the leadership team of Chris Hipkins and Carmel Sepuloni. This indicates the caucus does not consider his past mistakes to be electoral poison.

But it’s mostly a grassroots door-knocking campaign with face-to-face interaction. There is a sense of Wood having to earn back his stripes.

“That’s the kind of philosophy we’re taking into this campaign. We’re not taking anyone’s support for granted. We know there are people we lost last time that we need to earn back, and we’ll try and do that through respectful conversations and hard work.

“The way I want to win the seat back is through genuine connection with people.”

His door-knocking has seen him confronted with questions about his handling of his shares “very occasionally”, while the extended Covid lockdowns that contributed to Labour’s slide in Auckland come up “hardly ever”.

He says the key issue, as many polls have shown, is the cost of living, which Labour has been focusing on with its recent flurry of policy announcements.

Wood has been on Labour’s policy council, and his position as co-chair of the transport committee indicates his hand in the promise of a weekly cap on public transport costs ($20 in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and $10 elsewhere).

This isn’t the kind of policy that the Ministry of Transport is a fan of.

In advice to the Government this year on the spiking cost of fuel due to the US-Iran conflict, officials said broad public transport subsidies were inefficient because they give money to those who don’t need it. Targeted schemes were also problematic due to “significant setup issues”, officials said. (The Government opted to boost the in-work tax credit by $50 per week.)

Wood agrees the policy would help those who didn’t need it, while setting up a targeted system could see the costs outweigh the benefits. But it’s still a worthy policy, he argues.

“It benefits everyone, the public transport system, car drivers, we reduce our emissions, and it’s a cost-of-living measure as well.

“And every person who saves money as a result of this, maybe it means that they’ll be a little more able to support a small business in their community. No one has any money to spend at the moment, and it’s causing small businesses to close down all around the place.”

Part of his door-knocking sales pitch is the policy wins he won as a minister, including Fair Pay Agreements and the Clean Car Discount, though these have been axed under the current Government.

He also cites local advocacy, including the reestablishment of a local police station, in 2021, and finding a place to live for a local homeless man.

“He’d lost his house some time ago in a complicated series of events. He’d been living in a garden shed of some people he knew, but got kicked out because they didn’t want his dog there anymore, so he was sleeping on the streets.

“He’d tried to engage with MSD [Ministry of Social Development] but because of his mental health and other issues, he would get upset and start yelling, so he wasn’t getting anywhere with them.”

Wood said he and his team were able to find a place for the man and his dog in a Housing NZ home.

“Basically, the fact he was able to get into a decent basic house changed his life. He set up a little local lawn mowing business. We were able to help change this guy’s life. That, for me, is ultimately why you get into this.”

READ MORE: ‘Defining axis of social division’: How politics is feeding our housing crisis
