Stable and affordable housing is the foundation on which other social issues teeter, he says. Despite the drop in house prices since the 2021 peak, he wants to see them continue to fall in Auckland.

“Whether renting or owning, if families have stable housing, if their kids settle at the local school, if they’re linked into local support networks, they can deal with difficulties in their lives,” he says.

“But when families get shunted around and are getting uprooted constantly, everything else goes wrong. That’s when the kids go off the rails. That’s when petty crime starts to escalate into worse things in the community.

“We need to see house prices in real terms reduced in a sustainable way, if we want housing to be affordable for people.”

Part of the formula is increasing supply, and he is unsurprisingly critical of the Government’s reshaping of Kāinga Ora from a developer to a state housing landlord. This has turned around its finances at the expense of halting or changing development plans, including some in Wood’s electorate.

“There are huge areas in this electorate being developed as new housing but had funding pulled almost immediately when the new Government came in,” Wood says.

“Ultimately, you’ve got to have the right mix of policies across increasing housing supply as well as other settings – CGT [Capital Gains Tax] is a part of it as well – so we can get back to a more affordable housing market.”

Labour’s policy of three free doctor visits a year is, however, funded from the revenue from its proposed CGT.

This pot would be empty if house prices fell, which would further exacerbate lingering questions about how Labour would afford reversing the Government’s pay equity changes.

The controversial changes saw the Government bank nearly $13 billion over the forecast period from Budget 2025, money it says Labour will need to find to restore it to its previous form.

Wood steers clear of this fiscal territory. “We will present a fully costed plan for the election.”

His substantial drop in the pecking order probably diminishes his ability to comment on such matters. It was a different story, in early 2023, when he was Associate Finance Minister and a frontrunner for future Labour leader (and Prime Minister).

Is standing again the first stepping stone back towards those ambitions? “No. The focus is just on Mount Roskill.”

He concedes, though, that being a Cabinet minister again will give him more opportunity to implement the change he seeks.

“But I also go into this process with some humility. My focus is on winning the seat, being a good MP for the seat. Any decisions beyond that then get made by the leader,” he says.

“For me, the mission has always been the dignity, security, and opportunity for working people, and people who otherwise don’t have a voice.

“That’s what I stand for and will always stand for. That’s what I want to try and influence in politics.”

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

Lunch with... Shane Cameron - former heavyweight boxer on David Tua, rising from the canvas, resilience and redemption, and fears of a lasting toll

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

The remarkable and inspirational story of Shane Cameron and a life inside and outside the ring: 'It’s not how you fall, it’s how you rise.' Photos / Greg Bowker, Photosport, supplied

‘It’s not how you fall, it’s how you rise’: Shane Cameron’s new book is a raw portrayal of how a kid who thought he was ‘dumb’ rose to be a champion boxer, businessman, and public speaker. Only recently diagnosed with ADHD and dyslexia, his story of resilience is also tinged with fears of repercussions from years in the ring.

He’s watched the fight just twice. The first time, three years ago; the second time more recently. It’s a brutal encounter, and it knocked Shane Cameron down literally and figuratively. But it also delivered a powerful lesson.

“Only time heals,” Cameron writes in his new book about his 200-second boxing bout against David Tua in 2009. “It’s now over 15 years later, and only recently have I come to peace with it. Even a year ago, I hated people talking about it.”

The bout was dubbed the Fight of the Century, and it drew a staggering 88,000 pay-per-view sign-ups on Sky TV – still easily a record for a boxing match in New Zealand.

But it quickly became a one-sided affair – Tua, the former world heavyweight contender, rained punches on Cameron, sending him to hospital and into despair. The fight was over 20 seconds into the second round.

Cameron remembers little about the fight, and nothing at all of those final seconds.

“I’ve taken shots before, and normally you just go, ‘oh shit, Jesus Christ, I don’t want to take too many of those’,” Cameron says over a steak-and-beer lunchtime interview at the Northcote Tavern on Auckland’s North Shore.

“But that one was different. I don’t remember anything that happened afterwards. It was a tragic night – for me anyway, and my supporters and my family.”

He writes further in his book: “I was taken straight to an ambulance ... and off to hospital. I don’t really remember that part either. When I finally started coming around, I just felt devastated. You can handle losing. But to have such a huge build-up and then to lose in that fashion was incredibly difficult to take. When you talk it up, and you don’t deliver, it’s quite humbling.”

A lesser athlete might have thrown in the towel on their career there and then. But Cameron is no quitter – he went on to six further big wins after the Tua fight, including a huge knockout victory over Monte Barrett in June 2012. (Barrett had beaten Tua in 2011).

“Winning that fight was ... I was going to say the best night of my life, but definitely the best night of my life in boxing. 100%,” says Cameron. “I just felt on top of the world.”

Later came a tilt at a world cruiserweight title – a unanimous points loss to Danny Green. He finished with a career tally of 34 professional bouts – 29 of them wins, 22 by way of knockout.

If there’s a theme that runs through his new biography, Shane Cameron Mountain Warrior, it’s resilience and the way he has fought back from knocks in the ring – and some knockers outside it.

“It’s not how you fall, it’s how you rise,” says Cameron, a mantra he comes back to over lunch.

Seven years after that ill-fated Tua fight, Cameron was mowing the lawns at his then Mt Albert house. His famous opponent came to mind. He texted Tua and invited him and his wife over for a BBQ. He wanted to clear the air.

There had been a lot of high emotion and trash talking before the fight in 2009 – “of course I said I wanted to knock him out”. Cameron says he was saying and doing things that he’d normally not say. On reflection, he says, he and his manager Kenny Reinsfield “really pissed David off”.

“We had a good night – it was such a good night. We were playing pool in the man cave and [drinking] tequilas,” Cameron tells me of his reunion with Tua.

He says he apologised to Tua for the trash-talking.

“David and I talked and talked and drank tequila after tequila,” Cameron writes in the book. “It was a special night, and we had a lot of respect for each other. I remember he told me he’d been worried about my body shots. ‘David, you didn’t give me a f****** chance to throw them’.”

Over lunch, Cameron says he realises the Tua fight does not define his life. From humble beginnings and a decorated boxing career, he is now a successful businessman, public speaker, property investor, and trainer, as well as a dad of three.

“It’s part of me. It’s how you rise, and that’s the only positive way you can do it. At the end of the day, I lost to a great fighter – David Tua.

“My God, man, he’s put a lot of people to sleep. He’s a beast.”

There’s an anecdote in Cameron’s book that neatly and somewhat hilariously illustrates his determination. He was raised in the back-blocks of the East Coast – the book outlines a simple, happy life at Tiniroto, an hour inland from Gisborne.

“I can remember one Saturday morning wanting a can of Coke. The closest Coke was down at the Tiniroto Tavern. Mum said she wouldn’t drive me, so I decided to walk.

“It took me half a day to get there. I walked to the pub, got my Coke, drank it within a hundred metres of leaving the pub, and kicked the can all the way home until it disintegrated. I got back in the early evening.”

He asked his brother last year how far it was from where they lived to the pub; his brother drove the distance. “Bro, you walked 22 kilometres for a can of Coke.”

Cameron writes: “I tell that story when I do public speaking, to illustrate the lesson that if you want something badly enough, you’ll make it happen.”

Cameron hated high school in Gisborne, and persuaded his parents that he should do Correspondence School. But even that was too much; he was keener to work on the land. At the age of 12, he went off to work for a local farmer, Mike Sherriff.

“I just thought I was a dumb kid because I couldn’t read or write,” Cameron tells me over lunch. “You put yourself in that category of dumb, but one thing I did was I knew how to work. You work, you find your way.”

“To my amazement”, he writes in the book, his mum stepped in to do his schoolwork.

“I went home one weekend and walked inside and said hello to my mum, and she responded by saying: ‘Hey, look, I got an A in maths!’

“I told that story years later when I was on Celebrity Treasure Island, and it made it through the edit onto TV. Mum rang me up. ‘Hey, what did you tell them that for? I got an A in science, not in maths!’"

Cameron realised, as he read an independent synopsis of his proposed book, that he had a story to tell.

“Once I read the synopsis, I’m like, oh man, this is quite inspiring for people or young kids that are not really that good at school,” he says over lunch.

“I’ve got tools that I just focus on, like setting goals, and if that goal is strong enough, you’ll do whatever it takes to achieve that goal.

“It might be a huge goal like fighting for a world title – that might be the ultimate, but the short-term goal is you’ve got to win your next fight, and you’ve got to get better every time.”

He looks at 15-year-olds now. “Literally they’re kids. I was a man at that age.”

“By that time, I’d already been working for Mike Sherriff. I’d already been used to big days, starting in the dark and finishing in the dark for seven days a week.”

That work included learning how to shear a sheep, shoe and train a horse, and break in a dog.

“You find your own way. I’ve been undereducated, and I thought I was dumb, but I’m like, I can outwork people, so that was a big coup for me.”

Cameron found his way into the boxing ring at a relatively late age, as a 19-year-old now on an OE in the UK. His Scottish grandfather was a successful amateur boxer – so the legacy and history were there – but it wasn’t until he saw Prince Naseem Hamed on television that he was inspired to don the gloves.

Dozens of amateur fights for Cameron led to an early pinnacle – representing New Zealand at the Commonwealth Games in Manchester in 2002.

Cameron won a bronze medal. He has it framed on the wall.

“It’s the only bit of boxing memorabilia I have in my house. I used to have a big man cave in Mt Albert, but I ended up selling the house and [the belts are] in plastic bins until I find another man cave,” he laughs.

He turned professional after the Games, winning 15 of his first 16 fights, before taking on Tua.

As he did on the farm as a young teenager, he observed others around him, and how they worked. His favourite fighter was Evander Holyfield. Like Cameron, Holyfield wasn’t a big heavyweight, but “he was a warrior – I didn’t have the skill that he had, but there’s certain things that I just picked up with him”.

Same with Mike Tyson.

“I can’t fight like Tyson or Tua or Lennox Lewis or any of those guys, but I can fight like me. If I pick a little bit of each one of those fighters, then I’ve got my own style. You portray it your own way.

“It’s the same way in life, and how you do business. I like how this person operates; that’s a good decision... you know.”

Cameron sparred with Tyson for two weeks in Las Vegas in 2005. That camp not only gave him a huge confidence boost, but he came away with a mean impression of one of the world’s greatest boxers.

“We were sparring one day, and he threw a hook, but I caught the counter, and he dug me low in the groin. ‘Hey Mike, watch the low shots,’ I said gently. And in that high-pitched voice of his, he said: ‘Sowwy, Shane’.”

Over lunch, Cameron breaks into his Tyson impression.

More broadly, he says: “I survived two weeks sparring Mike Tyson; we would have sparred over 30 rounds. He didn’t knock me out, and I survived. I’m like, I’m not f****** scared of anyone. If I can survive two weeks sparring Mike Tyson, I can f****** fight anyone.”

For a considerable period of his career, the Warriors rugby league club took Cameron on board, promoting and funding him. In the book, former Warriors chief executive Mick Watson talks about how close Cameron came to being a Warrior player.

“Shane was winning everything at training because he was just so committed and dedicated, and it was Daniel [former Warriors coach Daniel Anderson] who said to me, ‘How would you feel if we actually turned this guy into a back row forward?’” Watson says in the book.

Cameron had no idea, and ultimately it never eventuated.

“I would have loved it – I remember training with them. I did a lot of running. I loved to push myself to see how I compared with them and all those sort of things in terms of the fitness. That was the mindset – ‘I can go faster than you’.”

While physical and even psychological scars were evident in the immediate aftermath of the Tua fight, the longer-term impact of Cameron’s boxing career is more difficult to pinpoint.

Cameron says he has no regrets about his boxing career. He loves the sport, and is still heavily involved in a business sense – with his equipment and accessories business Counterpunch, fitness centre and helping amateurs. For him, the sport has been a passport to a wonderful career.

But after a 34-fight professional career, during which he won 29 of his first 31 bouts, Cameron fears he may now be paying a price.

“People liked the way I boxed,” he writes. “I came forward, I traded punches, I didn’t shy away from going to war. It looked good on the television cameras, especially when the blood flowed, and it got the fans at ringside excited.

“But I wore a lot of punishment over the years, particularly in those final fights against Danny Green, Brian Minto and Kali Meehan.

“I’ve begun to suspect – or fear – that I am now paying the price for that punishment.

“CTE – which stands for chronic traumatic encephalopathy – is a progressive and degenerative brain disorder linked to repeated concussions and head impacts, particularly in athletes in contact sports like rugby, league and ... boxing. It can lead to cognitive, behavioural and mood problems that may get worse over time.”

Over lunch at the Northcote Tavern, Cameron explains his feelings candidly.

His long-term memory is good; the short-term memory can be a struggle.

He says he gets down a lot. “I don’t know if that’s depression,” he says. He’s had depression in the past. His brain races “100 miles an hour”.

“I’ve got so many things going on in my head. I put all the pressure on myself. When I get down, it’s because of me, because I haven’t done certain things or haven’t achieved enough or forgotten.

“As soon as I wake up in the morning, my brain just goes ‘boom boom boom boom’, and I’m like, ‘Oh, I’ve got to do this, I’ve got to do that’. All of a sudden I put myself in a whirlwind, and sometimes I’ll just go back to bed if I’m able to – if I don’t have to do anything – and just sleep it off. Then I’ll wake up and feel better.”

He is also sometimes quick to anger. “I’m still an angry person; I’ve always sort of been a bit like that.”

He’s seen a specialist recently, but did not feel he received any answers. He wouldn’t mind returning to neuropsychologist James Cunningham, who he saw a decade or so ago to see if he can undergo any comparative testing. “I don’t know what it will achieve. I definitely know, I reckon I’ve gone backwards.”

Over lunch, Cameron also shows me his right hand – it’s bent out of shape, with two fingers permanently crooked. He sometimes finds it difficult to shake hands, with a semi-closed fist.

Cameron broke his hand six or seven times in his boxing career, including in training before his Gisborne homecoming fight in March 2009 – just eight months before the Tua fight.

Bone from his wrist was grafted into the top of his hand, fusing his knuckles – it was the best medical advice at the time, but he wonders now if it should have been left alone to heal.

The hand causes pain each day. He can’t straighten it out properly.

“I just keep training, just keep doing burpees [flattening his hand on the ground], otherwise I reckon my hands would seize up.

“Sometimes I go to shake people’s hands, and it comes in like that,” he says, showing his curled down fingers. “It’s like a permanent hang loose sign.”

He reflects: “Just battered, eh man, just battered.”

Cameron has three children - Georgia, 21, Shane jnr, 11, and Kōwhai, 5.

He and his wife Casey met years ago, and were together for three years, before they rekindled their relationship later in life. Their daughter Kōwhai was born in the Covid period.

According to his book, Casey – a successful fitness instructor in her own right and who manages the fitness centre – calls Cameron ‘HM’, as in high maintenance. He credits her for “keeping me in line ... and not putting up with my shit”.

He is on good terms with the mums of Georgia and Shane jnr.

Kōwhai is a chip off the block. “She’s a fighter. She’s got a bit of hunger in there. I think it’s good for any kid to do boxing, or combat sports for when they’re growing up.

“It’s the discipline and about turning up and being punctual and pushing through hard times, hard situations, hard training. Cold, wet, sweaty, uncomfortable situations – that all helps for later on in life. And if they are good athletes, that brings more confidence that helps later in life.

“There’s absolutely no way I’d have achieved the things that I’ve achieved if I hadn’t gone into boxing.”

Nothing is as daunting as getting in a ring and fighting, he says. Not public speaking, and not appearing live on television on Sunday evenings to perform the cha-cha as part of Dancing with the Stars.

“Fighters that have been to the top of their game ... man, they can do anything.”

Dancing with the Stars was “probably the second toughest thing I’ve done in my life”.

He was training with Nerida Jantti (formerly Nerida Cortese) for 40 hours a week in 2015. “Ninety seconds [live on air] is a long time ... everything is choreographed. You can’t just move the hips.”

A little like boxing, judges will then come in and scrutinise your performance. Nerida and Shane stayed on the show for six weeks.

Much of Cameron’s focus now is on his businesses. He owns Shane Cameron Fitness on Auckland’s North Shore and his own boxing equipment line, Counterpunch.

He is also especially proud of a deal he’s secured with The Warehouse to stock another of his brands, Champ. That’s taken seven years, and a lot of patience and determination.

He hopes people will draw that sort of inspiration from his book.

In 2019, Cameron told the Herald: “Mostly I just want to be remembered for being a good bastard.”

Over lunch, he tells me: “I’m a pretty determined human – focused. And for my kids, to see that through hard work you’re going to achieve.

“And if you don’t want to do something, do something else. If you do something that you’re a bit half-assed about, you’ll fall off the wagon and make excuses.

“I f***ing hate people that make excuses. It pisses me off – don’t make excuses, do something that excites you.”

Editor-at-Large Shayne Currie is one of New Zealand’s most experienced senior journalists and media leaders. He has held executive and senior editorial roles at NZME, including Managing Editor, NZ Herald Editor and Herald on Sunday Editor. Wolvnie Ding: Friend pays tribute to ‘kind, funny and passionate’ 20-year-old woman found dead in Swanson

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

Wolvnie Ding (left) and Shuyan Liu in 2022. Photo / Shuyan Liu

A 20-year-old Auckland woman found dead after going missing for six days has been remembered as a kind, funny and passionate person who showed she cared through actions instead of words.

Police believe a body recovered in the Swanson area on Thursday is Wolvnie Ding, who was last seen walking along Birdwood Rd about 8.20am last Friday.

Ding lived in Auckland CBD but had been visiting family in West Auckland when she disappeared, police said earlier this week.

Contact the Herald newsroom

One of her closest and oldest friends, Shuyan Liu, told the Herald they were informed on Thursday that Ding’s body was found in a body of water close to her family home.

Shuyan said they will miss Ding’s sense of humour, deep chats about “serious life topics” and her fun personality.

“It’s one of those things where you never expect it to happen to someone you know personally,” they said, calling it a “tragic” loss.

Shuyan said Ding was “a woman of few words” who instead showed she cared through her actions.

“In her presence, it just felt like we understood each other. It was a very comfortable, unspoken understanding. And I’m sure that a lot of other people who have interacted with her would say the same.

“She was a very accepting, very kind person, and she shows her care through action a lot more than words.

“I loved laughing with her. She was a very funny person. Every time we talked, it felt like it was a coming-of-age movie from the early 2010s.”

Police said while formal identification of the body is still underway, they believe the body found on Thursday is that of Ding.

“Police extend their deepest condolences to the woman’s family at this incredibly difficult time,” acting Detective Inspector Megan Goldie, of Waitematā CIB, said.

“Family members have been informed and are being supported by police. Police would like to thank those who assisted in search efforts.

“Her death will be referred to the coroner.”

Shuyan said Ding loved to write, was a big fan of indie rock artist Phoebe Bridgers and the band Boygenius, and was passionate about feminist issues.

“A lot of the media that she would listen to and watch, a lot of it is talking about women’s issues.

“I think that if she could speak to everyone in the world, she would be speaking about women’s rights. So I want everyone who cares about her to honour her by spending more time reading and talking about these kinds of issues.”

In a tribute on Instagram, Shuyan described Ding as “one of the most gentle, thoughtful, passionate, inquisitive, gorgeous and resilient people I have ever had the honour of getting to know”.

“She was one of the few people who made me feel understood, cared for and appreciated without even saying a word. I wish I could go back and spend so much more time with her.”

West Otago’s Kylie Dorr named Supreme Winner at NZI Rural Women Business Awards

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

The 2026 NZI Rural Women Business Awards Supreme Winner, Kylie Dorr.

Kylie Dorr has taken out the Supreme Winner title at the 2026 NZI Rural Women Business Awards.

The awards, organised by Rural Women New Zealand and sponsored by NZI, recognise innovation, business excellence and community impact among women-led rural enterprises.

Dorr, who earlier won the Emerging Enterprise category, received the top honour at a gala dinner in Parliament’s Banquet Hall last night.

Based in West Otago, Dorr is the owner of Southern Reproductive, an independent reproductive services and training business.

She began the business five years ago after returning from eight years in the US, where she worked in reproduction and helped run grass-based farms for a large group of New Zealand dairy investors.

“I saw a really big gap in the market and thought things could be done better,” Dorr told The Country’s Jamie Mackay.

When she returned home, she began providing Artificial Insemination (AI) services as an independent technician in West Otago.

“It’s certainly grown over the last five years,” she said.

Revenue has doubled year on year, and the business now has 12 AI technicians across the South Island, with a team of over 20 seasonal staff.

“We cover most parts of the South Island with our artificial insemination service,” Dorr said.

Southern Reproductive also provides pregnancy scanning services and became the national distributor for IMV Technologies ultrasound equipment 18 months ago.

“We’re the nationwide distributor and repairer for that stuff, which is currently the largest part of our business.“

The business has also launched an AI training school, allowing people from across New Zealand to learn artificial insemination techniques at its facilities.

Dorr said Southern Reproductive planned to expand into Australia over the next 12 months.

“So yeah, it’s been pretty busy. That’s an understatement.”

Dorr is not a West Otago native; she was born in Hawaii to an American father and New Zealand mother.

“I moved back to New Zealand when my dad passed away when I was 5 and grew up in Northland,” she said.

“My grandparents were dairy farmers up there, and then my mum met a chap that was a dairy farmer.”

Dorr said the family moved down south to follow the dairy boom.

“[We] were pretty transient and seemed to change jobs every 12 months.”

She said the experience helped shape her.

“As a teenager I moved a lot, lived all over the country, which was both challenging but when you reflect on it, pretty darn good.

“I really learnt some very, very valuable skills at a very, very early age.“

This included milking and calving cows and doing a feed budget.

Listen below:

When she was 18, Dorr moved to Tapanui for her first job away from home, as an apprentice mechanic for Dwayne’s Service Centre.

“I rode and raced dirt bikes a little bit and thought that that would be a pretty cool job.”

Despite this, she returned to dairy farming.

“I couldn’t sit still long enough and went back to milking cows on weekends and eventually went back to dairy farming, which took me over to America and now here we are.”

But her interest in dirt bikes never went away.

After starting Southern Reproductive, Dorr bought a dirt bike as a hobby to share with her two sons.

“The plan was just to ride on the weekend,” she said.

Twelve months later, she had won a national championship and been selected to represent New Zealand on the world stage.

“So less than two years after stepping back onto a bike, I was over in Spain representing New Zealand as part of the first women’s team at the International Six Days Enduro.”

Passionate about endurance sports, she is the president of one motorcycle club and the secretary of another.

Mackay asked if she was more famous as an international motocross rider or an award-winning rural businesswoman.

“Today I think I’m a bit more famous for being a businesswoman than I am a bike rider,” Dorr said.

Stuart and Sarah Nash’s last political interview: ‘Stuart is many things, but he is not sexist’

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Stuart Nash has called Napier MP Katie Nimon to apologise for the late-night text he sent about her, that ended his bid for a political comeback.

In what he and wife Sarah expect will be their final interview about politics, they say they’re frustrated by the “distortion” of Nash’s message, and feel the level of backlash to it was motivated by political gain.

Stuart Nash didn’t fact-check his now-infamous text message to podcast host and former politician Chris Finlayson.

He says he never thought he’d need to, because it was meant to be the start of a private joust with a friend.

That message, criticising Napier MP Katie Nimon, triggered yet another political whirlwind with Nash at its centre, after Finlayson made it public this week.

“Katie took 9 months off on full pay, went back for a week, then took another month off,” Nash claimed in the text.

It appeared to Finlayson – and most eyes – to be a swipe at Nimon’s parliamentary leave when giving birth to her first child Lochie in 2025.

It was also inaccurate.

Nimon was away from Parliament for six months, and went back to work part-time in her electorate 10 weeks after Lochie was born.

That made the next part of the text problematic too.

“Laziest MP I’ve ever come across,” Nash texted Finlayson.

He finished with: “Nice woman but ill suited to the rigours of being an electorate MP”.

By Wednesday afternoon, the Prime Minister had labelled the text “sexist”, Chris Bishop had described it as “disgusting” and labelled Nash as a “d***head”.

Nimon herself hit back at Nash’s inaccuracies.

By Wednesday night, Nash had resigned his candidacy for NZ First in Napier, his political comeback over at the first sign of a hurdle.

He says he could barely read the headlines with his name beside the word “sexist”, they were so mortifying.

He continues to insist the widely-publicised interpretation of his message has been incorrect.

“I am mortified that people think that I was criticising Katie for taking maternity leave.

“Nothing could be further from the truth.

“I am absolutely devastated ... that a private message I had sent has been interpreted in the way that it has when it absolutely does not represent the views I have, at all,” Nash said.

“To read that I’m sexist is an anathema to every single thing I’ve believed, every single thing I’ve done throughout my career, and everything that I will continue to do.”

Nash said before he sent the message, he’d spent the past two and a half years hearing feedback from the electorate that “they felt Katie had been invisible”.

“In my mind, I wasn’t linking the laziness to the maternity leave, I was making a series of points.

“It was based on feedback that I had received over two-and-a-half years, and that was one of the reasons I had decided to stand, because I had felt, subtly, I offered something Katie didn’t.”

Wife Sarah Nash, a public relations professional, has now stood alongside him through several rounds of headlines triggered by Nash’s own errors – from breaches of the Cabinet manual to his crass description of what it means to be a woman on a radio show last year.

She says it’s telling how “quickly and disproportionately” the text was amplified.

“When you look at what other people are saying in the media, other politicians, I just think it was an easy way to get Stuart out of the picture, and make a much clearer running for Katie,” Sarah says.

“Stuart is many things, but he is not sexist, and I found reading that incredibly offensive.

“We’ve got two daughters, and the ripple effect of that is enormous, for a message that was so distorted.

“Stuart, love it or hate him, I feel like he is – and we’ve said this over the years – he’s too trusting in politics.

“And I think it’s really unfortunate now that politics is so toxic.

“You can’t trust anyone – I think it’s an endearing quality of Stuart’s that he thinks you can, but at the same time, it keeps, it’s landed us where we are now.”

Given Nash’s insistence that the text was not about Nimon’s maternity leave, why then, did he decide to stand down?

“I consider Winston Peters a very good friend of mine and I had thrown my hat in the ring because I thought I could add significant value to New Zealand First,” Nash says.

“I thought that, not just in this campaign, but in terms of policy development and advocacy, that I had a lot to offer.

“The one thing that I did not want to do is be seen as someone who pulled New Zealand First down or someone who Winston had to defend when he should be talking about solutions to the issues that are important.

“And when I saw that this had become a major distraction, I thought that the only honourable thing to do was step aside.”

Nash said watching the backlash unfold on Wednesday afternoon, as he was going back and forth with NZ First’s leader’s office to issue a public statement, was difficult.

“I think I just lost the narrative very, very early on.

“And by the time I responded, the message was so distorted that there was no way of reclaiming back that message or actually putting my side of the story that would have introduced a level of balance.

“And when that happened, I realised that I had actually become a liability and I needed to step back or else I was damaging the party.”

Nash said his campaign was meant to be around what he thought he could bring to Napier, the city he loves, and the region of Hawke’s Bay.

He had wanted to focus on “track record, work ethic and my experience” and had felt he had the slimmest of chances of winning the seat if his campaign had gone smoothly.

“Going after Katie as a mother is something I would never do because, first of all, that’s not how I play politics.

“Second of all, I celebrate motherhood, I mean, I have four children of my own.

“That was never part of the plan.

“Perhaps I am old-fashioned in my belief that private messages between friends should remain private.”

Nash plans to use the time he would have spent campaigning on street corners or door knocking – which he had already started – on reconnecting with his fledgling business helping people overseas attain golden visas. Other trade opportunities are also on the cards.

He said he wished his replacement NZ First candidate Te Kira Lawrence well, and he would support her, but he would not be involved in her campaign.

He also said he’d spoken to Nimon. She confirmed to Hawke’s Bay Today he had called her on Thursday night.

She claimed he had apologised “for offending me”.

“My apology to Katie was heartfelt and fulsome,” Nash said.

“And the thought that I had maligned her because she was a mother, it mortifies me because that’s not what I believe, it’s not who I am and it’s never been the sort of politics I have ever played.

“I wish her the very best of luck.

“She herself has said that being a young mother in Parliament is incredibly challenging.

“And Sarah and I know the challenges that her and her husband and her children and her wider family face.

“And I celebrate the fact that Parliament is a place where young mothers can also contribute.

“I’ve apologised to Katie, and I mean that 100%.”

Nash said he would now be spending more time at home with Sarah and his family on the weekend.

“I’ve said this before, but this is the end of any sort of political aspirations I have.

“That’s it.”

As he says this, Nash’s Apple Watch interrupts the interview to speak to him.

It calls out three words – “GPS signal lost”.

“I’ve lost my politics, and also my GPS,” Nash says with a laugh. As the laugh trails off, there’s a tear in his eye.

Letters: Political courage, not centrists, required to answer hard questions

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

Fast-track housing development proposals are leading us into another construction disaster. Photo / Getty Images

The article (July 24) by Richard Shaw, a professor of politics at Massey University, proposes that the political centre is a strategy not a set of beliefs.

It was enlightening and reinforces the need for the public and the media to not accept claims of political parties and politicians being centralist as a way of avoiding difficult questions.

The explanation, that centralist politicians also tend to describe themselves as policy moderates for the same reason is important. Asking what a moderate position on climate change is, is a good example of how political parties and politicians generally avoid this issue - which will have catastrophic consequences for the planet.

The age we live in requires us to reorganise global governance, and of course resource use, which we are all avoiding as an issue for political discussion.

We need to look for leaders who have the courage to state their positions clearly and offer solutions. The public and the media must have the courage to ask the right questions and not accept claims of being centralist or moderate as an excuse for inaction on anthropogenic climate change.

Dennis Worley, Birkenhead.

The fast-track approval of the Delmore subdivision near Orewa is another example of fast-track development proposals leading us into another leaky home disaster.

Several development proposals have been approved by the fast-track process without proper infrastructure solutions to water and waste treatment, let alone adequate access and infrastructure solutions.

In Delmore’s case we have a return to the old “night cart” regime where sewerage will be trucked out of the development for, wait for it, the next 30 years at least. No wonder it’s essential that the RONS project to get an expressway to Whangārei is also on the fast track - to ship truckloads of human waste up north, so their ratepayers can process it.

Looking back at the leaky homes crisis, ratepayers, taxpayers and poor unsuspecting homeowners got lumbered with the costs of remedial work when developers failed and their building guarantees went with them. Are we on a fast track to another crisis, one where developers can no longer service the sewerage and we have a “s…t happens" crisis?

Neil Anderson, Algies Bay.

Wellington city councillors have been told the amalgamation of Wellington’s Super City could cost $273 million and that “studies have found no evidence large amalgamation authorities are more or less efficient than smaller ones”.

Why is the coalition trying to push this before the election under fast track? Surely ratepayers should have a say. With a population of 208,000 in the city, plus the wider region of approximately 400,000, this means a family of four will pay nearly 1800. Why, when it seems to be an ideological desire by Chris Bishop, is this happening? We should have a say. It should be an election policy so we can vote on it. How much will this cost the whole of New Zealand? We are paying for the cost of “waters done well”, now amalgamation, and we’re told to keep rates rises under 5%.

Frankie Letford, Hamilton.

I’m happy to see Invercargill citizens querulous about the foreign-owned AI data centre. They should go further and seek guarantees for the 20 jobs alluded to; question the doubtful assertion that the south’s cold temparature will obviate use of water; demand their contingency plans for a hot summer; and seek guarantees from government that energy prices will not rise because American business will pay more but energy shareholders will benefit.

Why do Kiwis lie down and die, without a single political party to represent us? Or is there no " us" anymore?

Keith Burgess, Christchurch.

The Herald (July 23)revealed the truth about gold mining. There’s wealth to be made, but the ones who make it are overseas companies, not us.

Since 2019, New Zealand has gained a total of $54 million, or less than $10 million a year in royalties. This is peanuts. The company, meanwhile, made more than a billion profit last year alone – a proportion of which came from NZ.

The royalty rate increased in 2013 from 1% to 2% of revenue. Mining is an incredibly lucrative activity, but not for us.

We are the suckers left with vast piles of tailings and landscapes destroyed. The plan is now to tear up Central Otago – and what will we end up with – huge piles, not of money but of toxic tailings.

Susan Grimsdell, Auckland Central.

Wealth tax - clutch your pearls! Michael Cullen had a good phrase for this kind of comment - an “ideological burp”.

In 2007 former prime minister John Key called Kiwisaver a “cruel hoax”; in 2001 the Cullen fund was labelled a “political gimmick” and any other good move was attacked. Surely, it’s better to understand how unprecedented wealth expansion has damaged our economy and prevented growth. How? Super wealthy people buy assets, driving up the prices, which leads to unprecedented private debt, which inversely correlates with lower spending into our economy. Investigate this.

Michael Laurie, Eden Terrace.

Last night I watched the movie Sgt. Haane. Powerful emotionally, it should be compulsory viewing for everybody in this country. The men of the 28th Maori Battalion exemplified everything about what it means to be a New Zealander.

What bravery, not just by Haane Manahi, though he was exceptional, but by the entire battalion. What ferocious warriors.

No wonder the Italians and Nazis were scared witless when confronted by them.

Manahi and his comrades climbed a near-vertical cliff face without ropes or pitons to capture strategically vital high ground at Takrouna in Tunisia.

Three generals and Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery himself recommended Manahi for the Victoria Cross yet some bureaucrat in Whitehall downgraded it to a Distinguished Conduct Medal. What a disgrace.

David Morris, Hillsborough.

Winston Peters is looking for the future in his rearview mirror if he thinks spending $1 billion on a speculating gamble has merit. Fossil fuels are last year’s technology and a financial return (if any) from fossil fuel prospecting would not provide a return until 2050, when fossil fuels will be even more redundant.

We need younger minds with bright ideas in Parliament.

Ian Brady, Titirangi.

Regardless of the outcome of the “Shoot, shag, marry” game on Radio Hauraki, it appalls me that the item exists at all, and that some male politicians engage in it. It’s a crass example of the predatory mindset of the manosphere.

Aspiring MPs crave publicity and no doubt fear that a refusal to participate would brand them humourless and a bad sport.

In my view it would indicate that they have a sense of propriety and a respect for others, especially women.

Norm Murray, Browns Bay.

Message to NZ First: do not waste $1 billion on oil and gas exploration; spend it on renewable energy to get a much higher return for taxpayer money and NZs future.

Marie Kaire, Whangārei.

Whangārei ratepayers should be very proud of the sewage processing plant they have funded, for an Auckland housing development, but I am not sure they anticipated providing this service for Aucklanders as well? Waiting for answers in the “little room”!

Don Ashby, Whangārei.

Why do pointy top beanie woollen hats these days (with no " bobble"), make a wearer look like an elf?

Bring back the genuine beanie with the “tea cosy” look.

Larry Mitchell, Rothesay Bay.

I agree completely with Harvey White: please NZ Rugby get the names of our All Blacks on their backs. Far more enjoyable to watch if we know who we are looking at. Only way to get to know our new players.

Marilyn Newland, Blockhouse Bay.

I can understand the reasoning behind reducing the hot water temperature at the tap, but restricting it to 50C is too low. At this temperature the water in the kitchen sink is less than that. Add in cold greasy dishes and it can’t do the job properly.

Utter madness.

Angela Thomas, Greenlane.

Rotorua locals rally to save Prince’s Gate Archway, call for tenders to be reopened

New Zealand Herald July 24, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Rotorua locals are rallying to save the city’s Prince’s Gate Archway before “irreversible” work is done to take it down.

Those with construction experience say they want to work with Rotorua Lakes Council to restore the “iconic” arches after the council confirmed it would be deconstructed for safety reasons.

Locals have also called for the council to reopen tenders after one for the structure’s “full renovation” closed in April without success.

On July 14, the council said engineering assessments found the archway could pose a safety risk during extreme wind events and it had deteriorated to the point it was unsafe.

Deconstruction was expected to begin in two to three months.

The council this week said this remained the expected timeframe, however, a further assessment was planned to “confirm the extent of works required to address the public safety risk”.

An update would be provided if the timeframe changed after this assessment.

Meanwhile, no decisions have been made on reopening tenders.

The Prince’s Gate Archway was built in 1901 to mark the visit of the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York, who later became King George V and Queen Mary.

It is built from steel and native timbers including tōtara, rimu and kauri.

Rotorua resident Alex Wills, who has experience in building and woodwork, said he contacted Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell on Tuesday to offer his services to project-manage a rebuild at a third of his usual hourly rate.

In his view, “it’s not that complicated of a structure”.

“It’s modular... it doesn’t need to be an overly expensive or crazy undertaking to replace.”

He did not have a cost estimate but said it would be “very reasonable”.

Wills said he did not want Rotorua to lose the “iconic” arches.

Rotorua ITM co-owner Sam Milner said he and the business’ three other local owners had about 120 years’ experience in the construction industry.

Without knowing the plan for the archway, “it’s hard to say what we can do, but we definitely want to be involved in some way, shape or form”.

Milner said it would be “sad to see it go”.

Rotorua resident Peyton Tell said the arches had “welcomed generations of locals and visitors” and were a Rotorua “landmark”.

“Once they are dismantled, that original piece of our heritage can never truly be replaced.”

She agreed public safety should come first but was concerned about transparency.

Tell hoped for “a pause on any irreversible work”, all reports and assessments to be released, and community engagement “before an irreplaceable heritage landmark is lost”.

Tell, who started the Save our Rotorua Arches Facebook page, said she would like to see the council’s tender process reopened.

Rotorua ratepayer Lex Waterreus said he was “extremely disappointed” about the planned deconstruction.

Rotorua-born Waterreus, who runs the Nostalgic Rotorua Facebook page and lives in Australia, said there was time to reopen the tender process.

“I’d like to see it restored.”

He understood the importance of public health and safety but believed the council should seek a second opinion after the initial assessment.

Council group manager of community experience Alex Wilson said it had received “many thoughtful and generous offers and suggestions” regarding the archway from community members, including Wills.

“All offers and ideas are being collated and will be considered as the council works through the next steps to determine the best way forward for the future of the arches.”

The council received three tenders for the archway’s renovation but evaluations found “cost and delivery risks” in all of them and none was approved, Wilson said.

No decision had been made about reopening tenders.

“We have a process underway to consider options and present recommendations to the council for consideration.”

She said maintenance work in recent years included the replacement of broken lattice work, repairs to the top, checks of steel brackets and removal of “non-structural timber that has become loose”.

“The deterioration has accelerated since 2022 due to a large number of high and extreme wind events that have further affected the structure, blowing off or loosening weak or aged timber.”

Wilson said another assessment was planned within the next few weeks “to confirm the extent of work required to address the public safety risk”.

On community consultation, decisions relating to public safety risk were operational decisions and dealing with that risk was the council’s immediate priority.

“No decision has yet been made on how to proceed once the immediate risk has been addressed.”

Wilson said a team had been established to assess options and make recommendations for elected members to consider for decision-making.

Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga communications and marketing manager Adrienne Hannan said the agency’s conservation advisers and the council had discussed the structure’s “poor condition”.

Hannan said it was working with the council to “achieve appropriate heritage outcomes” for the structure and any replacement.

The Prince’s Arch and Gateway appears on the New Zealand Heritage list as a Category 2 historic place and is considered to have “historical or cultural significance or value”.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

You probably never wonder who’s packing your parcels. Perhaps you will now

Sydney Morning Herald July 25, 2026

Kat Stewart stars in a new Australian play that might just be our answer to Death of a Salesman.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When actor Kat Stewart and director Sarah Goodes were hunting for a script to collaborate on, they started with the classics. “The usual suspects, the Albees, who I adore, Tennessee Williams, a couple of Sam Shepard plays,” says Stewart. “The recurring theme was the American dream, the heartbreak or the disappointment of the American dream.”

But then Goodes brought in Break of Day, a script by veteran actor and playwright Steve Rodgers. A heartfelt and moving ode to the dreams and disappointments of ordinary yet recognisable people, it felt like an Australian version of those US classics. “Why aren’t we exploring that?” Stewart asked. “This is real. This is right now. And this is what we’re not shining a light on.”

Stewart plays Pam, a single mother barely making ends meet by pulling the night shift at one of those gargantuan warehouses that ship every product imaginable 24 hours a day. The customer unboxing their new smoothie machine or beard trimmer or yoga ball never spares a thought for the many hands that got it there. Pam is one member of that invisible army.

As in Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman, this isn’t the life our protagonist envisioned. Pam juggles her night work alongside caring for her wildly incapable dad and her 17-year-old daughter Rae. She’s devoted most of her adult life to giving her daughter chances she never had, but has reached a point of crisis: to give Rae those opportunities, she has to let her go.

Stewart has two kids of her own, so she can connect with how conflicted Pam must be. “She’s made her life all about elevating Rae,” she says. “She’s on that really interesting cusp, which I’m dreading, where Rae’s doing year 12 and she’s got so much potential. She’s about to leave the nest and start making her own decisions, which leaves Pamela at a real pressure point where she’s working out who she is in that context and how she can best look after her beautiful girl.”

In putting her daughter first, Pam doesn’t know who she would become if Rae does end up leaving. Her lack of self-identity is only compounded by the way her job is designed to depersonalise workers, hide them from public view. All of these factors mean that Pam finds herself facing a dilemma familiar to many women as they age: she feels she’s growing invisible.

If Pam’s circumstances sound grim, Rodgers’ handling is a reminder that Australian humour thrives under pressure. “What really rang true for me in Stevie’s writing is the humour of it and the way Australians talk,” Stewart says. “We use humour to deflect. We’re really great at that. It’s our armour.”

The armour that Pam has donned is the kind that’s instantly recognisable. “She’s really funny,” says Stewart. “She’s dry and she’s tough, but she’s funny. She takes the piss out of [her boss] Sunny a lot, but they’re really dear old friends. And she’s got a fraught relationship with her dad, but they really like doing quiz shows together on telly.”

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

1:35

A new Australian classic?

Kat Stewart on why Break of Day speaks to all of us

One of the reasons Break of Day brings to mind those classic American plays is in the way it humanises its characters, warts and all. Pam makes decisions that are questionable, though we never doubt the motivations behind them.

“Pam’s not a saint,” says Stewart. “She’s not exceptional. But we’re all on our own hero’s journey, trying to map things out as best we can and make the best decisions we can. I always work with the adage that it’s impossible to hate a person whose story you know. At the beginning people will make assumptions about Pamela, but hopefully by the end they will see her in a more complete and compassionate way.”

Rodgers’ script stipulates that the production be set in a satellite city, the kind of semi-regional urban centre that is itself often overlooked by outsiders. We’re more accustomed to romanticised portraits of rural Australia or gritty dramas set on the streets of a bustling metropolis. It’s less common to see a play set somewhere in between.

Which is, coincidentally, not dissimilar to the town where Stewart grew up. “It’s bigger now, but in those days Bairnsdale’s population was about 10,000,” she says. “That’s what rang true for me, the vernacular humour, the way the characters talk to each other. They’re voices that I grew up around and still hear.”

Stewart lived in Bairnsdale until she was 14. She understands Rae’s ambivalence, torn between the lure of city life and the familiar world that’s all she has ever known.

“I didn’t want to leave. The whole family left, so I had to, but I left kicking and screaming. I loved it and I had great friends there. I understood that there was a bigger world and that this might be the best thing for the family but I didn’t want to go.”

The kinds of warehouses Pam works at are often built in towns that are economically depressed, and so they give rise to another kind of ambivalence. They can put huge demands on employees, but they’re also providing work to regions that sorely need it. “This warehouse would be the lifeblood of this town, you know?” says Stewart.

This isn’t poverty porn: the playwright himself has worked in such a warehouse, and there’s a real authenticity to the details that are littered throughout the script. It’s less about grand tragedy and more about the quiet frustrations that the cost of living today invokes in most of us.

“I have so much respect for these characters and I feel so protective of Pamela’s dignity,” says Stewart. “Stevie has written something that’s kind of like a love song to the unseen workers. To family and to sacrifice and to yearning.”

Break of Day is at Malthouse Theatre from August 7.

Budjerah grew up in the national spotlight. Now he’s ready to reintroduce himself

Sydney Morning Herald July 25, 2026

The ARIA winner’s long-awaited debut album brings in Diane Warren and tackles toxic masculinity.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

At a time when the manosphere has taken over corners of social media, with figures like Andrew Tate and Myron Gaines pushing a conservative and aggressive take on what it means to be a man, singer Budjerah wants to recapture what it means to be a gentleman.

The 24-year-old, a Coodjinburra man from the Bundjalung nation, says the way masculinity was represented in his life was consistently positive. “I was very blessed to have so many incredible role models in my family. My dad, my cousins, my brothers, they influenced me in a good way,” he says.

“You hear a lot of bad stereotypes about Aboriginal men in particular that aren’t always true. That’s the definition of prejudice.”

The idea is at the centre of his debut album, Gentleman. ”I wanted this album to represent positive ways that men can be and the positive effects we can have on other people,” he says. “I think there are positive qualities in a gentleman that everyone can have, like opening doors for someone. Whether you’re a gentleman or not, or you believe in chivalry or not, it’s always best to lead with kindness and respect.”

Gentleman is funky, upbeat and assured. The titular opening track oozes swagger, while the swirling Pretty is emblematic of the confidence that Budjerah’s found as an artist. “I like the idea of the gentleman as an aspirational character I could play – this idea of being cool, calm, collected, put together, suave. Really putting in the effort, getting dressed up. I thought that was something cool I could aspire to be.”

The album arrives after years of percolation, and finds Budjerah carrying the weight of expectation on his shoulders. The singer won the ARIA award for Michael Gudinski Breakthrough Artist in 2021, and has spent the better part of the last decade adding to that success, amassing tens of millions of streams and collaborating with the likes of Ed Sheeran and Kylie Minogue, all off the back of a 2021 self-titled EP and a 2022 EP called Conversations. It’s a career trajectory that is seldom seen in Australia where, all too often, artists aren’t given the time to grow into themselves.

The release of Gentleman, then, is a coming-of-age for an artist who has grown up in the national spotlight, and he’s understandably itching for the album to be out. “The day before a release is always the worst day of my life,” he says. “I just can’t wait for it to be out in the world and I don’t have to think about it any more, and the people can just have their opinions on it. I’m just really excited for that ‘let go’ moment.”

That feeling would be understandable for any artist, but especially for Budjerah. Work began on Gentleman when he was 20. He’s now 24, married, and has lived a lot more life. “Since I released my first single, it’s just been about learning and getting myself together. I feel like it was artist development in a way, getting mentored by all these incredible artists and producers and musicians,” he says.

With Grammy-winning producer Om’Mas Keith at the helm, Gentleman is an album that is lush and expansive, painting a full picture of Budjerah’s musical journey. “It’s been a whirlwind, a lot of trial and error, trying different things and experimenting. We could do whatever we wanted,” he says.

“I felt like I definitely was challenged a lot in the making of this, and my skill was pushed to the limit. I had to really push my singing harder than I’ve sung before, and learning how to dance and sing at the same time was a challenge.”

His family’s influence is present throughout Gentleman. Budjerah’s parents are both licensed pastors, and he cut his teeth performing at his local church in Fingal Head, long before the world discovered his talents. His band, meanwhile, is made up of his cousins, and his little brother plays keys on Remember Your Name.

His family always hears his music before anyone else. “I always show my demos to my dad and my mum as soon as I leave a studio. It’s straight to them immediately. It’s always good to have honest feedback,” he says with a smile.

Budjerah wears his musical influences on his sleeve, looking to Michael Jackson, Usher and Beyoncé for inspiration. The latter even launched a moment of serendipity while he was in Los Angeles and contemplating a trip to Las Vegas to sample the city’s high-profile residencies.

“I was gonna see Lady Gaga because she was doing a big band jazz concert, but then I saw Beyoncé was doing the Renaissance tour that weekend and I booked the tickets,” he recalls. “She sang a song called Flaws and All, which is a gratitude song to her fans. I was like, I need a song like Flaws and All. I wanted something to express my gratitude to my family and to my fans.”

The day after the concert, his producer Keith (who he affectionately describes as “uncle”) told him they were off to work with the legendary songwriter Diane Warren. Warren, a Grammy-winner and 17-time Oscar nominee, penned I Was Here from Beyoncé‘s Four, Budjerah’s favourite album. During the session, she played the pair Even At My Worst, which became Gentleman’s closing track.

He beams from ear to ear recounting their time together. “She has written so many songs that I love, so getting to meet her and go to her studio, someone I’ve learned from as a songwriter myself, and to be able to hear her songs and to hear her as I’m singing the song, and she’s telling me how to sing it, how to shape the vowels, the specific notes. And if I was a little bit off, she’d correct it and tell me to do it again.”

Gentleman is a reintroduction of sorts to the world of Budjerah, a summary of the personal growth he’s experienced over the last half-decade. “A lot of people met me when I was like 16 or 17. Now I’m 24 and the content of the lyrics is a little bit more mature, singing about romance and heartbreak and stuff like that in a different kind of way than what I did six or seven years ago,” he says.

“I think of this as the album that the seven-year-old version of me would have loved. I wanted to be the artist that he would have loved.”

Budjerah’s debut album Gentleman is out now. He will perform at Melbourne’s The Espy on October 31, Anglesea’s The Sound Doctor on November 1, Sydney’s Metro Social on November 7, Gold Coast’s Miami Marketta on November 20, and Brisbane’s Triffid Beer Garden on November 21.

Confused by the gods, monsters and mortals of The Odyssey? This is your cheat sheet

Sydney Morning Herald July 25, 2026

Can’t tell your Zeus from your Zelus? Or think Scylla is some kind of hip-hop fusion band? Don’t worry, we’ve got you.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

So you’ve seen The Odyssey, or you’re planning on seeing it, but can’t tell your Zeus from your Zelus*? Or think Scylla is some kind of hip-hop fusion band? Don’t worry, you don’t need a detailed knowledge of Greek mythology to get through Christopher Nolan’s three-hour epic, but a little bit goes a long way. Consider this your starter guide to this Troy story filled with the gods, monsters and mortals of Homer’s epic 3000-year-old tale.

The king of Ithaca and a cunning and wise warrior. His journey home from the Trojan War (more on that later) should have taken about two weeks, but it turned into a 10-year epic that is the basis of Homer’s The Odyssey. Married to Penelope, with a son, Telemachus, and faithful dog Argos. Susceptible to witches, sea nymphs and long detours. Odysseus is a faithful yet forgetful husband in the film, which pretty much lines up with the original story, but skips over the bit where he also fathered a son with the witch Circe during his “lost weekend”, aka year on the island of Aeaea.

Odysseus’ wife, who spent 20 years fending off suitors while her husband was fighting in the Trojan War and then taking a “shortcut” to get home. To deter the suitors, who have essentially moved into the palace, she announces she will only marry once she has finished weaving the burial shroud for her father-in-law, which she unravels every night. Smart! Penelope is also the cousin of Helen, whose affair with Paris kicked off the Trojan War (he was kinda tricked by Zeus and Aphrodite into falling for Helen, but that story is in The Iliad).

The son of Odysseus and Penelope. In his 20s, he is a young man keen to do the right thing by his mum, but also has no real idea of who his dad is. He is the ultimate nepo baby but generally a good guy, who – post-Odyssey – goes with his mum to hang out with Circe and his half-brother Telegonus.

A real jerk who takes advantage of Penelope’s hospitality while trying to woo her. A walking red flag.

Odysseus’ faithful hunting dog who waits 20 years for his master’s return. The original good boy.

Trailer for Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey

The Odyssey is an epic fantasy action film written and directed by Christopher Nolan

Essentially, two countries, Greece and Troy, went to war because Helen (played by Lupita Nyong’o), widely considered the most beautiful woman to have ever lived, left her husband, King Menelaus of Sparta (Jon Bernthal), for pretty boy Paris of Troy. Menelaus’ brother Agamemnon (Benny Safdie) then decided war was the next best step. Odysseus became involved because, as one of Helen’s former suitors, he made a pact to always defend her chosen husband. The war lasted roughly 10 years, coming to a bloody conclusion when the Greeks hid in a giant statue of a horse that the Trojans then unwittingly dragged inside the city gates, giving rise to the saying, “Never look a gift horse in the mouth”. Helen, who by this point was married to Paris’ brother Deiphobus after Paris was killed in battle, was dragged back home to Menelaus where they lived unhappily ever after.

Daughter of Zeus (ruler of Mount Olympus, aka No.1 God) and the goddess of wisdom and warfare. She sprung fully grown directly from Zeus’ head, after he – totally normally – swallowed her mother Metis, while she was pregnant. In The Odyssey, Athena acts as Odysseus’ protector and mentor. She is a bit of a downer in the film, whereas in the Greek myths, Athena is a total badass who also guided the demigods Perseus and Heracles, defeated a fire-breathing giant and wore armour emblazoned with the head of Medusa.

An independent woman living her best life on the island of Aeaea who just so happens to be a powerful witch. Daughter of the sun god Helios, she bewitches Odysseus’ men, but he manages to talk his way out of it. In the film, Odysseus and his men leave after lunch, but in Homer’s epic, Circe and Odysseus spend one year together after Hermes, the messenger god, convinces Odysseus that sleeping with Circe is the best way to solve his problems. It is not! In another post-Odyssey twist – and real Housewives of Aeaea situation – Circe and Penelope end up living together on Circe’s island, and Circe and Telemachus eventually marry. Write that sequel, Christopher Nolan!

A sea nymph and minor goddess and possibly the daughter of the Titan Atlas (the Titans ruled before they were overthrown by Zeus etc). She enchants Odysseus and keeps him as her (sex) slave for seven years on the island of Ogygia, while he cries on the beach and sleeps in a cave. Again, this is not in the movie! In the film, she eventually helps Odysseus on his way, but in Homer’s telling, Zeus and Hermes have a stern word before she lets him go.

A giant man-eating cyclops who lives in a cave in Sicily tending to his sheep and making artisanal cheese (this is not in the original text). The son of the sea god Poseidon (who is the brother of Zeus and Hades, the god of the underworld), Polyphemus is blinded by Odysseus, who was trying to steal his sheep (again, Odysseus is the, ahem, hero in all of this). As revenge, Polyphemus prays to his father, who then curses Odysseus’ trip home. It works.

More giants who also enjoy eating humans. They, apparently, came from one of Poseidon’s sons, making them the nephews of Polyphemus (kind of). They destroy 11 of 12 of Odysseus’ boats. Not happy.

On the advice of Circe, Odysseus and his men head to the Underworld, which is ruled by Hades, to honour the dead (including the Greek soldier Sinon, played by Eliot Page, a character Nolan borrowed from Virgil’s Aeneid) and seek guidance from the blind prophet Tiresias. In Greek mythology, he’s considered a bit of a gender bender, having also spent seven years as a woman before switching back. In the film, Tiresias is the one giving Odysseus good but dangerous advice about getting home, whereas in the original text, it’s Circe who points Odysseus correctly in the right direction. #justiceforcirce.

The ultimate triple-threat. Charybdis is the sea monster/whirlpool, another child of Poseidon, who was sent to the bottom of the sea after she angered Uncle Zeus. Spends her days guarding the Strait of Messina with Scylla, a once beautiful sea nymph who angered Circe, so was, of course, turned into a man-eating monster. The Sirens, meanwhile, are the ones who alluringly sing songs that send men to their fate. Think of them as the original Sabrina Carpenters of the sea.

*Zelus is a cranky minor god, son of the Goddess Styx, an enforcer for Zeus and brother Nike, the God of Victory, not the shoe.

The Odyssey is now showing in cinemas.
