Australia had a chance to do something big. Then came weak leadership and fatal errors

Sydney Morning Herald July 25, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A little over a week after his wife Nanette and six-year-old daughters Alannah and Madeline were gunned down in Australia’s deadliest mass shooting, Walter Mikac sat down to write a letter to John Howard.

“As the person who lost his wife and two beautiful daughters at Port Arthur, I am writing to you to give you the strength to ensure no person in Australia ever has to suffer such a loss,” he pleaded with the then-prime minister.

Spurred on by the note, which is now held at the National Museum of Australia, Howard announced his legacy-defining national gun buyback scheme. Some 644,000 newly prohibited semi-automatic and pump-action firearms – one-third of all privately owned guns in Australia – were eventually handed over and destroyed.

Mikac had hoped to witness a similar national moment following December’s Bondi terror attack, in which 15 people were killed and many more physically and mentally scarred. But a potential repeat of Howard’s 1996 triumph has collapsed under the weight of shifting politics, absent leadership, and disagreement over who foots the bill.

Of Australia’s eight states and major territories, just two are proceeding with a post-Bondi buyback: NSW and the ACT.

Under the terms initially laid out by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, states and territories were meant to agree to reforms by March, and legislate the changes no later than July 1. Both deadlines have come and gone, and a mooted September start date in NSW is looking unlikely.

Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan rejected a key recommendation by her own independent expert, Ken Lay, to place a cap on how many guns a person can have, fearful of regional voters angrily handing back firearms at the same time as her beleaguered Labor government heads to the polls in November. Victoria Police also wanted a cap and was ignored.

Queensland is also out, as is South Australia. Tasmania won’t have a cap and Western Australia has just had 83,000 guns returned under a voluntary return program and feels no need to tie itself to Albanese’s proposal.

It took Howard just five months to announce, negotiate and begin his national gun buyback scheme following the Port Arthur massacre. By contrast, more than seven months have passed since the Bondi Beach antisemitic attack with no agreement.

Howard told this masthead this week: “Although the circumstances do vary, I am very disappointed that Anthony Albanese hasn’t got everybody on side.”

To make matters worse, the small number of jurisdictions that do want to take part in Albanese’s scheme still haven’t been able to finish the design of the scheme and strike a funding deal with Canberra.

In the Jewish community, patience is wearing thin. Farmers and recreational shooters who will be caught up in the fallout are also in a state of limbo.

The failure to land a new national gun buyback scheme – one of the key policy responses to flow from the Bondi atrocity – offers an insight into the state of politics in 2026 and the profound power of self-interest.

The rot set in the day Albanese announced his plan for a national buyback nearly a week after father and son duo Naveed and Sajid Akram allegedly opened fire on Jewish families at Bondi Beach.

Billed as “the largest since the Howard government in 1996”, Albanese said the buyback was critical and argued there were now 4 million firearms in Australia – more than at the time of the Port Arthur massacre.

But there were three problems with the prime minister’s commitment that meant the idea was fatally flawed from the start.

The first was who would pay. Unlike Howard’s buyback, which was federally funded via a temporary increase to the Medicare levy from 1.5 to 1.7 per cent, Albanese’s model called for a 50:50 cost sharing with the states.

Would the deal have got up had Albanese stumped up 100 per cent of the funding? “I’m not so sure,” Australian Gun Safety Alliance convenor Stephen Bendle said this week. “What we’ve seen is that there has been political hesitation more than financial.”

Either way, an argument over costs gave leaders an easy way to sidestep the scheme. Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro was the first leader to baulk at forking out. “We welcome the federal government to have a gun buyback scheme, but Territorians won’t be the ones footing the bill,” she said. “I’ve been very upfront and honest about that from day one.”

Albanese’s second failure was his initial refusal to announce other strong measures. His stubborn resistance to calling a royal commission into the deadly attack meant the measures outlined in his early response – however well-intentioned or needed – suffered by association.

Ironically, Howard – who supports the principle of a fresh buyback – damaged its chances of success in the days after Bondi. Savaging what he said was a failure of Albanese to combat antisemitism, Howard dubbed the prime minister’s proposed buyback a “diversion”.

“I do not want this debate post this horrible event to be used, the focus on guns be used, as a pretext to avoid the broader debate about the spread of hatred of Jewish people and antisemitism,” Howard said in December.

Albanese eventually relented and agreed to a royal commission – but the father of gun reform speaking in such negative terms offered conservatives cover to shirk bipartisan support.

The third setback was Albanese’s apparent unwillingness to use his prime ministerial authority to campaign for the changes. Whereas Howard travelled around the country making the case for a buyback, Albanese has been nowhere to be seen. He has spoken of the scheme publicly just a handful of times since February, according to an analysis of Hansard and his own transcripts.

But there is much blame to go around. The majority of states have refused to take part even though Virginia Bell explicitly recommended a national buyback in her interim report from the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

Costs are one factor. However, the rise of One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson has seriously spooked state leaders and oppositions. One Nation, which is vehemently opposed to a buyback and has pledged to repeal it, poses a real threat in Labor and Coalition-held electorates with high rates of gun ownership.

Federal Labor MP Dan Repacholi, who represents the NSW seat of Hunter, supports a buyback scheme but has criticised the four-weapon cap for recreational shooters proposed by NSW Premier Chris Minns. Allan, the Victorian premier, holds the regional seat of Bendigo East but denies her political survival was a factor in not following the lead of her NSW Labor counterpart.

Critics don’t buy it. The leader of the Victorian Greens, Ellen Sandell, said Allan’s refusal to support a cap was a “total capitulation to One Nation, the gun lobby, or probably both”.

Estimates based on current Victorian firearms ownership data have revealed that less than 20 per cent of the state’s firearms users would be impacted by the cap rejected by Allan.

Despite that proportionately small number, 287,000 firearms could have been disposed of had she agreed to the limit and participated in the national buyback.

“Any leader worth their weight would do what’s necessary to keep the community safe after such a horrific massacre as Bondi,” Sandell said in an interview this week. “People expect leaders to stand up and do what is right, even if that might be difficult and requires you to show some guts.

“And that’s why this is so disappointing with what Jacinta Allan has done here – she just does not have the guts to do what must be done.”

One senior Labor figure defended Albanese’s handling of the matter and said weak state leaders like Allan were really to blame for the scheme’s collapse. “They all need to explain why they are ignoring the recommendation of a royal commission that everyone was demanding,” the source, who declined to be named, said.

The department of Home Affairs, the domestic spy agency ASIO and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission have also endorsed a buyback, arguing it would help manage individuals with violent extremist ideologies, and frustrate serious and organised crime from obtaining lawful access.

Stolen or missing registered firearms account for nearly 10 per cent of illicit longarms and around 31 per cent of illicit handguns in Australia. Authorities estimate there are at least 250,000 illegal longarms and handguns in Australia, and potentially as many as 500,000.

Bendle also said limiting access would have other benefits, noting the “No.1 cause of firearm deaths is still by suicide”.

Shooting Industry Foundation of Australia chief executive officer James Walsh argued a cap in NSW and other states would not target the right gun owners. “These policies are not going to take a single firearm off a terrorist or a criminal – you’re just taking guns out of a safe,” he said.

“Taking those guns doesn’t increase public safety. Go out and go hard in south-western Sydney and take all the illegal pistols, illegal firearms, and the semi-automatic firearms that are being used. That will actually have tangible public-safety benefits.”

The argument that law-abiding owners saddle the biggest burden in any buyback was given short shrift by Howard in 1996. In his response to Mikac’s emotional letter of early 1996, the then-prime minister replied, saying: “I regret that many people who have never done anything wrong in their lives will be inconvenienced by the new laws, but this is ultimately a small price to pay for a community that feels, and is, more secure.”

Of course, Howard could rely on the crucial support of his deputy, Nationals leader Tim Fischer, who was instrumental in persuading rural Australia of the need for change.

Walsh said claims his industry and its lobbying arm had too much influence over the failed buyback were wrong. He claimed his organisation had to do little if any campaigning before most states pledged to not take part, and said the Minns government had “refused to speak to us”.

“We have his backbenchers calling, going, ‘there’s nothing that we can do. We know it’s going to cost us our jobs. We know we’re going to lose votes over this, but it’s a captain’s call. He won’t change his mind’.”

An analysis commissioned by his association recently found the cost of buying back weapons in NSW would be about $415 million before other costs such as compensation and administration were added. The government has not publicly disputed the findings of that study.

The delay in securing an agreement between Macquarie Street and Canberra has caused legitimate angst among recreational shooters and primary producers in NSW, who still have no idea whether the government will pay market value for a firearm, rather than a lower set price.

Walsh was scathing of Albanese’s handling of the issue, and his absence from the debate over recent months. “The prime minister seems to say a lot and then change his mind, doesn’t he?

“He came out in an emotion-fuelled speech saying he was going to do this and going to do that. But he hadn’t come to the industry. He hadn’t gone to the states. He didn’t know how many firearms are out there.

“There were questions he should have asked before he came out with this.”

The Herald and The Age asked the prime minister a series of questions, including why he had not been more forceful in his public advocacy for the scheme and whether promising to fully fund the program might have delivered more participation by the states.

In a statement, he said: “We’re continuing to work on the buyback scheme. We’re confident it will lead to a significant reduction in the number of firearms in our community, and that’s a good thing.

“I want fewer guns on our streets.

“The states and territories will make their own decisions about how they choose to participate – but all governments have a responsibility to do all they can to keep Australians safe.”

Chris Minns, whose premiership was redefined by the horror of Bondi, remains 100 per cent behind the gun buyback and has been overheard telling colleagues he thinks it’s an issue worth losing an election over.

Laws that passed parliament in December restrict firearms licences to Australian citizens, reduce the standard term for firearm licences from five years to two years, cap the number of firearms an individual may possess at four, with a higher limit of 10 for primary producers, and restrict access to pump-action, button or lever-release, or straight-pull firearms – such as those used in the Bondi attack – to primary producers.

However, progress on making those laws reality has been painfully slow. Some of the yet-to-be-resolved issues include whether the state can afford to offer market value for guns, which will increase the cost of the scheme, how much should be paid for ammunition and other soon-to-be redundant firearm paraphernalia, potential compensation for gun clubs and stores, and what other exemptions may need to be written into the regulation. There is also a huge amount of work being done on the mechanics of how guns would be collected and destroyed, which NSW Police have had to play a central role in navigating.

One senior member of the Minns government, who declined to be named due to cabinet confidentiality, said the work had been frustrating, “but I am sure there will be a deal and this will go ahead”.

Minns and Albanese have been under little political pressure to hurry up because oppositions state and federally do not see a political dividend in supporting the buyback.

NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane told a NSW Farmers’ conference in Sydney this week that while the NSW Liberals supported Minns’ gun laws in December, they wanted changes.

Bondi is personal for Sloane – she was one of the first on the scene to render assistance to the dead and wounded – but like her Victorian counterparts she is being squeezed by One Nation ahead of the March election.

“There were two terrorists that caused that attack,” Sloane told the crowd. “It was not farmers. I know you feel like you’re being punished. I know that those 10-gun caps in your communities feel unworkable. So I want to say that we are working with the government, with stakeholders, to make amends.”

Privately, the state government is angry at other states for capitulating to the threat of a backlash and does not blame Albanese.

Minns told this masthead on Friday: “There is goodwill from both the NSW and federal governments on this, and we’ll get it done. We remain absolutely committed to the buyback scheme.”

Minns has previously argued NSW will end up with the “strongest gun laws in Australia”. That may be true, but it would be easy for someone to cross a border and more easily obtain weapons in states with a higher supply.

Perhaps aware of the potential for states to go their own ways, the royal commission’s interim report warned against patchy laws. “There is a public interest in national consistency in firearms regulation in Australia, where extensive and largely unmonitored state and territory borders make it possible for people and firearms to move between jurisdictions with relative ease,” the report noted.

Bendle from the Gun Safety Alliance agreed things had not landed where he had hoped. “There was some hope among public health experts that there might be some light come out of the shadow of a Bondi,” he said.

He said while some states won’t sign up to a full national gun buyback, many may still alter their gun laws, and that would be a good thing. “But it won’t be the same as 1996.”

Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone review – the self-serving narcissist ruins this documentary

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 21:30:24 GMT

Just by his being there, the ex-prime minister undermines the honour of every brave fighter he meets in this tour of the war’s frontline. It should never have made it to TV

Here is the caption viewers are presented with at the start of Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone, an hour-long documentary following the former prime minister on his journey to the frontline of the ongoing hostilities between Russia and its coveted neighbour:

“This film presents Boris Johnson’s perspective on the conflict in Ukraine. The views expressed are subjective and reflect his own interpretations of events.”

What is this? A disclaimer? Arse-covering by a company that saw the rushes and took fright? A reminder of the inherent bias in all accounts of history, in all stories? Or is it as blatant a warning as possible that what you are about to see is presented by a known liar, a shapeshifting, self-serving narcissist whose mask long ago ate the face? Did the first draft of the caption read “Yes, we know, he’s full of it” or “Regrets? We have a few”? Or perhaps just “Sorry”?

From the moment it begins, you are beset by such questions instead of the ones Boris wants you to be thinking about (“Does Putin’s cruelty have any chance of success?”), as he interrupts the soldiers trying to explain their individual and national situation with his painful attempts at blokey camaraderie. He refers endlessly to their guns as “50 cal [calibre], right?”. He crows, “You shot the arse off that one!” He assures an army chaplain “I’ll pray for Ukraine’s victory all right!”

Your own questions nag throughout. One which I suspect many people will be asking is: does putting a man who long ago ceded any kind of moral authority, a man whose reputation for untruth taints everything he touches, in charge of a documentary not instantly hole the entire endeavour below the waterline?

I would say yes, and that the thing lists further and further with just about every contribution made by its ever-blustering presenter. Over the course of the hour, he turns it from serious undertaking to a new edition of the Boris Show, which most of us hoped had been cancelled for good after its increasingly shabby three-year run, 2019-22.

Much dwelt on is the fact that he needs to remain incognito to keep himself and his companions safe. So he clumsily – such a natural clown! – puts on a balaclava. Then he gets his flak jacket on backwards, and even once it is fitted properly on him it rides up at the back so that he looks ridiculous. This could be sorted. This is not real, nags that background voice again. This is showmanship in a war zone.

The dazzling rhetoric for which he was always so unjustly famed is on full, matte display here. When he and the crew spend their first night in an apartment at the edge of the kill zone, he is woken by the sound of bombs exploding nearby. “The truth is,” he says the next day, “if it had come through our window, we wouldn’t have known a thing about it, and there you go.” It really makes the endless suffering of the civilians and soldiers who have been under bombardment for the last four years live, you know? Sometimes it is combined with a faux modest heroism that grates even more than the blokey camaraderie. When they have to leave a street whose bomb damage they are inspecting with local troops because a drone is incoming, he assures us it is because “I don’t want to query the authority of a battalion commander. If he says we’ve gotta pull out, we’ve gotta pull out.” The careful elision to connote real emotion is really nicely done.

Maybe he will make up for the fly-on-the-wall stuff with the film of Reflective Boris back in the studio? Surely then we will get some political analysis of the situation, how it came to be, how it might be solved, what options are open to national and international powers? “I just don’t think I’ve ever seen such a clear case of right and wrong … This thing has gotta stop and the west has just gotta snap out of its complacency … It’s wrong.” And there you go.

At best, you might think it’s Alan Partridge Does Geopolitics. But then it ends with this caption: “It is widely acknowledged, including by Ukrainian officials, that Mr Johnson played a direct part in persuading Kyiv to abandon the Istanbul talks of spring 2022 – that were close to a settlement – in favour of continued fighting. He therefore has a share of responsibility for the resulting loss of life, Ukrainian, Russian and British alike.”

And you realise that your worst take was right. This is not merely a shambolic programme shambolically presented. It is a programme on which the plug should have been pulled early, instead of gifted to a man who undermines the honour and dignity of every fierce, brave, homesick fighter he meets just by being there.

Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone aired on Channel 5

Trump threatens EU with ‘substantial’ tariffs over fines of US tech giants

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 21:22:39 GMT

After Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Europe was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayers

What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countries

Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with additional and “substantial” tariffs after Brussels imposed a series of steep fines on US tech giants.

The US president accused Brussels of taking “direct aim” at several American companies including Apple, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Google, writing in a Truth Social post: “The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!”

Days earlier, Google was fined €890m ($1bn) by the EU after its search and app store services were found to have breached online competition laws. Last year Apple and Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, were also fined.

Trump claimed in his social media post on Friday that the US would “immediately” launch an investigation into the EU’s practice of “‘ROBBING’ American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer,” and said that the EU will “pay a very big price” for its actions.

It came just a day after the Trump administration separately imposed a sweeping round of tariffs on more than 80 countries, including those in the EU.

The European Commission did not immediately comment on Trump’s threat on Friday. Announcing the fine on Google on Wednesday, it said the tech company had given “preferential treatment to its own services, including shopping, hotels, transport and sports results”.

Google welcomed Trump’s intervention on Friday.

Jose Castaneda, a spokesperson for the company, said Google had worked hard to comply with the EU’s Digital Markets Act and expressed its concerns about the effects of recent decisions by the European Commission. “We appreciate the engagement by the administration and U. S. government,” he said.

Trump has often used tariffs – or simply the threat of them – as a way to retaliate against countries for decisions outside trade policy. Last year, he threatened a tax on imports from Mexico and Canada until the two countries agreed to implement measures on border security.

Despite challenges from the supreme court, Trump has persisted in implementing tariffs globally, claiming that they will help boost US jobs and manufacturing. The tariffs he announced yesterday would impose a 10% levy on the EU, and were designed to clamp down on what Trump claimed were unfair labor practices.

The EU has cracked down on a handful of large tech companies since before the start of Trump’s presidency after passing the Digital Markets Act, meant to help regulate competition among digital media companies.

Rampant Wigan sweep to derby win as St Helens’ Rowley sacking fails to spark change

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 21:04:46 GMT

Super League: Wigan 38-16 St Helens

Saints thrashed day after sacking head coach Rowley

There may only be eight miles between rugby league’s two greatest rivals but in sporting terms, Wigan Warriors and St Helens are simply worlds apart right now.

The most tumultuous of weeks for the Saints ended in the way many it expected to: with a straightforward derby defeat. There was no shortage of effort, but there are bigger problems at a club that expects greatness – which is why Paul Rowley was relieved of his duties as Saints coach after nine months in charge on the eve of this game.

The timing was perhaps a surprise; the decision, not so much. It simply didn’t work out, with the Saints regressing under Rowley to such an extent that he became their shortest-serving coach in 50 years. His successor has a huge job on his hands; not just to make the playoffs this year, but to oversee a rebuild beyond.

The very fact there was some talk of St Helens keeping this respectable representing a successful outcome for a club world champions just three years ago should be humiliating for all associated with their downfall. Yes, they are struggling with injuries, but their lowly league position underlines the size of the task Rowley’s successor has ahead.

But that talk is for another day. Here, this was Wigan’s night – and there is perhaps no player that emphasises the gulf between these two legendary clubs quite like the man who stole the show here: the Warriors’ talismanic half-back, Bevan French.

Back from a hamstring injury, French scored one try and created another four and added further weight to the argument he is Super League’s greatest-ever overseas player. It was in the balance at the break, with Saints’ players providing a response to Rowley’s sacking to trail by six at half-time.

Tries for Jacob Douglas and Jack Welsby put them ahead on two separate occasions either side of French’s try. The Australian then produced two superb assists for Zach Eckersley to put Wigan in front; they didn’t go behind again as they ran riot after the break, with the Saints’ young bench unable to keep up amid three more injuries to add to their mounting list.

But tellingly, even after an ultimately comfortable win, Wigan’s coach demanded more. “There’s elements we can do better,” Matt Peet said. “It shows how far we’ve come as a group though that we could still get the win.”

It was closely contested in the first half. The second was a mismatch. French teed up Oli Partington to score four minutes after the restart, before the half-back decided to let someone else make mischief for a brief moment, as Harry Smith’s kick sent Partington over for a second as the contest rapidly moved away from the Saints.

Adam Keighran then claimed a kick from – who else – French before Wigan’s maestro was withdrawn to a standing ovation with 15 minutes left. Lewis Murphy scored a late consolation for the Saints but realistically, there is only one of these sides heading to Old Trafford for the Grand Final in October: and it is not the Saints.

Their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll, was right to praise the effort his side displayed post-match. England full-back Welsby’s performance offered some hope too. But the problems at this club run much deeper, and Rowley’s replacement will have watched this contest from wherever in the world he is currently based and seen a club with a transitional period ahead of them.

Chuck Russell, director of The Mask and The Blob, dies aged 74

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 20:51:21 GMT

Director Chuck Russell, who helped propel actors such as Jim Carrey, Cameron Diaz and Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson to the Hollywood A-list, was found dead in his San Diego, California, home on Wednesday. He was 74.

Russell directed several box office hits in his decades-long career including A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors, The Blob and The Mask. In 2002, his film The Scorpion King featured The Rock in his first leading role.

The local fire department was called to Russell’s home on Wednesday afternoon with reports of an unconscious male, the director’s family said in a statement to TMZ. His death was confirmed by his attorney to Variety; a cause of death has not been confirmed.

Born in Park Ridge, Illinois, Russell first entered the film industry as an executive producer on the cult 1981 slasher Hell Night, starring Linda Blair, before co-writing 1984’s Dreamscape, a sci-fi adventure led by Dennis Quaid.

His directorial debut came with A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors in 1987, which Russell also wrote. The film which was hailed as a return to form for the horror franchise after mixed notices for 1985’s A Nightmare on Elm Street 2: Freddy’s Revenge.

After the 1988 remake of the cult B-movie The Blob, Russell hit the Hollywood big time with The Mask, the 1994 blockbuster that made global stars of Carrey and Diaz. Collaborating with George Lucas’s Industrial Light & Magic company brought the film acclaim for its practical effects, which were nominated for an Academy Award.

The Mask was originally envisioned as a horror flick. “New Line wanted another shocking horror film,” Russell said in 2024. “There was a comic book of The Mask that was quite terrifying. I said it’s going to be too much like Freddy Krueger. It’s going to be horrible.” Russell won his argument with the studio and the film grossed more than $350m on an $18m production budget.

Russell followed by working with Arnold Schwarzenegger on the 1996 action film Eraser and 2000 horror Bless the Child starring Kim Basinger and Christina Ricci. In 2002, he directed The Scorpion King, a spin-off to the popular The Mummy adventure films.

The director’s final film was 2024’s Witchboard, a remake of the 1986 horror starring Tawny Kitaen.

Paramount ⁠Skydance ⁠has agreed to ​pause its $110bn acquisition ⁠of ​Warner ‌Bros ‌Discovery until a ‌ruling on several states’ challenge ‌to the deal, or ​until 1 June ⁠2027, according ​to court ​papers ​filed ​on Friday.

A group of 12 US states headed by California obtained a temporary restraining order this week that blocked the merger from closing for 28 days, pending the outcome of a motion for a preliminary injunction.

The states allege that the deal should be blocked because it will reduce competition in the cable and theatrical markets.

A Warner-Paramount merger would bring together two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood, as well as a host of TV networks, titles filling streaming libraries and news operations. That would include Warner’s HBO Max and CNN coming under the same roof of Paramount-owned CBS, movies including Top Gun and the Paramount+ streaming service.

The ⁠delay could cost Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Ellison family, about $7m a ‌day in fees ‌it agreed to pay Warner Bros ‌shareholders if the merger does not close by 30 September. Similar merger ​challenges have taken an ​average ‌of eight ​months for ​a judge to rule on, a Reuters review of recent cases found.

Journalists at CBS News and CNN have expressed concerns about the possibility of the networks being merged and the likely resulting job losses. Press freedom groups have also voiced fears over political influence around the deal.

David Ellison and his father, Larry, a longtime Trump associate, have reoriented the CBS network in an editorial direction more favorable to the president, especially under the leadership of CBS News’s embattled editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss.

However, David Ellison pledged in March that CNN’s editorial independence would be protected amid speculation that he could put Bari Weiss in charge of the cable network.

At the time the deal was approved by the Trump administration in June, Elizabeth Warren, the progressive Democratic senator, said in a social media post that the development was “terrible news for every American who doesn’t want Trump-aligned billionaires to control what they watch and how much they pay”, adding that the merger “has reeked of corruption and influence-peddling”.

In a statement, Paramount said: “Today’s agreement is a significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence.”

It added: “This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers and good for creators – a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached … We look forward to proving our case at trial.”

Rebel Wilson had a legal win but didn’t come out of The Deb defamation trial unscathed

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 20:30:22 GMT

Judgment dismissing Charlotte MacInnes’s case expressed doubts about credibility of three key witnesses, and is likely to be appealed

Rebel Wilson’s self-styled brand as a truth teller was put to the test during a fiery defamation feud where rivals called her a bully.

But the Hollywood A-lister, referred to as “very difficult to be around” and “fucking nuts” during an at-times bruising trial, emerged from the federal court battle with the last laugh.

The Pitch Perfect star came under fire while being sued by the Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut film The Deb.

MacInnes claimed she was defamed by Wilson in four social media posts implying she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.

Wilson wrote the young actor confided – and later recanted – she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.

MacInnes denied making a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.

But in her ruling handed down on Wednesday, Justice Elizabeth Raper found evidence established MacInnes did make a complaint about feeling uncomfortable.

The young actor then walked it back, at least partially because she was concerned about losing control of the situation and wanted to contain it, the judge determined.

She ruled none of the four social media posts were defamatory in a comprehensive win for Wilson.

“This has been a long process and throughout I have tried to stay grounded in my values and what I believed was right,” Wilson wrote upon her victory. “I’m thankful that process has now reached its conclusion.”

Yet the Bridesmaids star did not escape the hotly contested trial without wounds.

For all Wilson’s protestations that she was known as a truth teller, Raper found the actor’s testimony had been untruthful on occasion, self-serving at times and punctuated with exaggeration.

MacInnes’s claims the first-time director would be believed because of her status in the entertainment industry were dismissed.

“It was my impression from all the evidence Ms Wilson is known for being outspoken but not necessarily reliable,” Raper wrote.

MacInnes faced the same scrutiny, with the judge finding she had been less than frank at times and combative when asked to accept reasonable suggestions.

She determined the young actor gave multiple inconsistent accounts of what happened in the Bondi apartment after the medical episode, as had Ghost.

“I have serious misgivings as to the truthfulness of the testimony of each of Ms MacInnes, Ms Ghost and Ms Wilson,” she wrote.

The scathing assessments may have MacInnes questioning why she sued her famous co-star. But the defamation law expert Prof David Rolph said the case highlighted the risk of defamation litigation. “People who sue for defamation or become involved in defamation cases don’t know and can’t control what’s going to come out in court,” the University of Sydney law professor said. “Once you start, it’s difficult to control and it’s difficult to stop what may be said about you in court.”

That became abundantly clear for Wilson, who was labelled a bully and a liar during the weeks-long hearing.

The Deb director denied the claims, labelling accusations of private and public bullying as nonsense and insisting she had been a champion of women throughout her 25-year career.

Raper noted she maintained her composure while being repeatedly charged with lying and fabricating evidence during her two-day cross-examination.

The accusations included that Wilson lied about having no involvement in the creation of smear websites attacking Ghost as the “Indian Ghislaine Maxwell” and a sex trafficker.

Raper made no determination of the contentious websites that loomed large during the trial, nor MacInnes’s allegation that Wilson was involved in a hack that resulted in a nude photo of hers being leaked.

Ultimately, the judge found, even if one of the posts had been defamatory, she could not be satisfied MacInnes had shown that she suffered serious harm.

The four posts had been visible to Wilson’s 11 million followers for 24 hours.

“The ordinary reasonable reader would have scrolled through the post relatively quickly and his or her reaction would have been impressionistic and fleeting,” she said.

The threshold of serious harm is a relatively new requirement yet to be tested in the country’s highest court, Rolph noted.

“The courts haven’t yet worked out precisely how to approach this issue and what’s required of it,” he said.

“It wouldn’t surprise me if a ground of appeal is raised in relation to serious harm because of the novelty of the issues and the novelty of the law.”

MacInnes indicated her intention to appeal against the decision, which has left her holding a hefty bill for the costs incurred by Wilson during the legal fight.

Rolph suggested such a high-profile loss may have a chilling effect on others considering litigation.

With a possible appeal looming, neither Wilson nor MacInnes can be said to have escaped without a scratch.

The actors began their relationship full of mutual admiration, working together on a film that was to elevate both of their careers.

But ended it on opposite sides of a stale Sydney courtroom, slinging accusations of lying and greed.

As Wilson wrote in her affidavit to the court: “Unfortunately, what started as a dream has turned out to be a nightmare.”

US surpasses 2025’s record number of measles infections as cases climb

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 19:09:29 GMT

The latest milestone, a recorded 2,318 infections, makes 2026 the worst year for measles in the US since 1991

The US has officially surpassed last year’s record number of measles infections, marking the highest case count since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000.

New figures from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released on Friday show the country has recorded 2,318 measles cases in 2026, overtaking the 2,289 cases reported during all of 2025 – with five months still remaining in the year. The country crossed the 2,000-case threshold last month before climbing even higher in July.

The latest milestone makes 2026 the worst year for measles in the US since 1991. Large outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona have infected hundreds of people, while additional clusters have emerged in several other states.

The growing outbreak makes it increasingly likely that the US could be entering a period in which measles once again becomes a regularly circulating disease, capable of sickening thousands of people each year.

International health officials are scheduled to meet in November to decide whether the US and Mexico should lose their measles-free status. The US achieved elimination of local measles transmission in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but coverage has declined in recent years, falling below the 95% level considered necessary to prevent outbreaks.

Even as reported cases continue to rise, the true scope of the outbreak may never be fully known. Public health officials and disease researchers have long said official totals are incomplete because some infected people never seek medical care.

Experts say reversing the current trend would require a nationwide effort to increase vaccination rates, but such an undertaking appears unlikely under the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long history of downplaying the importance of immunizations and grossly overstating their risks.

The American Academy of Pediatrics, which has sharply criticized the Trump administration’s approach to vaccines, described the new record as “an avoidable crisis that disproportionally hurts children”.

“These thousands of cases represent real people in communities across the country, including babies hospitalized with pneumonia, students who have missed weeks of school, and parents forced to miss work to stay home and care for sick children,” the statement said. “We should not accept this as our new normal. Unless we reverse this trend, America’s children will continue to pay the price.”

The measles surge comes as the US continues to face multiple public health threats, including hantavirus, screwworm, Ebola, cyclosporiasis, whooping cough and bird flu, highlighting growing concerns about the nation’s ability to prevent, detect and contain infectious disease outbreaks, especially as the Trump administration has cut staffing and funding to several preventive and response programs.

Former top CDC officials say the rapid dismantling of the US public health system at every level has left the country in a weaker position than it was before the Covid pandemic.

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 18:58:21 GMT

More than 180,000 people have fled or been ordered to lock down as huge wildfires sweep Spain and France, prompting Madrid to declare a national emergency and the French authorities to order the total evacuation, by land and sea, of one of the country’s best-known holiday spots.

Authorities in south-west France ordered the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast to be evacuated “village by village” in the face of an “intense, highly unpredictable” wildfire that has burned through more than 19,000 hectares (46,950 acres) of forest.

Spain’s government declared its first national emergency for a wildfire as two large blazes merged into one outside Madrid and a third was on the verge of joining them, amid searing heat and tinder-dry conditions across much of southern Europe.

Both countries sought EU help. “This is the worst wildfire in our region’s history,” said Madrid’s regional leader, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, describing “an unprecedented situation: a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds”.

More than 110,000 people had been evacuated in two days to escape the Cap Ferret fire, the Gironde prefecture said, including thousands of holidaymakers in campsites and rental homes.

Boats ferried hundreds off piers on the peninsula on Friday as the blaze threatened to cut off the only access road.

Scientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading to thousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate.

About 800 firefighters and four water-bombing planes were battling the Gironde blaze north of Arcachon Bay, but the fire, which began on Wednesday near the village of Saumos 25 miles (40km) west of Bordeaux, was not yet stabilised.

Numerous roads in the area, including those leading to Cap Ferret, which contains many villas owned by celebrities and millionaires, were closed to all but essential traffic. Eighty houses had burned.

“I’ve seen plenty of fires before, but never one of this intensity,” Jean Mazodier, 86, who owns 150 hectares of forest and was evacuated from his home at 6am, told Le Monde. “Everything’s burned. It’s like losing a child.”

A second fire raging in the region, farther south near the popular holiday resort of Biscarrosse, had also burned through more than 2,500 hectares, the Landes prefect, Gilles Clavreul, said on Friday, and led to the evacuation of about 31,000 people.

More than 600 firefighters were struggling to contain that blaze, Clavreul said.“There are a great many new fire starts ahead of the main blaze. The situation is highly dynamic and unfavourable,” he added.

In 2022, a wildfire burned more than 30,000 hectares in France’s south-west, forcing 50,000 evacuations. In parched conditions and fanned by strong winds, the two latest blazes have torn through coastal pine forests with flames up to 10 metres (30ft) high.

France’s president, ​Emmanuel Macron, said he had activated the EU’s civil protection mechanism as the country, which has endured three almost back-to-back heatwaves since May, battled numerous wildfires.

“We will soon be able to count ‌on reinforcements from two Croatian aircraft, two Portuguese planes, as well as two heavy helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia,” Macron said.

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Friday that 32 wildfires were burning, with 50,000 hectares scorched already so far this year – nearly four times the total by the same date last year.

About 800 firefighters were battling a blaze in the south-eastern Var area, where weather conditions were improving, Nuñez said, allowing some firefighting resources to be redeployed to the south-west.

A national emergency, which allows central government to assume overall control of powers and responsibilities that are usually the domain of Spain’s self-governing regions, has only been declared once before, during the countrywide blackout of April 2025.

The regional government of Madrid requested assistance, describing the situation as one of “extreme gravity”. It said at least four active fires could advance “beyond current extinguishing capacity”. The fires remained uncontained on Friday.

Spanish authorities said on Friday afternoon there was “very little time left” before the blaze in Madrid, already made up of two merged fires, combined with the Ávila fire.

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 18:43:41 GMT

Exclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sector

Hundreds of thousands of care workers could be exempted from the home secretary’s plans to toughen up the immigration system under proposals being considered by Andy Burnham as he looks for ways to relieve pressure on the social care sector.

The prime minister will give a speech next week spelling out his determination to start creating a National Care Service before the next general election as he looks to accelerate the process set up by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

In a highly personal speech, Burnham will talk about his experience of the care system through his father, Roy, who has Alzheimer’s, and announce that he is bringing forward Louise Casey’s review into the sector, which was due to conclude in 2028.

He is now also considering granting widespread exemptions from Shabana Mahmood’s plans to make it harder for people to achieve settled status in the UK.

The measure is not likely to be included in next week’s speech but could come later in the year once the Home Office has considered responses to a public consultation on the issue.

One person briefed on the plans said: “Andy is determined to do something about the social care system, and quickly. This is highly personal for him, and he will talk about why he wants to push some of it through before the election, even if that comes at a political price.”

Burnham has put reform of the social care system near the top of his list of priorities, having tried and failed to do so as health secretary more than 15 years ago.

He told broadcasters this week: “I think it’s about being prepared to grasp the nettle. I’ve got personal experience of the system. My dad has Alzheimer’s, and you see what the staff have to put up with. It’s not their fault. The system’s broken.”

He added: “You can’t leave social care like this. And this is part of my criticism of Westminster. It has flinched over the years from these big decisions.”

The prime minister has previously argued for replacing inheritance tax with a 10% levy on all estates once a person dies to pay directly for a universal care system, but those proposals were scrapped after the Conservatives labelled them a “death tax”.

People in England get state-funded care if they have less than £23,250 in assets, but those with more must pay the entire cost themselves.

Meanwhile, social care providers say they are financially stretched and increasingly unable to provide the services for which they have been contracted given the low value of their contracts with local authorities.

Many have complained bitterly about the likely impact of Mahmood’s plans to double the length of time it takes migrant workers to qualify for settled status, known as indefinite leave to remain, which could disproportionately affect the care sector.

Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, the country’s biggest union, said: “Vulnerable people and those with complex needs won’t get the help they deserve unless ministers focus on recruitment and retention. That means dropping plans to push migrant care workers out of the UK.”

Mahmood has said she will consider exemptions to the new ILR (indefinite leave to remain) rules, though carving out those on social care visas would make a significant dent in the numbers affected.

The Home Office has granted about 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more coming as their dependants.

Burnham is understood to be considering exempting those already in the country from the changes but allowing them to be applied to new entrants.

While the changes are not likely to be included in his speech next week, he is set to lay out some short-term fixes to alleviate the burden on the sector.

They could include putting more money into the £9bn Better Care Fund, a ringfenced pot of money designed to be used to boost social care where doing so would relieve pressure on the NHS.

One option he is understood to be looking at is increasing the fund to offer patients free short-term care once they leave hospital in an attempt to prevent them having to go back into acute care.

The prime minister will also leave the door open to levying extra taxes to pay for a new system in the longer term, saying that funding options should be considered as part of Lady Casey’s review.

Casey was commissioned by the former health secretary Wes Streeting to publish an interim report this year and a final one in 2028 but those close to the process say she could now simply accelerate her final report instead.

Burnham told the Guardian last month he would like to see the review published by the end of the year, though sector experts said this is likely to prove overambitious.

Casey has said the UK faces a “moment of reckoning” over its longstanding failure to match sufficient resources and action to the demands of growing numbers of frail elderly people and disabled adults.

She has been scathing of the way patients with dementia or Alzheimer’s are undermined by institutional fights over whether a person qualifies for free NHS care or is means-tested and charged for social care, and smoothing the fault lines between the services is expected to be a key focus of the review.

Casey will launch a public consultation in the next two weeks calling for a “challenging conversation” with the public this summer.

Sources said she wants to answer a series of questions including who should qualify for social care, how far families should provide care for loved ones, and how far individuals should pay for care.

Member states vote to remove British barrister after allegations of sexual abuse

The prosecutor of the international criminal court, Karim Khan, has been removed from office after the court’s governing body concluded in June that he had committed serious misconduct in connection to allegations of sexual abuse.

The ICC’s member states voted on Friday to oust the British prosecutor in an unprecedented move that concludes a damaging episode for the court two years after the allegations were first raised.

According to sources familiar with the result, 82 of the court’s 125 member states voted in favour of removing Khan at a special meeting at the UN’s headquarters in New York.

The vote follows a drawn-out disciplinary process that examined the abuse allegations, which were made by a woman who worked for Khan at the ICC.

Khan has repeatedly denied all the allegations against him, which include claims that he engaged in coercive and non-consensual sexual behaviour over an extended period.

His lawyers have criticised the disciplinary process as procedurally unfair. Responding to the vote, they said Khan would “challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the decision through all available legal mechanisms”.

The prominent British barrister was elected in 2021 to serve a nine-year mandate running the court’s prosecution division, which is tasked with investigating and bringing to trial individuals accused of atrocities.

During his tenure, Khan’s decisions to obtain arrest warrants for the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, raised the ICC’s profile and thrust it into the crosshairs of major powers.

The warrants, issued by judges, are unaffected by his removal. However, the court’s prosecution division, which has about 400 staff, has been left bruised by a protracted scandal and convoluted process to resolve the matter.

Last month, the executive committee of the ICC’s governing body suspended Khan after concluding he had committed serious misconduct in connection to the sexual abuse claims, referring the outcome to member states for a decision on whether to permanently remove him.

In a closed-door session on Friday, diplomats voted after reviewing the findings of the executive committee, alongside a fact-finding report by a UN watchdog and a legal analysis of its investigation by a panel of judges.

Thirteen member states voted against removing Khan in the secret ballot, while 11 countries abstained.

After the allegations first emerged in 2024, Khan’s representatives have sought to suggest the claims may be part of a plot to discredit him in response to his 2024 decision to seek arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his then defence minister.

In a report detailing the outcome of the disciplinary process against Khan, the ICC’s governing body found there was no evidence to support claims the woman was “being used by third parties, including intelligence agencies”.

Last week, the staffer spoke out against claims she was some sort of “state agent” in an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour. She said: “My complaint was because of what happened to me, not for any other reason.”

Danya Chaikel, the International Federation for Human Rights’ representative to the ICC, said the vote was a testament to the complainant’s “extraordinary courage in coming forward, despite everything she risked in doing so”.

Khan also faced sexual misconduct allegations from a second woman. She came forward to the Guardian last year and accused Khan of mistreating her while she was working for him as an intern earlier in his career.

Khan lawyers have previously said he categorically denies having “harassed or mistreated any individual”.

In a statement, his lawyer Tayab Ali said: “Khan’s removal was determined by a process in which he was never given a fair opportunity to be heard.” He said the decision was “unsupported by any lawful or properly reasoned finding”.

Khan’s dismissal comes as the court faces an array of pressures, including renewed threats from the US. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on several ICC judges and prosecutors and last week vowed to “systematically disable the ICC’s ability to operate”.

Senior officials at the court’s headquarters in The Hague do not expect the US government’s hostility towards the court to diminish with a change in prosecutor.

Against this backdrop, the court must now appoint a new prosecutor. After Khan stepped aside last year pending an outcome to the disciplinary process, his two deputies took over the running of the court’s prosecution office.

Prosecutors are elected by the ICC’s member states. Some in the prosecution division believe one of the deputies should take over, while others feel it needs a fresh start after two years of turmoil.

If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 18:14:12 GMT

Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all

US politics live – latest updates

Don’t believe the Trump administration’s rationale for its new volley of tariffs against everybody.

The new levies, ostensibly to punish countries for failing to do enough to curb forced labor, switched on at 12.01am on Friday, to coincide with the expiration of a temporary 10% blanket duty that Donald Trump imposed in February, ostensibly to protect the United States from a balance-of-payments crisis.

That duty was imposed right after the supreme court struck down tariffs the president unleashed on US trading partners last year on the also spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies.

The shifting justifications alone underscore how Trump’s arguments are bullshit. But the specific nature of the latest accusation truly takes the cake.

The US is arguing that tariffs of 10% or 12.5% are justified against 60 trading partners because they import stuff made with forced labor, unfairly undercutting American producers. But the charge omits that forced labor is not only prevalent across the US. It is also actively enforced by the state.

Americans import lots of stuff made with forced labor: $170bn worth of imported goods are at risk of being tainted at some stage along the supply chain, according to the Global Slavery Index (GSI), from raw materials through to finished products. In 2023, this was the most among the countries in the G20.

It includes electronics imported from China and Malaysia; clothing from India, Vietnam and Bangladesh; fish from Ghana; and timber from Russia, Brazil and Peru. The mining of essential minerals used in many electronics the US buys from abroad, from cobalt and copper to lithium and nickel, is rife with allegations of human rights abuses.

To be sure, until recently the US was the only country that explicitly prohibited importing goods made with forced, convict or indentured labor. Still, the GSI reports no evidence that penalties are enforced against companies that fail to comply with reporting mandates, due diligence or other procurement regulations.

Then there’s the issue of forced labor at home. There were 1.1 million people living in modern slavery in the US on any given day in 2021, according to the GSI, mostly doing domestic work, or toiling in agriculture, construction, retail, hospitality and illicit activities.

That amounts to 3.3 forced workers for every thousand people in the population, which is more than in many of the countries Trump wants to punish. In the Netherlands and Germany, there are 0.6 forced workers per thousand people. In Britain there are 1.8.

Canada also has a law on the books prohibiting imports made with forced labor. The prevalence of slave labor in Canada is only 1.8 per thousand people. Still, it just got hit with a 10% tariff because according to the US trade representative it is not doing enough to enforce the law. (The European Union will ban imports that involve forced labor starting in 2027.)

But here is the real rub: a significant share of modern slavery in the US is enforced by the state.

The US stands out among the world’s democracies by allowing forced labor in prisons. And there is no legal obstacle to export goods made by prisoners forced to work against their will.

The 13th amendment to the constitution bans slavery and involuntary servitude, but it exempts work “as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted”. In Alabama prisons, they call the forced labor “mandatory chores”.

after newsletter promotion

About 800,000 of the 1.2 million people in state and federal prisons work, according to a report in 2022 by the American Civil Liberties Union and the University of Chicago – often against their will, under the threat of further punishment. Incarcerated workers, the report adds, “are under the complete control of their employers, and they have been stripped of even the most minimal protections against labor exploitation and abuse”.

Most work for the prisons themselves and other government businesses. In Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and Texas, more than 10,000 prisoners are assigned to agricultural work on penal plantations or prison farms, according to the ACLU report. They are also often farmed out to the private sector. In Alabama, according to an investigation by the Associated Press, they were leased out to at least 500 private businesses between 2018 and mid-March 2024.

Prisoners toil in poultry processing plants and work in the kitchens of some of the biggest fast-food chains. They cook, wash dishes, fix plumbing and clean buildings. They are paid pennies an hour. And their wages are often garnished by the state.

In seven southern states – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas – almost all work by prisoners remains unpaid.

If he is so inclined, Trump could help the fight against slave labor by taking a hard line against the US’s southern states, which generally raise less tax revenue and thus rely more on “free” work by the incarcerated to both operate prisons and generate revenue for the public sector.

The ACLU report estimated that the incarcerated produce stuff worth more than $2bn a year and provide $9bn worth of services to their prisons.

Other countries could help by slapping some tariffs on American goods to retaliate against these blatantly unfair practices.

Relaxed and tanned, Enzo Maresca offered a warm note with his first words to the media as the manager of Manchester City, who must somehow follow the generational Pep Guardiola. “Before we start, I would like to send a message and a big hug to Kevin Keegan’s family for this moment,” said the Italian in tribute to a football legend, following his death on Monday.

Keegan, of course, was a former City manager who had at Newcastle famously locked horns with Sir Alex Ferguson when he led Manchester United, the fierce rivals of Maresca’s new team. When the 46-year-old, sat on the dais occupied for 10 mostly glittering years by Guardiola, offered an unsolicited reference to Ferguson – and Arsène Wenger – you could see he comprehended the mammoth task before him.

How do you follow the man who claimed 20 trophies in a decade and who ranks alongside Ferguson? Well, by mentioning, and so trying to tame, the elephant in the room. “The history of the manager with many years in the same club always struggled a little bit. After Sir Alex, after Arsène,” Maresca said. “But also, it’s a challenge to try to do the right things immediately for this organisation, for the fans, for everyone.”

Speaking in front of a giant “Welcome back Enzo” billboard, a reference to his previous leading of City’s elite development squad in 2020-21 as well as his stint as Guardiola’s assistant manager in the 2022-23 treble season, Maresca would have been aware the font of goodwill will not prove deep if results go south. Certainly not from that most fickle of constituencies – fans. So Maresca cutely pointed to the patience of City’s chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, and his executive. “This club has had three managers in 17 years,” he said. “This is not normal, so this is one of the things that I’m confident we can do a great job and continue to do the job that has been done in the last years. Roberto [Mancini] was here, then Manuel [Pellegrini] and then Pep – for 10 years.”

Mancini’s tenure began in December 2009, ended with his sacking in May 2013, and was angst-ridden: anathema to al-Mubarak and his chief executive, Ferran Soriano. If Mancini could be volatile, Pellegrini proved serene, and Guardiola was, simply, a genius. Al-Mubarak’s and Soriano’s experience of Maresca during his two previous seasons at City obviously convinced them that he is the full package: an accomplished football man who is of equable character.

Yet Maresca’s exit from his previous post at Chelsea on New Year’s Day ended with an apology from him, and City paying the west London club £17m in compensation. Maresca’s shutters came down for the first – and only – time when his conduct was raised. “I feel quite lucky in terms of my former clubs – Leicester, Chelsea – I think we did a great job,” he said. “In both clubs, the identity of the team was clear, the success of the team was clear, and I feel very lucky to be part of these clubs. But now we are here today. That is the most important thing, just about City. And nothing to add.”

Maresca made Leicester Championship champions and the next season took Chelsea to fourth in the Premier League and a Conference League triumph before claiming the Fifa Club World Cup last summer, a 3-0 evisceration of Paris Saint-Germain in the final a calling card that may well have sealed the City job.

He talked of “titles” for the coming season. To aid this mission, Maresca has Elliot Anderson, a £116m buy from Nottingham Forest, to patrol midfield, and potentially Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, who shone for Morocco at the World Cup, to further bolster this department. He also retains an interest in Malo Gusto, one of his right-backs when at Chelsea, and if Omar Marmoush leaves, the market will be entered for a similar, pacy forward.

One player Maresca certainly does not wish to lose is the peerless Rodri, who lifted the World Cup for Spain on Sunday and received the Golden Ball, and whose control of a contest in the ever-more frantic domestic game is priceless. The 30-year-old will have surgery on a back problem on Monday. The word is it is not too serious, though he will miss out when City host Bournemouth on the opening weekend of the season. The more important date is 1 September, when the transfer window closes: will Real Madrid have made a move for a footballer who has a year left on his terms and is declining to sign the new deal offered by City?

Of more immediate concern for Maresca is flying out on Tuesday for a pre‑season tour of Asia that features matches with Inter in Hong Kong and K-League All Stars and Atlético Madrid in Seoul. For the trip Maresca will have back City’s A-listers who exited the World Cup early, including Josko Gvardiol, Mateo Kovacic and Abdukodir Khusanov.

“I’m working at the moment with many young players,” he said. “That is always good because they are full of energy and some of them are very good. The last group of players are going to join three or four days before the Community Shield and we will have all the squad.” After that Cardiff game with Arsenal on Sunday 16 August, the bid to successfully succeed Guardiola begins in earnest.

“You need to adapt, evolve,” Maresca added in reference to his playing style. “Set pieces, man to man – it’s a little bit the direction where football is going. We managers, it’s our duty to find solutions.” We are about to discover how good he is at this.

The hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing, Brendon McCullum, rather than taking full control of both red- and white-ball squads.

Some high-profile candidates have been unwilling to work within such a setup, either because they want full oversight over the senior men’s teams or because of the unique ­challenge of working alongside ­the person who was sacked as Test coach earlier this month.

The issue is exacerbated by next year’s schedule: though the Test side will be the focus of attention until the end of the Ashes in early August they would then take a backseat to the ODI team before the World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in October and November. Even with the Ashes on the horizon the white-ball coach would be expected to argue that multi-format players, including the current white-ball captain, Harry Brook, should play the five-game ODI series against Pakistan that starts the international summer, while the Test coach could demand they concentrate on the one-off Test against Bangladesh that begins less than 48 hours after its conclusion.

As a result the process of appointing a new coach is taking longer than first hoped. Rob Key, the ­managing director of men’s cricket at the ­England and Wales Cricket Board, who is leading the recruitment ­process, was initially optimistic that someone would be in place before the three-match Test series against ­Pakistan that starts on 19 August. But the ECB is increasingly resigned to – and relaxed about – the process dragging on beyond that date. Once that series ends on 13 September there is a gap of 87 days before the team is next in action, when their tour of South Africa starts with a three-day game against a CSA Invitational XI in ­Durban, and sources say they are determined to pursue the best appointment rather than the quickest.

The ECB has started the process of meeting leading candidates, and expect to hold multiple rounds of interviews over several weeks. ­Justin Langer, the Australian who is ­coaching Manchester Super Giants in the Hundred, is believed to have fallen from favour, with the former England batter Jonathan Trott, the Glamorgan head coach, Richard ­Dawson, and McCullum’s former New Zealand teammate Stephen Fleming among those still in contention.

If there is no permanent appointment before the Pakistan series, Key will name both an interim coach and an interim captain, with ­Marcus Trescothick – who worked as ­assistant coach under ­ McCullum – the presumptive frontrunner to take the coaching role, though ­alternatives are being considered, and Joe Root the clear frontrunner to lead the team once again.

Ferdinand Geus is proud of the positive, global impact his small speciality coffee business is having.

“We sell their coffee to cafes across five continents, fuelling employment for an entire chain of people that spans the seas and reaches into local high streets and neighbourhoods around the UK.”

Despite Geus’s enthusiasm, Sheba has been struggling under the weight of increased energy bills and a soaring cost of living.

“Coffee is a luxury and people are cutting back,” he said. “To survive at this point in our business journey, we need to expand – to employ more people – but we can’t do that.”

He might have been able, however, had Andy Burnham’s 20% cut to business rates bills embraced cafes and restaurants. But to Geus’s frustration, the targeted package, worth roughly £100m a year, will only support specific high street sectors: pubs, social clubs and live music venues across England.

“Burnham says he wants to support high streets but independent cafes are more than retail businesses; they are workplaces, meeting places and important parts of their local communities,” he added.

“Supporting pubs while excluding cafes risks creating an artificial distinction between businesses facing many of the same commercial pressures.”

Hakan Elbir, founder of the deaf-run Dialogue Cafe, an inclusive social enterprise based at the University of East London that supports deaf and hard of hearing baristas, is also frustrated.

“We’ve been trying to hold down our prices – despite the rise in the cost of coffee beans, which came on top of all the other price hikes we’ve had to absorb – because any increase will push footfall down even further,” he said.

“But this incentive to our competitors is definitely going to affect us in a bad way. Our customers will now prefer to go to the pub for their hot drinks because they’ll be able to undercut our prices. It’s not fair.”

Elbir said he is particularly disappointed because, listening to Burnham’s speeches since he became prime minister, he had been anticipating receiving help.

“I feel that he has missed an important point,” he said. “We are helping the government employ disabled people. We’re saving them money – but instead of rewarding us, they put more barriers in our way.”

Elbir also argues that Burnham’s exclusive focus on venues that sell alcohol is based on a fundamental misunderstanding of where people want their community hubs to be.

“Our cafe actually does have an alcohol licence but predominantly and increasingly, people prefer to buy coffee or tea,” he said.

“If Burnham wants to help communities, he needs to look at what communities really want, rather than what he thinks they want, and focus his support there.”

Water bosses’ pay rises despite bonus ban and public fury over bills and pollution

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 17:09:50 GMT

Exclusive: Eight companies expect to be covered by the ban for 2025-26, the Guardian can reveal

Water company bosses’ total pay rose over the past year despite a government bonus ban and public outrage over pollution and bills, the Guardian can reveal.

One chief executive, Mark Thurston of Anglian Water, received £1.9m – including a £500,000 “retention payment”, despite the bonus ban.

The biggest package went to Louise Beardmore, chief executive of United Utilities, who received £2.5m – £1.1m more than the previous year.

Overall reported pay packets rose by 1.5% to £25.3m for chief executives and chief financial officers in the year, thanks to salary rises and the use of pay loopholes, according to analysis of the 14 companies that serve most of England and Wales.

With water bills soaring and with Britain’s biggest water company, Thames, on the brink of insolvency and about 23 million people covered by hosepipe bans as drought status looms, the revelation sparked criticism of companies for allegedly finding ways to pay their bosses more, despite the bonus ban being introduced in 2025.

The news will add to pressure on Andy Burnham to clamp down on the industry. Burnham has said he wants to exert “more public control” over the water industry, and has suggested he could move Thames into temporary government ownership after years of financial struggles and mismanagement.

Adrian Ramsay, a Green party MP, said: “The astronomical sums paid to water company executives are a perfect illustration of everything that is wrong with treating this essential public resource as a private commodity.

“Andy Burnham must surely now reach the obvious conclusion that water should be brought back into public ownership, as the Green party would do, so that any money raised goes back into the system, not into shareholders’ pockets and excessive executive pay.”

Water company pay has come under intense scrutiny in recent years because of persistent dumping of sewage into Britain’s rivers and seas. The utilities have been allowed to raise bills sharply to make belated investments in their leaking pipes, ageing treatment works and new reservoirs. Recent hot weather has added to the frustrations of customers.

Eight companies said they expect to be covered by the bonus ban for 2025-26, with bans applied retrospectively to companies responsible for the most serious pollution incidents or financial failings.

Yet despite the ban and heavy criticism, total pay for chief executives and chief financial officers reported by water companies was £25.3m for the year to the end of March, up from £24.9m the year before, according to analysis of company accounts. It is the second year in a row that executive pay has risen despite the bonus ban.

In some cases the companies have given their bosses extra awards that they claim are not “performance-related payments”, or bonuses, which they argue means the cash is not covered by the ban.

Anglian Water said it will be caught by the bonus ban, but still gave more to Thurston. The chief executive, who was Britain’s best-paid public servant when he ran the late and hugely over-budget HS2 rail project, received the bulk of his pay through Anglian’s parent company, including a £500,000 “retention payment”.

Anglian, which provides water and sewerage services to nearly 7 million customers in the East of England, claimed the payment did not count as a bonus because it was not linked to the regulated water company’s performance. The company said the payout was funded by shareholders for work outside the regulated company, and it needed “targeted, time-limited retention arrangements to maintain leadership continuity”.

Yorkshire Water said it was likely to be banned from paying bonuses, but its parent company, Kelda Holdings, paid another £600,000 to its chief executive, Nicola Shaw, on top of her fixed pay of £732,000. The regular payment – which Yorkshire has said is not related to the water company’s performance – was first revealed last year by the Guardian.

Gary Carter, a national officer for the GMB union, which represents many water workers, said: “Finding ways round the bonus ban further tarnishes the reputations of private water companies. It makes them look like money-grabbing asset strippers who care more about lining their own pockets than providing fresh, clean water for the UK public.

“Senior executive pay is out of control and the government needs to fundamentally overhaul the water companies – with more public control – to fix it.”
