Executive pay dropped at some of the companies covered by the ban, including Severn Trent, Southern Water and Northumbrian Water – although Northumbrian also made a £300,000 “retention payment” to its chief executive, Heidi Mottram. However, the High Pay Centre, which scrutinises executive pay, said the analysis raises questions over whether the government’s bonus ban has been effective in cutting pay for those companies who are responsible for serious pollution, or which have failed financially.

Andrew Speke, the High Pay Centre’s interim director, said: “These figures show the government’s current measures have not gone far enough. Restricting bonuses makes little difference if executives continue to receive broadly the same overall level of pay through other forms of remuneration. The government could go further by introducing measures such as maximum pay ratios, but more fundamentally it needs to address the corporate governance model that has allowed these levels of executive pay to persist despite years of poor performance.

“If Thames Water does come under public ownership or control, ministers should seize the opportunity to demonstrate a different approach to executive pay and corporate governance. Setting clear expectations that pay should reflect performance and the public interest would establish a benchmark for the rest of the sector and increase pressure on other water companies to follow suit.”

The water company reports showed other ways used by water companies and their owners to reward executives. United Utilities does not expect to be banned from paying bonuses this year, but it still gave Beardmore a £435,000 “annual allowance” with no performance conditions, on top of a 16% increase in fixed pay to £971,000. The FTSE 100 company, which has 7.3million customers, said the money came from shareholders, and was required to retain its leaders.

Wessex Water was also banned from paying bonuses. However, it granted its chief executive, Ruth Jefferson, a 14% salary increase. Wessex said the higher salary better reflected the job’s responsibilities.

The other companies that indicated they would be covered by the ban were Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water and Thames. Thames still paid £4.1m in bonuses to senior staff not covered by the ban.

The water regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, is not expected to confirm formally which companies are subject to the bonus ban until the autumn. However, the ban applies retrospectively to any company responsible for the most serious pollution incidents during that year, as well as those such as Thames Water which are failing financially.

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “We have banned undeserved bonuses for water company bosses. Any attempt to circumvent the rules is completely unacceptable.

“We will leave no stone unturned in ensuring bonuses can only be paid where companies deliver environmental and customer outcomes and Ofwat’s review of the bonus rule will carefully consider if any requirements need to be tightened.”

Water UK, which represents companies across country, declined to comment.

The Guardian’s analysis included pay awarded to all people who held chief executive or chief financial officer roles during the respective years, including from parent companies where reported. Two companies did not disclose pay for chief financial officers.

Parts of England under heat alert with 30C temperatures possible

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:52:31 GMT

Warning in place until Sunday morning in southern and central regions after drought declared in parts of Wales

Heat alerts are in place across parts of England, with possible highs of 30C (86F) and officials saying temperatures are likely to have an impact on health and wellbeing.

The yellow heat health alerts issued for the East Midlands, east of England, London, south-east, south-west and West Midlands are in place until 9am on Sunday.

Temperatures in the affected areas are forecast to reach the mid- to high 20s, with a high of 30C a possibility, as a prolonged period of dry, warm weather continues in much of the country.

The heat health warning from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) comes after drought was declared in north Wales and the upper Severn region, following record dry conditions, heatwaves, wildfires and dwindling rivers.

It was the first part of the UK to declare drought status amid a summer of record-breaking heatwaves.

Many parts of England have had prolonged dry weather as the country has received just 3% of its average July rainfall. Hosepipe bans are in place for 23 million customers and suppliers are warning they may last all summer.

Wildfires have been raging in England, while Scotland has also been hit by a major fire in the Cairngorms. In Ireland, a nationwide hosepipe ban is in place.

This summer’s dry conditions follow last year’s summer drought, as the UK increasingly faces more extreme weather fuelled by human-caused climate change, mostly from burning fossil fuels.

The Met Office said temperatures could reach 30C in parts of south-east England on Friday, while parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will see patches of cloud.

The forecaster Craig Snell said outbreaks of rain would move southwards on Saturday, spreading from Scotland and Northern Ireland into northern England and parts of Wales.

By Sunday, temperatures were expected to become “fresher” across much of the UK, with rain possible in “areas that haven’t seen much” over the past few weeks, he added.

The Met Office said that while some areas would experience rain and showers, the wettest conditions were likely to remain confined to northern and north-western parts of the UK.

The Met Office chief meteorologist, Dan Suri, said: “For much of southern England, dry conditions are expected to remain the dominant feature, with temperatures recovering quickly next week and the potential for very warm or locally hot weather to return.”

The UK’s climatic extremes are becoming increasingly normal, the Met Office’s annual State of the UK Climate report found, with last year the hottest on record and further “unprecedented changes” likely to break the record again soon.

Data stretching back to 1884 shows the UK has never experienced a year as hot as 2025, according to the report, with temperatures pushed to dizzying heights by carbon pollution clogging the atmosphere.

While the UK’s climate is becoming wetter overall, punishing droughts amid hot and dry summers are expected to worsen as average temperatures increase further, the report found.

Earlier this month, the Met Office said the UK had already recorded as many 30C days in 2026 as in the extraordinarily hot year of 1976.

“What we used to think of as extreme, we increasingly consider as normal,” said Mike Kendon, a scientist at the National Climate Information Centre and lead author of the report. “We are seeing unprecedented changes continuing … and every year adds to this body of evidence.”

The heat alerts are in place at the beginning of a period in which millions of motorists are expected to take to the roads for summer getaways. The AA said about 6.3 million drivers were planning a road trip of more than 100 miles between Friday and next Thursday.

The port of Dover is expecting another busy weekend but has worked to smooth any delays caused by new EU border checks.

The ferry company DFDS said its waiting times at Dover were up to 60 minutes at border controls but “free-flowing” at check-in.

The weather health alerting system is provided by the UKHSA in partnership with the Met Office and is intended to provide early warning to the health and social care sector, emergency services, the voluntary and community sector and government departments when temperatures are likely to affect people’s health and wellbeing.

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s first week: polished politics allow an upbeat start

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:49:21 GMT

With a flurry of cost-of-living measures and a day in Number 10 North, the new prime minister has hit the right early notes

Appropriately enough, Andy Burnham ended a week of political signalling and first impressions back in Manchester on Friday. At the offices of the new No 10 North – where the prime minister hopes to work at least one day a week – regional mayors sat alongside ministers in an example of Burnhamism at work. It was an early statement of intent, ahead of what Mr Burnham bills as “the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen”.

The same could be said of the series of cost of living measures fired out during the new government’s first few days in office. A £2 cap on bus fares, a cut in VAT on electricity, and some business rates relief for pubs, clubs and smaller music venues were all modest moves. But they were cleverly indicative ones, nodding empathetically to people’s need to have the chance to enjoy themselves as well as pay the bills.

They also sent a distinctively optimistic message to the public, compared to the Starmer government’s fateful early decision to cut winter fuel payments. Mr Burnham needed to sound and act differently from the off. In short order he has demonstrated the political sure-footedness so sadly lacking in his predecessor.

Given the relatively small scale of the spending involved, the eagerness of sections of the media to locate Liz Truss-style “unfunded commitments” has been faintly risible. There will, of course, be much more of that to come in the autumn, as Mr Burnham’s surprise choice of chancellor, John Healey, puts together his first budget. But with parliament now in recess and Nigel Farage distracted by a political farce of his own making in Clacton, the prime minister and his team will feel they have navigated the opening act of his premiership with some aplomb.

The more difficult work begins now. Recent polling, as Mr Burnham prepared to take office, pointed to an exasperated and impatient electorate which will give him only a limited window of opportunity. He intends to use the summer to visit constituencies identified as losers from a 40-year political settlement in which “power was centralised, economic power was privatised and communities were deindustrialised”. But having arrived in No 10 after a quicker handover than he may have preferred, and without the scrutiny of a contest, the coming weeks will also be crucial in refining the strategy for reform on all three of those fronts.

As economic headwinds continue to blow from the Middle East, and fiscal caution is urged upon the new government from the usual quarters, it will need to be bold. Mr Burnham’s analysis of the flawed political economy which has ill-served Britain in recent decades is the right one. But from radical devolution to public control of utilities and launching the biggest public housing programme since the Attlee government, his prescriptions for change will challenge entrenched orthodoxies. The viability of the 10-year plan that the prime minister intends to unveil later this year will depend on his government’s ability – and willingness – to successfully take them on.

As England progressed to the semi-finals of the men’s World Cup this month, it looked at one point as if Mr Burnham might move into No 10 the day after football finally came home. Lionel Messi and Argentina denied him that “lucky general” moment. But the prime minister’s first week has been upbeat and politically polished. Trickier tests are yet to come.

The Guardian view on ponds: these freshwater havens need a law of their own

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:48:12 GMT

Small pools don’t get the same attention as polluted rivers or seas. But they have a vital role to play in boosting nature

Frogs; newts; small fish such as minnows and sticklebacks; dragonflies; water boatmen and water snails: these are just a few of the hundreds of animal species that make their homes in Britain’s ponds alongside diverse wetland plants, some of which are endangered. Yet while small bodies of water are cherished by hobbyists as well as scientists, they have startlingly few protections – even at a time when the polluted state of rivers, lakes and coastlines is a key focus of environmentalists.

With a clean water bill expected soon, this official neglect of ponds should soon be consigned to the past. While rewilding projects have overseen the rediscovery of older “ghost ponds” as well as the creation of new, and householders are encouraged to create miniature ones in their gardens, charities including the specialist Freshwater Habitats Trust point to the growing body of international research that testifies to their ecological importance. In 1996 the first-ever national survey estimated that there were 228,900 ponds in Britain. Thirty years on would be an apt moment to grant them enhanced status.

The decline of ponds is part of a wider story of damage to the UK’s waterways by a combination of intensive agriculture, building development, pollution and the failure to manage it. One local study in Leicestershire has found an average 1% species loss every year for 15 years. But unlike rivers, many of which disappeared underground when they were culverted by the Victorians, around two-thirds of ancient ponds in England and Wales have vanished altogether either through drainage or infilling for farmland. When horses were replaced by tractors, it was wrongly thought that these pools had served their purpose.

To the extent that ponds have been legally shielded, this has been largely due to great-crested newts – a protected species since 1981 and one that cannot thrive in rivers with large fish. These rare amphibians even had the dubious honour of becoming an anti-red-tape trope, with Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, among senior politicians to have suggested that rules were overly tilted towards wildlife.

More recently, Rachel Reeves, then chancellor, criticised the way that a development in Sussex was delayed by concerns about another freshwater creature, the little whirlpool ramshorn snail. While it is right for regulation to take account of individual species, the broader point about ponds is their contribution to biodiversity overall.

Increasing heat and drought, and the stress they impose on natural systems, make the presence of water in landscapes all the more urgent. Ministers should heed calls to add targets for ponds to the plans that govern England’s 10 river basin districts. They should also embrace a broader lifting of ambition, whereby the target of high ecological status would be set for a limited number of streams, rivers and lakes.

Compared with the challenges around water companies, sewage and pollution from roads and farming, ponds and streams might sound unimportant. But the Climate Change Committee and other experts consistently stress the importance of nature recovery – and one of the distinctive benefits offered by small water bodies is the speed at which they are capable of being restored under careful management. What is good for newts and snails could also be good for politicians and the public.

Shirtless heroes, bucket hats and gold: reimagined Games find their glow

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:40:19 GMT

Some big stars are absent, but day one in Glasgow showed the Commonwealth Games have retained plenty of soul

There will be many extraordinary sights at these Commonwealth Games in Glasgow over the next 10 days. But few, you imagine, will top that of a volunteer ripping his T-shirt off and nosediving under the water, without goggles, to fix a broken rope while Adam Ramsay-Peaty waited on at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre.

The crowd, who had watched other volunteers fail to deal with the problem using large nets, cheered. And, after a 10-minute delay, Ramsay-Peaty was back smoking his rivals in the heats of the 100m breaststroke.

So was the double Olympic champion tempted to jump in and retrieve the item himself? “Definitely not,” he said. “Even if it’s a first – scoreboards break, clocks break – the guys got it together pretty well. Hopefully it doesn’t happen again.”

Over at the para powerlifting, meanwhile, there was more confusion as England’s Mark Swan won the first gold of these Games – but couldn’t fathom why it was given when he had ended with the same score as Nigeria’s Roland Ezuruike.

Only an hour or so later did officials explain that a second decimal point had separated them.

But do you know what? Despite these initial teething problems, and a fair number of empty seats, it didn’t matter. These Games might be “reimagined” – which is management speak for “made smaller”. But, as the first full day of action showed, they retain plenty of soul and glow.

The soul? That was provided by the Botswanan lawn bowler Diza Mphotho, who delighted the crowd at the indoor SEC arena with his bucket hat and languid style, even if he ended up being on the reverse of a 10-3, 16-1 thrashing by Guernsey’s Jason Greenslade.

“It’s very hot in Botswana,” said Mphotho, an IT worker who took up the sport 10 years ago when his mother’s friend told him it could be his passport to see the world. “So I always play in my bucket hat.”

Bowls is not big in Botswana. Only about 200 people play it across four clubs. There was a fifth, Mphotho explained, but then a copper mine shut down and the funding dried up. But it has proven life-changing to him.

There was one other message Mphotho wanted to impart: he gets 20 days of annual leave a year – and he is using pretty much all of them to play in Glasgow. “We’ve already been here two weeks,” he said. “And it’s completely worth it.”

And the glow? That came from watching Swan’s celebration after he bench-pressed 222kg to win gold – a weight that, staggeringly, is more than three times his bodyweight.

It has also been some journey for the 25-year-old geordie, who started his powerlifting journey at an event for the Dwarf Sports Association Games, where he lifted 70kg to earn a bronze medal.

And it helped that he was roared on by a packed Armadillo Arena, partly because members of the Tartan Army were given four free tickets each to certain events to fill the blank spaces.

However, it is noticeable that there are fewer fans than usual from around the globe. That is largely explained by simple economics. When Glasgow rescued the Games after Victoria dropped out in 2023, there was no time to build an athletes’ village. And so athletes and officials are staying in hotels and other accommodation, which means a lack of supply – and crazy high prices – for everyone else.

One person said they were paying nearly £300 a night for a tiny room in a three-star hotel. And the kicker? It doesn’t even have a window. However, Phil Batty, the chief executive of Glasgow 2026, insists that plenty of people are still coming to Scotland to watch – but are staying outside the city.

And despite the empty seats, he insists momentum is building.

“We’ve got facilities like the velodrome where we’re completely sold out,” he said.

“But we have taken bold and brave decisions, like taking netball centre stage in the Hydro for nine days with 21 sessions. A Commonwealth Games of the past would have just had the final and the bronze medal match there.”

Insiders have told the Guardian that the 10,000-seater Hydro will look very empty for some netball matches. Batty’s response? “We have sold more tickets for netball than have ever been sold in the history of Scotland. But, yes, there’s still midweek netball tickets for £10 to buy.”

There have been some other missteps. When you walk through the city centre it is not obvious that a major event is taking place.

That is in striking contrast to Birmingham 2022, when Commonwealth branding was everywhere – and the bull from the opening ceremony became an overnight tourist attraction.

Yet the sense is that Glasgow is making a decent fist of staging a budget games where many of the big stars, including the Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson, have stayed away.

In the arenas, the commentators are enthusiastic, the crowds involved and the music upbeat. Although as the Stone Roses’ Made of Stone segues to another indie classic, it was tempting to ask whether Andy Burnham had hijacked the playlist.

But perhaps the abiding memory of day one was watching two young boys being utterly transfixed by Australia’s men’s 3x3 basketball team squeeze past New Zealand 21-15.

Their mother, Eilidh Rooney, who paid £150 for four tickets, said it had been worth it. “It’s lower key this year compared to 2014, when the entire city felt alive,” she said. “But there is a great buzz here.”

The roar that followed shortly after as Australia celebrated their victory suggested that plenty of others agreed.

Pogacar conquers Alpe d’Huez in record climb to win stage 19 and extend Tour de France lead

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:25:54 GMT

Slovenian only second man to win in yellow on mountain

Leader opens up gap of more than seven minutes

Tadej Pogacar put further distance between himself and his last remaining rivals, winning the Alpe d’Huez stage of the Tour de France and extending his overall lead to more than seven minutes.

There was a brutal inevitability about the defending Tour champion’s win on the legendary climb of the Alpe, despite all the rumours of illness and gastric problems within his UAE Emirates XRG team.

Pogacar’s climbing time, of 35 minutes and 26 seconds, shattered the longstanding record set by Marco Pantani in 1997, by more than a minute.

“I don’t know what the time of Pantani was,” he said. “I don’t take too much into that, but I heard that I broke the record, so I’m happy.

“I would say this means as much as any other win, but now everyone has emphasised how big this win is, maybe I will start to realise it is quite important.

“I just wanted to do a good race and to win. A thirtysomething year record finally broken is good for us.”

So feverish was the speculation over Pogacar switching from yellow shorts to black earlier this week, that one French TV commentator even suggested it was to conceal an excess of flatulence. But on the Alpe, it didn’t matter what colour Pogacar’s shorts were: he still won.

The only wind emanating from the four-time Tour winner, now close to taking a record-equalling fifth win in Paris on Sunday, came from the metronomic climbing style that took him to a record-breaking ascent of the Alpe’s 21 hairpin bends.

The Slovene looked the picture of health as he sped up the 13.8 kilometre climb, the theatre for many of the Tour’s most dramatic finishes, and with one final mountain stage still to come, now seems assured of overall victory in Paris.

The old adage, that the Tour is won on the Alpe, was proven again with Pogacar’s latest demolition of his hapless rivals. With 25km left to race, the day’s breakaway led by almost four minutes, but three kilometres from the finish, Pogacar had caught and overtaken them.

Pogacar’s sports director, Matxin Fernández, was reduced to tears by his rider’s performance. “I don’t know why they get so emotional,” Pogacar said of his team management. “I don’t cry often. I guess it meant a lot to the team and also the way we are riding as a team, the team spirit we have. It cannot be better, so when we win, the emotions come to the surface.”

Huge and rowdy crowds, estimated to be in the region of 500,000, and at times out of control, greeted the riders at the foot of the Alpe. Some had arrived six days in advance, while others seemed too intoxicated to know why they were there in the first place.

“It was a crazy atmosphere on the climb,” Pogacar said.

The damage done to his rivals was extensive, with Remco Evenepoel the least wounded by the onslaught. The Belgian remains in second place overall, but any hopes of challenging for the final victory are long gone. He and Pogacar’s teammate, Isaac del Toro, are now the only riders within 10 minutes of the race leader.

On another day of desperation for the teams that have yet to taste success in this year’s Tour, a big breakaway took shape on the early climbs of the Bayard and Noyer.

In that leading group of 40 were some now familiar names, including past stage winners, Richard Carapaz, Thymen Arensman, winner of two stages in 2025, and the recovering Adam Yates, teammate to Pogacar, who won in Bilbao in 2023.

It was a Lazarus-like performance from Yates, who was so sick earlier this week that he was barely able to pedal through the finish line to his team bus after Wednesday’s stage to Voiron. But as soon as the main contenders began to climb the first steep ramps of the Alpe, the stage took on a new look, as Pogacar shifted up a gear.

His decisive acceleration came 12km from the summit and immediately left his closest rivals in his wake. After joining forces with Yates, the pair ate into the break’s advantage, until with 10km remaining, Pogacar set off alone.

The denouement was obvious. It was a cruel and relentless win, wholly in character with Pogacar’s domination of the Tour. He has taken five wins in 19 stages. Saturday’s “queen” stage, over four of the hardest climbs in the Alps, now offers him the chance to take a sixth. Another victory now seems almost inevitable.

Scoff at cheaper bus fares and No 10 North if you like, but Andy Burnham knows what he’s doing

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:01:30 GMT

Retail politics while taking power out of London: if this works, Burnham’s premiership could be seriously transformational

One of Andy Burnham’s first policy moves brought back a sharp memory. On Wednesday, he announced that single bus fares across England would be capped at £2, starting from January. It was part of a series of small, practical measures designed, said the new prime minister, to offer a little “breathing space” to a hard-pressed public, but this was the one that registered with me most. That’s because it echoed the first time I ever experienced a specific public policy that I realised affected me directly.

It was in the autumn of 1981 when the newly elected Greater London Council, led by Labour’s Ken Livingstone, slashed bus fares in the city. The headline-grabber was a new, short-hop fare of only 10p. I was 14 years old at the time, so for me it was even better: all child tickets were reduced to 5p. They called the scheme Fares Fair.

It became a legal and political battle – Margaret Thatcher’s government objected to the extra local tax levied on Londoners to pay for it – and eventually Fares Fair was declared illegal and shut down. But I never forgot it and nor, I suspect, did many of the residents of the capital who would make Livingstone London’s first elected mayor nearly 20 years later.

Fares Fair had what no one at the time called cut-through. It was a simple, clear offer to voters that had a direct, positive impact on their lives, one they would remember long after bigger, grander strategies had been lost to oblivion. It worked because politics is, in part, a retail business.

Burnham’s first week as PM, and his tenure as mayor of Greater Manchester, suggest he understands that very well. Yes, there can be grand talk of ending a 40-year model of political centralisation and economic privatisation, but you also need to do something for voters that is immediate, tangible and uncomplicated. Everyone understands a lower energy bill or, indeed, a cheaper bus fare.

Kemi Badenoch’s response to these first moves of Burnham’s was unintentionally revealing. They were too unambitious, the Conservative leader said, amounting to “small answers to big problems”. As she put it: “He is not the mayor of Manchester. These are mayor of Manchester ideas. Where is our prime minister?”

Obviously, it’s daft to deliver a verdict on an administration a few days old, not least when Burnham has said that bigger decisions are coming, including a 10-year plan for the country to be unveiled in the autumn. But the language of her dismissal was telling, and not only because it confirms that she does not grasp the retail dimension of politics or its value.

She associates such things with the municipal realm and therefore sees them as insufficient and unserious: they are mere “mayor of Manchester ideas”. It’s true that municipal leaders often do retail well. Several of them made their name that way – think Rudy Giuliani, before his disgrace, and his “broken windows” policing strategy that cracked down on relatively minor offences, whether a stolen bike or a snatched handbag. That’s in the nature of a local politician’s job. They’re closer to the ground than national governments, able to improve voters’ immediate circumstances directly. But Badenoch is wrong to see that as a weakness: for a politician, it’s a strength.

For national leaders, envious of that municipal impact, there are two possible responses. One option is to think retail, even when operating on the largest scale. Harold Wilson named as his greatest achievement the Open University, a simple idea that made higher education available to those who’d been denied it. Thatcher defined an era by allowing council house tenants the right to buy their homes. Or consider the ultimate retail offer – the guarantee of free medical care – in the form of what went on to become Britain’s most cherished institution, the National Health Service.

The other option is for a government not to emulate the municipal so much as to empower it. This seems to be the animating project of Burnham government, embodied by his No 10 North plan to decentralise the running of the country. Opening the new site in Manchester on Friday, the PM described it as “the best day of my life”.

Burnham’s view is that the key to Britain’s future is allowing more and more places to repeat Manchester’s experience. As he wrote in the Guardian: “We built a city-region with twice the economic growth of anywhere else in the UK. What we did in Greater Manchester, we can do across the nation.” What Badenoch meant as an insult, Burnham regards as a badge of honour: these are indeed “mayor of Manchester ideas”.

The core belief is that devolution, giving more powers to cities and regions, is Britain’s best shot at grabbing the prize that has proved so elusive for so long: economic growth. A new paper from the Harvard Kennedy School and King’s College London, authored by Ed Balls and others, argues that Britain’s national productivity problem is a function of its “persistent regional productivity problem”, with the divide between the south-east and the rest leading to “productivity gaps wider than between east and west Germany”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It argues that Keir Starmer’s government talked a good game on devolution but didn’t match words with deeds – and says this has been the story of British governance for decades. The Harvard-Kings team did 95 hour-long interviews, including with 10 former prime ministers or chancellors, and found not only a Whitehall machine reluctant to let go, but politicians failing to act boldly enough, early enough. John Major, Tony Blair and George Osborne all spoke of their regret that they did not push regional growth from the start, when they had the political capital to do so.

This time, it could be different. At long last there is, simultaneously, a devolution true believer in No 10 and allies in both No 11 and the key Whitehall department. As Balls puts it, the combination of Burnham, John Healey and Angela Rayner makes this “the best moment we have ever had on this agenda”.

Badenoch is not the only one grumbling that Burnham’s opening days have offered small beer. Even some Labour voices have wondered when they will see the equivalent of Gordon Brown’s 1997 granting of independence to the Bank of England or windfall tax on the privatised utilities, both of which came in week one. That fails to take account of the obstacles that stand in Burnham’s path: he has to find many billions to fund increased spending on defence, social care and much else, and yet is hemmed in by a 2024 manifesto that blocks off the most obvious routes to raising the cash.

But those grumbling may also be missing what is right in front of them. A rebalancing of British power is shaping up to be the big-ticket item of the Burnham government. If it works, it will unleash myriad policy moves as yet unimagined across the country, bringing the growth that is the prerequisite for all else. And, who knows, it might even improve the life of a teenager somehow and somewhere – one who will never forget it.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

‘Netflix has to evolve’: can the upstart survive the end of the binge-watch era?

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 16:00:11 GMT

Streaming pioneer that transformed TV faces slowing growth and battle for viewers’ attention from YouTube

When Netflix offered viewers the chance to binge on an entire season of House of Cards it revolutionised the TV industry and started on a path to becoming the world’s most popular streaming service.

Almost 15 years on, however, the upstart’s strategy of pumping its service with an avalanche of content and an almost-as-rapid penchant for mercilessly cancelling shows has viewers reaching for the remote.

A recent analysis of a number of Netflix’s top shows, such as One Piece, Beef, The Night Agent and Avatar: The Last Airbender, revealed audience declines of 30% to 70% in their second seasons and further declines in their third.

Last week, Netflix said it would scale back the viewership data it releases to once a year, following the scrapping of the quarterly reporting of subscriber growth last year, further fuelling fears that its years of juggernaut-like engagement growth may have passed its peak.

“We’ve been saying to TV producers to be careful, it might be tempting to take the big money being offered to make a show for Netflix, but the saying goes that it’s often the case of ‘one and done’ – you’re cancelled,” says one senior TV industry executive. “What is happening with binge model audiences has been clear for years now. Fifteen years ago it was a means to an end, creating a market leader, but look how different the world is today. Netflix is looking out of date.”

While there is a popular perception that Netflix is quicker to cancel shows than its competitors, research from Ampere shows that it is a facet of the streaming model. A look at cancellations of scripted programmes made last year shows that across all the big streamers this usually occurred after series two or three.

Netflix has announced the fate of about 180 unscripted and scripted shows annually over the last three years, with a cancellation rate averaging about 22%, with a similar ratio seen across the other global streaming players.

The reason streaming cancellation rates seem so high is largely because they are, but only compared to traditional broadcasters. For example, an analysis of the rate of cancellations last year at the BBC shows that a scripted show was typically cancelled after its fifth or sixth season, a lifespan typical across major traditional broadcasters.

“I remember always having to defend the weekly broadcast model by saying there is value in deferred pleasure,” says Peter Fincham, a former senior executive at the BBC and ITV who is a co-chief executive of the production company Expectation. “Linear broadcasting is biased towards recommissioning, because you have a schedule. And there are plenty of examples of a series that has shown some promise, but maybe not done quite as well as hoped, building over time. In the world of streamers, which is much more data driven, it is much less sentimental.”

Netflix does dabble with how it releases some content, such as its flagship franchise Stranger Things, which has been released in multi-episode tranches, and Love is Blind as a weekly drop.

However, competitors such as Disney+, HBO Max and Apple TV have had huge success using the traditional TV-style, slower-burn drip-feed for hits such as Rivals, The Pitt and Widows Bay respectively.

Investors started showing concern about Netflix’s hit content pipeline when it stunned the market by making an $83bn (£62bn) bid to buy Warner Bros Discovery’s (WBD) studios and streaming business.

While it was positioned by bosses as a rare chance to pick up a trove of assets – including the Hollywood studio behind franchises including Harry Potter, Superman and Batman, as well as HBO, home to shows including Game of Thrones, The White Lotus and Succession – that bid marked the first time Netflix had hoped to bolster its content firepower through an acquisition.

With the mega-franchise Stranger Things and Squid Game coming to an end, and the new hit Wednesday not scheduled to return to screens until next year, investors worry the move was instigated in recognition of a need to shore up a patchy content slate to keep viewing in growth mode.

The company’s share price has tumbled 40% over the last year.

Emarketer forecasts that time spent on the streamer in the US, by far and away Netflix’s largest market, will grow just two minutes this year to 36 minutes, and just one minute in each of 2027 and 2028.

But again, while investors have reacted to a perceived engagement problem at Netflix, that appears to be a factor at rivals too. Emarketer forecasts that the amount of time spent by viewers on Disney+ will only increase by 1 minute this year, half that of Netflix.

Profits at Disney’s streaming operations nearly doubled year on year in its most recent quarterly results, reporting its first double-digit streaming margin. Nevertheless, an analyst at Wells Fargo recently suggested Disney should get out of streaming and focus on producing and licensing to boost a share price down almost a quarter over the past year.

Almost a decade ago, the founder of Netflix, Reed Hastings, quipped that the market opportunity was so vast that his biggest competitor wasn’t rivals but sleep, as viewers flocked to binge-watch its hosepipe of content. However, while Netflix has enjoyed golden years as a first-choice streamer it faces newer competitors in the battle for consumers’ attention.

And when it comes to screen time, YouTube has become a force to be reckoned with. Last year, average daily viewing on YouTube passed Netflix for the first time, according to a report by Digital-i. The 20 market report found that while YouTube viewing rose from 87.2 minutes to 99.1 minutes per day on average, Netflix fell from 100.5 to 93.4 minutes per account.

Figures from eMarketer also put TikTok in the attention competition mix, with average daily viewing per user in the US at 57 minutes. However, it is YouTube’s drive into the living room that marks it out as the biggest threat to the existing streaming hegemony.

Last year, YouTube said TV screens officially overtook mobile phones and desktop computers as the primary device for viewing the platform’s content in the US, a milestone that was also reached in the UK as four- to 15-year-olds joined older demographics that had already made the jump to television formost of their viewing on the video platform.

UK data from the audience body Barb showed that TV sets became the first-choice device for YouTube viewing for over-55s in October 2023, for those between 35 and 54 in April 2024, and for 16- to 34-year-olds in December 2024.

YouTube’s combined share of UK television and streaming viewing is now second only to the BBC – 18.3% to 20.55% – according to Barb’s most recent figures for June.

And in terms of content, viewers have moved beyond videos of cats on skateboards and gamers’ videos of themselves playing Minecraft. Digital-i estimates that the share of viewing to long-form content on YouTube, that is videos more than 20 minutes long, is about 68%.

Netflix itself acknowledged the YouTube threat when it was bidding to take over WBD, as is Sky and ITV in their argument to gain takeover clearance.

Paramount, rival and ultimate victor for WBD, claimed that a Netflix deal would give it too much dominance over the streaming market in the US. Netflix countered by saying that as a video-platform YouTube should be included as a competitor in the market.

“The problem is Netflix isn’t distinctive any more, it is now just part of the firmament,” said the senior TV executive. “It is not head and shoulders above everyone else any more, and is no longer the first choice destination for discovery, and I think that is massive. Everyone else has changed and evolved, why hasn’t Netflix?”

Johnny Depp is playing Scrooge? I am not here for his big Hollywood comeback

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:51:49 GMT

‘It’s good to be back,’ says the actor in a new trailer for the forthcoming Ebenezer. Has everyone forgotten about the ghosts of his past?

It is fair to say that, professionally speaking, Johnny Depp has had a quiet few years. Since he and Amber Heard sued each other amid a whirlwind of genuinely ugly accusations in 2019, and went to trial in 2022, Depp has struggled to reclaim his position in Hollywood.

His 2020 film Minimata made less than a million dollars at the box office. Jeanne du Barry fared better in 2023, although its Cannes premiere was marked by feminist demonstrations and an open letter signed by 100 members of the French film industry, furious that the festival appeared to be offering alleged abusers institutional protection. Aside from that, he voiced a Puffin called Johnny Puff in a cartoon series called Puffins, and that’s about it.

Rather, it was. Because now Depp is back on top. Yesterday he made a surprise appearance at Comic-Con in San Diego in costume as Ebenezer Scrooge, shuffling and slurring in front of a crowd of delighted onlookers. He shouted insults (“Have you people no jobs?”) and made Trump jokes (threatening to put a tariff on some railings) and interrupted a Directors on Directing panel to wander about and mutter.

The reason for Depp’s appearance is simple. Paramount has made a film about Ebenezer Scrooge, and he is playing the lead. The trailer could not be more clear that this is to be Depp’s big comeback vehicle, either. As Scrooge hobbles about the screen, the trailer’s captions proclaim: “He brought us Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands and the Mad Hatter. This November, the master of misfits returns.” And then Depp, his face as close to the camera as it can possibly be, whispers, “It’s good to be back.”

It is hard to see how the trailer could have made the comeback any more explicit, although some people might take the trailer’s wording with a pinch of salt. It is, after all, a piece of extraordinary public relations to take a man who was found by a UK civil court to have repeatedly punched his wife in her head while screaming “I fucking hate you” and rebrand him as “the master of misfits”. It does seem like booking Bill Cosby for a film and calling him “TV’s Mr Sex”.

Still, the trailer has received almost universal approval from commenters on YouTube, whose feedback ranges from “I think many will go see this film even if it’s not good, just to see Johnny back on the screen” to “Good to see Johnny Depp back!!!”. Which is great and everything, but where were you when Minimata came out, you cowards?

And in fairness, the film does seem to offer precisely what people expect from a mainstream Johnny Depp performance. His Scrooge is an overblown caricature of a thing, all hunched and cackling, and filled with the sort of overblown reaction shots that have come to be his stock in trade. His eyes bulge. His tongue sticks out. He folds his mouth upside down like Silvio from The Sopranos. It’s like watching Jack Sparrow after a few too many years on the pies, or Willy Wonka after being hauled to a riverbank with a lawn rake after being found face-down.

What’s more, Ebenezer is being directed by Ti West, a man who knows his way around a horror movie better than almost anyone. He made MaXXXine, Pearl and House of the Devil, and there are elements of the Ebenezer trailer that hint at something much darker than its breezy homecoming trailer would suggest.

That would be a good thing, because as things stand, it would take all manner of mental gymnastics to square the cutesy double-taking character in the trailer with a man who, let’s not forget, was accused of banging his wife’s head on a countertop and then writing messages about her sexual activity on the walls in his own blood. Perhaps a horror movie would be the best way to ease him back into the mainstream. If nothing else, it would fit the public perception of him.

As comebacks go, it’s hard to fault the boldness here. The true test will come in November, when audiences will either flock to Ebenzer or stay away in droves. Still, it could be worse. At least Depp isn’t selling cheap rings on the internet like Kevin Spacey yet.

Our blueprint for Andy Burnham’s success

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:42:41 GMT

Readers advise the new prime minister and his party on how to turn Labour’s fortunes, and the country’s, around

Rafael Behr neatly summarises Andy Burnham’s strengths as a potential leader and he rightly emphasises that he needs a united party behind him (Andy Burnham is playing the long game in an age of short attention spans, 22 July).

He then accurately identifies what Burnham needs to do, but makes no reference to what the parliamentary Labour party needs to do. Leadership is interactional, and Labour MPs outside the government – particularly those (in Behr’s words) with hair triggers on the radical left and those aggrieved Starmer loyalists – have to realise that Labour is in the last-chance saloon here, and they have just as much a role as he does to ensure the success that leads to a second term.

If Burnham is to succeed, there is no place for the kind of self-indulgent social media posts made by Darren Jones on funding for removing VAT on electricity bills, which provide instant fodder for the Tories, Reform UK and the rightwing media. Of course, there will be policy disagreements, but all Labour MPs must find ways to debate these while retaining a fundamental commitment to the success of this new government, given the sceptical mood of the country, and exercising appropriate judgment in the way they express their differences, however sincerely held. Dr Roger BookerClapham, London

If Andy Burnham is looking for ways to fund the cost of living crisis (Andy Burnham urges cabinet to examine ‘all possible ways’ to tackle cost of living crisis, 21 July), why doesn’t he just do the obvious and increase the top rate of income tax which now sits at 45%? During the second world war the top rate was 99.25%; during the Wilson government of the 1960s it was 90%; and it was 83% when Margaret Thatcher became prime minister. Back then high earners mostly lived in the UK, and it was only from the 1980s that high earners such as Rod Stewart and later Phil Collins started bleating about high taxes.

The reduction of the top rate of income tax has not resulted in better compliance, as avoidance and evasion are rife, nor has it boosted enterprise. It has, however, produced a more divided and less fair society that has more millionaires and an alarming number of people struggling with the cost of living. Sadly, and I know it’s early days for Burnham, tinkering with small reductions in electricity bills and fixing bus fares won’t have the required effect.

Raising income tax for wealthier people (not just the super rich) will both ensure a fairer, more cohesive society and increase the funding available for genuinely radical change. I don’t understand why no one appears to be considering this. Steve PennyAbergavenny, Monmouthshire

Reading Monday’s Guardian, optimistic about a fresh start with a new prime minister, I suffered abrupt heart-sink on reaching the business section when I saw the headlines (Wessex Water chief pockets above-inflation pay rise despite bonus ban over sewage spills, 18 July; Pay gap widens as UK bosses get 130 times average worker’s salary, 20 July).

What can be done to stop these obscenely avaricious and selfish people from further dividing our country into a nation of haves and have-nots? It is well known that a wide disparity between the pay of rich and poor leads to discontent and unrest. Please, Andy Burnham, introduce a swingeing income tax on earned/unearned income and bonuses in excess of, for example, £1m per annum. Jane SutherlandDry Drayton, Cambridgeshire

Learning that Andy Burnham’s father is unable to understand that his son is the prime minister was one of those moments when the prospect of changing a muddled social care system came very much closer (The Guardian view on social care reform: Andy Burnham is right – this issue must be gripped, 21 July). When the Blair government found it easy to kick the findings of the Royal Commission on Long Term Care into the long grass, some of us involved in campaigning believed that if only someone with power and influence could relate to the issues at a personal level the situation might change.

As the author of the reforms legislated by the Thatcher government said at the time, “Community care is everybody’s distant relative, but nobody’s baby”. Perhaps Burnham’s elevation will mean that this “orphan” will now receive the serious cross-party attention that has eluded it for so long. Until then, those in need of care and their families will continue to be confused, anxious and disappointed by the options open to them. Les BrightExeter

Tom Clark is right that transformative governments have usually been enabled by emergencies (Andy Burnham says he will go ‘faster’ than Starmer. Why is that so hard?, 20 July). Roosevelt, wartime Britain and the pandemic all show that when leaders are honest about the scale of a threat, the public are willing to support extraordinary action.

Yet there is one question his piece leaves hanging: what if the emergency is already here? Extreme heat, flooding, crop losses and mounting pressures on health services, infrastructure and the economy are no longer future risks; they are today’s reality. Yet politically we continue to treat them as isolated policy problems, rather than symptoms of a climate and nature crisis with severe implications for the country.

This is not simply a failure of political courage. It is also a failure of public communication. Democracies can only move at the speed that public understanding allows.

If Andy Burnham wants to govern “faster and bolder”, his first task should not be announcing another initiative. It should be treating the public as adults: explaining honestly the scale and immediacy of the crisis, how it is already driving up the cost of living, and the opportunities that decisive action would bring.

Britain does not lack an emergency. What it needs is political leadership to describe it honestly – and begin building a public mandate for bold national renewal. Prof Mike Berners-LeeChair, National Emergency Briefing

It has been suggested in some quarters that the Burnham premiership will take the country back to the 1970s. Here are just a few of the things that existed then. No food banks, little homelessness, little energy poverty, council houses, rent controls, British industry making things, a funded defence force, water, energy and public transport under the public’s control, and membership of the Common Market. John GarnhamAmpthill, Bedfordshire

Migraines are so much more than just banging headaches

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:41:33 GMT

Until migraines are recognised as a multi-system condition, sufferers will continue to be dismissed, writes Sarah Khan. Plus a letter from Rab Hallett

Thank you for your article about migraines – a maligned, misunderstood condition (The truth about migraines: what causes them – and how to find relief, 19 July). But framing it around the headache understates what it is: a systemic neurological event in which head pain is only one component.

For me, until perimenopause, the head pain was minor. The disabling symptoms were profound fatigue, body aches and cognitive fog, which dominated even the “prodrome”. This is why my migraines went undiagnosed for decades, blamed on a “poor immune system” rather than a neurological disorder.

The piece also underplays how little control sufferers have. Telling patients to manage their triggers ignores those navigating puberty, or women whose reproductive years bring hormonal shifts entirely beyond their control. Many face a predictable menstrual attack plus a second at ovulation, which in severe cases can consume up to half the month. In perimenopause, hormonal triggers can be daily; the nervous system responds by lowering the threshold until attacks come ever easier. I’ve had daily migraine for over two years, prodrome and postdrome overlapping without pause.

This is also why migraine cannot be left to neurologists alone. When the driver is fundamentally hormonal, gynaecological care matters – yet very few gynaecologists understand the migraine brain, and some prescribe perimenopause treatments that actively worsen it.

With regard to treatment, gepants have been transformative, and GPs can now prescribe Rimegepant where triptans fall short. Yet access remains a postcode lottery.

Migraine is not a banging headache. Until medicine treats it as a genetic, multi-system condition, sufferers – disproportionately women – will keep getting dismissed, even though treatment is available. Sarah KhanLondon

While all the new research pathways are interesting, the most important thing is go and talk to your GP; don’t suffer in silence trying to self-manage, avoiding triggers. For me, it was only after years that a pain management consultant finally said: “Why has nobody ever prescribed you triptans?” Now I get on with life the best I can, with some emergency tablets in my pocket. Rab HallettEdinburgh

Children are the longest-lasting casualties of war

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:39:08 GMT

Responding to a new exhibition that explores how children have experienced conflict, Arabella Dorman says they live with the consequences long after the fighting has ended

Your article on the Imperial War Museum’s forthcoming exhibition Childhood in War is a timely reminder that the deepest wounds of conflict are often carried by those who never chose it (‘There was absolutely no chance of being a kid’: new exhibition explores how war shapes children’s lives, 19 July). While wars are recorded through battles, borders and political decisions, children experience them very differently: through interrupted childhoods, fractured families and the loss of what should have been ordinary days.

Over many years working in war zones, I came to understand that children are not simply among the victims of war; they are its longest-lasting casualties. Long after the fighting has moved on, they continue to live with its consequences – in their bodies, their memories and the futures they must somehow rebuild.

My series Child of War grew out of those encounters. It was never intended to document conflict itself, but rather its enduring imprint on young lives: children whose resilience was remarkable, but whose suffering should never be mistaken for acceptance or inevitability.

Art cannot change the past, but it can bear witness. If this exhibition encourages us to look beyond the headlines and recognise the human cost of conflict through the eyes of a child, it will have performed a profound service. Arabella DormanLondon

Was Keir Starmer’s leaving party the boozy birth of a new Labour force?

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:33:41 GMT

A £10,000 bar tab was drunk, there was a ‘lot of anger’, and now ex-ministers are thinking how to cooperate in future

Keir Starmer’s leaving party had been planned for some time. But in years to come it might be seen as the birth of a new Labour movement.

Dozens of ministers, aides and Starmer himself headed to the Grafton pub in Kentish Town on Monday night to drown their sorrows, hours after the former prime minister left Downing Street for the last time.

By 7pm, revellers had exhausted a £10,000 bar tab. But as a boozy late-night karaoke session started, several were learning they had lost their ministerial jobs, victims of what some believe was a purge of Starmer allies being punished for their loyalty to the former prime minister.

Now the group – at the centre of which are 11 former cabinet ministers – are considering how to cooperate in the future, whether in supporting the government of Andy Burnham or, occasionally, pointing out where it is going wrong.

“There was a lot of anger at the party,” said one person who was there. “There were some decent, competent people who seemed to be losing their jobs simply because they did not call for Keir Starmer to quit.”

One of Starmer’s biggest problems in government was that he did not have an identifiable faction of people who were willing to defend him at all costs – a symptom of both his late entry into politics and of his relative lack of ideology.

But many of those whom Burnham sacked or demoted after entering office did have one thing in common: they were close to the former prime minister and had not called for him to resign.

They included the chancellor, Rachel Reeves, who turned down the chance to be education secretary; the prime minister’s chief secretary, Darren Jones; the attorney general and longtime Starmer friend, Richard Hermer, and the housing secretary, Steve Reed.

Many had been expected to lose their jobs as Burnham made space for his own allies. But others were more of a surprise. Nick Thomas-Symonds was ousted from his position as chief negotiator with the EU, Hilary Benn lost his job as Northern Ireland secretary, and at a more junior level, Alison Levitt, who worked with Starmer at the Crown Prosecution Service, was sacked from the Ministry of Justice.

Two people who previously worked at the heart of Starmer’s office in opposition, Jenny Chapman and Chris Ward, both lost their positions.

“Obviously Andy was always going to bring his own people in,” one Starmer ally said, “but the fact that he kept in everyone who called for Keir to go and ousted everyone who didn’t feels very deliberate.”

Burnham has said his cabinet “reflects the party, the country, all backgrounds”, and has promised to take a “one-team approach” within the Labour party.

Guardian analysis shows his first cabinet has a better gender balance than any other in history, although it is more privately educated than Starmer’s and less ethnically diverse than Rishi Sunak’s.

Now Starmer’s former ministers and advisers are thinking about how they can best contribute to the Labour party from outside the government. Jones showed one possible route on Tuesday morning when he publicly pointed out the flaws in Burnham’s plan to scrap the government’s digital ID scheme to pay for a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

“Good news that VAT will be cut on electricity bills. It’s a simple way for families to save a few quid, and to mechanically help to keep inflation that little bit lower,” he posted on X.

“But the DigitalID program was unfunded. The government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget.”

That post had an immediate impact, as Downing Street found itself having to defend how the policy was costed. Burnham told cabinet ministers to take a “hard look” at their budgets in a sign that they could soon be asked to make spending cuts to pay for some of his commitments.

Despite that, some close to Starmer believe Jones was wrong to question the new prime minister in such a public way. “I’m not sure that helped,” said one. “There is a risk it just makes us look bitter.”

But those who served at the top of Starmer’s government want to keep posing difficult questions to the prime minister, whether in public or private. There is talk of a new WhatsApp group, to be set up when MPs return in September, to help coordinate their efforts.

Some MPs are likely to take up committee roles, while others, including Starmer, will sit on the backbenches and only intervene on a limited number of issues. Several have careers in other fields that they can now return to, such as Hermer, who was a practising KC before Starmer appointed him to the government.

But given that many know the government’s accounts and priorities in detail, they are in a unique position to scrutinise Burnham’s decisions or point the way for others who wish to do so.

“Yes, we know where the bodies are buried,” said one Starmer ally. “But it’s not so much that, it’s more a case of explaining why we made the decisions we did, and what the downsides are of the ones Burnham might make instead.”

Others believe they will need to keep quiet at least in the short term, given the weight of support Burnham has in the party and, increasingly, the country.

But they say the example he has set in appointing his first government could come back to haunt him. “He has chosen not to reward loyalty to the leader,” said one Starmer ally. “That is sending out a message he may come to regret.”

‘Future generations will curse us for its loss’: can nothing save Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh’s masterpiece?

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:04:36 GMT

Stratospheric costs could prevent the fire-damaged landmark from returning to its former glory. Now, unless a wealthy patron is found, the building seems destined for ‘soulless’ facade retention or ‘curated decay’

Doubly destroyed by two fires, Scotland’s finest piece of architecture, the Mackintosh building at the Glasgow School of Art (GSA), cuts a lamentable sight.

A 12-year saga of destruction, rebuilding and yet more destruction, all underscored by an unedifying seam of political and institutional wrangling, reached an apologetic conclusion of sorts, with the recent announcement that Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s exquisite art nouveau creation is unlikely to be rebuilt in its original form because of stratospheric cost.

The GSA said a full rebuild or “faithful reinstatement” of the burnt-out 1909 landmark, which, while still remaining a long-term ambition, would cost £265m, four times previous estimates and five times the GSA’s annual turnover.

The school admitted that it could not afford this comprehensive reconstruction on its own, and outlined how it was moving forward by stabilising the building’s remaining shell and removing external scaffolding. The plastic shroud will also be removed, revealing the surviving stone walls. How things progress from there is still the subject of debate. The cost of the stabilisation work, though unconfirmed, is understood to have been covered by a recent settlement with insurers following arbitration.

The fate of a building considered Scotland’s equivalent of Gaudí’s epic Sagrada Familia in Barcelona or Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris still hangs precariously in the balance. But while Notre Dame, damaged by fire in 2019, was the subject of a concerted national rebuilding that allowed it to reopen five years later, Mackintosh’s masterpiece still languishes more than a decade on, and seems no closer to being restored as a working art school.

Professional bodies including the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland and the Royal Institute of British Architects have given a cautious welcome to the current interim strategy but said that “faithful reinstatement should remain everyone’s preferred outcome”.

In a joint statement, they added: “We need leadership from the Scottish and UK governments to find the resources needed to ensure the faithful reinstatement of the Mackintosh building and to secure its future as a revitalised creative hub serving Glasgow, Scotland and the world. A building of such national importance requires a national response if future generations are not to curse us for its loss or mutilation.”

Writing in the Architects’ Journal, Labour MSP for Glasgow Paul Sweeney echoed this call. Sweeney, who has long campaigned for full restoration of the building, argued that a joint venture partnership approach to rebuilding the Mac should now be considered. “It’s about the Scottish and UK governments putting their arms around the art school and trying to support the restoration as a national project,” he said.

But in a cost of living crisis, riven with attendant political and cultural jeopardy, it’s highly doubtful whether such resources can or will be found. Time for a wealthy patron to sponsor the project of a lifetime?

Others have been more critical. “The loss of the Mackintosh building would be catastrophic,” says architect and former GSA lecturer Gordon Gibb. “Even a partial rebuild, or a soulless facade retention with highlights, would result in the loss of our heritage and in the further diminution of Glasgow. If you do not rebuild it as it was imagined, you lose all of its integrity – and you do nothing more than celebrate the incompetence of its temporary custodians that led to its demise.”

The entire sorry debacle began with a small fire breaking out at an end-of-year student show in 2014, when an aerosol canister of expanding foam placed near a hot projector caused flammable gases to ignite. It could and should have been contained, but Mackintosh’s arrangement of timber-lined voids and ducts contrived to spread the flames. Nonetheless, almost all of the building was saved, and a £35m restoration commenced. Weeks before its completion in 2018, the building was gutted by a second fire.

Cosily familiar to patrons of museum gift shops, it’s perhaps hard to envisage just how radical and unsettling Mackintosh’s art and architecture were in his day. A temperamental dandy who took his cue from movements in fin de siècle Europe – art nouveau, Japonism, symbolism – his oeuvre was a zinging riposte to the conventions of Victorian neoclassicism. “How absurd it is to see modern buildings made in imitation of Greek temples!” he fulminated in 1893. “We must clothe modern ideas in modern dress.”

Mackintosh experienced extreme reversals of fortune. In 1900, his fame was such that during a trip to Vienna, “Toshie” and his wife, artist Margaret Macdonald, were feted as Caledonian heroes by the secessionist movement and cheered through the streets in a flower-decked cart. But the first world war sundered connections with Europe and a slow decline into poverty and obscurity ensued. By 1928, Mackintosh was dead of mouth cancer at 60, induced by his penchant for drinking and smoking, a grimly bohemian end to a fitfully stellar life.

If the Mac is not to be rebuilt as it was, there are precedents for a strategy of what might be described as “curated decay”, mixing new and old parts to relate the wider story of the building. Gutted by wartime bombing, Berlin’s neoclassical Neues Museum lay in ruins for more than 40 years until an evocative scheme by David Chipperfield, abetted by conservative specialist Julian Harrap, transformed its fortunes. The city’s Reichstag building, remodelled by Norman Foster, retained graffiti scrawled by victorious Russian soldiers.

Yet the glory of the Mac is the fact that it is all of a piece, from door handles to furniture, stained glass to light fittings, all minutely considered by Mackintosh as an exemplary Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. Its double destruction has been a disaster, but, at present, its rebirth as a hugely costly phoenix from the flames feels as far away as it ever was.

In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan worries the end of politeness will destroy civilisation. I fear he’s right

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:00:20 GMT

Since I saw the movie, I have found it difficult not to see Trojan horses everywhere. We live now in a state of perpetual distrustfulness

Prior to the release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, I’m not sure many of us would have conceived of the Trojan Horse as a kind of proto-atomic bomb, the sort of norm-obliterating device from which civilisation cannot turn back. If anything, the horse has long existed in our collective imaginations as at best a credulity-stretching plot device – why did those overly trusting Trojans not think to look that particular horse in its wooden mouth? – and at worst a cutely comedic non-threat. The greatest civilisation of its age was taken down by a timber what?

But the true masterstroke of Nolan’s film is its parallels to the last one he dropped on us, Oppenheimer. Like that film, The Odyssey is about a haunted genius who, when presented with a problem, solves it with such speed and significance that he must necessarily cast aside implication. But rather than splitting the atom, Odysseus (Matt Damon), dismembers something considerably more significant – the social fabric.

The world of Nolan’s The Odyssey is one obsessed with civility and rules. Characters talk endlessly about Zeus’ law: a basic currency of interpersonal kindness, where each human being is treated as though they might contain the divine. Odysseus, upstanding man of the world that he is, will not even kill a deer without alerting it of his arrival via a twang of his bow: to sneak up on prey without warning is to turn a “fight” into a “hunt”, he tells us.

Of course, no such bow twanging accompanies the Trojan horse. Odysseus even hides its threat from his own cousin, Sinon (Elliot Page), who is impaled on its wooden side in the opening minutes of the movie. Poor hapless Sinon isn’t even aware of what he’s dying for. And when the horse breaches Troy’s walls, the resulting massacre is depicted by Nolan as exactly that: a massacre.

But, Nolan frets, the cost is greater than just bloodshed. The horse only succeeds in a world where humans are used to taking each other at their word; where a gift is a gift, and a surrender is a surrender. Turns out the Trojans weren’t comically ignorant. They were just decent. And so, in Nolan’s film, what Odysseus invents is the world’s first lie – its first impoliteness.

Such a concern might strike us oddly these days. In our world, handwringing over rudeness too often has the blush of quaint conservatism to it, and for decades now the centre-right have lectured the left on the importance of keeping the world “civil” even when the world in question is burning. Sure, polluters might be destroying all life on the planet, but there’s no need to deface a painting to protest them or block traffic for an hour or so. That’s just rude.

For that reason, the cynical could be forgiven for bristling at Nolan’s suggestion that telling a grand ole fib damned us to eternal destruction. There are surely larger fish to fry; problems more significant than a lie. Nolan even seems to understand that bigger picture himself: the sorceress Circe (Samantha Morton) tells Odysseus that men’s evil has existed a lot longer than the construction of some wretched horse. As she explains it, civility has just been a thin layer on top of a deep wellspring of rot. And in this version, Circe doesn’t turn Odysseus’ men into pigs. She reveals them for what they are. Which is pigs.

But, Nolan seems to say, at least they were once pigs who told each other the truth. And I must admit, such a framing shook me far more deeply than the bomb testing that wrenches Oppenheimer in two. Fire is fire; a nuke is a nuke. A horse that is not a horse does something perhaps less immediately destructive, but no less horrifying. It casts aside the notion that there are things we have all agreed not to do.

In the days since I saw The Odyssey, I have found it difficult not to see Trojan horses everywhere. We live now in a state of perpetual distrustfulness. The paranoiacs, it turns out, are right – there is poison in every water supply. Thanks to AI, no picture is a picture. To borrow a turn of phrase from David Foster Wallace, the content we endlessly consume – whether it be on our phones, or our TV screens – is not being made by people who love us. It’s being made by people who want something from us. Our politicians will lie to us, endlessly, for no other reason than they can. Cruelty now takes a friendly face, and our biggest polluters have carefully curated Instagram pages.

In short, I can’t remember the last time I saw a stranger as containing the divine; a horse as just a horse. And looking back from the point of view of our post-fall of Troy world, politeness no longer seems like the vaguely pathetic instruction that we mind our p’s and q’s. Instead it’s a bond, a default approach of care that says, the other is not a demon, but possibly a God in disguise. An approach that says, this person you do not know has something for you, and you should take it. Because, after all, what are the chances that they mean you harm?

Joseph Earp is a critic, painter and novelist. His latest book is Painting Portraits of Everyone I’ve Ever Dated

Feeling lost without the World Cup? Six ways to survive the weekend

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 14:36:08 GMT

What to watch on TV plus other ways to occupy your time now that the party is over

The 2026 World Cup is over, and the millions of people who enjoyed it now find themselves presented with a yawning chasm this weekend. In the UK alone, ITV and the BBC broadcast approximately 275 hours of live coverage over the duration of the tournament, and something that colossal will be hard to replace.

But fear not. Just because the football is over, we are still brimming with things similarly designed to take our minds off the screaming hellpit that is the world around us. Here’s a guide, hope it helps.

The good news is that, while the World Cup is over, the Commonwealth Games have just begun in Glasgow with a wealth of sports to watch, including swimming, netball, boxing, gymnastics and bowls. The bad news, however, is that all of this will be crammed into a single hour of joyless highlights on Channel 5 at 10.30pm, because TNT bought the rights and you need a subscription to watch it.

The same goes for the Tour de France, now that ITV’s 24 years of coverage has ended.

If it’s normal, old-fashioned, free-to-air televised sport you’re after, you’ll have a harder time getting your fill. There’s a rugby league match on BBC Two this afternoon, and some cricket tomorrow, but other than that your best hope is to put ITV4 on today and just let its trickle of low-level sport wash over you. Highlights of Man Utd v Nottingham Forest from December 1979 at 6.20am. World rally highlights at 7.20am. Racing at Ascot at 9.30am. Then Formula E. To top it off, Sean Bean in Sharpe this afternoon and Tom Cruise, who gave the opening speech at the World Cup final, is back again in Top Gun at 10.05pm.

That’s basically the same as the World Cup, isn’t it? Isn’t it?

You should really go and watch The Odyssey. Christopher Nolan’s epic film is breaking box office records left and right, with tickets in his preferred format (70mm Imax) genuinely hard to come by.

And, quite honestly, it isn’t so different from the World Cup. It is loud and long and exciting. It offers no end of topics to get mock-angry about (where were the Phaeacians? What happened to all the sex? What was Nolan thinking, infusing Judeo-Christian themes of guilt into an ancient poem whose climactic solution is an orgy of violent vengeance?).

Also, it is essentially the story of a man who, in the cold light of day, looks back at a period of intense tribalism with a sense of newfound regret, and if that isn’t the post-World Cup mood writ large, I don’t know what is.

Perhaps you have simply grown accustomed in the UK to staying on American time, and that habit is proving hard to shift. If that’s the case, then you have some options to prolong your new nocturnal hours. If you’re a Netflix subscriber, then WWE SummerSlam starts at 11pm BST on 1 August and will run for several hours. Also, the San Diego Comic-Con starts tonight, and runs on California time, providing you with the chance to stay up all night refreshing social media in the hope that you get to see a cool new trailer in real time.

Alternatively, the Delta Aquariid meteor shower is likely to peak on the night of 30 July. It isn’t guaranteed that you’ll see it from the UK, but it’s that or going to bed like a loser.

Go and drink something. Urinary tract infections are no fun, especially at this time of year. And watch an advert while you’re at it, just for the full FIFA effect.

Most of the fun of the World Cup is all the second-guessing and conjecture that goes with it. Luckily, British political life is especially ripe for this exact thing at the moment. We have (another) new prime minister, providing us with endless potential for amateur punditry. Is Angela Rayner being played out of position? Has Ed Miliband still got the legs for international diplomacy? How many disappointing performances will it take before the country begins demanding yet another change of manager?

Even better, the Clacton byelection is coming up, which is a great opportunity to get an office sweepstake going. Which of the 34 candidates will you draw? Binface? Farage? Baron Von Thunderclap? Abi Hookway from Channel 5’s Rich House Poor House? Woke Trump Carrzee? Laurence Fox? What excitement.

This is the best news of all. It was reported this week that Donald Trump wants America to host the 2038 World Cup. He would be in his fifth term as president by then, too. Joy upon joy.
