13 surprising reasons you’re always dog tired – and what to do about it

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 14:00:16 GMT

Feel lethargic even after a full night’s sleep? From not enough fibre to too much sitting, experts explain why your get up and go has got up and gone

The very air you breathe could be an issue. “Close the door, shut the window, add a partner and a heater, and by 3am a typical bedroom sits at 1,500 to 2,500 parts per million of carbon dioxide,” says Dr Jemma King, author of Sleep First: Sleep Smarter, Think Sharper, Feel Better. “Research shows that above 1,000 ppm sleep efficiency drops, deep sleep reduces and salivary cortisol rises on waking. You’re sleeping, but your nervous system is mildly activated all night.” Luckily, it’s an easy fix: open a window – even 2cm will do the job, according to King.

This supplement isn’t just for bodybuilders. What we think of as “energy” is a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP), produced by mitochondria. It stores and then delivers energy to cells. As you age, you have fewer mitochondria, so your body struggles to produce enough ATP.

Creatine can help. “When creatine is combined with phosphagen (a compound linked to energy), you get phosphocreatine, which regenerates ATP,” says Justin Roberts, professor of nutritional physiology at Anglia Ruskin University.

As well as older adults, research consistently shows benefits for regular exercisers, women, vegans and vegetarians (as creatine largely comes from meat and fish), says Roberts. Research shows supplementing can improve mental fatigue and reduce fatigue during exercise.

In terms of sleep, in three separate studies people taking 5g daily showed improved mood and cognitive function after a poor night’s sleep, slept for longer and experienced improved sleep quality. Look for micronised creatine monohydrate and take 3-5g daily to increase muscle stores of ATP over two to four weeks. You cycle creatine, so try taking it for six weeks, then come off it for two to four weeks, and repeat.

“Emerging evidence suggests that exposure to daylight improves our sleep and blood sugar control,” says Dr Brendan Gabriel, whose research at the University of Aberdeen focuses on metabolic biochemistry. It’s all down to our circadian rhythms. “We have a body clock in nearly every cell in our body,” says Gabriel. “One of the most important is the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus, which is most responsive to daylight. Getting exposure to outdoor daylight helps our body distinguish between day and night, which can improve sleep quality.”

A massive 96% of people in the UK don’t meet daily fibre recommendations of at least 30g. But a fibre-rich meal can help to slow the release of sugar into your bloodstream, giving you longer lasting, steadier energy, says Dr Emily Leeming, research fellow at King’s College London and author of Fibre Power: Transform Your Energy and Feel Amazing. She thinks we’re confused and discouraged by “a rather unfortunate PR run that fibre hasn’t been able to shake off. We think fibre is brown stodge.”

Time for a fibre rebrand, then. She suggests we all add “the BGBGs to our diets – beans, greens, berries, grains and seeds – and nuts. Make those the foundation of your meal, then add other things.”

Getting eight hours sleep but still exhausted? “We live in a world that equates our worth with productivity,” says Zahabiyah Yamasaki, author of Protect Your Energy. She believes we need to stop rushing when we don’t have to and start to “move at a slower pace, be intentional about commitments, and choose presence over productivity. That might mean closing your eyes rather than reaching for your phone, or sitting quietly looking out the window. Over time, these small shifts help make rest more accessible.” So nap, listen to a podcast, stretch, read, sit in nature, turn down a plan, cuddle your pet.

Foggy head? A lack of polyphenols could be to blame. “These antioxidants give pigment to fruits and vegetables – the deep purple of an aubergine, the redness of a strawberry,” says Leeming. We get most of ours from tea and coffee, but dark chocolate, black beans and herbs and spices are particularly concentrated sources, alongside berries.

Leeming points to research showing polyphenol supplements help with oxygen and nutrient delivery to the brain, improving reaction time and mental fatigue. But you don’t need to supplement, just eat the rainbow – or blitz it. “A small study gave people a 400ml smoothie containing blueberry, strawberry, raspberry and blackberry, or a placebo, and tracked them across a work day. The berry smoothie people maintained accuracy and response times throughout the day.”

Sworn off smoothies or juice over sugar concerns? “Your blood sugar going up is a very normal response,” says Leeming. “It’s when it stays elevated out of range for a long time that it’s problematic – 150ml of fruit juice is a good source of polyphenols and is one of your five a day.” And include berries. “Blending fruit with seeds gives less of a blood sugar response than something like a banana.”

While you sleep, your brain is putting in a shift. Dr Jemma King provides an analogy: “Imagine all the events that happen during the day get documented and put into a manila folder that’s stacked on the desk of your personal librarian, who works through the night, deciding what to keep and what to discard. Usually this happens smoothly, but sometimes folders need the boss to decide, and you’ll be woken at 3am with a burning thought that makes you feel stressed. The stress hormone cortisol has a half-life of at least 30 minutes, so if you engage with that thought, you have at least until 3.30am before your stress levels go back to a ‘sleep-permissive’ level.”

Help your midnight librarian by spending a few minutes in the early evening creating a list of what you’ll address tomorrow. “Be sure to add times,” says King. “For example: call Sammy’s teachers at 10.30am; call my tax accountant at 11.15am.”

Ideally you need to clear your plate by 7.30pm, especially on steak night. “Protein – particularly big chunks of meat – takes four to six hours to leave the stomach,” says King. “Fat slows it further, while digestion raises core body temperature and draws blood toward the gut, pushing against the nocturnal cooling trend needed for deep sleep.” This is why eating within three hours of bedtime decreases the quality of your sleep. “Your body doesn’t like digesting and repairing at the same time, and will opt to get rid of meat over replenishing maintenance.” Eat heavier protein and fat at lunchtime, and build evening meals around veggies, lighter protein such as fish, chicken or tofu, and plant-based carbohydrates.

“There is two-way communication between your gut and your brain via the vagus nerve, and 80-90% of that communication goes in the direction of gut to brain,” says Leeming. “If things are sluggish, that can make you feel lethargic because your gut is communicating back to your brain that things are not optimal.” According to one study, there’s an incredibly simple fix: eat two kiwis a day (skins optional – the research was done without). “There are different types of fibre, and the particular type found in kiwis helps to draw water in to soften the stool and move it through.”

Protein is definitely having a moment – the UK market for it is expected to be worth £643m by 2031. But sacrificing carbs to make way for more protein could be detrimental. As sports dietitian and personal trainer Kerri Major says: “If this puts carb intake too low for someone’s activity levels, it can impact energy.” As a general rule, for a steady energy releasing meal, half your plate should be made up of colourful veggies, a quarter carbs and a quarter protein, alongside some healthy fats.

There’s a reason you sleep soundly in those fresh hotel bedsheets. “Mite droppings, fragranced laundry powder and synthetic fibres can all trigger low-grade inflammatory responses, producing nocturnal congestion, itching and microarousals you don’t consciously remember,” says King. “People with house dust mite allergies are far likelier to report insomnia.” Wash your bedding weekly using fragrance-free detergent, put dust mite covers on your mattress and pillows, and air your bed for 10 minutes in the morning.

Our ancestors spent their days hunting and gathering, rarely sitting, so from an evolutionary perspective, “long hours of being sedentary sends a message that something is wrong,” says King. “One theory suggests that in order to conserve energy to fight potential sickness and to promote sleeping to heal, our brains will make us feel sleepy, despite not actually being ill. It will also make us withdraw and isolate so we don’t infect the other tribe members.” Every 30 minutes, stand and move for two minutes. “A 10-minute walk after lunch lowers postprandial glucose and supports afternoon energy.”

Has your GP ruled out iron or B12 deficiency, or thyroid problems, asks Dr Linia Patel, dietitian and author of Food for Menopause? Iron deficiency, she says, produces “a heavy, physical exhaustion and breathlessness on exertion, heart palpitations, pale skin and that frustrating inability to get through the day despite adequate sleep. It can also trigger restless legs, disrupting sleep further.”

B12 deficiency fatigue “feels more neurological, so brain fog, poor concentration, low mood, tingling in the hands or feet, and a deep, bone-level weariness.” Thyroid problems, whether under or overactive, cause tiredness. “An underactive thyroid brings sluggishness, weight gain and feeling cold; an overactive one can cause anxious, wired exhaustion.” Request a blood test from your GP.

Wedding gift registries are great – but divorce registries would be a lifesaver

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 14:00:16 GMT

Marriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?

It’s peak wedding season, and my own divorce is waiting on a judge’s signature. People are being congratulated with Dutch ovens and serving bowls for dinner parties they may not ever host.

Marriage comes with an etiquette system for asking people to help build a home. The registry says the embarrassing part for you. Divorce deserves the same grace.

Meanwhile, I was standing alone in my new-to-me condo kitchen, rereading a text I had drafted to my mother, trying to make quartz countertops sound like a normal thing to need.

“Would you and Fred consider making this my birthday, Christmas, divorce and condo-warming gift?” I wrote, referring to the countertops and single-basin sink I had been fixating on. I attached a screenshot of Calacatta almond quartz, as if the visual aid might make the request seem less unhinged.

The price point is why I piled on the occasions. But I am a 44-year-old man with a mortgage and two dogs, so “birthday and Christmas” was not really the headline. Divorce was.

My mother’s response was not yes.

“Your stepdad and I are in the ER. I can’t think about this right now.”

Fair. Terrible timing, but the shame had been there before she even replied.

It’s hard now to imagine a wedding without a registry, but that etiquette had to start somewhere. Marshall Field’s, the Chicago department store whose State Street flagship is now a Macy’s, is often credited with introducing the modern bridal registry in 1924, when the list helped couples steer family and friends toward china, silver and crystal patterns. A century later, couples don’t even have to pretend they want china. Home funds are now common enough that The Knot has said the share of couples including them in registries has increased 55% since 2018.

A few years ago, when my now ex-husband and I got married, his parents paid to finish turfing the backyard of our house so we could have the wedding there. My parents covered the tents, tables, chairs and sound system. These were not small gifts. But they turned a backyard into a wedding, so nobody had to defend the cost.

For the registry itself, we mostly wanted cash. We were new homeowners in Los Angeles with nothing left for a honeymoon, so we used a platform called Hitchd to let guests click a link and donate to our new life. It helped pay for Hawaii and the house. I was a newlywed, so the ask came pre-forgiven.

Then the marriage ended, and the household went with it.

You can’t roll up half a backyard and bring it to a condo. The things that once meant “our future” became community property: the patio furniture, the dog bowls, the good knives, the drawer organizer that only made sense in that kitchen. Things to divide, keep, sell or leave behind.

Someone should build the divorce version of Hitchd. Call it Ditchd.

Actually, people already have. The Associated Press reported that Fresh Starts Registry, a divorce-registry service, had 50,000 to 70,000 monthly visitors, part of a broader shift toward talking more openly about divorce. So the need is not hypothetical. What still feels missing is the etiquette – a graceful way to say: we did not make it, but I’m accepting contributions toward a vacuum.

A divorce registry sounds tacky because gifts are supposed to be fun, and replacing the half of a home that didn’t come with you is mostly just sad. I took the Instant Pot; the air fryer stayed. Asking for another one felt like showing everyone exactly how we split the kitchen. I did most of the cooking, and I didn’t realize how much I loved our beautiful countertops until they weren’t mine any more. So yes. Countertops made the list too.

Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats. First come the lawyers, movers, closing costs and a new internet account. Then come the dumber purchases: trash bags, forks, a shower curtain, a couch the puppy has not peed on yet. None of it feels giftable. All of it has to be bought anyway.

I wasn’t destitute. That almost made the asking harder. I landed in the annoying middle: technically OK, but still buying my life back one receipt at a time.

By the time I drafted that text to my mother, I had already spent my share of the house making the new condo feel like mine. The beige living room carpet became blonde oak flooring because the new puppy I “won” in the divorce still wasn’t potty trained. A handyperson painted the dated dark cabinets soft sage; I switched the hardware to matte black myself. I put bougainvillea and olive trees on the balcony, because maybe the dogs wouldn’t notice they had lost their backyard. At the old house, bougainvillea had covered the pergola in papery magenta blooms. Here, I had one in a pot.

But in LA, the money runs out quickly.

I left the bedroom carpet and dated bathrooms alone. After the floors and cabinets, the old counters dragged the whole open-concept room back into “this was what I could afford”. Replacing them would mean I could stop balancing a cutting board over a burner. At the sink, I wouldn’t have to stretch on to my tiptoes – and I am tall – just to see my dogs asleep on and beside the couch.

This was the case I made. My mother used to be horrified by how much my husband and I spent on Uber Eats. She gave us gift cards for Christmas that I joked would barely cover a dinner and a half. Now I was cooking almost every meal at home. The kitchen was where I could save money, feed myself and two expensive dogs on one income, and make the condo work as a home.

The ER text made the timing comically indefensible. But the shame wasn’t really about timing. Marriage gets a table at Crate & Barrel. Divorce gets a Target cart full of things you already owned in another life.

Maybe I’ll get the counters, maybe I won’t. For now, the quote sits there like one more line in a ledger that already has a mediator, a new floor and moving costs on it – one more number I keep staring at like it might solve something.

I didn’t want a party for the divorce. I wanted permission to ask for help with the life I now had to build.

Still, I can see the kitchen as it could be. The new sink. The cleared counter. Dinner at home. The dogs asleep in view. The bougainvillea on the balcony, doing the best it can.

Nick Dothée is a Los Angeles-based writer whose work has appeared in the Atlantic; he is working on a memoir about the last-chance Hollywood recovery house where he got sober

‘It’s generations of decline’: can Andy Burnham really end rough sleeping?

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 13:31:38 GMT

Outreach workers on the frontline of England’s homelessness crisis react to PM’s flagship policy pledge

UK politics live – latest updates

It is close to midnight as two outreach workers from Spear, a homelessness charity in south London, shine their torches around bushes on the edge of a park in Twickenham.

Suddenly they alight on an array of sleeping bags, airbeds, toilet rolls and plastic bags stuffed with belongings – a rough sleeping encampment that has popped up in the last two days.

“We are seeing numbers going up which is really not what we want,” said Peter Bancroft, the operations manager at the charity. “And it is everyone from individuals with complex mental health and substance use issues, to people who have either had a relationship breakdown or lost their job and fallen behind with their rental payments.”

In a bold first pledge in his first speech as prime minister, Andy Burnham promised to eradicate rough sleeping in England, allocating an extra £340m of funding.

The move was welcomed by homelessness charities, but with some scepticism: Boris Johnson said he would end rough sleeping when he was prime minister, and Keir Starmer vowed to halve long-term rough sleeping during his time in office.

Yet rough sleeping numbers have risen to 4,793, the highest on record.

On their shift, Spear outreach workers are following up nine referrals for new rough sleepers who have been spotted throughout Wandsworth and Richmond in the past 48 hours, as well as checking on the people they already know and speaking to others they spot on the way.

Their journey takes them into graveyards, parks, front gardens, shop doorways and car parks, where people have been spotted sleeping in tents, in cars and on the ground. Some people are happy to chat to the workers – they accept water, the offer of a mobile phone and a housing assessment – but others turn down all offers of help.

Two people with drug addiction issues sleeping in a haphazard tent in the corner of a graveyard had emergency council accommodation until two weeks ago, but they didn’t use it and it was revoked.

Bancroft said: “I would love to be able to say homelessness services can deal with this, but I’ve been playing the game a long time now and I know the best results have been in partnership with other services.

“You’ve got to get drug and alcohol services, mental health services, social services, all onboard, everybody working collaboratively to wrap around the person or it just falls apart. Ultimately, my dream is to be out of a job because that would mean we’ve solved it, but it’s not easy.”

The details on Burnham’s rough sleeping plans are still unclear but it is likely he will build on the success of his A Bed Every Night scheme in Manchester, which departed from the norm by allowing all rough sleepers to access support – even those without local connections or recourse to public funds.

It also provided individuals with case workers to deal with multiple issues, not just housing, and it ran alongside a Housing First pilot scheme targeted at the most complex rough sleeping cases, which guided more than 300 people into long-term tenancies.

There is a growing consensus that funnelling lots of vulnerable rough sleepers, many with complex needs, illnesses and addictions, into communal living spaces such as hostels and houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) often pushes people back into homelessness.

Social housing is still being built at a painfully slow rate in England – Burnham has pledged the “biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”, but his housing minister, Angela Rayner, has since acknowledged the country is still very far off this building pace.

Francesca Albanese, the executive director of policy and social change at Crisis, said: “For a long time in England we’ve just been maintaining the status quo, so putting lots of money into hostels, emergency and temporary accommodation – managing homelessness not ending it.

“What we need is to get people off the streets into permanent homes, not into temporary accommodation. Housing First is the most evidence-led intervention we know that works to end rough sleeping so we need to see that rolled out nationally. We know about Andy’s track record and there’s real optimism this can be done.”

Ray, 53, spent four years drifting between sofa surfing, street homelessness and temporary accommodation that was “barely nicer than a prison cell” in Liverpool after experiencing sudden sight loss. It was only when he was given support from Crisis and finally offered a social home that he was able to turn his life around.

“The biggest thing for me is the government should be opening front doors again for people to come into and not putting all the pressure on charities,” he said. “I think Andy Burnham brings positivity to this and a different outlook. Housing is a right and shouldn’t be a fight. But this is not about one individual, it’s about a country that’s been in decline for generations.”

As well as the wider cost of living crisis, there are a range of policies thought to be driving up rough sleeping. Local housing allowance rates have been frozen which has increased the gap between what benefits cover and what landlords are charging, pushing more people into rent arrears.

Charities also said an increasing number of people on the streets are people who have left prison, or asylum seekers who have been granted refugee status and moved out of Home Office accommodation.

Any attempt to eradicate rough sleeping must deal with all these issues, experts said, not forgetting that a lot of rough sleepers – especially women – are not represented in the national statistics.

Lucy Campbell of the Single Homeless Project said: “If Andy Burnham is serious about ending rough sleeping, he needs to be the first political leader who’s not going to shy away from saying, actually, the figures are much higher than we think they are.

“And we cannot expect generic homelessness initiatives to work the same for men as they do for women and the LGBTQ community.”

Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G film

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 13:15:29 GMT

Sacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice-of-yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?

The Wimbledon lawn tennis championships are not generally a hotbed of crime. Yet this year, unprecedented infringements ocurred. Eleven players were fined a total of £34,000 for “audible obscenities” and “racquet abuse”. Meanwhile, a spectator at the men’s singles final called a heckler a “bumbaclat” before inviting them to fight, badgered Prince William to repay a drugs debt of £1,400 allegedly owed to him by Prince Harry from his days at Eton, and attempted to sell illegal substances to those seated near him – and beyond. “If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed,” he posted on Instagram, touting for business, “I iz here wif de hookup.”

The culprit was Ali G, real name Alistair Leslie Graham, AKA the malapropism-dropping home counties wide boy played by Sacha Baron Cohen, kitted out for the occasion in trademark skullcap and gold chain, plus custom Wimbledon jacket, traditional crossed rackets replaced with cannabis leaves. Security released him without penalty, but the reprimand was captured on scores of smartphones – including one held by Cohen himself.

Such footage is likely to find its way into a movie that will be released worldwide on 23 October and whose existence was only revealed four days before the Wimbledon incident. This week, a title was announced – Ali G: Who Iz I? – as well as the fact the film is to be the directorial debut of its star: a new development in the career of one of the UK’s most audacious, ambitious – and powerful – comedy actors, apparently taking greater agency over his projects as his own political engagement intensifies. (The appalled reaction to his recent Netflix comedy Ladies First, which he neither wrote nor directed, suggests this is a sage move.)

It also makes sense logistically: Ali G is a character who would energetically embrace selfie-mode shooting, which presumably streamlines a film crew considerably. Meanwhile the absence of a US theatrical release for the first Ali G film, 2002’s Indahouse, means targets in America would be easier to hoodwink.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Cohen first rose to fame as the tracksuit-wearing naïf and committed cultural appropriator in 1998, when Ali G was introduced as the “voice of the yoof” on Channel 4’s The 11 O’Clock Show. His own show followed in the early 2000s, constructed around interviews with unsuspecting subjects including Buzz Aldrin (whom he called Buzz Lightyear and asked if he was “ever jealous of Louis Armstrong”), Naomi Wolf (whom he complimented by telling her she’s attractive enough to be a sex worker) and Tony Benn. The late MP was outraged by the character’s dismissal of striking workers in 1984 as lazy skivers; Cohen later told Benn he was the only interviewee who had “dealt seriously with his loud, sexist, materialist image of youth”. (Benn’s letter of reply ended with the words: “You’re my main man.”)

Although Cohen declared both Ali G and Borat – his Kazakh TV presenter and the star of a 2006 film that was a commercial and critical hit – retired in 2007, both have since returned. Borat was resurrected in 2020, for Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, intended by Baron Cohen as an intervention in the impending US presidential election. As with his 2018 series Who is America?, it secured a number of high-profile and highly-embarrassing scalps – most notably Rudy Giuliani, who was caught with his hand down his trousers in a hotel room with an actor pretending to be Borat’s 15-year-old daughter.

Before his recent reappearance, Ali G was last seen presenting an award at the 2016 Oscars: a surprise even to the show’s producers, who understood Cohen would appear as himself. The ruse involved the star feigning food poisoning then locking himself and then-wife Isla Fisher in a disabled loo for 40 minutes to change into his costume.

While Ali G Indahouse was a scripted comedy concerning the character’s inadvertent role in the downfall of the government, indications are that its sequel will be closer to the more politically intentional Borat followup, returning Ali G to his origins as an interviewer whose dubious views prompt his subjects to reveal their own.

The film was shot in secret – as was 2009’s Brüno, in which Baron Cohen skewered the fashion industry – but some of the leaked locations in the UK and US give early clues as to whom Cohen may have had in his crosshairs.

Last summer, there were sightings of the character in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire - home to the likes of David Cameron, Rebekah Brooks, Ellen DeGeneres and Jeremy Clarkson. The town was also, during the dates Ali G was spotted, playing host to US vice president JD Vance and his family, there to enjoy a Cotswolds holiday.

Vance travelled with a considerable security detail, so it remains uncertain how close Cohen would have been able to get, had he been in pursuit. The Sun ran a photograph of the character sporting a Rastafarian beret while filming at a nearby wildlife park in Burford. A source told the paper: “He was with a whole film crew and was in full character. He seemed very comfortable in the role. I was amazed, I thought to myself, ‘that’s Ali G’.”

A crew member on the film to whom the Guardian spoke said an NDA prevented them from comment, but added: “I CAN tell you that it’s gonna be big. And packed full of laughs.”

Representatives for Kellie Bright, Charles Dance and Martin Freeman, all of who had roles in the original film, did not respond to enquiries, but the actor Adam Deacon confirmed he was not returning, “even though I would have loved to be a part of it”. He added that he could also do a “perfect” Borat accent so would be happy to be kept in mind for further films featuring that character too. “I’m a massive fan of what Sacha creates and I hope the new movie is a success.”

In the first film, Deacon played a member of the East Staines Massiv, the rivals of Ali G’s less-than-intimidating gang from the other end of town. The Surrey commuter town was sceptical about the fame bestowed on it by the Ali G connection, and in 2010, a group spearheaded by the Spelthorne business forum lobbied the borough council to change the town’s name to Staines-upon-Thames in an attempt to add distance. The area, said Alex Tribick, chair of the forum at the time, “is really rather nice and it has some fantastic natural beauty around it”.

He added: “Staines has had some adverse press further to that with it being portrayed as an urban wasteland off the end of the M25. The purpose of the exercise is to improve the image of Staines, rebrand it, and denote its greatest natural resource.”

The then MP for Spelthorne, Kwasi Kwarteng, supported the move – which was duly voted through by the local council in 2011 – saying “if anyone knows anything about Staines, then one would know that Ali G is a million miles from it. It’s a very charming place actually.”

Yet in his Thursday video announcing the title and release date, Ali G announces himself as “representing the westside of Staines-upon-Thames” – suggesting the area is unlikely to shake off the association any time soon.

Happily, the sitting Spelthorne MP, Lincoln Jopp, said he welcomed news of the return of the town’s prodigal son. “I can’t believe Ali G is coming back!” he said. “I loved Ali G Indahouse; it’s hilarious. Sacha Baron Cohen is a genius.”

Jopp, who specified to the Guardian that his constituency includes the “West Staines Massiv”, added that the town was “a great place. We can take a bit of mickey-taking, trust me. Booyakasha!”

Posts on local Facebook forums suggest resurgent grassroots support for the character putting the town on the map. “Oh happy days, loved the film,” wrote Blossom Welch, while longtime Staines resident Joanna Barlow added: “Loved Ali G not ashamed saw the show being filmed thought it was hilarious.”

However one user, Bettafisheye, demurred, venturing that Ali G is “like a bad smell that never leaves. I just say I’m from Laleham now. If u say Staines it’s like being around a constipated dog talking through there arse.”

Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visit

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 13:00:48 GMT

Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the rightwing US influencer Laura Loomer, amid signs the White House’s traditional hostility towards Ukraine is beginning to crumble.

In an interview with Loomer, the Ukraine president said he will probably attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham and hold talks with Trump, which will take place as the latest version of the Russian sanctions bill makes its way through Congress.

Loomer interviewed Zelenskyy in the garden of the presidential palace in Kyiv – a remarkable move for the online provocateur who has previously minimised Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and amplified Kremlin propaganda to her nearly 2 million followers on social media.

This week, however, she performed a stunning about-turn. “Just experienced my first air raid in Ukraine. Sirens blaring. This is every day for every Ukrainian,” Loomer wrote on X. “I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. We need to have moral clarity.”

Loomer posted a photo of her one-on-one meeting with Zelenskyy as well as a clip from her interview with him in which she asks about his infamous confrontation last year with Trump and the US vice-president, JD Vance, in the Oval Office. No questions were off limits, she said.

In the clip, Zelenskyy said his relationship with Trump had significantly improved and describes their brief conversation in the Vatican in April 2025 as a “historic moment”.

“We changed the relations during 15, 20 minutes,” Zelenskyy added.

Writing on Truth Social, Trump praised Loomer’s interview, calling it “Very good!!!!”. The White House later confirmed that the two leaders were scheduled to meet on Tuesday, while commentators in Kyiv said Trump’s message confirmed his administration’s once negative view of Kyiv was changing at a time when Ukrainian long-range drones are pummelling Russia.

Russia has continued to strike Ukraine, with a daytime ballistic missile attack on Friday killing ten people in the Kyiv region and injuring nearly 100 more. Another five people died when an air bomb hit the eastern city of Sloviansk.

Expressing support for US sanctions on Russia, Loomer said the Kremlin was a close ally of the Iranian regime. “Russia is funding Iran and providing them with explosives to murder US soldiers as Iran has called for President Trump’s assassination,” she wrote, arguing: “The United States needs to break Russia’s economy until they submit to peace.”

Loomer’s comments are a reversal for a woman who has spent years criticising US support for Ukraine’s defence, declaring it “a country full of Nazi apologists” – a claim used by Russia to justify its full-scale 2022 invasion – and “led by a Jihadi apologist”.

Her scepticism towards Kyiv has been shared by other major conservative influencers, including Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host. The issue became a big point of contention between more traditional Republicans, such as Mike Pence, a former vice-president, and Trump’s Maga base.

Anton Gerashchenko, a popular blogger and former Ukrainian government adviser, described Loomer’s interview with Zelenskyy as “important and necessary”. “It records a public break with Russian narratives and propaganda by part of the Maga movement. We are seeing a shift in rhetoric regarding Russian aggression,” he said.

“It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are,” Zelenskyy’s office added this week. “It takes courage to come to Ukraine and not be deterred by Russian propaganda or air raid sirens. Thank you, Laura.”

Loomer also visited the Dormition Cathedral of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of the country’s most significant religious landmarks, which came under Russian drone attack in June.

In a video recorded from inside the church, she accused Vladimir Putin of hypocrisy by portraying Russia as a pro-Christian nation – a perspective many US evangelicals appear to share. “I just don’t think that you should be allowed to say that you’re protecting Christianity if you’re trying to drone strike Jesus Christ,” Loomer remarked.

Loomer also met Ukraine’s chief rabbi, Moshe Reuven Azman, and toured a branch of McDonald’s hit repeatedly by Russian missiles. Loomer ordered a cheeseburger and sat demonstratively on an outside table in front of a wrecked building, in Kyiv’s much-bombed Lukianivka district.

On Friday, the chief rabbi wrote: “I had the honour of welcoming @LauraLoomer – whose views have a significant influence on the U. S. audience and who is well known for her close ties to President Donald Trump – to the Central Synagogue of Ukraine.

“The conversation was candid. I told her the truth about this terrible war – about the daily Russian shelling, the children and civilians killed, the destroyed cities and villages, and the pain that Ukrainian families endure every day.”

When is an apology not an apology? When it comes from an AI boss with an out-of-control chatbot

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 12:32:58 GMT

An incident in which an autonomous OpenAI agent hacked a startup either confirms that the end is nigh – or that the product is just amazingly sophisticated

Throughout history, many things have been seen by terrified populaces as a harbinger of doom. A comet. A crow on the battlefield. A solar eclipse. A mutant livestock birth. Yet times move on. In the modern era, the leading harbinger of doom is literally any picture of the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, attached to a news story. You know it’s not going to be good, right? You know that by the time you’ve read it, you’ll be begging to go back to the time when the worst thing that could happen to us at the hands of the techlords was just some democracy-subversion, or childhood destruction, usually followed by Mark Zuckerberg putting on a suit and claiming: “We will learn from this.”

Anyway: a lot of pictures of Sam Altman in the news of late. Most recently, this week, one darkened the skies alongside the tale of how an OpenAI autonomous agent went rogue during a supposedly sandboxed/guardrailed test, and hacked a major startup that functions as a repository of coding information. (I’m slightly obsessed with the fact that the startup in question is called Hugging Face, adding weight to my suspicion that some vast, tweely benign emoji is the last face humanity will see before it dies.)

Needless to say, an affectless OpenAI statement broke the news. “We are sharing preliminary findings at this stage to help defenders understand what happened and to help calibrate on what models are now capable of,” this droned calmly, trundling on toward its inevitable “learnings”. “We’re improving and adding stronger protections around future training and evaluations.” It’s such a particular tone, isn’t it, dressed in the psychopathically desiccated language of management speak. Like having to listen to a homicidal sex criminal talk about killing people by “close of play”, and then “circling back” to victims to remove a trophy.

Then again, for a company that likes to present itself as the planet’s leading agent of revolutionary prosperity when things go right, OpenAI lapses tellingly into the passive when things go wrong. Bad things seem to happen to it, not because of it, at which point it takes on the role of tirelessly unflappable investigator, like one of those firemen who moonlights as a serial arsonist.

Amazingly, it was possible to detect even a note of self-congratulation in OpenAI’s take on the whole situation. “We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber-incident,” the company’s statement remarked, “involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities.” I don’t know what you’d call this general vibe for Earthlings. Death by humblebrag? I increasingly feel we’ll find out the answer to the question “What’s the worst that can happen?” in a blog post from OpenAI entitled “OpenAI first to discover the worst that can happen”. Already, a significant section of AI watchers are convinced that the only reason OpenAI would tell the world about this incident is as a marketing tool, or even a come-and-get-me plea for regulation that will in effect protect them and burn the bridge behind them for smaller competitors.

After all, these are testing times for the firm. This is a month in which Open AI was discovered to be exploiting a legal loophole to sell its advanced AI models to Chinese tech firms blacklisted by the Pentagon. S&P Global Ratings cited OpenAI as a “key credit risk” in the course of downgrading US tech giant Oracle to BBB-, which is one notch above junk status. And it seems to be on track to miss its five-year ad revenue projection by 90 – NINETY – per cent. Which, without getting too financially technical, feels like a lot of per cent. And it’s not great news on the hardware front, either, with Apple suing it, alleging that its consumer hardware plans are based on stolen intellectual property. Meanwhile China’s much cheaper provider, DeepSeek, is believed to be preparing for an IPO, maybe even filing this year.

Back to the old worst-that-can-happen question again, though, with a reminder that the Pentagon dramatically binned off and threatened to destroy another AI firm, Anthropic, earlier this year after it resisted loosening its ethical guidelines that prevented use of its technology for, among other things, autonomous lethal weapons. Needless to say, a certain more relaxed company was only too glad to step into the breach, with OpenAI initially claiming its deal had the same guardrails as Anthropic’s, before it emerged – inevitably – that it didn’t.

No doubt no one too invested wishes to extrapolate too much from the Hugging Face incident. Yet the fact is that AI safety researchers have already spent literally years warning of three particularly dangerous scenarios: deception (when the model decides against solving tasks honestly in favour of achieving the goal via any means necessary); reward hacking (when the model finds a way to maximise its score without actually doing the work it was told to do); and escaping oversight (let’s just say in this case that no one at OpenAI seems to have realised what was happening for an entire weekend). All of these were part of the latest incident.

In terms of what happens next, something tells you that we will not be experiencing a downturn in photos of Sam Altman attached to news reports. The co-founder of Hugging Face said it should serve as a “wake-up call” to the industry. Maybe! As I think I’ve mentioned before, at university I had a friend who pressed snooze on his alarm clock every 10 minutes for eight-and-a-half hours, which feels a lot like the way this particular industry experiences its wake-up calls. Definitely getting up when the next one goes, seriously, I promise …

Most people arrested during Henry Nowak protests had been reported for domestic abuse

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 12:00:13 GMT

Exclusive: Hampshire police data reveals 22 of 37 detained had been accused or convicted of intimate partner violence

Most people arrested during violent protests after the sentencing of Henry Nowak’s murderer had previously been reported to the police for domestic abuse, the Guardian can disclose.

Data released by Hampshire police under freedom of information laws shows that 22 of 37 people (59%) detained in Southampton after Vickrum Digwa was jailed for life have been reported for crimes associated with intimate partner violence.

Protests took place on 2 June after police bodycam footage was released showing Nowak, 18, handcuffed as he lay dying after being stabbed by Digwa, who had falsely accused him of racism. Nowak repeatedly said he had been stabbed.

Digwa stabbed Nowak with a large blade he claimed to carry as part of his Sikh faith, before falsely telling police he had been the victim of a racist attack, leading officers to initially arrest the white teenager rather than his killer.

The footage led to claims from Nigel Farage and others that it was evidence of “two-tier policing” and “anti-white prejudice” within police forces.

Demonstrators initially gathered outside a city centre police station, with several hundred people then attempting to march towards the murder location and the street where Digwa’s family lived. During prolonged violent disorder, 12 police officers were injured, and nearby properties and vehicles were damaged.

Harry Varney, 34, claimed he attended the public gathering to pay his respects to Nowak, but was later filmed swearing at police and punching their riot shields. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment.

In 2023, he pleaded guilty to assault by beating after pinning his partner against a bedroom wall, bruising her neck. He claimed she deserved to be beaten by a previous abusive ex-partner and continued to threaten her after this attack.

She said in a written statement read out in court: “I suffer with flashbacks, anxiety attacks and nightmares. I also now struggle with my social life trusting people. I can’t be left alone with a man without feeling scared.”

Dillon Crawford, 29, was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment after throwing a brown bin and a metal chair “with some force” at police officers during the disturbances. He has 19 previous convictions, including for domestic abuse offences. During one incident, he broke a partner’s front teeth, punching her unconscious, and, after she woke up, told her he had put bleach in her hair.

Andrew Summerhayes, 38, was seen throwing a wheelie bin at police during the disorder. He was sentenced to three years and two months for violent disorder and possession of an offensive weapon.

Hampshire police confirmed that 33 people had now been charged for their involvement in the public disorder. The force has referred itself to the police watchdog, with two officers who attended the scene being investigated for potential gross misconduct by the Independent Office for Police Conduct. The investigation is considering potential failures to identify that Nowak needed urgent medical help and the decision to arrest and handcuff him before providing first aid.

The Guardian previously revealed that two out of every five arrested for participating in riots in 2024 had been the subject of a domestic abuse report before their involvement, with one in five subsequently being reported for domestic abuse.

Farah Nazeer, the chief executive of Women’s Aid, said: “Over the last two years, we have seen recurrent anti-migrant protests that have erupted into violence, with many of those arrested also carrying convictions for domestic abuse or other crimes against women and girls. It is not surprising that someone who is violent in public may also be violent at home, as there is a proven correlation between the two.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Violence against women and girls is a national emergency. We will continue to deploy the full power of the state to bring perpetrators to justice and prevent harm before it occurs.

“Our violence against women and girls strategy sets out how we will pursue and manage domestic abuse perpetrators, including through the rollout of new domestic abuse protection orders.”

‘You can’t paper over the cracks of history. It will haunt you’: Gugu Mbatha-Raw on her race-horror thriller

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 12:00:12 GMT

She paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things up

Gugu Mbatha-Raw seems blissfully immune to the heat. London is pushing 40C on one of those heatwave mornings when everyone is wearing the weather: damp collars, flushed faces, hair slicked to foreheads. Arriving at the cafe of the central London hotel where we meet, however, the star looks as if she’s stepped in from an altogether different climate. Dressed in a pristine white linen two-piece, makeup free, hair scraped back, she carries herself with a composure that makes everyone else’s perspiration seem faintly melodramatic.

She is, in every sense of the word, cool. This impression is only reinforced as we settle in for some small talk and she mentions that she’s been to the hotel once before.

“I stayed here during the premiere of Belle – gosh, almost 15 years ago now,” she says. Then, almost as an afterthought: “And Prince performed at the afterparty.” She laughs at the look on my face. “It was incredible,” she says. “Just completely surreal.” It’s the sort of global cut-through all British actors dream of, and an anecdote that perhaps feels slightly out of place in the orbit of Mbatha-Raw’s career. Since Belle – Amma Asante’s luminous 2013 period drama about Dido Elizabeth Belle, the real-life mixed-race daughter of an enslaved African woman raised in the English aristocracy – Mbatha-Raw has become one of Britain’s most fascinating actors.

From playing the lead in Charlie Brooker’s acclaimed queer Black Mirror episode San Junipero and starring in Jennifer Aniston and Reese Witherspoon’s workplace #MeToo drama The Morning Show to leading Apple TV’s identity-bending psychological thriller Surface in which she plays a woman recovering after a suicide attempt, the 43-year-old has consistently chosen projects that are intellectually and politically ambitious – roles one might summarise as having “something to say”.

“I don’t want to do the same thing all of the time,” Mbatha-Raw tells me. “It’s fun for me to go from a period drama to a romantic drama to a comedy – it keeps me stimulated.”

That instinct is precisely what drew her to Possession, Sky’s new supernatural thriller. Mbatha-Raw plays Claudia, a Bristol lawyer dispatched to Jamaica after a white plantation owner’s wealthy descendant dies suddenly, leaving his fortune not to his family but to a Jamaican man nobody can seem to track down. Claudia is assigned the case partly because, as one colleague bluntly puts it, having a Black, half-Jamaican lawyer would be “better optics”. But the legal work slowly gives way to something far more unsettling: the ghosts of Britain’s colonial legacy – both literal and metaphorical – intrude upon the present.

“I was fascinated by Claudia because she’s caught between her professional obligations and her own personal history,” says Mbatha-Raw. “[She goes] from this relatively detached, brittle, ambitious career woman who was quite numb to her heritage and disconnected from her Jamaican background to becoming more grounded and rooted.”

The story slips between modern Jamaica and the brutal realities of plantation slavery. But the enslaved do not remain confined to history: the enigmatic Cudjoe East, the man at the centre of the inheritance dispute, claims to be an enslaved man cursed centuries earlier to wander the Earth. In the past, a plantation mistress keeps grisly relics – locks of hair, severed ears – to perform magic on the bodies of those she enslaved. Present-day characters find themselves possessed by the spirits of enslavers, while Claudia struggles to resist being claimed herself.

Filmed on location, much of the show’s richness comes from the vision of its Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, whose work has long explored the country’s layered histories and identity. The island is rendered in full polyphonic Technicolor: music and traditional masquerade rituals punctuate the narrative, while Obeah – the African-Caribbean spiritual practice of contacting ancestors, long feared by colonial authorities for its association with resistance and rebellion – becomes one of the show’s recurring motifs.

“We wanted everything to feel as real as possible – the beauty of the colour, music and smells of Jamaica, but also its darkness,” says Mbatha-Raw. “We filmed at a real plantation house – all the scenes in the grounds, with enslaved people working on the land – real people lived and died there. Driving up the hill towards the house, you could really feel the weight of history.”

The show belongs to the same lineage as Jordan Peele’s Get Out – racially conscious horror, in which the supernatural is merely a conduit for the far more terrifying legacy of racism. It is a provocation about reparations, colonial wealth and Britain’s historic relationship with slavery. In one pointed exchange, Claudia and the son of the plantation owner discuss the fact that the British government compensated former slave owners after abolition – a debt underwritten by taxpayers until 2015 – while those who had been enslaved received nothing. These are conversations that feel particularly pointed with the rise of far-right nationalism and racism in the UK and beyond. Is this something she was conscious of when making the show?

“It’s uncomfortable to talk about reparations, it’s hard to talk about slavery and how we make peace with that history,” she says. “I think that’s what makes [the show] so compelling,” she continues. “You can’t just paper over the cracks of history. If we don’t deal with it, it will find ways of haunting us.”

More than a decade separates Possession and Belle, but the two projects feel in conversation with one another in their meditations on empire.

“It’s funny because it wasn’t like a huge blockbuster film,” she says when I ask how the movie changed her life. “But it was my first lead role, and it opened up lots of opportunities for me. And it was an important story to tell. A lot of people didn’t know that mixed-race characters existed in history – certainly not of any status, because you never saw them in movies unless they were a slave or being brutalised in some way.”

Before we meet, she tells me she took a walk through Hampstead Heath to Kenwood House, once the stately home where Dido lived. “I wanted to immerse myself in that history again before speaking to you,” she says. Looking back now, she believes Belle helped widen ideas about who gets to exist in Britain’s period dramas.

“I do think Belle helped pave the way for a show like Bridgerton,” she adds. “Just having Black and brown people visible is a huge change in the last 10 years or so.” Belle also marked the beginning of her friendship with Oprah, who was an early champion and offered to help with its US marketing; the pair have remained in touch ever since.

Sign up to What's On

after newsletter promotion

Politics has never been optional in Mbatha-Raw’s life. She was born in 1983 in Witney, a town just outside Oxford. Her father was a student anti-apartheid activist and ANC campaigner who fled South Africa to avoid imprisonment on Robben Island, eventually rebuilding his life with support from the UN’s Refugee Agency.

“I remember we would talk about politics at the dinner table, but when you’re South African, you don’t know any different,” she says.

She grew up an only child, living with her mother, a British nurse. Her parents split when she was young, but her father remained in her life. Ballet was her first love, as well as music – she trained with the National Youth Music Theatre before going on to Rada.

As a young, biracial aspiring actor – particularly one growing up outside of London – has she ever felt held back by her race? She demurs.

“There were certainly some roles that would have been closed off to me, like those early Regency-era roles, but the industry is changing in a really positive direction,” she says.

She does mention that early on in her career, an older – white – actor suggested she change her name to something easier to pronounce. It was advice she politely ignored.

“I love my name, it’s what makes me who I am,” she says. “I don’t think it’s that hard to pronounce. Plus, it translates to ‘our pride’ in Zulu, so changing that would feel so wrong – the opposite of what it means!”

After graduating from Rada in 2004, Mbatha-Raw built her career the old-fashioned way: on stage. In 2005, she appeared in Antony and Cleopatra before landing one of her first major roles opposite Andrew Garfield in Romeo and Juliet at Manchester’s Royal Exchange. Supporting screen roles in Bad Girls, Marple and Doctor Who followed, before a celebrated turn as Ophelia opposite Jude Law’s Hamlet in the West End and on Broadway. JJ Abrams saw the production and cast her in his American spy drama Undercovers, opening the door to Hollywood. For years she lived peripatetically, dividing her life between sets in the US and London. For now, she is London-based again.

Her move coincided with a broader exodus of Black British actors across the Atlantic. Daniel Kaluuya has spoken about not getting roles in the UK “because of the colour of my skin”; David Oyelowo has talked of being “pushed out” because of the racial “glass ceiling”, as has David Harewood. Blockbuster names such as Cynthia Erivo and Damson Idris have found some of their biggest roles in the US, fuelling a long-running debate about whether Britain’s film and television industry truly nurtures its Black talent.

“It’s definitely something I’ve heard, but it hasn’t been my personal experience,” she says when I ask about this. “I didn’t go to the US looking for opportunities; I got offered a role in Hollywood because of the work I’d already done here – and that’s not really something you turn down. I was very lucky.”

Mbatha-Raw is thoughtful and politically engaged, but I get the sense she would rather speak through her characters. “I wouldn’t ever want to tell people what to think or experience,” she says. “Maybe Possession will inspire people to think about the more thought-provoking conversations around slavery, the idea of reparations and the complexity of that. But mostly, I just hope people find it entertaining.”

Possession starts on 6 August on Sky Atlantic at 9pm.

Digested week: History shrugs off Keir and makes room for brilliant Kerr

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 11:54:39 GMT

A low-key PM leaves the stage briskly, while a breathtaking athlete misses out on the attention he deserves

And so it was over. You normally get a bit more notice when a prime minister is about to deliver their resignation speech outside No 10. The buildup. The sense of occasion. Keir Starmer did things differently.

No sooner had “Hot Podium Guy” set up the lectern in Downing Street than Keir was out the front door. As if he couldn’t wait for it all to be over. His speech was done in little more than five minutes.

There was no David Cameron confected nonchalance. No tears as there were with Theresa May. No unconcealed bitterness and resentment like Boris Johnson. No bewilderment at the speed of the ending like Liz Truss. And no symbolic rainstorm as with Rish Sunak.

Keir said he was going with good grace and he looked as though he meant it. He may still feel angry at the way some of his cabinet turned on him, but it was no longer consuming his every waking minute. What was done was done. He would miss the attention but could see the upside of no longer being the bloke who got woken up at 4am to be told of Donald Trump’s latest efforts to start world war three.

Despite the rapid turnover of prime ministers in the last 10 years, there is still something quite poignant about these moments. To see the very public end of a frontline political career. Keir did his best to cement his legacy by saying he had left the country in a better place than he had found it. Which was probably true. He just hadn’t changed the country enough. Or given us a reason to believe in him. And now it was like watching him being airbrushed out of history.

From now on, anything that goes wrong for Andy will be Keir’s fault. And anything that goes right, Andy will take the credit for. It was always thus.

We’re going to have to reset the clock. Coming in to the World Cup, all the talk was of ending “60 years of hurt”. Now we’re going to have to up that to “64 years of hurt” for the next tournament in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. I feel like I really should know better, but this time round I did allow myself to believe that this might be the year when we got to the final and maybe even win it.

A team that seemed to be able to play as a team and a manager with the nous to be able to find a way to win matches that we appeared to be losing. Then came the Argentina semi-final. It was like watching Spurs again. Mind you, I knew the game was up when we took the lead. It was far too early in the second half. Far too much time to think about all the ways they could screw it up.

The only way we were ever going to win that game was to keep the score at 0-0 until injury time and then go for the winner. Whose idea it was to try and defend for the last 40 minutes is still not clear.

I was just screaming at the TV for England to carry on playing in the way that had got them the lead and had kept Lionel Messi relatively quiet. Desperate for someone on the pitch to realise that another way to have won the game was to score a second goal.

Still, we did get to participate in the most entertaining match of the whole World Cup when we took on France in the third-place playoff. Not that we should read too much into the 6-4 scoreline other than that it was a joy to watch what was basically a friendly between two teams that were demob happy. And we did get to miss out on Trump making a fool of himself by trying to gatecrash the celebrations. Swings and roundabouts.

This time last year, Reform was setting the political agenda. While Labour and the Tories seemed to have shut up shop, having decided the public must have been as fed up with politics as they were, Nigel Farage and co were dominating the headlines with new policy announcements every week. Now it seems that the two main parties are trying not to make the same mistake again.

Andy Burnham’s government is dripping us a new policy every day while Kemi Badenoch has become desperate to get television airtime at every opportunity. The latest is to tell us that she doesn’t really trust Andy. Who would have guessed?

As for Reform, it appears to have stalled somewhat. From leading the polls it now finds itself neck and neck with Labour in many samples and it feels more and more as if Nige can’t stand the level of scrutiny he is coming under with regard to his own finances. Ever since the Guardian revealed he had received a £5m gift from the Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, Nige has rather gone to ground. Refusing to do regular press conferences, taking no questions from the media and reduced to posting videos on social media from the middle of random fields. Moreover, his financial affairs are becoming more opaque the more he tries to explain them. First the £5m was to pay for his security, then a gift. Now it is alleged it was a downpayment on his demand for £1m a year to stand as an MP for Clacton. All this before we get to the donations both in kind and cash from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell and his mum, Fiona. It’s not very Man of the People.

Also, despite protestations to the contrary, it becomes more and more clear that Reform is really a one-man band. Dicky Tice is a halfwit, Robert Jenrick a liability and Zia Yusuf so dislikable that even Reform constituency associations don’t want him to stand as their MP. All of which seems to be getting to Nige. This week he turned up at a rally – if you can call it that – in Norfolk and appeared as bored as the 200 people in the audience. Just a rehash of some of his favourite lines that we’ve all heard before. Nothing new to say. Just a need for some attention. And no questions from anyone. He’s desperate for all the talk about his finances to go away but the more he deflects, the greater the interest. The Reform bubble might just be bursting.

Regular readers of this column will have realised that I was away two weeks ago while visiting my daughter in Minneapolis. At least that was the plan. But a couple of days before we were due to fly, my wife tripped on an uneven pavement and broke her shoulder. So we had to stay at home. Chemo can make the bones more brittle, so that’s another thing to blame cancer for.

The charge sheet gets ever longer. It was meant as a short trip – I was going for four days, my wife for eight – but I was still gutted. This was the second trip to the US we have had to cancel in the past year and we are yet to see Anna’s new house – she moved in the middle of last year – or to meet her new dog, Pearl.

I have also yet to discover whether I will actually be allowed into the US or if I will be put on the first return flight home. Fingers crossed that border security have better things to do than read satirical sketches about the president in the Guardian. We are now planning/hoping/not counting our chickens that we can get to Minnesota for Christmas. So I guess I will find out then. Maybe Trump will still be too moany about the midterm election results to bother with the odd UK journalist.

Talking of dogs, we have also had a massive disappointment. We had made it down to the last two to rehome a six-year-old cockapoo called Tinka whose owner had died unexpectedly. We did get to meet Tinka once and take her for a walk. She was very different to Herbie, much more nervy and insecure. But we had fallen in love with her on the spot and had dared to look forward to making her a part of our lives. But it was not to be.

So the hunt goes on. If any of you knows of a house-trained cockapoo that is in need of a home or even a cockapoo puppy that nobody wants, then please do get in touch. We are both feeling very much dog deprived. The last year has been unremittingly shit. We are due a break.

Maybe it was the excitement of the third place playoff and the buildup to the World Cup final. Maybe it’s just that the UK no longer cares that much about athletics. The Commonwealth Games start today and they barely register on the public consciousness.

Ticket sales are sluggish and they aren’t even being broadcast on terrestrial TV. When I was young they were almost as big a deal as the Olympics. Probably because it was the one Games back then when we won a shedload of medals.

But even so, I can’t help feeling that Josh Kerr hasn’t got quite the credit he deserves for breaking the world record for the mile at the London Stadium last Saturday. A remarkable achievement by any standard, but all the more so because he beat the record set by Hicham El Guerrouj in 1999 by nearly half a second. A breathtaking piece of running that had been more than a year in the planning. Kerr had dedicated his whole season – he called it Project 222 because that’s the precise number of seconds he needed to run to finish in 3.42 – to this one race.

From March this year, he was telling the world what he planned to do. The time and place he would achieve sporting immortality. And yet … While most papers covered the world record on the night, Kerr seems to have rather slipped out of the British public’s mind since. As if, everyone was thinking, “That’s nice”, before forgetting about it.

The US media seem far more impressed, with the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both having written in-depth analysis of how Kerr did it. All very different from the late 70s and early 80s when Steve Ovett and Sebastian Coe were regularly swapping the mile record. Back then almost everyone had a favourite – mine was Ovett; I found Coe unbearably smug. Still do, in fact – and their races didn’t just lead the sports pages, they made front-page news as well.

They were both personalities as well as athletics greats. Instantly recognisable. Josh Kerr could walk into a pub and there’s a fair chance no one would know who he was. So let’s hear it for Josh. I’m biased, of course. I used to run myself. Though my best 10K time was 10 minutes outside the world record. Call this the start of a campaign for Josh to win this year’s sports personality of the year. Let’s face it. No other athlete is going to come close to achieving what he has.

Masked men invading and taking Amazon communities ‘hostage’ in organised crime surge, say local leaders

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 11:49:19 GMT

Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon

Indigenous leaders on the Brazilian-Peruvian border have said their communities are being “taken hostage” by organised crime groups who are running rampant across the region, destroying rainforest, building roads and trafficking drugs.

Earlier this month, masked men armed with semi-automatic weapons entered homes in Apiwtxa, a village in the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory, intimidating people and searching for targets.

The Asháninka people, who have faced threats from intruders for decades because of their efforts to protect the forest and eject narco smugglers, say this is the worst danger they have faced, prompting an emergency delegation to Brasília this week to appeal for support from the government of the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

“Either the state steps in to provide protection, or communities will start organising to defend themselves – and that would be disastrous,” said Francisco Piyãko, the general coordinator of the Organisation of Indigenous People of the Juruá River, who is part of the delegation. “We are not facing a local conflict. We are facing the expansion of transnational criminal networks into Indigenous territories that currently represent one of the last barriers against the illegal occupation of this region of the Amazon.”

The petition of the Asháninka people comes amid growing concerns about the nexus of drug trafficking and environmental crime, which Brazilian climate scientist Carlos Nobre has described as the greatest new threat to the Amazon Forest.

The Brazilian side of the border is in Acre state, where the forest is still relatively healthy compared with the Peruvian side, which has experienced heavy logging and violence. Acre has sometimes been a perilous area for environmental and land defenders. One of the country’s most celebrated forest campaigners, Chico Mendes, was shot dead there in 1988. After that, there was a period of relative peace in Acre, compared with other countries in the Amazon or other Brazilian states such as Pará. More recently, however, there has been a rise in tension, much of it from the outside. Isolated Indigenous communities from Peru have been increasingly crossing the border to escape confrontation with loggers and drug cartels.

Apiwtxa was the last Indigenous village visited by the British journalist Dom Phillips before he was murdered in the neighbouring Brazilian border state of Amazonas in 2022 while researching illegal extractivist activities in another area menaced by arms and drug smugglers.

According to the Asháninka petition to the Brazilian government, the most recent intrusion into Apiwtxa involved five heavily armed, Spanish-speaking men arriving on the evening of 6 July at the home of one of the Asháninka leaders, who was out of the village at the time. “They were clearly poised to attack with lethal intent,” said one member of the community. It was the second time in several days that masked gunmen had entered the village looking for leaders.

Frightened villagers took their children into one building for protection and notified the authorities. The army arrived at midnight, by which time the would-be assassins had disappeared back into the forest, leaving only tracks.

“For us, this was a threat unlike any other, because they came right into our home – they entered our house,” said Piyãko. “We realise that the context we’re living in now isn’t just about drug trafficking; you can see it’s a movement involving everything from wildcat mining and illegal mining to illegal logging, drug trafficking and other issues.”

The Asháninka delegation in Brasília is calling for a permanent security presence along the border to prevent the free movement of drug traffickers, illegal loggers and the illicit construction of “virus roads” that push into the forest without environmental oversight. They also want greater protection for their leaders and operations to combat organised crime in the area.

The neighbouring Peruvian department of Ucayali has the widest network of illegal roads in the Peruvian Amazon, providing transport for gangs involved in environmental crime, gold, money laundering and drugs. In the past five years, coca cultivation in Ucayali has tripled.

The Igarapé Institute, a public security thinktank, has said that organised crime – which often intersects with narcotics and illegal extraction of natural resources – needs a more robust response by governments across the region: “It is increasingly clear that the fight against organised environmental crime in the Amazon ultimately demands better intelligence and strategic prioritisation. The goal must be to strengthen Brazilian state authority to deter and repress crimes and those who commit them.”

Piyãko said this was now a matter of urgency. He added: “If the Peruvian and Brazilian governments joined forces and wanted to resolve the situation, they could. Because they have the means to combat this.”

“If the state doesn’t protect these territories, they will be dominated by this criminal system, or the people will be forced to defend themselves on their own. This could lead to very serious situations, because as the net tightens around these territories, tensions rise.”
