‘The captain told me to wear a nappy on board’ – why is air travel so humiliating for disabled passengers?

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 10:04:05 GMT

From being abused by staff and other travellers to being denied access to toilets, flying is an increasingly distressing and frustrating experience for many wheelchair users. Here, they share their stories

When Hannah Babalola boarded KLM flight 598 on 26 May, she was tired. A Paralympic athlete, she had been competing at an event in South Africa’s Cape Town, and was hoping there would be no hold ups on her journey back home to Chicago.

Babalola, 37, is well-travelled. A former wheelchair racer, she now competes in marathons and has flown to dozens of countries over the years without big problems.

The first stretch of her journey home was a flight of almost 11 hours to Amsterdam. After boarding, she was told by the captain and crew that she wouldn’t be able to access an onboard wheelchair, known as an aisle chair. These narrow wheelchairs are used by people with disabilities so they can access the toilet during a flight. Crew members told her when she boarded the plane that if she needed to use the toilet, she would have to do so without a wheelchair – if this wasn’t possible, she was told she would have to get off the flight altogether.

Astounded by this – aisle chairs are generally available on wide-bodied aircraft – Babalola stood her ground, despite becoming increasingly distressed. The crew offered various justifications for their position, including the captain’s fears that the chair would be unsafe to use if there was turbulence. She was also wrongly told that she hadn’t booked the flight as a disabled person (disabled passengers are advised to book special assistance at least 48 hours before taking a flight – which Babalola had done). She had bought a return ticket​ and had​ had no trouble receiv​ing assistance as a disabled passenger on her outward journey​.

“It was the first time anything like this had happened to me on a plane,” says Babalola. “They made me feel as if I wasn’t a human.” The crew called the police and security. Both declined to take any action against her, as there was no evidence she had done anything wrong. Desperate to get home, she finally agreed not to use the toilet during the flight. “The humiliation was unbearable,” she says.

What happened to her is not an isolated incident. When the Guardian first reported on Babalola’s case, a flurry of emails followed from others who had had similar experiences.

According to data published by the World Health Organization in 2023 approximately 16% of the global population experiences significant disability – about 1.3 billion people. The UK’s Civil Aviation Authority outlines the rights of passengers to accessible air travel, which includes assistance moving through airports, and when boarding and disembarking planes. But such assistance has limitations. It applies only to people flying from UK airports on any airline, and for returns to the UK on either UK or EU airlines.

The National Centre for Accessible Transport published a report in July 2025, called Invisible Barriers: How public attitudes affect inclusive travel. It found that people with impairments or access needs that fall outside certain models have to fight to get those needs met. Those who were interviewed for the report said they had experienced negative treatment when travelling, due to assumptions and stereotypes around disability. The report looked at various types of transport, including planes; it found that disabled travellers sometimes have to endure abuse from other passengers, and that transport staff have a limited understanding of disability. One wheelchair user quoted in the report, who was travelling by plane, was denied assistance as they had limited mobility; they could stand up and walk in certain circumstances, but were unable to get down the plane steps without assistance. A crew member said: “Well you can stand, you can get off, you can go down the stairs.”

Sophie Morgan, a British TV presenter, writer and disability rights campaigner, is co-founder of Rights on Flights and an energetic campaigner for people with disabilities who fly. She was paralysed from the chest down after a car accident at 18, and began campaigning because her wheelchair was broken so many times by airport staff when she flew.

“I honestly think that if the airlines could ban us from flying, they would,” she says. “I feel sad that the same problems that were happening three years ago are still happening now. It feels like a case of one step forward, 200 steps back. When I was campaigning in the beginning I thought: ‘They just need to be told.’ In fact, they actually know full well, but they just don’t care. Where are we? We are nowhere. One plane captain told me I should wear a nappy on board.”

Sarah Richardson has a disability called arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, which causes severe problems with her joints and bones. This makes travel, including plane travel, very challenging, and led her to conduct research for her MBA with 36 disabled travellers from around the world. Half the respondents encountered problems “almost always”. None reported no problems.

More than 83% of her respondents experienced stress and anxiety when travelling, and restricted food and drink in the hours before travelling to avoid the struggle of using the onboard toilet. Some resorted to wearing nappies on flights in case toilet access was impossible.

“I was really shocked by what I found in the interviews,” says Richardson. “Travelling systems are just not made for people with disabilities, and things have got worse with automation.” While researching her thesis, Richardson found that, as travel infrastructures have become more automated to boost efficiency and economic return, accessibility for disabled travellers is increasingly treated as a conditional service rather than something baked into the design of systems. “Travel systems are designed for average bodies and toilets are not designed for people with disabilities. It is particularly terrifying on long-haul flights.”

On a recent flight, she asked if she could move to a seat with more leg room, which was vacant, but was told she could only switch if she paid an extra $300. “When you are up in the air, you are a hostage. Disability is not a niche market. We are part of the community. Being disabled is seen as not important, not sexy, not interesting,” she says.

Some disabled travellers say they have to prepare for the worst when they book a plane ticket. Hasan Adeel has muscular dystrophy and flies frequently to visit family and to speak at conferences about his disability. He says he is frequently wrongly handled when being transferred between his wheelchair and his plane seat. “I have never yet used an aeroplane bathroom, as I can’t get through the door,” he says. “I feel that for airlines, rules are ranked higher than humanity. But you can’t argue with the airlines or they won’t let you get on the plane.”

On one trip, Adeel landed in Doha in Qatar and asked staff to help him transfer from his aeroplane seat to his wheelchair. He was left for 20 minutes. “They said they had never transferred a person like me before but that they would try,” says Adeel. “First they transferred me to the narrow aisle chair and from there into my wheelchair. They did not know the correct way to transfer someone with my disability and the transfer was not done in a professional way.”

Payal Shrishrimal, an artist who lives in India, is determined not to let the significant challenges of air travel get her down. She also has muscular dystrophy and, at 41, has far outlived the life expectancy of 20 that she was given as a child. “On one journey, when I was travelling home after recovering from surgery, the crew started whispering about me and my disability. They kept asking why I was using a wheelchair, and it made me feel very nervous and humiliated … Two or three hours before I leave home to travel to the airport I have to stop drinking water, because I know I won’t be able to use the toilet on the plane. Once, I was even asked to pay for the transport of my wheelchair, although there are [supposed to be] no charges for this.”

A recurrent complaint among wheelchair users is that, when their chairs are stored in the hold – in perfectly good condition – on landing they are returned to them battered and broken. One man discovered his electric wheelchair had been badly damaged when he arrived in London on an Emirates flight on 18 May. He is completely reliant on the chair and, as a result of the damage, has been confined to his home. “I have effectively been trapped inside my home, and unable to attend medical appointments, shop independently, or carry out normal daily activities,” he says. “This situation has caused significant distress, loss of independence, emotional suffering and disruption to my life.” He received no response from the airline, and nor did others who wrote to Emirates trying to advocate for him.

After the Guardian contacted Emirates, the airline agreed to take action. A spokesperson said: “We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience he experienced. We are in direct contact with him and have arranged a temporary mobility device. We are also assessing options to replace his wheelchair as a permanent solution, and will continue to support him until the issue is fully resolved.”

Even those who are powerful and high-profile report appalling experiences when they travel by plane. Samanta Bullock, Brazil’s former No 1 wheelchair tennis player, now lives in the UK. She founded Bullock Inclusion, which creates social projects in fashion and sport to promote inclusion for all, and aims to change attitudes to transform the lives of people living with disabilities. Last month, she flew to New York to take part in the UN’s 19th Conference of States Parties to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which aims to further the rights of people with disabilities. She and her team had organised a fashion show for the event and discussed with officials how best to advance the rights of disabled people. But when she arrived at JFK airport for her flight back to the UK, she was told by British Airways staff that she couldn’t board the flight without a carer to take her to the toilet, as the flight crew wouldn’t be able to assist her. This would have required her to buy an expensive extra ticket.

“I have travelled my whole life and never had this experience before,” she says. “Eventually, they said they could transfer me to an American Airlines flight. I thought about not accepting the transfer and fighting this. But I was so tired from my trip and I just wanted to get home, so I agreed to the change.”

A British Airways spokesperson said: “We want to ensure a seamless flying experience for everyone and we’re sorry that our customer had a negative experience on this occasion. We are aware our customer has expressed concerns regarding her experience and we have reached out to her to discuss further.

“We serve hundreds of thousands of customers who require additional assistance every year and while we’re committed to continually improving our service, we work hard to support accessibility requirements throughout their journey.”

Morgan says that, because cases like Bullock’s continue to happen, she will keep on fighting. “I fly with my rights in my pocket, but our rights continue to be violated. We need to rebrand this as a crisis.”

As for Babalola, she continues to fight KLM. When the Guardian asked the airline to comment on her case, KLM said in a statement: “We regret that an incident occurred involving one of our passengers on the flight from Cape Town to Amsterdam on 26 May. Out of respect for the privacy of both the passenger and our crew, we find it inappropriate to discuss the details of the situation.”

Babalola has now engaged a lawyer to help her. “I need to take legal action, because otherwise this abuse of power against disabled people will continue. The experience I had on that KLM flight was distressing, degrading and humiliating. I felt intimidated by the flight crew.” On 19 June, she received a further letter from KLM, saying it was important to the company that all passengers are treated with “the utmost respect and dignity”.

“We are disappointed that we fell short of that expectation,” the airline added. It went on to apologise for the fact she hadn’t received the assistance she requested and included “sincere apologies” for her experience. The letter concluded: “We once again apologise for Ms Babalola’s experience on board flight KL598 and are making efforts to ensure that such a situation does not reoccur in the future.”

None of the people interviewed for this piece are holding their breath.

So many British people have it better than they think – it’s up to Burnham to make them see that

The Guardian Fri, 24 Jul 2026 10:00:10 GMT

A new survey suggests voters are becoming more cynical and pessimistic. A few goodwill gestures from No 10 won’t change all that – but it’s a start

Who are we, the people Andy Burnham now governs? He inherits a miserable lot: grudging, angry pessimists, expecting the worst of all politicians, trusting no one to lead the country well, according to a long-running study. British folk feel the social contract is broken, they feel let down. Ignorant of basic facts, they are wilfully misled by malevolents.

Over half a century of taking their pulse, Ipsos has collected data on shifting attitudes for the mighty Understanding Society, the largest longitudinal household study in the world, run by the Institute for Social and Economic Research. By chance, this latest national portrait will be the benchmark for Burnham’s era. Here are his people: can he make them feel better? In the end, that’s the great purpose of all politics: you can have good policies, make improvements, do your honest best, as Keir Starmer tried, but if you don’t make the people feel it, then it’s a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, as Paul told the Corinthians. Can Burnham lift up their hearts, a bit?

Reading this survey, he may sink his head in his hands. Earning any trust is a Himalayan climb: it was bad enough back in 1989 when just 33% believed politicians were good people in general, but now that’s fallen to 20%.

The people’s contradictory desires are many: they want lower taxes and better services – a higher standard of living without paying for it. They admire Sweden above all other countries, yet show little sign they would accept Swedish taxes at 42% of GDP, while ours are about 33%.

Impossibilism is everywhere. Launching the report, Gideon Skinner, Ipsos’s director of UK politics in public affairs, said: “We are seeing a sharpening public friction between high expectations for public services like the NHS and a declining appetite for the taxation required to sustain them.” Belief in the welfare state remains high, but it has slipped. The old divide between collectivists and individualists has deepened: “a society which emphasises the social and collective provision of welfare” gets 46% support, fallen from 54% in 1989, while 47% now want “a society where the individual is encouraged to look after themselves”, compared with 40% in 1989.

But people are contradictory, torn between public spirit and private greed. Asked if they would prefer “a mainly socialist society in which public interests and a more controlled economy are most important” or “a mainly capitalist society in which private interest and free enterprise are most important”, support for socialism has risen to 57%, which is 10 percentage points higher than in 1989. More people now support “a society which emphasises similar incomes and rewards for everyone” than in 1989. What does that mean and how can Labour seize on those sentiments, not the meaner impulses?

People see some glaring truths – they are not hoodwinked by the Americanised myth that everyone can make it if they only try harder. “Belief in social mobility has halved since 1989”, as only one in four (26%) now believe that the best people rise to the top regardless of their start in life, down from 52% in 1989. The facts show how birth and inheritances are cementing future chances.

Pessimism is at its worst in 50 years and 72% expect a world war within the next 25 years (many more than at the height of the cold war in 1983). And yet people are not unhappy: “The clear majority of Britons remain happy with their life at present, even if fewer are ‘very happy’ than in 1991.” Live-and-let-live liberal values have made the country more tolerant since the 1980s.

Yet here’s the alarm sounded by Ipsos. “This moment feels different in character to the cycles of political dissatisfaction we have seen before,” Gideon Skinner warns. “What is worrying is that pessimism risks becoming more embedded in Britons’ sense of national identity.”

People may be less despairing if they knew the basics of the social contract they think is broken. Wild misunderstanding of what they pay in tax and what they get from the state fuels resentment of government. The political psephologist Peter Kellner, poring over the Office for National Statistics’s treasure trove “Effects of taxes and benefits on household income”, finds that 53% of the population gets back more from the state than they pay in: that includes not just all taxes and VAT, and cash transfers in benefits and pensions, but non-cash benefits such as the NHS, social care, education and transport subsidies (omitting collective benefits, such as the police and the armed forces).

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But very few know it: only 12% think they get more than they pay in. Very few over-65s recognise the ONS calculation that 90% of them gain more: even those on incomes over £70,000 on average get more than they pay, mostly because of how much they use care services and the NHS. Everyone needs a well-funded state, the old most of all, yet they vote against it.

That’s the ignorance and the ingratitude Burnham faces. When he says, “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity,” it needs a burst of public education to counter the daily blast of bad-faith misinformation from the right and its media. Ignorance is inexcusable when it has never been easier to find out anything at the click of a mouse.

Starmer and Rachel Reeves tried to square with the people, telling brutal truths about hard choices and high debts. The people hated it. That’s Burnham’s template for what not to do. But how does he revive faith in the state? He starts with small goodwill gestures to show the government is there to help – with cuts to electricity bills, bus fares, tax for state pensioners, and business rates for pubs and clubs. Saving music venues chimes with his aim to change the mood of the nation. The public’s demand for urgent change is no guide: it points chaotically in contrary directions. Good leaders seize on guiding the better parts of human nature to believe things can be better.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Paramount Agrees to Delay Warner Bros. Merger for Months

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Paramount-Warner Bros. Deal

Advertisement

Supported by

The company agreed to a proposed freeze until June 2027, unless a judge issues a ruling before then on a lawsuit blocking the deal.

By Benjamin MullinDavid McCabe and Lauren Hirsch

Paramount said on Friday that it had agreed to halt its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery until next June at the latest while a judge considers a lawsuit from state attorneys general who sued to block the deal. The delay is the latest curveball in a deal that would remake Hollywood.

In a legal filing, Paramount and the state attorneys general said that they had reached an agreement to freeze the $111 billion merger while the case works its way through court, extending a shorter pause imposed this week by a federal judge in California. The merger agreement expires on June 4, 2027, if the deal has not closed by that date.

The delay could be costly for Paramount. The company, run by the tech scion David Ellison, has agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders a fee of $650 million for every quarter that the deal does not close, beginning in October. Larry Ellison, David Ellison’s father, has personally guaranteed the acquisition.

But Paramount framed it as a “significant win” that would help it close the deal. The company said the move would speed up the legal process by pushing the case to a trial sooner. It will also help avoid prolonged back-and-forth over some legal issues, like the merits of a court-ordered delay.

The proposed delay does not take effect until it is approved by Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, who is overseeing the case in the U. S. District Court for the Northern District of California.

“This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers, and good for creators,” a Paramount spokeswoman said in a statement.

The coalition of 12 states led by California includes New York, Connecticut, Oregon and Arizona. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the states, said in a statement that the delay was “great news for audiences.” Letitia James, the New York attorney general, called the freeze “a crucial victory” in a statement.

The deal would unite under one roof two major movie studios, the streaming services HBO Max and Paramount+ and networks including CBS and CNN. Mr. Ellison has aggressively pushed to acquire Warner Bros., ultimately outbidding Netflix after proposing a handful of escalating offers.

The lawsuit from the state attorneys general argues that combining with Warner Bros. would give Paramount too much leverage over the release of feature films and, in particular, the tent-pole blockbusters that are the backbone of studio revenues. It also claims Paramount would be too dominant in the market for basic cable channels.

The Writers Guild of America has filed its own lawsuit against the deal, arguing it would financially harm screenwriters. The Friday filing proposing a delay to the deal’s closing also covers the union’s case.

Paramount has argued that the deal will give the combined company enough heft to serve as a counterweight to streaming powerhouses like YouTube and Netflix. It has also argued that the states are too narrowly defining the market for basic cable and films, particularly by excluding players like streamers.

The merger raised similar alarms in Hollywood among creative professionals who feared that bringing two major studios into the same conglomerate would lead to fewer productions and less investment in show business.

Norm Eisen, a lawyer who led opposition against the deal in Hollywood through his organization Democracy Defenders Fund, applauded the delay in a statement, saying that the merger was “anti-competitive, anti-consumer and anti-creator.”

The delay comes after a week of wrangling over how the lawsuits challenging the deal would proceed. Judge Martínez-Olguín was preparing to hear arguments on an injunction that would freeze the deal for an indefinite period of time while the lawsuits moved forward. Friday’s proposal is likely to render that kind of injunction unnecessary.

Seamus Hughes contributed research.

Democrats Vote to Put South Carolina First in 2028 Primary

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The state, along with several others still being chosen, appears set to play an important role in determining the party’s next presidential nominee.

By Shane Goldmacher

Reporting from Washington

A powerful panel of the Democratic National Committee voted on Friday to make South Carolina the first state in the party’s fight for the 2028 presidential nomination, after a lobbying push that at times fractured Democrats along racial, geographic and ideological lines.

In addition to putting South Carolina first on the calendar, the party preliminarily approved three other states to vote before Super Tuesday in early March: New Hampshire, Michigan and Nevada. The order of other states had not yet been set, and up to two more states could still be added to the so-called early window.

In the 49-person committee’s balloting on the first state, South Carolina received 26 votes, Nevada drew 19, and New Hampshire earned four.

“The South is not the past, it is the future,” Christale Spain, the chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party, said in her final speech lobbying for her state before the vote.

The panel, the D. N. C. Rules and Bylaws Committee, was meeting inside the Salamander hotel in Washington on Friday and still needed to vote on the full order of states; the full committee must ratify it at a meeting next month.

The fight between South Carolina and Nevada to be at the front of the line was intense, and the outcome is seen as profoundly important in deciding who ultimately emerges as the nominee.

“We’re shaping the proving ground for the next Democratic nominee,” said Maria Cardona, a veteran D. N. C. member who supported Nevada.

For decades, Iowa and New Hampshire kicked off every presidential nomination fight. But in 2024, Joseph R. Biden Jr., then the president, put South Carolina at the front of the line, after the state helped him win the nomination in 2020.

The state lobbied aggressively to keep its slot.

The first states to vote typically winnow the presidential field — and Democrats are expected to have a sprawling set of candidates in 2028. A dozen states had applied, and the party set rules to choose at least one state each from four regions — the West, the Northeast, the South and the Midwest — with a bonus fifth state from any region.

On Friday, the committee moved to add a sixth state that would vote before Super Tuesday.

Committee members debated the importance of the cost of campaigning in these early states, and even the logistics of how they count votes.

Stuart Appelbaum, a D. N. C. member and a union president, said he had backed South Carolina over Nevada in part because Nevada allows for the counting of ballots after Primary Day — which could delay the final results in a close race.

“With the stakes so incredibly high in this election, I feel we need certainty in 2028,” Mr. Appelbaum said.

But some uncertainty remained. Most notably, New Hampshire has a law requiring that the state hold the first primary. New Hampshire did so in 2024, even though the Democratic Party had placed South Carolina first.

Asked immediately after the vote what New Hampshire would do, the party’s longtime chairman, Raymond Buckley, said he did not know.

The debate inside the committee was ongoing on Friday.

This article will be updated.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

The New York Times July 24, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Even after the collapse of the cease-fire between the United States and Iran, American universities expect to teach in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and a new outpost is on track to open in Saudi Arabia.

By Alan Blinder

The Middle East campuses of American universities are expecting — or perhaps just hoping — to be open for classes as usual for the coming semester, even as the United States’ conflict with Iran poses new risks in the region.

Some American schools have long run programs in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The war, however, meant that students spent much of the spring semester enduring shutdowns, evacuations, online courses and other emergency measures. But the unraveling of the cease-fire between Washington and Tehran is not yet curbing universities’ ambitions to teach as they ordinarily would in the Middle East.

The University of New Haven is still planning to inaugurate its new campus in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, though probably without some faculty members it intended to send from the United States.

“The word in Saudi is that students are going to school and it’s business as usual,” Jens Frederiksen, New Haven’s president, said in an interview. “We’re proceeding with the launch.”

For American universities, campuses in wealthy Persian Gulf states can offer new revenue and welcome clout. Those perks, though, come with sporadic political headaches at home, reputational perils and regional safety concerns. After a strike on a physics building at a university in Tehran, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps warned in March that “American universities in the West Asia region are legitimate targets for us.”

By then, American schools had begun closing campuses and turning to remote classes. But the relative lull of recent months left many administrators encouraged and publicly optimistic that the campuses would be able to run normally as students return for another semester.

Virginia Commonwealth University, which has a presence in Qatar, said it was “planning to begin the fall semester with in-person instruction and campus operations as scheduled.” But the school said it was “prepared to transition temporarily to remote instruction and operations should circumstances warrant.”

Spokesmen for Carnegie Mellon University and Northwestern University described similar approaches for their Qatar campuses.

Cornell University, whose medical school has a presence in the country, said the campus would “continue to follow guidance from the Qatar Ministry of Interior, monitor developments and provide timely updates.”

Meghan Dubyak, a spokeswoman for Georgetown University, said she did not “have any updates to share at this time” about plans for the university’s Qatari operation, which has been describing the campus as “open with limited services.”

A spokesman for Texas A&M University, which moved in 2024 to begin winding down its campus in Qatar, said the school was continuing to monitor the situation. But he noted that the university’s presence had been already “much reduced” as it worked toward the 2028 shutdown.

In the Emirates, New York University’s Abu Dhabi campus is “planning for in person,” said Wiley Norvell, a school spokesman.

The U. S. government warned this week that the security situation could shift unpredictably.

“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U. S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U. S. businesses and other institutions,” the State Department wrote in an alert that said Americans “should reconsider travel to and through” the Middle East.

Americans already in the region, the State Department said, “should exercise caution and heightened vigilance.”

As New Haven prepares to open its branch in Riyadh, Dr. Frederiksen, the university president, acknowledged that the student body might be different than once envisioned. He said he expected most of the debut cohort’s students to be from Saudi Arabia and that the campus would probably be “light,” for the time being, on pupils from elsewhere.

He said that he and other university officials were in close contact with the Saudi authorities so they can better discern whether to invoke contingency plans for the campus.

“We’re incredibly, acutely aware of how dynamic situations are and what are sort of responsible for trigger points to say, ‘OK, then let’s go hybrid for a while,’” Dr. Frederiksen said.

But Dr. Frederiksen cautioned against relying on the decisions of other campuses across the region.

“You can draw lessons and pay attention, but, obviously, Riyadh or Saudi is not Bahrain or another one of the Gulf states, so I think there are some nuances there,” he said.

Sharon Otterman contributed reporting.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

What We Know About the Police Shooting in Madison

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A Black man was shot and killed by the police on Wednesday, not far from the Wisconsin Capitol. An investigation is underway.

By Jacey FortinPooja Salhotra and Robert Chiarito

The fatal shooting of a Black man by a police officer in Madison, Wis., on Wednesday has prompted protests, vigils and a state investigation.

The killing occurred in the city’s Marquette neighborhood, where officers were responding to reports of a man stealing bicycles and looking into parked vehicles, officials said. The police approached the man, who pulled out a knife during an ensuing struggle, they said.

Officers tried to incapacitate the man with a Taser, but it was deployed unsuccessfully, according to the police. An officer who was injured by the knife fired at the man, who was taken to a hospital and died.

Here’s what we know.

The killing happened on a busy street near the State Capitol. Multiple people captured cellphone footage, and videos of the shooting have circulated widely on social media.

They show a man surrounded by four officers. He falls to the ground during a struggle, and one officer deploys a Taser. As three officers try to hold the man, one fires his weapon, and multiple gunshots can be heard.

Chief John Patterson of the Madison Police Department said the footage on social media was only “one perspective” and added that “not all perspectives are online right now.”

Most Madison police officers do not wear body cameras, though some officials, including Chief Patterson, have been pushing for them.

Madison’s mayor, Satya Rhodes-Conway, identified the victim as Corey Ruiz, 38. In a news release, Noah Lieberman, a city alderman, identified Mr. Ruiz as Black and called for more police oversight. Police records listed Mr. Ruiz’s race as African American.

At a news conference on Friday, family members said that Mr. Ruiz, father of a 13-year-daughter, was caring, smart and beloved by the people who knew him.

“My son was an exceptional guy,” his mother, Elsa Ruiz, said. “He was my love. He loved his daughter. He loved his family. He did not deserve to be taken out like that. They took my baby from me.”

Public records showed a Madison address as Mr. Ruiz’s residence. He had a criminal record that included convictions for drug possession, theft and resisting or obstructing an officer, records showed.

His sister Veronica Ruiz said that “his criminal record tells a tale of trauma, of pain, of struggle.”

She continued: “It does not define who my brother was.”

Mr. Ruiz’s daughter, Kah’liyah Ali Omar, whose walk to school takes her close to the spot where her father was killed, said that he had “tried to do his best for me and his family.”

“I wish he was still here.”

The Wisconsin Justice Department is leading a homicide investigation into the shooting.

At a news conference on Thursday that was disrupted by protesters, Chief Patterson pledged he would cooperate fully with state investigators.

“We will not hide from any aspect of this investigation,” he said, adding that the police department would review its training and use of force policy.

After state officials finish investigating, they will share their findings with the district attorney’s office, which will decide whether to bring charges against the officer, Chief Patterson said.

The Madison police did not release the name of the officer who fired, but Chief Patterson said he hoped state investigators would release it soon. He added that all four officers involved have been placed on administrative leave.

In 2015, in the same neighborhood where Mr. Ruiz was shot, a white police officer shot and killed Anthony Robinson, a 19-year-old Black man, and protests followed. The district attorney did not file charges, deeming that the officer’s actions had been justified.

And in 2012, Paul Heenan, a white man, was fatally shot by the police after he had mistakenly entered the wrong home. The same district attorney found that the use of deadly force had been justified, and the officer was not charged.

Wisconsin Democrats will select their candidate for governor in less than three weeks, and the primary has been chaotic. An establishment front-runner recently left the race, and a state legislator who is a democratic socialist, Francesca Hong, is polling well, raising questions about how she would fare in the general election.

Wisconsin is a narrowly divided state where Republicans and Democrats have fought bitterly over elections. Republicans are expected to choose Representative Tom Tiffany, who grew up on a dairy farm and campaigns as the “common sense” candidate, as their nominee.

Ms. Hong, whose campaign office is a few blocks from the site of the killing, has referred to the shooting as an “execution,” while Mr. Tiffany has accused her of rushing to judgment. Both have called for an investigation.

Julie Bosman contributed reporting. Georgia Gee contributed research.

Jacey Fortin covers a wide range of subjects for The Times, including extreme weather, court cases and state politics across the country.

Pooja Salhotra covers breaking news across the United States.

F. D. A. Panel’s Vote on Peptides Raises Concerns About a Prescribing Boom

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The committee endorsed broader use of the peptides in lightly regulated compounding pharmacies that have grown into a multibillion-dollar business.

By Christina Jewett and Dana G. Smith

Christina Jewett reported from Washington, and Dana Smith from North Carolina.

A Food and Drug Administration advisory panel recommended broader use of six unproven peptides, raising concerns that wellness and telehealth companies could adopt a once-obscure pathway to bring unapproved drugs to the commercial market.

The votes directed the F. D. A. to add some peptides to the list of substances that specialized, so-called compounding pharmacies can make for patients. That kind of prescribing, typically meant for exceptional cases, has grown into a booming business that has largely been limited to copycat GLP-1 drugs.

The panel’s decisions alarmed F. D. A. scientists who spoke extensively at sessions on Thursday and Friday. But they are likely to be well received by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and signaled an increasing openness in the Trump administration to products popular with wellness influencers. These peptides in particular have prompted concerns, since they are mostly injected into the body, and have not gone through the F. D. A.’s thorough approval process.

The committee endorsed four peptides on Thursday and two more on Friday, though it also voted down the broader use of one rarely used peptide.

Some F. D. A. scientists during the panel meetings on Thursday and Friday pointed out that the peptides under review had not been proven to be safe or effective, and could present risks to patients.

Any hazards that emerge could be hard to track, the federal scientists said this week, since the advised action would push peptide use into a lightly regulated market largely overseen by state pharmacy boards.

Peptides have become a pet project for Mr. Kennedy, who has used the substances and has said publicly and privately that the agency should broaden access. His office took the unusual step of appointing eight new members to the committee that met this week, including six who market peptides in terms like “revolutionary” or able to “enhance disease resistance.”

The substances are chains of amino acids that prompt cells to perform actions like decreasing inflammation or increasing collagen production. Peptides that have been fully vetted by the F. D. A. include drugs like insulin or GLP-1s.

But unproven peptides with names like BPC-157 and MOTS-c have become popular items for social media influencers who unbox new peptides on camera and suggest that they improve skin tone and overall health. Some videos mock the F. D. A. and refer to peptides as “peppers,” to avoid content moderation.

Other users are people who feel failed by the medical system, and who distrust the pharmaceutical industry. Consumers buy peptides from longevity clinics, alternative health providers and even TikTok. The drugs are sometimes produced in unregulated Chinese labs and sold as “research grade” compounds.

In 2023, the F. D. A. essentially banned the peptides reviewed this week, over safety concerns. Before that, the compounds had been nominated for a list of acceptable items to compound, but had not been accepted by the agency.

Matthew Lash, an F. D. A. compliance official, said during Friday’s hearing that placing them on the legal-to-compound list would be a new action.

“I don’t think that we know what the potential explosion of use would look like,” he said.

The panel advisers, including some temporary voting members, do not have a final say. F. D. A. scientists and officials typically finalize such decisions, with sign-off from the agency’s commissioner. But Mr. Kennedy has expressed interest in making the decision himself, according to two people familiar with the matter who were not authorized to speak publicly.

The F. D. A. has struggled to keep up with compounding pharmacies and telehealth providers as they have grown into a multibillion-dollar industry marketing directly to the public.

Representatives from prominent telehealth companies, including Hims & Hers and Noom, testified during the hearings and signaled their interest in marketing the peptides under consideration.

John Hertig, a pharmacist and a board chair of the Collaborative for Evidence-Based Medicines, an advocacy group, said he was concerned that the additions would amount to an end-run around the F. D. A.’s careful approval process.

“This creates another parallel pathway to get this product in front of the public at much less rigor, fewer science-backed studies, and really does put the entire public and patient safety system at risk,” he said.

He added: “Once it’s on the list, you lose control.”

The most notable vote of the day was cast in favor of epitalon, a peptide that is marketed for longevity but that has been flagged as potentially increasing the risk of cancer.

Studies in cells found that epitalon can lengthen telomeres, something that is linked to a longer life span. F. D. A. scientists, however, cautioned that long-term, continuous exposure to epitalon could be carcinogenic.

Among the seven committee members voting in favor were physicians who sell peptides, including Dr. Melissa Loseke, the president and chief medical officer of the Re-new Institute in Omaha, Neb., and Dr. Kris Wusterhausen, the founder of the Resurge Clinic in Weatherford, Texas.

The Re-new Institute’s website describes peptide therapy as “a cutting-edge longevity treatment” that helps the body “reduce inflammation, improve cognition and accelerate recovery.” The Resurge Clinic offers them in efforts to lower body fat, increase lean muscle, repair tendons and ligaments, enhance sexual performance and protect against UV light.

Dr. Asare Christian, the founder of a Philadelphia-area clinic that sells peptides for “longevity,” said at the meeting on Friday that he voted in favor of every peptide because he treats pain in patients, which is managed with treatments like opioids, Tylenol and gabapentin, which carry their own risks.

“That’s why I’m making all these choices,” he said, adding that “a lot of the things that have been said here hasn’t really stressed a significant safety signal.”

Many committee members who sell peptides and people who testified in favor of broadening access to them called for guardrails on peptide quality, such as requirements for reports of harm or purity testing. The F. D. A. emphasized that the agency did not have the authority to set such conditions on unapproved drugs, saying Congress would need to step in.

On Friday, the advisory panel voted against broadening the use of the peptide emideltide, which is known as a sleep-inducing compound. It is naturally produced in the brain and connected to circadian rhythms. It has had a mixed record in small human studies, most from the 1980s, related to its use for insomnia. The studies did not report any adverse events, but because the peptide acts on the opioid pathway, some scientists at the meeting expressed concern about emideltide’s addictive potential.

The committee on Friday also voted 8 to 5 in favor of the widespread compounding of semax, which is marketed as a treatment for neurological conditions including strokes, migraines and facial nerve pain, as well as mental health disorders.

Animal studies suggest that semax could have anti-clotting and pain relieving effects, but one of the few human studies reported mixed results. Although the human research on semax is primarily as a nasal spray, it was endorsed by the committee as a spray and an injection.

The F. D. A. has said the final decision will be laid out in a proposed rule, giving the public an opportunity to comment.

Dr. Reshma Ramachandran, an assistant professor at the Yale School of Medicine who was not involved in the hearing, said she was concerned about how the peptides could be embraced by telehealth platforms. She said she worked on a recent study that found that such services issued GLP-1 prescriptions with little patient interaction, and often within five minutes.

“If F. D. A. moves to allow compounding of the peptides, you can expect these telehealth platforms to act as a pill mill for peptides with clinician oversight happening in name only,” she said in an email, “and not in practice.”

Rebecca Robbins contributed reporting.

Christina Jewett covers the Food and Drug Administration, which means keeping a close eye on drugs, medical devices, food safety and tobacco policy.

Dana G. Smith is a Times reporter covering personal health, particularly aging and brain health.

Trump Administration Admits Canceling Grants to States That Did Not Vote for Him

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Federal officials said in court documents that they halted billions of dollars in funding for energy projects to states “based solely” on whether they backed President Trump in the 2024 election.

By Tony Romm and Brad Plumer

Reporting from Washington

When the Trump administration canceled more than $7.5 billion in Biden-era federal grants for clean energy projects in October, it framed the move as an urgent corrective to protect taxpayer funds from waste.

But it wasn’t true.

In little-noticed court documents, federal officials acknowledged this month that they had terminated the funding “based solely” on political criteria, targeting projects in states that were represented by Democrats and had voted for Kamala Harris, the party’s presidential nominee, in the 2024 election.

The stunning admission offered an unvarnished glimpse into the way President Trump has weaponized the provision of federal education, energy, health, housing and infrastructure aid in his second term. Far from rooting out the sort of misspending that Mr. Trump sees as rife in Washington, the White House has instead sought to leverage the budget as a tool to assist its allies — or as a cudgel to hurt the president’s foes.

The saga illustrates the stakes as the Trump administration is completing a set of rules that would provide the president even greater control over more than $1 trillion in annual federal grants. To critics, the new regulation would only make it easier for Mr. Trump to strike wider tranches of congressionally approved funding over political differences.

“The risk that the Trump administration is willing to go to extreme lengths to politicize grant-making is not a hypothetical,” said Devin O’Connor, a senior fellow at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning group. He previously served at the White House budget office under former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

“If they are willing to be that blatant about it,” Mr. O’Connor said of the court filing, “then I think we should take seriously when they put forward a framework that would allow for the extreme politicization of grant-making across all of the federal government.”

The White House and the Energy Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The administration’s latest concession about the grants came in a lawsuit filed by a group of California researchers challenging various federal agencies that have canceled Biden-era funding.

After reviewing its spending, the Energy Department last fall created a list that recommended canceling more than 600 grants awarded by the Biden administration for a wide range of novel energy projects. That list included funding for projects in states represented by both Republicans and Democrats.

But in October, the White House budget office, led by Russell T. Vought, terminated only 284 of those grants. In a social media post announcing the news, Mr. Vought pointed to the motivations: “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled,” he said.

Months later, in court filings, federal officials indicated there was little else that had informed the final decision about which grants to cancel.

“With one exception,” a lawyer for the Energy Department conceded in a court filing this month, “the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing senators.”

The lawyer acknowledged that none of the grants were included in the October terminations “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor.”

In contrast, the administration left untouched hundreds of additional energy grants in states that were represented by Republicans and had backed Mr. Trump in the last election, even though the Energy Department had recommended canceling them, the government confirmed in the July court filing.

The cancellations coincided with a broader White House effort at the time to pressure Democratic lawmakers to cave in a fight over funding that had shut down the government. That month, Mr. Trump had vocalized the strategy: He threatened openly to slash what he described as “Democrat agencies,” while Mr. Vought announced a series of additional spending cuts targeting other Democratic-led states.

As a result, the administration’s actions halted funding for hundreds of energy projects, including upgrades to electrical grids in states like California and Oregon; efforts to reduce methane leaks from oil and gas operations in Colorado; and large hubs to produce clean-burning hydrogen fuels in California and the Pacific Northwest. Some awardees later sued the Trump administration in an effort to restore their grants.

Federal officials offered the new details about the grant cancellations as part of an agreement with plaintiffs meant to spare the government an exhaustive, evidence-uncovering process known as discovery, the court filings said. That process could have required federal agencies to hand over more damaging records.

The agreement applied to other federal agencies targeted by the lawsuit, including the Department of Transportation and the Department of Health and Human Services. Some agencies later revealed new details about the ways in which they reviewed their grants — using specific keywords tied to Mr. Trump’s political priorities and past directives — for possible cancellations, according to additional court documents this month. Lawyers for the plaintiffs did not respond to a request for comment.

The filings also appeared to undermine the congressional testimony of Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who spoke about the cancellations in a June House hearing: “No decisions were made on politics.”

The Energy Department previously conceded in two other cases that politics had been a “primary reason” for the cancellations. In those cases, Amit P. Mehta, a judge in U. S. District Court for the District of Columbia, eventually ruled that the agency had improperly canceled more than a dozen grants. But the latest concession is far more detailed and sweeping, and it sparked new anger on Capitol Hill.

Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the chamber’s appropriations committee, and Representative Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, a Democrat who leads her party on the House’s top energy appropriations panel, said in a joint statement on Friday that politically minded grant cuts amounted to an “outright un-American” weaponization of government.

“This administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: It terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the president in the 2024 election,” they added. “This is an astounding admission that the president and his team corruptly abused their power to kill good jobs and punish hard-working families because of their political views.”

Many Democrats have raised those same concerns as the White House looks to assert even greater control over federal grants. Those proposed regulations, which are expected to be completed by October, would require Mr. Trump’s political appointees to review all federal grants, with the power block or revoke money if they did not conform to administration priorities.

The White House has also sought to layer additional restrictions on grant recipients, limiting their political activities, memberships and even appearances at conferences, along with vague requirements that they cannot use the money for certain purposes, including those deemed “anti-American.”

The proposed rules have sparked widespread backlash from antipoverty groups, arts practitioners, city leaders, law enforcement officials, scientists and others. These critics flooded the government with thousands of comments arguing that the measures could undermine crucial government services.

But the administration has maintained that the new rules would help to prevent waste and align federal spending with Mr. Trump’s priorities. Testifying at a congressional hearing this month, Mr. Vought said it would ensure “that we have democratic control of the spending that is going out.”

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

Iranian Threat to Air Force One Prompted Plane Swap During NATO Summit

The New York Times July 24, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Times exclusive

The threat led the Secret Service to urge President Trump to fly out of Turkey on the old plane, raising questions about the security of the Qatari-donated jet.

By Tyler PagerJulian E. Barnes and Maggie Haberman

Reporting from Washington

President Trump abruptly switched aircraft when leaving Turkey this month after what officials judged to be a credible threat that Iranian proxy forces were targeting him and Air Force One, according to multiple people briefed on the matter.

The threat emerged while Mr. Trump was attending the NATO summit. He had flown into Ankara on the new Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8, which lacks the same advanced defensive capabilities of the old Air Force One, as The New York Times previously reported.

After the U. S. government picked up on the threat, the Secret Service urged Mr. Trump to change planes. He later announced that he would be using the old plane to leave the country.

The information about the nature of the threat, which has not been reported before, sheds light on why the White House moved swiftly to swap out the planes. It also underscores the concerns about the security of the donated jet, which Mr. Trump pressed to be ready as soon as possible for his use.

The information that U. S. officials had did not indicate that the proxy forces had any specific focus on the new plane, but rather that they were targeting Mr. Trump and whatever aircraft he was traveling in.

The people briefed on the matter spoke to The Times on condition of anonymity to discuss the information.

The White House did not comment. But in response to questions from The Times, a senior administration official pointed to Mr. Trump’s public remarks about Iran’s efforts to kill him and expressed confidence in the steps taken to protect the president and the traveling delegation. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.

The details of the threat were not disseminated widely even within the administration; some officials were told only that the switch in planes was a precautionary measure because of general concerns about Iran. Key members of Congress have not been briefed on the specific threat.

Mr. Trump initially said the switch in planes was to give American service members in Britain a chance to tour the new aircraft, and he denied the decision was security related. The Times reported that the Secret Service had urged him to switch planes.

After The Times reported this month that federal officials had significant concerns about the security capabilities of the jet, the government launched a leak investigation seeking grand jury testimony from several Times journalists as well as their phone records and those of their relatives. (The Justice Department withdrew the subpoenas on Thursday.)

The president appeared to acknowledge on Sunday that the plane was lacking some of the features that the older Boeings used as Air Force One have, telling a reporter who noted that the Qatari plane lacks antimissile defenses that it would soon be “maxed out.” The roughly 14-year-old plane went through a costly yet relatively rushed process to retrofit the aircraft to serve as Air Force One.

At the time of the swap, there were reports that Israel had shared intelligence with the United States about Iranian efforts to kill Mr. Trump. Some American officials viewed Israel’s intelligence with skepticism, believing it was an effort to provoke Mr. Trump to intensify attacks against Iran.

The threat to Air Force One in Turkey that prompted the change in airplanes was separate from the one attributed to Israeli intelligence, according to some of the people briefed on the matter.

The United States had resumed strikes against Iran while Mr. Trump was in Ankara, roughly 1,000 miles away from Tehran. While at the summit, Mr. Trump also spoke openly about Iranian efforts to try to kill him when asked about why he was swapping out the Qatari-donated jet for the older one.

“They want to take out the U. S. leader — me,” he said. “I’m on every list. I saw this morning, I’m on every single one of their lists. And so far, I guess I’ve been a little bit lucky, but that maybe doesn’t last very long.”

Forces with ties to Iran have long wanted to assassinate Mr. Trump, dating back to his first term when U. S. forces killed Qassim Suleimani, a top Iranian general.

Mr. Trump for years has complained about the state of the two airplanes that have served as Air Force One since 1990, saying they were not impressive enough to bring on foreign trips. Military officials separately expressed concerns that the current Air Force One jets had been used for many more years than had been intended.

Last year, Qatar said it was donating a Boeing 747-8 for Mr. Trump’s use, and Mr. Trump has said he plans to take it with him for his presidential library when he leaves office.

Officials have described the new plane as a “bridge” until the long-delayed Boeing jets commissioned by the Air Force are delivered.

Since Mr. Trump returned to the United States from Turkey, White House officials have said the new plane will be taken out of service for about one month this fall for additional upgrades.

“The new Air Force One is perfectly safe for the president’s travels, but will receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete,” Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said in a statement. “During that time, the president will fly on the old Air Force One.”

It is unclear what upgrades can be completed in such a short time frame.

At a briefing on Wednesday before the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, which was interrupted in April when a gunman rushed past a security checkpoint, Secret Service officials said the threat level for the agency’s protectees was the highest they had ever seen.

“The numbers at this agency, and certainly I’ve never seen in my 24-year career, they’re off the charts,” Sean Curran, the director of the Secret Service, told reporters. “I think the environment has become very volatile and that’s just across the board. I think not just to our protectees, but local officials. The threat picture and environment is as large as I’ve ever seen it.”

Mr. Curran was the head of Mr. Trump’s Secret Service protective detail between Mr. Trump’s two terms. He was among the agents with Mr. Trump when, as a candidate, he was shot in an assassination attempt during a rally in Butler, Pa., in July 2024.

Shawn McCreesh contributed reporting.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

C. D. C. Expands Cyclosporiasis Outbreak to Nine States

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Cyclospora Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania now join Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia in cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce.

By Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi

A large outbreak of cyclosporiasis associated with iceberg lettuce has been linked to another four states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At least 1,947 people have become ill and 98 have been hospitalized in the outbreak, which has expanded to include Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania. Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia were already part of the outbreak.

The Food and Drug Administration has linked the infections to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms and grown in central Mexico. On July 17, Taylor Farms recalled bagged iceberg lettuce sold in 27 states (including the nine states in the outbreak). The recalled lettuce was sent to restaurants, retail stores and food service distributors including Taco Bell and Walmart, but Taylor Farms has not provided clear information about exactly where the products were sold or served, and which specific products were affected.

The news comes as federal officials investigate other cyclospora outbreaks and illnesses across the country, which they say are unrelated to this outbreak. On Thursday, the F. D. A. announced a new outbreak with 72 cases, but did not identify the location or the potential source.

Nationwide, the C. D. C. has confirmed or is investigating more than 11,500 cases of cyclosporiasis, which is caused by a parasite typically spread through food or water contaminated with human feces.

The true number is likely far higher, health experts said. Many people with symptoms never get tested. And because it takes time for state health departments to report case numbers to the C. D. C. — and for the agency to confirm them — state totals often exceed those reported by the federal government.

The New York Times reached out to state health departments for their case counts, which collectively reached nearly 16,000 as of Friday afternoon.

In Michigan, which has reported the most cases, some labs have started to run out of the reagents that they need to test for cyclosporiasis, said Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, the state’s chief medical executive. Cases there climbed to 8,176 on Friday. Their tallies are “likely an undercount,” Dr. Bagdasarian said, given the shortage of lab supplies.

Health officials in Ohio, the state reporting the second highest number of infections, confirmed 2,576 cases on Thursday — more than double the number recorded on July 16.

Note: Data as of July 24. There are variations in how state health departments define cases and how frequently they update case counts. Some states report cumulative case counts for the entire year so far, though most cyclosporiasis cases usually occur between May 1 and August 31.

Source: Case data are from state health agencies.

Arfa Momin, Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi/The New York Times

On Friday, Sean Doyle, a spokesman for North Carolina’s health department, said that investigators there had not yet identified a single source of cyclosporiasis, but that parsley, cilantro, berries and romaine lettuce had come up most often during interviews with sick patients.

Mr. Doyle said that this wasn’t proof that those items were causing illnesses and that, relative to the other items on the list, berries were less likely to be the source.

On Tuesday, cases in North Carolina rose to 561 from 307 a week before.

This has been the worst year on record for cyclosporiasis in the United States, which has seen an average of about 2,800 cases per year nationwide since 2016. Because the parasite thrives in warmer temperatures, cases typically rise between May 1 and Aug. 30. Even so, this year’s count is far higher than the usual summer surge.

Cyclospora infections have continued to rise in the nine states included in the newly expanded outbreak. Indiana reported 710 cases on Friday, more than triple the count from July 14. And Kentucky’s tally shot up to 468 cases on Friday, compared with 192 on July 15.

On Friday, the F. D. A. said that the number of confirmed cases was expected to continue rising despite Taylor Farms’ recall. The agency said it can take as long as six weeks for the C. D. C. and state officials to determine if a sick person is part of the outbreak.

An earlier version of this article misstated the date of Ohio’s previous case count. It was July 16, not July 14.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi is a Times reporter focusing on nutrition and sleep.

Help! I Might Be a Tradwife!

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By JoAnna Novak

Ms. Novak, a poet and a professor of creative writing, writes a newsletter on culture and parenting.

When I heard that Netflix was rebooting “Little House on the Prairie,” I was hopeful, if a little wary. Though I’d never watched the original TV show, I’d grown up so besotted by Laura Ingalls Wilder’s novels that not only had I read them all but I even owned the supplemental “The Little House Cookbook,” by Barbara M. Walker. I paged through frontier recipes for fried salt pork and gravy with the same longing I experienced when reading Wilder’s prose: the wish to be transported. Tuning in to the new Netflix offering a few weeks after giving birth to my second son, I suppose I once again had that hope.

The new “Little House” isn’t exactly transporting, and that’s why I feel a little disappointed. To the contrary, it seems all too familiar, like cosplay for a fantasy frontier. It’s a visual feast of chemises, bonnets and limpid-eyed girls with flower crowns haloing their Pre-Raphaelite coifs. The show also appears, perhaps inevitably, like an infomercial for the tradwife lifestyle, set to a soundtrack of whinnying horses and chirring bugs. The Ingalls girls wash their clothes in pristine streams, stoke fires while sucking peppermint sticks and slumber under patchwork quilts. Who wouldn’t yearn for this life?

The “Little House” reboot arrives in the midst of a tradwife moment. Caro Claire Burke’s best-selling novel “Yesteryear” (soon to be a feature film starring Anne Hathaway) imagines a modern-day tradwife transported back to the real-life deprivations of 1855. One of the ur-tradwife influencers, Hannah Neeleman, who has nine children, has opened the Ballerina Farm Store in Midway, Utah, transforming that town into a trad tourist trap. Part of the reasoning, no doubt, for Netflix’s series is that the original, which debuted in 1974, was, according to Nielsen, the most streamed legacy title as recently as 2024, racking up 13.3 billion minutes of viewing time that year, which is roughly 40 minutes for every person living in America.

My first exposure to the world of tradwives came while I was teaching a food writing workshop, and a grad student wrote an admiring essay about a young mother from Texas whom she followed on Instagram. This young mother, Nara Smith, 24, makes homemade nut butter, cares for five children and, according to my student’s essay, shares “the joys of serving those she loves while still fulfilling her career as a model.” Ms. Smith also has 12.5 million followers on TikTok and 4.8 million followers on Instagram.

As a woman who’s always believed that my life purpose is synonymous not with my fecundity or my homemaking prowess but with my artistic ambitions, I’m decidedly not the audience for this kind of content. The tradwife performs wholesome homesteading for online public consumption — milking cows with apple-cheeked little ones trailing her long, organic cotton skirts — while I’ve always approached my maternal duties with a little more ambivalence, scribbling drafts of poems from my seat on a concrete bench in the muggy YMCA pool balcony as my 6-year-old shows off his cannonballs.

But maybe it was the moment when I was slicing strawberries from the farm share and scooping homemade coconut-almond granola into my son’s Greek yogurt that a startling revelation dawned on me. Or maybe it happened while I was watching “Little House” and its liberally tendered tropes of hardscrabble fairy tales. I’m definitely not a tradwife — but maybe I’m a little tradwife-curious? Maybe I have a few latent tradwife tendencies?

Maybe more than a few. Maybe more than tendencies.

I’m not suggesting I’m suited for raising a brood of children or for living on a 19th-century homestead like the influencer in “Yesteryear,” who wakes up having been whisked from her performance of 19th-century hardship to the real thing. I have no desire to cosplay as a milkmaid or shepherdess, and I can’t abide the overt tradwife staging of conservative social values, religious doctrine, traditional gender roles and natalism. I also don’t subscribe to the idea that the female spirit is best channeled into servitude and sustenance-providing at home, sweet heteronormative home.

But I have realized that my blanket aversion to the performance of domestic life as a source of fulfillment may be a little misguided. I was raised by a stay-at-home mom, herself raised by a mom who attended culinary school, and my mother always modeled to me the practice of finding purpose in the kitchen, punching down dough, laying a towel over the bowl, letting it rise. In my home today, cooking isn’t for show; it’s an expression of the beauty of making something tangible and nourishing.

How can I renounce the regressive side of tradwives while blissfully kneading my own milk bread dough? How can I deny the appeal of the Hannah Neelemans and Nara Smiths of the world when my own household habits help balance my workaholism, keep me present and mindful in my body? Anchored to a professional life that’s increasingly screenbound, I find that taking 20 minutes to, say, arrange stalks of scarlet rhubarb by height in a caramel-coated cast-iron pan really grounds me. Makes me happy, even. Many of my most tradwife-like proclivities — cooking and baking and taking what may be an above-average pleasure in polishing copper pots — are the very habits that help keep me sane.

So, like many others, I’m learning to reassess the value of so-called grandma hobbies, those frontier-adjacent activities that — surprise, surprise — don’t also require you to be a religious zealot or an antisuffragist. Of course, for women like my mother and her mother, these kinds of hobbies were acts of domestic generosity but also of necessity. All those hours of kitchen-bound chores weren’t performed for legions of online followers but were simply required by the demands of family life.

Toward the end of the first episode of “Little House,” titled “Independence,” Ma Ingalls lies in an ivory tent, bathed in a romantic shadow play of lamplight and the big Kansas night sky. She’s pregnant and has sustained a foot injury in her first days on the frontier, and, ever the stalwart spouse, she tells her husband that even though she’s frightened by their new circumstances, she believes in him. She counters her own fear with hope of what this new way of life might offer. “What if this is where we finally become who we were meant to be?” she says.

I guess the tradwife life may be just another waypost on a person’s journey to figuring out who she’s meant to be. And maybe I’m less a tradwife than someone who’s come to accept that she needs a regular infusion of domestic ephemerality. I love my kitchen pursuits for how invisible I become while doing them — how the practice even allows for a little psychological and philosophical space.

I imagine other people find this same kind of contemplation in sewing, or knitting, or mending, or, yes, even milking a cow. So even if I don’t live the full tradwife lifestyle — for anyone else’s consumption, or my own — I can still venerate those tasks that remind me that who I am meant to be is fluid and multitudinous. It can be expressed in how I stir a wooden spoon through water and flour to make the tangzhong that is the starter for my son’s favorite milk bread, and also in a poem I might write, born of my fascination with the same word.

I think you’ve hit on a key piece when you identify an influencer promoting the trad wife life, while running a business (her online presence is clearly a business) and being a model. It seems all the women promoting this life style don’t actually live it, ala Erika Kirk. They are professional women with careers that don’t conform to what they preach. I don’t like the either/or stance most take. The point of feminism is to say women have choices and those choices aren’t mutually exclusive. I’m highly educated, I raised three children, had a successful corporate career, love to cook, quilt, garden, read, travel, etc. those are all facets of the life I’ve lived. If someone else is happy raising six kids on a farm and churning her own butter, great. She’s found her place. My beef with the trad wife movement is the limitations it tries to impose. The do this - don’t do that mentally.

There is great joy to be found in domestic work if one is suited for it. Cooking, baking, gardening, nourishing children. adding beauty to the home. It can be fulfilling for some. This is not the same as being a trad wife influencer. Play acting for clicks and money is not living a fulfilling life. Fame and riches are toxic.
