Small Businesses Sue Just Hours After Trump’s Latest Tariffs

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The businesses are represented by the Liberty Justice Center, a legal group that has successfully challenged President Trump’s past duties.

By Tony Romm and Ana Swanson

Reporting from Washington

Two small businesses sued the Trump administration on Friday over the latest tariffs it has imposed around the world, touching off another legal battle that could redefine President Trump’s powers to wage a global trade war.

The new challenge concerned the tariffs that the government had put in place just hours earlier, covering more than 80 countries including Canada, Mexico and the 27 members of the European Union. The lawsuit, filed in a federal trade court, argued that the Trump administration had misused the law in its attempt to recreate the same system of duties that judges had already ruled illegal.

The plaintiffs in the case are Burlap and Barrel, a New York spice retailer, and Collective Horology, a California watch seller. They are represented by the Liberty Justice Center, a legal group that has successfully challenged Mr. Trump’s tariffs repeatedly in his second term.

Lawyers for the organization had previously joined state officials in invalidating the president’s original roster of punishing, country-by-country duties at the Supreme Court in February, and they similarly succeeded against Mr. Trump’s temporary replacement for those tariffs in the spring. The Liberty Justice Center has won over judges with arguments that Mr. Trump has violated the Constitution by usurping tariff powers reserved for Congress.

At the heart of the most recent fight is Mr. Trump’s use of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. In general, the provision of law allows the government to investigate other countries’ trade practices, and it permits the president to impose tariffs on those that are found to behave unfairly.

Generally, Section 301 is understood to be settled policy, unlike some of Mr. Trump’s earlier tariff actions, which relied on novel interpretations of federal law. In fact, the president’s use of Section 301 to impose duties on Chinese goods during his first term survived several court challenges.

But small businesses said that Mr. Trump had stretched the statute beyond its limit this time, pointing to the way that his administration conducted its investigations — and the fact that it had planned to impose tariffs even before its reviews concluded.

One of the investigations specifically concerned claims that other countries had failed to crack down on “forced labor,” which had left U. S. businesses that follow such laws prohibiting coercive practices at a disadvantage. In June, the administration said it found fault in 86 countries, including U. S. allies that have laws banning forced labor practices. The tariffs it levied on Friday range between 10 percent to 12.5 percent, with little differentiation based on the country or its labor laws.

Canada, which has a law prohibiting forced labor, faces a 10 percent tariff on its exports. China, which U. S. officials frequently criticize for using forced labor, is subject to a tariff that is only 2.5 percent higher. Foreign officials say they have also received assurances from the United States that their tariff rates will be the same as they were under the trade deals they previously negotiated.

In response, lawyers for the two small businesses argued in their lawsuit that Jamieson Greer, the U. S. trade representative, did not adequately investigate each country. They contend that the administration had erred by studying the countries and issuing its findings and subsequent tariffs in bulk.

The opponents also pointed to past statements from Mr. Trump and his deputies, who had said they hoped to use Section 301 to replicate the tariffs declared illegal previously by the courts. That, according to the lawyers, suggested that the outcome of the investigations were predetermined, not based on the facts uncovered.

“Those statements, in combination with the timing, scope and rate structure of the final action, support the inference that the Section 301 tariffs, by design, replace the invalidated global tariff regime rather than constitute measures selected to obtain elimination of identified economy-specific practices,” they argued in their lawsuit.

Lawyers for the Liberty Justice Center said it was not clear how taxing imports on such a wide set of goods would help to change other countries’ labor practices. And they said the scope of the administration’s efforts raised constitutional concerns, arguing that a blessing by the court would greatly expand Mr. Trump’s power to impose tariffs without Congress.

“Forced labor is morally indefensible, but an important objective does not give the government permission to ignore the law,” said Sara Albrecht, the chairman and chief executive of the center. “The administration allowed one global tariff to expire and immediately replaced it with another under a different statute. Changing the statute doesn’t change the law.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. But Mr. Trump, commenting on the tariffs on Friday, described them as “standard,” pointing to the fact he had used them in the past.

When asked if any country could take action that would fully remove the tariffs, a senior administration official said Thursday that the government welcomed countries to take action but that the tariffs probably could not be “eliminated overnight.”

The official said that it was “too simplistic” to say the new tariffs replicated the ones struck down by the Supreme Court, and that they differed in important ways. But the official added that Mr. Trump would always use the tools at his disposal to achieve his trade policy goals, and that the president was not going to allow his trade policy to be undermined simply because one tool was limited by a court.

The lawsuit from the Liberty Justice Center was not the only legal challenge to be filed on Friday. Another group of small businesses, including Learning Resources, an educational toy company, similarly sued the administration on Friday over its new tariffs under Section 301. That company had also participated in the successful, earlier fight against Mr. Trump’s original duties.

The new cases will send Mr. Trump and his opponents back to the Court of International Trade, a specialized federal circuit that has repeatedly found that the administration exceeded its power under law. The past fights have been tense, evident in the continuing battle over the roughly $160 billion that the government owes to importers who paid illegal tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Once again, states opposed to Mr. Trump’s tariffs could soon join the fight. Dan Rayfield, the attorney general of Oregon, said he was “reviewing the latest action to determine next steps.”

Citing Mr. Trump’s past tariff defeats, he criticized the president for “trying yet another way to impose the same costs on working families who are already struggling to get by.”

More duties are expected from Mr. Trump in the coming weeks, some of which could be affected by the new legal battle. The administration has explored a second tranche of tariffs using Section 301, targeting 15 countries and the European Union to offset what the White House calls unfair practices in their manufacturing sectors. And Mr. Trump on Friday said the government would open still another investigation into the European Union over its practice of fining U. S. tech companies.

The administration also invoked this week an obscure law to impose a 50 percent tariff on billions of dollars of Canadian exports. In that case, the president relied on a portion of the statute that has never been used to impose duties. That provision will not go into effect for 30 days. If it ultimately does go into effect, legal experts said it was also likely to be challenged.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Gretchen Whitmer Endorses Haley Stevens in Michigan Senate Race

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Whitmer, a popular second-term governor, is wading into one of the most contentious Democratic primaries of this year’s midterms.

By Tim Balk

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Representative Haley Stevens on Friday in Michigan’s hotly contested Democratic Senate primary race, seen as a major test of the Democratic Party’s direction.

The endorsement from Ms. Whitmer, a popular governor and one of the country’s highest-profile Democrats, arrived 11 days ahead of the primary. Ms. Stevens, a centrist and a favorite of the Democratic establishment, is working to fend off Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former health official running with support from left-wing leaders including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

Ms. Stevens has promised to offer an antidote to chaos on Washington, while Dr. El-Sayed has vowed to fight the political system and pursue ambitious policies including universal health care.

They have starkly different positions on Israel: Ms. Stevens has described herself as a “proud pro-Israel Democrat.” Dr. El-Sayed has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.

The winner of the primary is expected to face former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in one of the country’s most competitive Senate battlegrounds in November.

In a video statement, Ms. Whitmer compared herself to Ms. Stevens, saying, “Just like me, Haley will do whatever it takes to get things done for the people of Michigan.”

“We need her now more than ever,” Ms. Whitmer said. “Republicans in D. C. are making your life harder and more expensive. Tariffs. Cuts to Medicaid. Soaring gas prices. It’s all piling on. Luckily, Haley is taking them on.”

Ms. Whitmer, who defeated Dr. El-Sayed in the 2018 Democratic primary for governor in Michigan, also said Ms. Stevens “is as Michigan as it gets.”

The governor’s endorsement could be a boost for Ms. Stevens, who trails Dr. El-Sayed in some polls ahead of the Aug. 4 primary. A recent Detroit News/WDIV survey found that 52 percent of Michigan voters said they approved of Ms. Whitmer, compared with 39 percent who said they did not.

In a social media post, Ms. Stevens said she was “absolutely thrilled” to have the governor’s endorsement, calling Ms. Whitmer a “champion for our state” who “understands the stakes of this race.”

A spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, said in a statement that the “corporate establishment has closed ranks and made their pick — now, Michigan voters will get to make theirs.”

Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting.

Americans Told to Stay Home as Canada Opens International Bridge

The New York Times July 24, 2026

U. S. Tariffs and Trade

Advertisement

Supported by

After a delay ordered by President Trump and new tariffs against Canada, the bridge between Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit finally opened on Friday.

By Ian Austen

Reporting from Ottawa

When Canada and Michigan agreed to build a multibillion-dollar bridge at the busiest border crossing between the United States and Canada, the relationship between the two nations was dramatically different.

In 2012, President Barack Obama was admired by an overwhelming majority of Canadians in polls, and the countries were often in agreement, including on border security and increased military cooperation. To honor both countries, the bridge linking Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit was named after the Canadian hockey star Gordie Howe, who played 25 seasons with the Detroit Red Wings.

On Friday, the 6.4 billion Canadian dollar bridge (about $4.5 billion) opened, at least ceremonially, with a president in the White House who has shaken Canada’s economy with tariffs, mused about annexing the country and stalled the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge.

The latest blow came this week when President Trump, who is as disliked in Canada as Mr. Obama was acclaimed, announced 50 percent tariffs on a variety of Canadian products worth $20 billion. For Canada, it’s all been too much. It rescinded its invitations to American officials to jointly open the bridge. And it moved the ceremony from the international border line in the center of the bridge to a vast expanse of pavement at the inspection plaza of the Canada Border Services Agency.

“In light of trade action threatened by the United States earlier this week, it would be inappropriate to proceed with a celebratory event between the two countries,” the office of Canada’s infrastructure minister said in a statement. “The Gordie Howe International Bridge remains a vital infrastructure project that reflects years of hard work and will be a major economic driver.”

In the middle of the ceremony, which included a ribbon cutting and an Indigenous drumming ceremony, Mr. Trump remarked on social media about the change of plans.

“Canada disinvited the United States of America to the opening of the Gordie Howe Bridge, which is fine, considering they are paying substantial TARIFFS to the United States,” Mr. Trump wrote.

Mr. Trump added that the 2012 agreement between Canada and Michigan governing the bridge “no longer stands.” Speaking with reporters after the ceremony, Gregor Robertson, Canada’s infrastructure minister said that is not the case.

Some invitations for the ceremonial opening have now been withdrawn twice. At the apparent request of the Trump administration, an opening scheduled for June was canceled days before the event.

Cars and trucks won’t cross the Gordie Howe Bridge until Monday. But with soaring towers and animated lights on its suspension cables, the structure is a flashy version of the sort of big projects that Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, a Liberal, has championed as an antidote to Mr. Trump’s tariffs.

“It’s regretful that this is what it’s come to,” said Drew Dilkens, the mayor of Windsor and an invited guest. “It just speaks to where we’re at with our relationship with the United States.”

He added: “It is a bit underwhelming, but that’s OK. We are where we are.”

Mr. Dilkens is among the many Canadians who hope the opening will finally end a more than two-decade-long battle with Michigan’s wealthy Moroun family that owns the Ambassador Bridge, a nearly century-old span upstream that currently carries around $300 million a day in trade.

Legal action and political lobbying by Matthew Moroun, a Detroit-based trucking magnate, first meant that Canada was left entirely funding the construction of the new international bridge after lawmakers in Michigan, which shares ownership of it, refused to contribute.

In February, following a meeting between Mr. Moroun and Howard Lutnick, the secretary of commerce, Mr. Trump said he would block the bridge’s opening in a social media post citing several grievances. The New York Times reported that a month earlier, Mr. Moroun donated $1 million to a super PAC devoted to Mr. Trump.

A tentative deal that gives the United States a small portion of toll revenue for 15 years was reached this month, leading to the opening.

The agreement is vague on many key points. Originally, Canada planned to use any toll revenue that remained after covering the operating expenses of the bridge to pay back its construction costs — estimated to take at least 50 years. Then Michigan and Canada would split any profit.

Instead, for the first 15 years, the U. S. will get half of any surplus over operating costs, which it will use for economic development “for the benefit of the United States and trade between Canada and the United States.”

While Mr. Trump praised the agreement, forecasts published by the authority that will operate the bridge for Canada and Michigan suggested that it will initially generate nothing or relatively little money for the American fund.

For the current year, the authority estimates that it will only take in 35.8 million Canadian dollars while spending 135.6 million on operations, leaving a loss of nearly 100 million dollars. Next fiscal year it forecasts a 2.9 million loss followed by a profit (excluding repaying Canada’s construction costs) of 18 million dollars in 2028.

The United States has not announced how it will distribute the money from its fund. On Thursday, Mr. Carney said the government anticipated that the United States will receive about 5 percent of the cost of building the bridge, about 320 million Canadian dollars, over 15 years.

“I genuinely am hopeful that at some point in the future, we could close this bridge for a couple hours and have the proper celebration that it deserves,” Mr. Dilkens said. “It would have to be at a time when the relationship’s a little stronger than it is today.”

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes. com.

Your Car Lives Where?

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

No longer satisfied by regular parking garages, some drivers are upgrading their luxury vehicles’ homes.

By Jessica Shaw

Jessica Shaw drives a 2007 Prius and is probably looking for a parking spot in Brooklyn at this very moment.

Jack Griffin, a former racecar driver, owns a double-size condominium in Carrollton, Texas, complete with a library, fully stocked wet bar and custom-designed floors.

The big-screen television on the main level is 50 inches. A bigger-screen television on the mezzanine level is 75. Placed precisely throughout are photos of his races, from Le Mans (France) to Daytona (Florida), along with a few family heirlooms.

Griffin, 81, doesn’t live in the condo, but 11 of his 12 Porsches do.

Even thinking about relegating square footage to a car is enough to make a New Yorker go mad. To anyone who engages in the 45-minute ritualistic hunt for a neighborhood parking spot, praying to the car gods that the fire hydrant at the end of the block is just the devil’s mirage, there is nothing more luxurious than an assigned parking spot.

But to a growing number of autophiles around the country, assigned parking is incomprehensibly basic.

The status spot is now a “car condo,” which is essentially a pied-à-terre for wheels and the people who love them. It’s part garage and part club, and developments for these condos are now all over the country.

“It’s a remote man cave, a second home away from home,” said Jonathan Miller, president of Miller Samuel, a real estate consulting firm. “This is not just you park your car there and go back to your house. It’s a place to hang out in privacy from your own home.”

And while car condos are still “extremely niche,” Miller added, “we’re in an environment where it’s about acquiring other physical assets because of the wealth effect.” In other words, the ultrarich are making more and spending more.

Jon Summer, who owns Garaza Design in Scottsdale, Ariz., said his clients spend $400,000 to $1 million to customize their spaces. For “the first few garages we did,” he said, customers “would spend $50 to 100,000 on steel cabinetry.”

“Then,” he said, “it was, ‘Oh we need a mezzanine.’ Then ‘We need floors’ and ‘We need lifts.’”

At the Toy Barn in Scottsdale, he collaborated with Jaimee Rose Interiors to turn a car condo into a homage to Ralph Lauren.

It’s also about something money can’t buy: community. Griffin, the former racecar driver, said, “I know so many people my age who sit at home and watch ‘Gunsmoke’ all day long.”

He, by contrast, said he had become friendly with a retired Southwest Airlines pilot a few garages down and a well-known Texas rancher with 12 Corvettes. “We have something to get up in the morning for,” he said. “If someone doesn’t show up to the garage for a couple of weeks, we check up on them.”

Griffin owns Garages of America, which developed 14 stand-alone garages full of condos. He has started an in-person gathering called “Garages and Gearheads Getting Coffee,” named after Jerry Seinfeld’s series “Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee.”

If the car-condo business is booming, it’s because the car craze has never been hotter. According to a study released in December by the Boston Consulting Group, the U. S. luxury and exotic car market is expected to nearly double to up to $215 billion from $110 billion in the next decade.

A 62-car condo garage called The Hangar in the Hamptons is scheduled to open next year, the first in the Hamptons. “It took five years to find the spot,” said Scott Cunningham, the Hangar’s founder and chief executive. “We love that area, but the issue was finding enough land that would allow us to build.”

In the end, he scored space near the Francis S. Gabreski Airport, a joint airstrip for military and private customers, in Southampton, N. Y., because the plane noise made it undesirable for potential homeowners (and more accommodating to things like car condos).

Cunningham would not reveal prices, but he said he had a list of more than 100 people interested in buying condos and expected to sell out before the building was completed. “Our owners don’t have what they call ‘price sensitivity,’” Cunningham said. “We want to be the Four Seasons, not the Holiday Inn.”

Some car lovers laugh at the over-the-top trend. “These condos are just an extension of the competition guys have every time they get together,” joked Tom Yang, a former audio engineer for the “Late Show With David Letterman” who now restores Ferraris in Hudson, N. Y. “It’s like the arms race.”

The former roller rink he owned next door to his shop will open on Sept. 1 as Hudson Valley Car Storage, a $400-a-month luxury garage — decidedly not condos. As he put it, “I want to do stuff with cars — not be a real estate developer.”

Opposing Defense Bill, Democrats Shift Their Tactics

The New York Times July 24, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Crossing what was once seen as a political red line, Democrats voted against the usually bipartisan measure, registering dissent about the war in Iran.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from the Capitol

Senator Angus King, the Maine independent aligned with Democrats, has never in more than a decade in Congress opposed the annual Pentagon policy measure, a bill that traditionally draws overwhelming bipartisan backing by lawmakers eager to show support for America’s military.

Yet Mr. King this month crossed what was once considered a political red line, by joining Senate Democrats in unanimously blocking a bill that would lay out more than $1.15 trillion in Pentagon spending.

On Wednesday, 205 House Democrats voted against that chamber’s version of the legislation, a striking break from the past when only the most liberal Democrats dared to oppose the annual defense bill.

The shift underscored the hardening partisan divide over the war with Iran and its elevation as an issue in the coming midterm campaigns. It also highlighted an evolution in the strategy of leading Democrats in Congress, who have become more responsive in recent months to pressure from voters to reject the status quo.

“It is hard to go home and say we need this level of increase when I just learned that, for example, over 4,000 kids are losing SNAP benefits in Maine,” Mr. King said, referring to federal nutrition assistance.

The turnaround reflects what Democrats see as strong voter sentiment against the war. It also points to a realization born of the two recent government shutdown fights Democrats waged with President Trump and congressional Republicans that positions that were once viewed as politically treacherous — such as opposing a defense bill, voting against homeland security spending or blocking government funding overall — can sometimes be political winners instead.

“I said to our caucus, ‘We cannot do business as usual,’” Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said in recounting the argument he made for Democrats to band together to block the Pentagon legislation as a proxy for their resistance to the war in Iran.

In an interview, he called the war a “horrible fiasco.”

“It is not just political,” Mr. Schumer said. “It is how we really feel and how the American people feel. So we are just doing our job by voting against these things.”

The Pentagon measure is just one notable break from ingrained voting patterns by Democrats who have become more responsive to pressure from voters.

This month, almost half of House Democrats voted to cut off federal aid to Israel over its conduct of the war in Gaza, an almost unthinkable rupture after decades of unflinching support for the Jewish state. Democrats, along with a handful of Republicans, have also blocked the extension of a terror surveillance tool that was previously sacrosanct in a fight with the president over his appointment of an inexperienced loyalist to a key intelligence position.

The votes came after Democrats, in a running spending fight with Republicans and Mr. Trump, voted multiple times to block funding for government agencies and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown after years of avoiding such votes out of a fear of causing a constituent backlash.

The unwritten rule in Washington has long been that the party deemed responsible for opposing a national security measure, blocking government funding or standing in the way of a raise for the troops would pay a steep political price. But the old rules do not appear to be applying the way they once did. Instead, when Mr. Schumer initially cleared the way last year for a spending deal with Republicans to avert a shutdown, he faced an onslaught of criticism from the Democratic ranks.

Democrats say their opposition votes have now been proved correct, particularly in light of public opinion against federal immigration tactics and the war.

“I think sometimes members of Congress put themselves in the Washington bubble and scared themselves in a way that was not justified by public sentiment,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland. “But when it comes to a bill that essentially endorses an illegal war in Iran, you better stand up because the American people have been way ahead of Congress on some issues.”

Republicans quickly sought to blame Democrats for playing politics and shame them for stalling Pentagon legislation that Democrats had helped mold.

“Do Democrats think that voting against our national defense and our nation’s military will gain them points with their base?” Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, asked on the Senate floor. “Or do they simply think they can afford to ignore our nation’s defense needs until some hostile actor takes advantage of our weakness?”

“I don’t know,” he added, “but I do know that our nation is less safe because of Democratic actions.”

Democrats, however, believe they are on solid ground given their reservations about the conduct of the war and the substantial spending increases being demanded by the Trump administration.

They shrugged off the potential political repercussions for opposing what is officially known as the National Defense Authorization Act, a bill that has passed annually for more than 60 years and is a particular point of congressional pride.

“I have never voted against the N. D. A. A., but I will because it is perceived, understandably, as a referendum on the Iran war,” said Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut and a member of the Armed Services Committee. “We’ve been given no opportunity to vote on the war, which is not only our obligation but our right. We have been stonewalled.”

Even the two top Democrats on the military panels, Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Representative Adam Smith of Washington, are opposing the measures they were closely involved in writing. It has been a wrenching decision for both.

“They are taking us down roads that I think are incredibly dangerous and make it very hard to maintain that bipartisan spirit,” Mr. Smith said on Wednesday about the Trump administration as he voted against the Pentagon legislation. “I can’t support this bill. It profoundly hurts me, because I believe in this process.”

Other Democrats say there are too many unanswered questions about the war and the administration’s strategy, as well as the spending increases being sought, for them to agree to move forward now with the Pentagon legislation. It has in the past been approved late in the year, and Democratic defense hawks still see a path to backing it at a later date.

“I hope that I am going to be able to vote for an N. D. A. A. before the year is over,” said Senator Jeanne Shaheen, Democrat of New Hampshire.

For now, Democrats are holding tight against it despite their track record of support.

“Although the bill doesn’t specifically address Iran, it is inevitably part of the discussion,” Mr. King said. “It’d be hard to explain a vote to say: ‘Well, I’m against the Iran war. It’s never been justified. It’s never been authorized. But I voted for a bill that funds the department.’”

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Measles Cases Hit New Record in U. S., as Vaccination Rates Wane

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

More measles cases have been reported in the United States in the last two years than in all the years from 2000 through 2024 combined.

By Teddy Rosenbluth

The United States has now recorded more cases of measles in 2026 than in any other year since the virus was declared eliminated in 2000, a grim sign that the country may be headed toward a new era in which the disease regularly sickens thousands every year.

On Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced that there have been 2,318 confirmed cases of measles so far this year. The case count toppled the record set last year, when measles infected more than 2,200 Americans and killed two unvaccinated children. More measles cases have been reported in the United States in the last two years than in all the years from 2000 through 2024 combined.

Reversing course on measles would require a nationwide push to improve vaccination rates, a prospect that experts said seemed unlikely under the leadership of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has halted funding for vaccine hesitancy research, downplayed the risks of measles and spearheaded a hunt for evidence that vaccines are unsafe.

In November, a panel of international experts will meet to determine whether the United States has lost its elimination status, which has long been viewed as one of the country’s crowning public health achievements.

“This is just going to keep happening,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “It’s going to mean living in a perpetual state of vulnerability and risk until we get vaccination levels up.”

Many of the cases reported this year were tied to a large outbreak in South Carolina that took root last October in a close-knit, evangelical Slavic community and quickly became the largest outbreak in the United States since 2000. The outbreak, which ultimately sickened nearly 1,000 people, was declared over by state health officials in April.

Still, the virus is far from contained. Utah is fighting an outbreak that began along its border with Arizona last summer and has led to more than 700 cases, spread across every jurisdiction in the state. Virginia health officials have reported more than 170 cases from an outbreak that began in mid-May. Pennsylvania is grappling with an outbreak that has sickened more than 100 people this year.

In total, the C. D. C. has reported 35 new measles outbreaks this year. A vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccine status was unknown.

The string of outbreaks is no surprise to public health experts, who have watched vaccination rates tick down in recent years. Nationally, the measles vaccination rate fell during the Covid-19 pandemic and has not rebounded to the 95 percent required to stem the spread of the measles virus in a community. While the latest national data shows that about 93 percent of kindergartners have received the measles, mumps and rubella shot, that protection is uneven: Some communities have vaccination rates approaching 100 percent, while others have rates below 80 percent.

Measles, one of the most contagious diseases, is exceptionally good at exploiting those pockets with weak immunity.

“It’s going to find people who aren’t immune,” said Dr. David Kimberlin, a pediatric infectious disease expert at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. “It’s like a heat-seeking missile.”

Children have borne the brunt of the infections, making up more than 70 percent of confirmed cases. More than 80 children and adolescents have been hospitalized this year for complications like pneumonia, which leaves patients gasping for air, and brain swelling, which can cause lasting damage, including blindness, deafness and intellectual disabilities. (There are no treatments for measles, though researchers are trying to develop them.)

While many of the children who became ill were vulnerable to the virus because their parents opted them out of the measles vaccine, local health departments have also reported several cases in babies too young for the shot and people with health conditions that make them ineligible for the vaccine.

The outbreaks have taken a steep economic toll, as state and local public health departments strained to track down everyone exposed to the virus, start vaccination campaigns and analyze tests. Researchers have estimated that in 2025, each measles case cost the United States more than $100,000, when factoring in health care spending and the days of missed work for sick people or caretakers.

The United States is not the only country grappling with a measles resurgence. Canada, which lost its elimination status last year, has reported more than a thousand cases this year. Health officials in Bangladesh confirmed more than 8,000 infections since March.

Still, several experts said the Trump administration’s response — which has not included any national push to increase vaccination rates — has done the United States no favors.

Courtney Spencer, a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said the department has mounted an “aggressive outbreak response,” and pointed to the $8.5 million it has given states to help contain outbreaks and the technical assistance that the C. D. C. has provided to those areas.

She added that the department has said, referring to the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella, that “M. M. R. vaccination remains the best protection against measles.”

Dr. Jonathan Temte, a former chairman of the C. D. C.’s vaccine advisory committee, said: “We have seen virtually no national messaging. We’ve seen no ad campaigns.” He added, “I think that really tells us something about their priorities.”

Dispute Over Trump Tariffs Snarls Russia Sanctions Deal

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Lindsey Graham (1955-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

A bipartisan bill championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham has become mired in a dispute over expanding President Trump’s tariff power.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

A dispute between President Trump and Democrats in Congress over his tariff authority has emerged as the biggest obstacle to legislation imposing sweeping new sanctions on Russia, threatening bipartisan hopes to move quickly after Senator Lindsey Graham’s death on a bill he championed.

The dispute centers on a provision of the proposal that would allow — but not require — Mr. Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that purchase a significant amount of Russian oil and other energy products, and to lift them if he chose to.

Democrats had long bristled at giving the president such discretion, but Republicans argued that doing so was essential to increasing pressure on Moscow and asserted that Mr. Trump would veto any legislation that sought to force his hand.

But as the Trump administration continues its whipsawing tariff campaign, top Democrats have dug in against the move, unwilling to hand the president broader trade powers at a time when they argue he is already trampling over Congress to claim broad authority where he has none.

Representative Richard E. Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, and Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the ranking Democrat on the Finance Committee, warned in a joint statement this week that they could not support legislation that “hands President Trump a blank check to continue his chaotic tariff agenda.”

Their concerns took on added urgency just after midnight on Friday, when the Trump administration imposed tariffs of 10 percent to 12.5 percent on goods from dozens of trading partners. It was the latest expansion of Mr. Trump’s aggressive push to go around Congress and move unilaterally to shield the U. S. economy from foreign competition.

The disagreement has complicated what many lawmakers had hoped would be a bipartisan consensus to honor Mr. Graham, the South Carolina Republican, by enacting a key piece of his long campaign to increase economic pressure on Moscow.

The legislation would impose sweeping sanctions on Russia while targeting countries that purchase its oil, gas and uranium, an effort supporters argue is intended to cut off one of the Kremlin’s most important sources of revenue for its war against Ukraine.

Representative Michael McCaul, Republican of Texas and a former chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, has spent recent days trying to bridge the divide, a role he has often played in negotiations over major foreign policy legislation throughout his time on Capitol Hill.

He said lawmakers were working to preserve tariffs as a tool strong enough to secure Mr. Trump’s support while addressing Democrats’ concerns that the bill would unnecessarily expand presidential trade authority.

Those concerns center on Section 113 of the legislation, which would authorize the president to impose tariffs of “up to 100 percent” on imports from countries that knowingly purchase 15 percent or more of their energy as Russian-origin crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas or uranium.

Republicans contend the language is narrowly tailored to countries helping finance Russia’s war. Democrats worry it could establish a broader precedent for presidential tariff authority at a time when many in Congress are already uneasy with the administration’s expansive use of tariffs.

The Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate trade, but there are numerous laws that allow the president to issue tariffs in certain circumstances. Mr. Trump has waged an unyielding campaign to use those statutes to circumvent Congress, where Republicans have ceded much of the legislative branch’s power on trade, and do what he pleases with the U. S. tariff system.

Mr. McCaul said that the sanctions bill is “very clear” that it only grants the president tariff authority for its narrow purpose. He said he would be open to adding language explicitly saying so, if that would assuage Democrats’ concerns about how the president and his trade advisers may interpret the legislation.

Despite the impasse, supporters remain optimistic the measure can still advance. Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the bill’s leading Democratic co-sponsor, said this week that “nothing has been this close” to becoming law since he began working with Mr. Graham more than a year ago on the sanctions package.

Mr. McCaul said he had hoped Congress could send the legislation to the president before the House departed Washington for its five-week summer recess on Thursday and before Mr. Graham’s funeral on Tuesday, viewing both as critical milestones for legislation carrying forward one of the South Carolina Republican’s final legislative priorities.

But so far lawmakers have been unable to gain enough momentum to pass the bill in short order.

Instead, the House left Washington without an agreement, leaving the Senate to try to take up the legislation next week.

The bill — also sponsored by Senator Darline Graham, Republican of South Carolina, who was appointed this month to serve the remainder of her brother’s term — has enough backing to ultimately overcome the objections of Democrats expressing concern. But skeptics could drag out the process.

“Passing this legislation would honor my brother’s steadfast commitment to our national security and it would provide President Trump with additional leverage to bring this war to an end,” Ms. Graham said in a statement.

Robert Draper contributed reporting.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

Wildfires in France and Spain Drive Tens of Thousands From Their Homes

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Extreme Heat

Advertisement

Supported by

French officials ordered the evacuation of the Cap Ferret Peninsula, a popular holiday destination. Fires west of Madrid were closing in on populated areas.

By Carlos Barragán

Reporting from Madrid

Tens of thousands of people fled their homes on Friday as wildfires ravaged vast areas of France and Spain, with broiling summer temperatures across Western Europe exacerbating the ferocity of the blazes.

In southwestern France, the authorities ordered the evacuation of the Cap Ferret Peninsula, a popular Atlantic holiday destination. Hundreds of people fled by boat as a fast-moving wildfire approached.

Firefighters were battling what Sophie Brocas, the prefect of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, described as a highly unpredictable, “XXL” wildfire. She characterized the fire and another burning in the Landes, farther south, as the “two ogres of the summer.”

In total, more than 60,000 people in France have fled their homes, according to the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez. Thirty-two fires were blazing across the country, he said.

In Spain, wildfires in the mountains west of Madrid forced more than 19,000 people to evacuate and had burned almost 15,000 acres by Friday afternoon. The blazes were closing in on populated areas.

“This is the worst wildfire in the Madrid region’s history,” Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the regional president, said on Friday. “Our priority is to save lives, nothing else,” she said, adding that the authorities were working to evacuate residents from towns threatened by the fires.

The fires spread amid “a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds,” Ms. Díaz Ayuso said.

The Spanish government requested additional resources from the European Union — as did France — after declaring a national emergency over the fires in Madrid.

“We cannot be optimistic. Today is a critical day,” Fernando Grande-Marlaska, Spain’s interior minister, said on Friday. The authorities were particularly concerned that several fires burning in the area, including another one in the neighboring city of Ávila, could merge into a single, larger blaze.

If the fires were to converge, he said, the blaze would become “more virulent and aggressive.”

The fires in France and Spain are part of a broader wave of wildfires this summer across Europe, where repeated heat waves since late May have brought extreme temperatures and caused deaths. Last month was the hottest June on record in Western Europe, according to Copernicus, a European Union monitoring agency.

Connecting a specific heat wave or fire to global warming is hard to do, but experts agree that human-caused climate change is behind increasingly high temperatures that have made wildfires in general more destructive.

About two weeks ago, a wildfire in the southeastern Spanish province of Almería killed 13 people, making it one of the country’s deadliest fires on record.

France, too, has faced wildfires of unusual intensity. A few weeks ago, President Emmanuel Macron said that France had “never faced so many outbreaks of fire across the country since the end of World War II.”

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting from Paris.

Facing a Surge of Criticism, Argentines Have Something to Say

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Many Argentines condemned their players’ racist chants and aggressive behavior during the World Cup, but rejected what felt like a sweeping stigmatization of their entire nation.

Many Argentines condemned their players’ racist chants and aggressive behavior during the World Cup, but rejected what felt like a sweeping stigmatization of their entire nation.

Argentine supporters at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Argentina, after the World Cup final on Sunday. Credit... Sebastián López Brach for The New York Times

Supported by

By Emma Bubola and Daniel Politi

Emma Bubola and Daniel Politi are based in Buenos Aires.

Argentina was having enough of a rough week after watching their national team’s decisive defeat in the World Cup final and tears from Lionel Messi. Then came what felt like an enormous, persistent wave of global hatred against their nation.

Fans of opposing teams, celebrities of all kinds and a surge of social media users were directing their scorn not only at the Argentine team but at the country as a whole — turning the celebrated champions of the 2022 World Cup into the villains of 2026.

“We lost, and now we’re being called every name under the sun,” said Mercedes Maspero, an Argentine researcher.

In part, the animosity was fueled by speculation that Argentina had received favorable treatment from soccer’s global governing body, FIFA, and by the team’s sometimes aggressive style of play.

Then there was the post-match brawl after Sunday’s final, in which several Argentine players and staff attacked Spanish opponents.

The criticism was also linked to off-field behavior during the tournament, including Argentine players captured on video singing a racist chant about French players in 2024, an incident that critics resurfaced this year. An Argentine fan also apparently directed racist abuse at IShowSpeed, a Black streamer and social media influencer.

But the anti-Argentine sentiment came to be framed around a wider critique of Argentine society, history, and the country as a whole.

Samuel L. Jackson, the actor, reposted an Instagram story urging Black fans not to support Argentina for historically being “one of, if not the most racist country in the world.”

The American comedian Eric André celebrated Argentina’s loss against Spain in an expletive-laden Instagram story in which he accused Argentina of being racist, violent and full of crime.

Mr. André, in a statement, said that he “was referring to the history of their government’s policies, not every single citizen.” A representative for Mr. Jackson did not respond to a request for comment.

Some celebrities, like the singers Patti Smith and Rosalía, reposted (and later apologized for sharing) content that was interpreted as being critical of Argentina, and the connection between racism and anti-Argentine support even reached a hearing at the U. S. Congress.

Many bolstered their criticisms with accusations that the Argentine national team does not have any Black players, and online petitions to exclude Argentina from the World Cup attracted large numbers of signatures.

The denunciations of Argentina started weeks before the final, but Argentines seemed too busy living the dream of a consecutive World Cup title to pay much attention. Immediately after their loss in the final, they were overwhelmed with sadness. But this week, the lament that washed over Argentines has given way to indignation, confusion and anger over the global hatred directed at them.

Even President Javier Milei responded. “They are jealous of us,” he posted on Instagram. “We are good at almost everything.”

Some commentators tried to address the substance of the condemnations.

“The World Cup enabled some sort of international court in which Argentina is the accused,” said Pedro Rosemblat, a prominent Argentine journalist, on his streaming show.

Judgment was coming from people in the United States, he said, which has a long history of racism, or European nations that had started wars, engaged in colonization and still wrestle with xenophobia.

And verdicts were rendered, Mr. Rosemblat added, by actors and celebrities “who would not be able to explain anything about our history, our society and our civilization.”

Many Argentines condemned the racist chants of players and fans and the team’s physical attacks on their opponents. They admitted that their country, like many others, has problems with racism. But they rejected that problematic aspects of their history should prompt a sweeping stigmatization of their nation and team.

“Argentina has its share of racism, but no more than any other Latin American country,” an antiracism group made up of Argentines of Indigenous origins called “Identidad Marrón,” or “Brown Identity,” wrote in an Instagram post.

Daniel Schteingart, an Argentine researcher, pointed out on social media that the Integrated Values Survey, a study and survey that measures values in dozens of countries, found that 4 percent of Argentines said they would not like having an immigrant as a neighbor, and less than 3 percent would object to a neighbor of a different race.

Those figures, from the most recent study conducted between 2017 and 2022, were among the lowest in the world and lower than those in the United States, France, Spain or Mexico.

“It makes sense: Argentina has opened its doors to immigration since the 19th century and has one of the friendliest immigration laws on the planet,” Mr. Schteingart wrote.

Argentina has historically provided immigrants with broad access to public education and health care while offering accessible pathways to legal residency. And even though the Milei government has imposed some restrictions, Argentina’s immigration policy is still far less strict than that of the United States under President Trump.

“Pointing out real problems is one thing; turning an entire country into a caricature is another,” Mr. Schteingart wrote.

Racist incidents have been a dark fixture of European soccer for decades, though recent years have brought far stricter penalties as players started to speak out demanding action. Argentina, by contrast, has not yet undergone a similar reckoning, as casual slurs and racial innuendos continue to be used.

The criticism arising from the World Cup has also led to a broader look at race relations in Argentina and its treatment of Indigenous and Black people.

Black people once made up a much larger share of the population across the region that became Argentina.

There were many reasons for that decline. Black men were repeatedly and disproportionately mobilized for wars, while poor living conditions contributed to high infant mortality and lower birth rates. Intermarriage changed how many descendants were classified in official records, and mass European immigration sharply reduced the Black community’s relative size.

This helped cement an enduring image of Argentina as a white, European nation, one that minimized and left out its African roots and the contributions of Afro-Argentines from its official history.

Organizations like Identidad Marrón have said that Argentina actually has a much more diverse ethnic mix.

That includes many people of Indigenous descent, among them Argentina’s soccer demigod Diego Maradona, who spoke proudly of his native Guaraní roots.

Groups like Identidad Marrón have long said that Argentina’s nonwhite population is often the target of discrimination, but they condemned what he called an oversimplified debate.

“If it was so easy, it would mean that national teams with more players of African descent belong to nations that respect their rights,” said Alejandro Mamani, an Argentine lawyer of Indigenous descent who is part of the group. “And that at their borders, in their seas, there would not be bodies and dinghies adrift.”

As criticism of Argentina surged online after the World Cup final, many people outside of the country reached out to me to ask how Argentines were responding to it. This piece digs into where the criticism is coming from and how people here are making sense of it all.

Lucía Cholakian Herrera and Natalie Alcoba contributed reporting from Buenos Aires.

Emma Bubola is a Times reporter covering Argentina. She is based in Buenos Aires.

Iran’s New Leader Is More Open to Pursuing a Nuclear Weapon, U. S. Intelligence Says

The New York Times July 24, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The previous supreme leader, who was killed early in the war, had renounced nuclear weapons. U. S. spy agencies believe his son is more interested in building a bomb.

By Julian E. Barnes

Reporting from Washington

American intelligence agencies believe that Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, is far more interested than his father and predecessor in pursuing a nuclear weapon, according to officials briefed on the assessments.

Ayatollah Khamenei’s father, who was killed at the start of the war in an Israeli attack aided by U. S. intelligence, had sworn off developing a nuclear weapon. While American officials long asserted that Iran wanted to be capable of building a nuclear weapon, many believed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s hesitancy was genuine.

His successor has never publicly called for Iran to build a nuclear weapon. But U. S. intelligence agencies believe that Mojtaba Khamenei and the harder-line government that emerged after the United States and Israel killed many of Iran’s previous leaders have ambitions to develop advanced nuclear weaponry.

The current government has already worked to assert greater control over the Strait of Hormuz and proved a difficult negotiating partner. If the U. S.-Israeli war has made Tehran more, rather than less, likely to pursue a nuclear weapon, it would amount to one more grave consequence of the killing of the supreme leader and the steps toward regime change the Trump administration initially pursued.

American officials caution that most of the intelligence on Mojtaba Khamenei’s views comes from before the war. He was badly injured in the first part of the war, and American officials said he has limited his communications and public appearances because of his injuries and also because he does not want to be targeted in an airstrike.

The officials assess that he remains in charge of the government but does not have the absolute authority and influence of his father, who ruled for more than 36 years.

The assessment comes as President Trump is weighing whether to intensify the military campaign against Iran. A determination that the supreme leader is potentially open to pursuing a bomb would provide additional justification for an escalation.

While U. S. officials insist Tehran has not made any moves to restart its nuclear program, Iran has taken some steps to preserve its nuclear assets after the U. S. strikes on key facilities last year or during pauses in fighting during the current war.

Iran has moved at least some centrifuges, according to American officials, to a heavily fortified underground complex in central Iran that the United States refers to as Pickaxe Mountain. The Wall Street Journal first reported this week that Israeli intelligence had tracked the movement of the centrifuges.

While such a move could be a first step toward rebuilding enrichment capability, U. S. officials said they believe that for now Iran is more interested in preserving some of its equipment by trying to move it outside the range of American bombs.

In June 2025, Mr. Trump ordered the U. S. military to conduct strikes on three key nuclear facilities. B-2 stealth bombers dropped the largest conventional bombs in the Air Force inventory on two of the sites, Fordo and Natanz. A third site, at Isfahan, was hit with Tomahawk missiles.

Mr. Trump immediately claimed that the military operation had obliterated the facilities, but initial intelligence assessments were far more measured, suggesting the program had only been set back by months.

Iran’s nuclear site at Pickaxe Mountain was not targeted in the attacks last summer. And the facilities there are a far more difficult target for the U. S. military. The underground facilities are buried deep below a mountain, out of the range of the most powerful conventional U. S. bombs, according to multiple American officials.

After assessing the damage at the Fordo nuclear facility, the Iranians learned just how deep the U. S. weapons could penetrate, and are confident that Pickaxe’s even deeper underground halls are safe from conventional aerial attack.

But Iranians remain worried that U. S. forces could mount a commando raid against Pickaxe, potentially using ground forces to enter the site and destroy it from within. U. S. intelligence agencies have reported that Iran has moved ground forces to Pickaxe to deter any ground raid.

Mr. Trump this week threatened to attack the facility, calling it “a possible target for a nice big fat shot right in their front door.”

He also said the United States saw no activity there, a reference, officials said, to the fact that Iran has not restarted nuclear enrichment or other work, despite moving equipment there.

American officials declined to discuss the planning for any attack on the site, and said Mr. Trump has been presented a broad range of options and an array of potential targets. It was foolish, several officials said, to predict what targets Mr. Trump might approve.

Whatever missteps the United States has made in its war with Iran, the damage to the Iranian nuclear facilities, particularly in its strikes last year, succeeded in at least freezing progress on the nuclear program.

The intelligence agencies assessed that the damage would have set back the program by only six months, had the Iranians immediately moved to repair centrifuges or restart enrichment work at other sites. But, American officials said, the Iranians did not immediately dig out all of the facilities or restart enrichment at other locations.

Still, the building blocks of a bomb, most notably Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, remain intact and accessible to Tehran.

Ali Khamenei had issued a religious order, or fatwa, prohibiting the use of nuclear weapons by Iran, a stance publicly announced to the International Atomic Energy Agency in 2005.

The fatwa had its limits. While it prevented Iran from using a nuclear bomb, it did not block the government from developing its overall program or taking steps toward weaponization. Even after the fatwa was in place, harder-line elements in the Iranian government wanted to be able to quickly develop a nuclear weapon.

But based on public statements and intercepted conversations before the war, American intelligence officials assessed that Mojtaba Khamenei did not share his father’s hesitancy and was interested in pursuing an advanced nuclear weapon.

At the end of the Biden administration, U. S. officials said Iran was looking at ways to develop a cruder nuclear weapon, potentially like the Hiroshima-style bombs, that would be difficult to deliver but would provide something of a deterrent.

The new supreme leader, according to U. S. officials, sees less utility in that type of weapon but appears to support developing the kind of thermonuclear warhead that could eventually be miniaturized and placed on a long-range missile.

In his public statements, Ayatollah Khamenei has vowed to preserve Iran’s nuclear capabilities, but has not spoken directly of a need to obtain a weapon. He distanced himself from an agreement the United States and Iran signed in June that said Iran would not pursue a nuclear weapon. Ayatollah Khamenei said he had allowed the agreement, but did not agree with it as a “matter of principle.”

Rosemary Kelanic, the director of the Middle East program at Defense Priorities, a think tank skeptical of American military intervention, said the war and the announcement this week that the United States may help Saudi Arabia build enrichment facilities make it “significantly more likely” that Iran pursues a nuclear weapon.

“Iran now has a much greater incentive to weaponize to deter future U. S. or Israeli attempts at collapsing the regime or the Iranian state, which means that the war is counterproductive to its own ostensible goals of preventing Iranian proliferation,” she said.

Iranian officials who previously argued in internal debates that only a nuclear weapon could prevent an Israeli or American attack believe their position has been strengthened, U. S. officials have said.

Dustin Volz and Michael Crowley contributed reporting.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

A Tempting Remedy for Heat-Stricken France: Be More Like Spain

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Extreme Heat

Advertisement

Supported by

A French government delegation will travel to its southern neighbor to learn how it copes with long spells of hot weather.

By Mark Landler

Reporting from Paris

Jean-Pierre Farandou grew up in the sunbaked southwest of France, north of the Pyrénées mountain range, which divides France from Spain. His grandparents, he recalls, were farmers who rose to work in the cool predawn hours and rested in the heat of the day, the French equivalent of a Spanish siesta.

So, when Mr. Farandou, now France’s labor minister, was searching for ways to respond to the heat waves that have recently scorched France, he instinctively cast his eye toward Spain. Mr. Farandou contacted his Spanish counterpart, Yolanda Díaz, and proposed a field trip to Madrid, the capital, to explore how Spain has adapted to its torrid climate.

“France is discovering that in summer, it will become Spain,” Mr. Farandou, 69, said in a recent interview. “It is a country that resembles us,” he added. “We know that Spain works, even when it’s hot.”

In September, when the French government’s need to respond to heat waves will presumably have eased, Mr. Farandou and his small delegation will spend a few days in Spain, talking to government officials, business executives, union leaders, academics and ordinary people. The goal is to understand how Spaniards organize their society to cope with frequent spells of extreme heat.

Some of the measures are obvious and already being tried in France: shifting work hours to earlier in the day, particularly for outdoor or manual workers; frequent rests, which help people recover from sleep lost during heat waves; and an emphasis on drinking fluids.

Spain also provides paid leave during climate-related disruptions, though it adopted that after disastrous floods in Valencia in 2024 rather than because of heat waves. In France, the Green Party recently proposed five days a year of paid vacation to protect workers during extreme heat, an idea that drew headlines even if stands little chance of becoming law.

France and Spain share another climate-related scourge: wildfires. On Thursday, tens of thousands of people were evacuated after fires spread across both countries. In France, vacationers were forced to flee threatened campsites along the Atlantic coast in the southwest. In Spain, the authorities declared a national emergency in a region near Madrid, where several fires burned out of control.

To Mr. Farandou, Spain’s culture is as intriguing as its laws. Spanish habits of daily life — from midday siestas to late-night dinners — reflect a long history of living with heat. Transplanting those cultural adaptations to France, particularly the country’s north, would be tricky, he acknowledged.

“Adapting through regulations is one thing, but the real, major challenge is cultural adaptation,” said Mr. Farandou, a businessman who ran France’s national railway, S. N. C. F., before joining the government last year.

In seeking to change habits, experts say, France is looking for low-cost solutions to an expensive problem. Behavioral changes are cheaper than major investments in infrastructure, such as the widespread installation of air-conditioning and “net zero” policies, which seek to reduce the carbon emissions that are the main culprit for a warming climate.

“Acting on our time schedules, things like that — they don’t cost a penny,” said Sonia Lavadinho, an urban anthropologist in Bern, Switzerland. “You can understand why a government would like to implement these changes.”

But Spanish habits, other experts warn, should not be viewed as a magic bullet. For one, traditional Spanish customs, like the siesta or earlier workday, are neither ubiquitous nor available to the people most vulnerable to heat: agricultural laborers, construction workers, delivery people and cleaners.

Moreover, Spain still struggles to protect its population. Roughly one in three Spanish households are unable to keep their homes adequately cool in summer, said Christian Oltra, a senior researcher at the Center for Energy, Environmental and Technological Research, a government-affiliated think tank in Madrid.

“Spain can be genuinely more accustomed to heat than its neighbors and still carry a very substantial health burden,” Mr. Oltra said. “The most accurate description, in my view, is that Spain is partially and unevenly adapted — a valuable case to learn from, rather than a straightforward success story.”

However imperfect, Mr. Farandou said, Spain was better weatherproofed than France. He noted that many French administrative arrangements dated to the Napoleonic era and were singularly ill suited to a hotter climate.

While August is a vacation month, for example, when many flee stifling cities for cooler climes, June is typically hectic, packed with school exams, sports tournaments and construction projects. This year, all that activity coincided with the most intense June heat wave on record.

The French health authorities recorded nearly 6,000 excess deaths from June 17 to July 2, a period when the temperatures rose above 40 degrees Celsius, or 104 degrees Fahrenheit. Desperate for relief, thousands of people jumped into canals, rivers and other waterways, leading to 90 deaths.

Mr. Farandou suggested that local authorities keep pools open at night so families could use them after school and work. Schools, he said, should move up exams, though even that might not help, given that France’s first heat wave this year occurred in late May.

At workplaces that require a dress code, such as government ministries, he said he supported allowing employees to go without ties, jackets or long trousers in hot weather. The British, he noted, devised Bermuda shorts a century ago to make life bearable for officials working in tropical and desert climates.

Architecture is another area where Spain offers lessons. Its older houses have thick walls and narrow windows with shutters, blinds and awnings to block the sun. Many French houses have shutters, too, though in modern apartments, large windows are prized. In Paris, the familiar zinc roofs that cover almost four-fifths of the buildings sizzle under the sun, making life unbearable for those who live underneath them.

The most obvious change, of course, would be to install air-conditioning. In Spain’s hottest regions, Mr. Oltra said, three-quarters of the houses use cooling systems. But in France, as in other northern European countries, air-conditioning is a political lightning rod. Critics note that it worsens climate change by using lots of electricity and pumping hot air outside the buildings it cools.

Mr. Farandou, who began his career at an American mining company in Denver, said he favored installing cooling systems in schools, hospitals, nursing homes and other places with vulnerable people. But he said that American-style air-conditioning was not a solution that would work in France.

It is not an accident that Mr. Farandou is visiting Spain instead of the United States, Asia or the Middle East, where many buildings are also heavily air-conditioned. Those places are too distant, culturally and geographically, to be useful models for France, he said. Even trying to live more like their Spanish neighbors will be a stretch for the French, he said, though they will have little choice.

“Deep down, I have this conviction,” Mr. Farandou said: The French people “will have to change something relatively profound in order to adapt to these very long periods of intense heat.”

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

Mark Landler is the Paris bureau chief of The Times, covering France, as well as American foreign policy in Europe and the Middle East. He has been a journalist for more than three decades.

Crucial Interest Rate Jumps to Highest Level of Trump’s Second Term

The New York Times July 24, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond has risen steadily this year, as the Iran war rages, government spending worries intensify and artificial intelligence spending boosts growth.

By Joe Rennison and Gregory Schmidt

President Trump returned to office promising lower costs across the economy, but an important interest rate that his administration cites as a barometer of its success recently hit its highest level of Mr. Trump’s second term.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond, considered one of the most important interest rates in the world, jumped this week to 4.7 percent, up from less than 4 percent before the start of the war in Iran in late February. It was 4.6 percent on the day Mr. Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

The yield underpins borrowing costs across debt markets, from corporate bonds to mortgage loans, and its rise complicates Mr. Trump’s plans to keep costs affordable for companies and households across the United States.

Source: FactSet.

By The New York Times

The impact is apparent in the housing market. Rising yields have driven up mortgage rates in recent weeks, dampening hopes that moribund home sales would rebound this year. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, the most common home loan in the United States, is now 6.58 percent, Freddie Mac said Thursday. Mortgage rates had fallen below 6 percent in the week before the first U. S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.

“This latest leg up in rates is going to push sales down unless it’s quickly reversed,” said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead U. S. economist at Oxford Economics. “And it comes at a time when households are confronting other increased costs for energy and food due to the effects of the war.”

While some of the rising yields can be attributed to higher inflation expectations amid soaring oil prices, analysts said that longer-dated interest rates, like the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, had been caught in a swirl of higher growth expectations stemming from the build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The higher growth, if left unchecked by higher rates, could cause the economy to overheat and ramp up inflation. Another factor driving up the 10-year yield is investors’ worries about unsustainable fiscal spending by governments around the world.

“The Iran war isn’t helping, but it’s not obvious that the 10-year is being driven by inflation risk,” said Jonathan Hill, an inflation strategist at Barclays.

In Britain, 10-year gilts — the equivalent term to Treasuries for government debt — have risen 0.9 percentage points to over 5 percent since the war started, alongside concerns over the fiscal plans of the new prime minister, Andy Burnham. In Japan, 30-year government bonds have risen 0.7 percentage points, to 2.8 percent, over the same period, as the government has rolled out hefty spending plans. Concerns over high government spending also linger in the United States, as the government seeks to increase its military budget for the war with Iran.

As governments look to borrow more, investors are demanding a higher return to lend, and that higher return is reflected in higher interest rates throughout the economy, analysts said. The U. S. government has nearly $40 trillion in debt outstanding, more than double the amount 10 years ago.

“All bond yields are rising, and it is for some of the same reasons,” said Subadra Rajappa, an interest rate strategist at Société Générale. “It is about domestic debt and deficits. It’s happening globally.”

Analysts also pointed to the huge amounts being lent to big technology companies at the forefront of the A. I. build-out, which is forcing other companies that want to borrow money to attract investors by increasing the amount they are willing to pay in interest.

Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, has previously pointed to the 10-year bond as a “barometer” of his success in improving affordability.

“Lower Treasury borrowing costs mean lower corporate borrowing costs, lower mortgage rates and lower car payments — which all translates to greater affordability for all Americans,” he said in a speech in November.

Conversely, higher treasury yields mean higher borrowing costs for companies and consumers, hurting affordability.

The yield had fallen below 4 percent earlier this year, touching its lowest point of Mr. Trump’s second term on Feb. 27, the day before the United States and Israel attacked Iran. Since then, the 10-year yield has risen roughly 0.8 percentage points.

Although analysts said that inflation worries had been largely contained, there remains pressure on Kevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve chairman, to show his commitment to reining in the pace of price rises. Traders warn that inaction from the central bank risks extending those inflation worries over a longer period, potentially pushing yields on longer-dated Treasury notes even higher.

“The reality is we are coming up on five and a half years of above-target inflation,” said Mr. Hill of Barclays, “and the market is already saying we should anticipate the likelihood of that for additional years, not just months, to come.”

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Gregory Schmidt is a senior staff editor who has covered real estate since 2022.
