Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Johnny Itliong says Cesar Chavez stole credit from his father, the farmworker activist Larry Itliong. For years, he has been trying to correct the record.

“I have been fighting to get the story of my father out for decades and have been waiting for the U. F. W. to step up and honor Larry as they do Cesar,” said Johnny Itliong, at a mural commemorating his father. Credit...

Supported by

By Jill Cowan

Visuals by Mark Abramson for The New York Times

Jill Cowan interviewed Johnny Itliong over several months in Venice Beach in Los Angeles and in Santa Monica and Delano, Calif.

It was Magic Monday, the weekly convocation of roller skaters on Venice Beach in Los Angeles, and a nearly sacred observance for Johnny Itliong. As usual, he was helping out his entrepreneurial friends on the boardwalk by sporting their merch — a “Skate Famous” branded hat from one, stickers on his gear from others.

The music was bumping and the sun had come out. On most Magic Mondays, that and a little weed would have been all Itliong needed. But on this afternoon, as he felt his way through the steps of a line dance and passed a vape to a buddy, he had more on his mind.

Days before, the news that Cesar Chavez had been accused of sexually abusing girls landed like a bomb, forcing a reckoning over one of the nation’s few Latino civil rights icons.

Those girls were the daughters of farmworker organizers whose movement Chavez had famously led. Itliong, 61, felt sorrow for the victims, who included the sister of a close friend. But the revelation also brought something like vindication — and opportunity.

Itliong’s father was Larry Itliong, the Filipino American farmworker leader who was perennially overshadowed by the younger and more telegenic Chavez. While Chavez’s name was reverently bestowed on schools, streets and libraries, the Itliong name remained largely unknown even in Delano, the agricultural town in California’s Central Valley where Johnny was born and Larry died.

For decades, the son has made it his life’s work to change this. He has traveled California, attending United Farm Workers events and ceremonies honoring the farm labor movement to proclaim what he sees as the truth: After his father spent decades toiling in the fields, learning multiple languages to communicate better with workers and making grueling treks to find them, he said, Chavez and his followers muscled in on their work and took the credit.

“I have been fighting to get the story of my father out for decades and have been waiting for the U. F. W. to step up and honor Larry as they do Cesar,” he said at one such event.

His efforts, he said, have cost him money, untold time, three marriages and his relationships with his three children.

But now the world could find out what Itliong had believed for as long as he could remember.

“He was a narcissist,” Itliong told me, jabbing his two middle fingers into the air whenever he said Chavez’s name. He paused to nod at friends passing by on their skates.

“They’re writing about my dad!” he told them.

He was confident and breezy, joking and laughing as he glided around the rink. But later, he reflected on a life in which he has often felt thwarted — punished, even — for trying to carry forward his family’s legacy.

“I want this for my children,” he said. “I may be a piece of shit, but I want them to be proud of their grandfather.”

Everyone was waiting for Itliong, and when he finally appeared on the video call, he apologized; he had been looking for a place to plug in his laptop.

In the weeks since the Chavez news had broken, he had given about two dozen interviews reminding journalists that the movement Chavez had come to embody was actually about much more than a single person. He told The Los Angeles Times that his father’s purpose “was to raise everybody up.”

Members of a loosely organized group of Asian American civil rights advocates had read the coverage. Seeing an opportunity to highlight the work of Filipino American leaders, they asked Itliong to help them strategize.

“This is a very critical moment with this openness,” said Eric Chen, a pastor. He began working as an activist after a mass shooting at a ballroom that left 11 mostly older Asian Americans dead and devastated the Asian American enclave in Los Angeles County that he calls home. “We’ve got to strike while the iron is hot.”

The question was how. Chen and Itliong had identified a turning point, but they had a harder time figuring out a mission. All they knew was that they wanted to bring more attention to Larry Itliong’s contributions without deifying him or anyone else. In the end, they decided that they would host a kind of informational “round table” and news conference, both aimed at moving the celebration of the farmworker movement from Chavez’s birthday to some other day and elevating the stories of others in the movement.

Chen offered a benediction.

“I pray that as we embark on this journey to rewrite history, that it would be a journey of healing as well, a journey of redemption,” he said as the others nodded solemnly in their little boxes on the screen. “Because, Lord, we know that it was not about one man. It was a movement.”

Larry Itliong married six times, and Johnny’s mother was mostly absent from his childhood. He was cared for by a large, shifting group of aunts and uncles, related by blood and not, who were animated by the common goal of building a farmworker movement.

In his first memories, he is a toddler watching Mickey Mouse cartoons on a jet to the Philippines with one such couple — a Filipino American doctor and his wife. They took him to visit the rice paddies his father left behind when he came to the United States in 1929.

Larry Itliong had begun rallying agricultural workers up and down the West Coast in the 1930s, from the canneries of Alaska to the vegetable fields of the Coachella Valley. He spent decades pushing for higher pay and safer working conditions for farmworkers who were then, as now, nearly all immigrants.

As the leader of the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, he helped orchestrate the Delano, Calif., grape strike and boycott of 1965.

Historians say it was only after Larry Itliong helped persuade the predominantly Mexican and Mexican American leaders of the nascent National Farm Workers Association to join the Filipinos’ strike that the modern farm labor movement was born.

Growing up in Delano in the 1960s and ’70s, Johnny sometimes rose in the early hours of the morning to follow older relatives into the grapevines, where they did the backbreaking work it took to feed the nation.

Even as a child, he had a sense that his family was at the center of something important. After dinner, he and the other children would stay outside while the adults talked inside Delano’s Filipino Hall, their voices often erupting into shouts. In conversation, Itliong routinely rattles off names of other leaders who he says were harmed by the cult of personality surrounding Chavez. Many of these organizers, like his father, understood the sacrifices that it took to make it as a farm laborer. Itliong said he could relate to this struggle in a way that Chavez’s children could not.

But during those years, forces beyond Larry’s control were conspiring to change the course of history.

One of the founders of the National Farm Workers Association was Chavez. At the time, he was a young man amassing followers as he sought to transform the long effort to unionize migrant farmworkers into a broader civil rights movement.

Born on an Arizona farm just two years before Larry Itliong arrived on the West Coast, Chavez was a sharp strategist and strong-willed Mexican American leader who galvanized Latinos, a fast-growing demographic in search of their own Martin Luther King Jr.

In Itliong’s telling, Chavez’s growing fame created an opening for his ambitious cohort to elbow his father and other longtime organizers out of the way. The tension between Chavez’s mostly Latino followers and the Filipino Americans close to Itliong lingers even now.

Itliong remembered his father’s anger when Chavez moved the United Farm Workers’ headquarters from Delano to an isolated community in the Tehachapi Mountains, farther from farmworkers’ homes. He remembered how journalists and documentarians focused on Chavez and did not widen the frame to include Larry or other Filipinos.

“Their passion is a product of their frustration,” said Matt Garcia, a historian at Dartmouth College and a Chavez biographer who has written critically about the way Chavez wielded his power. “And that frustration is legit.”

While Professor Garcia said there was no evidence of a conspiracy by Chavez and his allies to exclude Larry Itliong or other Filipinos from the history books, he said that Itliong and Chavez represented clashing visions of the farmworker movement.

Larry was a strident “meat and potatoes” union organizer, eager to flex the untapped power of farmworkers like himself. Chavez, as a Mexican American, was a member of a demographic majority of farmworkers, and he saw the movement as a broader social one. Collective bargaining and the fine points of contracts, Professor Garcia said, didn’t interest him.

Chavez also had “a will to power,” Professor Garcia said, and it was fulfilled by society’s impulse to venerate individuals instead of the messy collectives who make change. And so Chavez became the face of the movement.

The United Farm Workers union he left behind had been grappling with his legacy since long before the revelations of abuse. In response to questions from The New York Times, the group acknowledged that there were “many, many names who don’t have enough recognition,” including but not limited to Itliong.

“The best way the modern U. F. W. can honor Larry Itliong’s legacy is to continue what he spent his incredible life doing,” the statement said: “organizing workers to win the dignity and protections of a union contract.”

The Chavez family declined to comment for this article.

Much of the maneuvering that ultimately sidelined Larry Itliong took place when his son Johnny was too young to understand what was happening. In 1971, Larry resigned from the union that became the United Farm Workers. His children helped care for him as he suffered from A. L. S., the harrowing degenerative disease, until his death in 1977.

“I just remember the doctor sitting in the white chair we had, or yellow leather, or something,” Itliong told me, wiping away tears. “And then the preacher came.”

At age 14, he left home, where life had become turbulent, and stayed with friends or in a car. With the help of an empathetic teacher, he graduated from high school in Delano and moved to the nearest big city, Bakersfield.

He said he worked as a contractor overseas in roles he maintains he can’t talk about. He worked as a chef. He lived in the San Francisco Bay Area and in Nevada, where the last of his marriages dissolved in acrimony.

He is estranged from his children — not by his choice, he said, though according to divorce court records, he has not taken opportunities to see them.

In 2004 he was convicted of domestic violence, after an incident in which his wife at the time, Kelly Cornell, said he slapped her and assaulted her while she was on the toilet. Itliong maintains he was not violent and said Cornell lied. More than two decades later, Cornell said she harbors no “hard feelings.” But after going for years without child support for their son, now an adult and also named Larry, she said, “I just wish his dad would step up a little bit.”

Reached by text message, the younger Larry, 25, said he didn’t want to talk about his father. He didn’t reply when asked if he felt any connection to his grandfather’s legacy.

On and off for about three decades, Itliong has lived in Los Angeles, mostly hanging around the beach. For money, he said, he helps mount televisions for wealthy customers. A skateboarder for decades, he has also taken up roller skating, joining an enthusiastic community that blasts music and wears glowing lights. He describes his living situation as mobile; he has eschewed many of his possessions to live “the way the manongs lived,” referring to Filipino immigrants like his father.

But when anyone — the office of an elected official, a Filipino American nonprofit, a reporter — calls asking to talk about his dad, he picks up. And after the accusations of sexual abuse by Chavez emerged, there were lots of calls.

In Delano as in other communities in the Central Valley, suburban neighborhoods have replaced some of the fields. Still, small reminders of Larry Itliong’s legacy are tucked throughout the town. On Memorial Day weekend, a crowd of siblings, cousins and in-laws held an impromptu gathering at Larry Itliong Unity Park, which was dedicated two years ago. Johnny Itliong had come to spend time with his sister, Sandra Itliong Bowman, who had driven down from the Seattle area.

Sandra’s adult children say that they remember being dismissed by classmates and teachers, even in Delano, when they talked about their grandfather as a historic figure of note. Sandra said she was grateful that her brother had continued to publicize their father’s accomplishments. She wants her seven grandchildren to know where they came from.

“I’m not here to judge anybody,” she said, reluctant to blame anyone for overlooking Larry. “I can only build on the future for the ones who will carry on the legacy.”

The next stop was an elementary school where Itliong’s half sister, Patricia Itliong Serda, worked for decades as a librarian. On the exterior wall of the library, a colorful mural depicts Larry’s journey from the Philippines, the Delano grape strike and symbols of his legacy. Johnny stopped to point out details, including an image of Patricia as a child standing at Larry’s knee as he reads from an open book. Patricia said she worked for years to secure a nonprofit grant to commission the piece.

Most of the students at the school are Filipino American, Latino or a combination of the two, and she said she had poured her energy into teaching them about their heritage. The mural has invited discussion.

“Coming from our little town, it means a lot,” she said. “This is where I can make the most impact.”

Later, Itliong stopped by the cemetery where his father was buried beneath a simple headstone. Itliong once worked there, helping to maintain the grounds.

“I’ve come here at times throughout the years, you know?” he said, almost to himself, as he plucked stray weeds and bits of trash from the grass. Not for the first time in our conversations, Itliong alluded to a sense that his own life hadn’t worked out entirely as he might have hoped.

“Struggling, because my life — you know, I get great satisfaction from helping people, right? But you know the old saying: No good deeds ever go unpunished.”

He said he talked to his father when he visited the grave but never told him about the work he was doing on his behalf. Accolades wouldn’t have interested Larry, Itliong said. He said he used to skip ceremonies and events himself until one day a friend helped him think of things another way.

“‘You’re the connection to him,’” Itliong recalled her saying. “All this weight on the shoulder? It increased a hundredfold. I’m like, ‘Are you kidding me?’”

Soon Itliong was back in Los Angeles, hosting a panel with other Asian American activists. He took his place at the center of a table facing a group of nonprofit workers and labor rights advocates at the Pilipino Workers Center, a nonprofit in Historic Filipinotown.

Itliong was joined on the panel by his longtime friend Desirée Rojas, a daughter of Al Rojas, a farmworker and labor organizer. Rojas’s sister Debra was among the women who upended Chavez’s legacy when they described how he had abused them as young teenage girls.

Itliong seemed nervous, getting up briefly to fiddle with the audiovisual setup. But as others on the makeshift dais spoke about his father’s work, he relaxed into his role as a kind of magnanimous convener.

“It’s always been an honor to be the son of Larry Itliong. Those are very, very hard shoes to step into,” he told the room. “But I’m here now. I’ve been here my whole life, doing exactly what he did, standing up for those who needed to be heard.”

Aquilina Soriano, the director of the Pilipino Workers Center, urged the audience not to let their stories or perspectives remain in that room.

Tell your leaders, she said, that it’s important to pick a different day to celebrate the farm workers’ movement, that it’s important not to simply swap in the name of another imperfect person on every street sign or school that now reads “Cesar Chavez.”

“This is a call to action,” she said. “We still have a lot of work to do.”

To end the day, Itliong invited the audience to join him in what has become known as the unity clap, which begins with a slow clap and builds to the cacophony of loud applause. The Filipino version is punctuated with a cry of “isang baksak,” which roughly translates from Tagalog to “one down” — another day completed, another task done.

“Yeah! Isang baksak!” Itliong yelled, pumping his fists as the applause rang out.

Another task done, many more left. In the days after, Itliong would meet with the others to discuss strategy as Los Angeles County officials debated how to rename things named after Cesar Chavez.

But first, he went skating.

I met Johnny while reporting on the aftermath of our Cesar Chavez investigation. His story really got me thinking about how family, trauma, and human messiness ultimately shape history.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

Jill Cowan is a Times reporter based in Los Angeles, covering the forces shaping life in Southern California and throughout the state.

No Wonder Elon Musk Hates ‘The Odyssey’

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Goldberg

By Michelle Goldberg

Opinion Columnist

Elon Musk is still mad about “The Odyssey.”

For months, he and his acolytes have been throwing an online tantrum about the casting of Christopher Nolan’s version of the ancient epic, particularly his choice to have the Black actress Lupita Nyong’o play Helen of Troy and the trans actor Elliot Page play the warrior Sinon. Now that the film is out, some conservatives have acknowledged that there’s nothing particularly woke about Nolan’s blockbuster tale of masculine honor and sacrifice. It takes liberties with the source material, as any Hollywood version would, but one of its chief departures is a moral framework that’s more Christian than pagan, which shouldn’t offend most social conservatives.

Nevertheless, Musk has been stewing. On Tuesday he promised to make a “historically accurate” A. I.-generated “Odyssey” movie by year’s end, posting an absurdly kitschy clip made by his Grok image generator. In doing so, he inadvertently highlighted one reason Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is so powerful — because it represents a revolt of the human in a world overstuffed with A. I. slop.

Despite its sprawling canvas, Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is often strikingly intimate in scale and sparing in its use of computer-generated effects. “We like to spend a lot of time in real places, on real locations, having stuff in front of the camera that is tangible and tactile,” his cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema told The New York Times. The Cyclops Polyphemus wasn’t an A. I. creation, but a 60-foot animatronic puppet. The Sirens are small figures in the distance, Hades a murky field. In The Telegraph, Robbie Collin described Nolan filming on a wooden ship amid a real-life storm that had extras clutching the sides and vomiting, creating the movie’s feeling of tempestuousness. Nolan knows how to build hyper-real fantasy realms, as he did in “Inception” and “Tenet,” but in “The Odyssey,” he’s opted for the earthy over the glossy and grandiose.

Some of the polarizing narrative choices Nolan has made seem downstream of this approach. The film does not create a lavish ancient dream world for viewers to get lost in. The gods are barely present, except for a subdued Athena played by Zendaya. “Nolan’s ‘Odyssey,’ unlike Homer’s, is a story completely disenchanted, devoid of the supernatural, aside from like the odd witch or two that shows up,” complained the right-wing influencer Matt Walsh, who compares the movie unfavorably to “Gladiator,” “The Lord of the Rings” and Mel Gibson’s “Apocalypto.” The film’s stakes feel more psychological than mythic.

That seems to be exactly what viewers are responding to, turning “The Odyssey” not just into a hit but a cultural phenomenon, with some people traveling by plane for the chance to see it in IMAX 70 millimeter. (As The New York Post reported, Manhattan’s only theater to show the film in that format is sold out for every screening through Aug. 19.) There might seem to be a contradiction between its absence of eye candy and its success as a spectacle. But A. I. has rendered eye candy cheap. Viewers long for the visceral.

One of this year’s few pleasant surprises is that people are going back to the movies. During the pandemic, there were many predictions that movie theaters were dying, replaced by the comforts of streaming video. While the gloomiest forecasts proved overwrought, in recent years, the trend has still been one of decline. American box office sales were lower in 2024 than they were in 2023, and continued to disappoint in 2025. This year, however, is on track to be the best one for ticket sales since 2019. Young people, eager for communal experiences, have been flocking to theaters; according to a study by Fandango, Gen Z is now the most active moviegoing demographic.

What’s striking, though, isn’t just that people are returning to theaters, it’s the sort of films they’re going to. Recent movies that look artificial — including “Supergirl,” the live-action “Moana” and “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu” — have flopped. By contrast, the low-budget horror movies “Obsession” and “Backrooms,” which rely on frightening premises rather than otherworldly imagery, have been enormous hits. “Audiences in 2026 are sending a clear message to filmmakers: We want movies to look real — and for you to sweat while making them,” wrote The Hollywood Reporter’s James Hibberd.

There is no greater champion of hands-on, analog filmmaking than Nolan, who doesn’t even own a smartphone. Speaking to The Telegraph’s Collin, he celebrated young people’s rejection of A. I. “I’ve never seen a more rapid wholesale dismissal of a supposedly foundational jump in technology in my lifetime,” said Nolan. As a result, he said, “after years of driving toward heavily virtual environments, we’re seeing a renewed interest in more tactile, more real forms of storytelling.”

It is this ethos, more than multiracial casting, that makes “The Odyssey” a rebuke to Musk’s ideology, with its video game-derived visions of grandeur and conviction that algorithms can make art. He’s probably right to hate it. He’s wrong that his machines could ever conjure anything close.

If the rejection of AI overkill means a movement away from the endless parade of superhero comic book movie spectacles that we've been seeing over the past decade, i'm all for it. There aren't any superheroes coming to save us in Trump's America. I want movies with characters I can relate to and who face the same dilemmas most of us face. If people aren't going to read books any more, let's at least have intelligent movies.

The Artist and Filmmaker Helping Trump Reshape Washington

The New York Times July 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Matthew Taylor, a conceptual artist and political strategist, made influential ads and documentaries produced by Steve Bannon. Now he’s assisting the White House.

By Zachary Small

Reporting from Washington, New York and Venice

Matthew Taylor officially holds one role in the Trump administration as a senior adviser at the National Endowment for the Humanities, but he has quietly become a key player behind many of the president’s bold initiatives to transform Washington and its cultural legacy.

This year, Mr. Trump appointed Mr. Taylor to the Commission of Fine Arts, a federal agency that reviews government construction in Washington, to rubber-stamp approvals for projects such as the White House ballroom and the world’s tallest triumphal arch. He secured a role overseeing the National Garden of American Heroes, which would include the installation of 250 new statues in the capital.

Mr. Taylor consulted on the White House’s scathing report about the Smithsonian, which accused the National Museum of American History of promoting “extreme ideological activism.” And he was a constant presence at the U. S. Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, where he appeared alongside the curator in orange aviator sunglasses and a Super Mario Bros. hat.

Unlike other culture czars for the administration who have quickly come and gone, Mr. Taylor has an artistic background that makes him a distinct and persistent champion of the president’s vision.

He is a Marcel Duchamp devotee with a degree in sculpture. He is a filmmaker behind right-wing documentaries produced by Stephen K. Bannon and the F. B. I. director Kash Patel. He is a campaign strategist who hosts podcasts and makes music videos.

“He is an artist first and then he is a conservative,” Mr. Bannon said. “We don’t have enough of those people on our side.”

Vince Haley, the director of the White House's Domestic Policy Council, asked Mr. Taylor to help fulfill the president’s desire to overhaul the capital’s cultural institutions.

“Matthew Taylor is absolutely committed to elevating beauty in the arts and culture and showcasing the best of American creative genius to the world,” Mr. Haley said.

Blocks away from the White House, Mr. Taylor’s handiwork is on display. Under the blazing sun last month, he unveiled 21 statues of soldiers and Revolutionary scenes that he designed to commemorate a $10 million renovation of Freedom Plaza. “A new icon of American liberty,” he said on Mr. Bannon’s talk show, pointing to a statue of a woman holding the Declaration of Independence in one hand and a raised sword in the other.

As a filmmaker, Mr. Taylor has been producing work on parallel tracks. He has directed a lauded documentary about Duchamp, the godfather of conceptual art. But under a different name, M. A. Taylor, he has promoted conspiracy theories and played an instrumental role in some of the most influential videos in modern political history.

He edited the windsurfing ad that characterized John Kerry as a flip-flopper while he was the Democratic presidential candidate in 2004. And he was the editor and cinematographer of “Hillary: The Movie,” which the Federal Election Commission said could not be aired on television in 2008 because of election rules. That dispute led to the Supreme Court ruling known as Citizens United, which ended political spending limits for corporations.

“He is still one of the best editors I have ever seen,” said Mr. Bannon, who credited Mr. Taylor with developing the opening sequence of his film about the 2008 financial crisis, “Generation Zero.”

Mr. Taylor, who declined to comment, describes himself online as a “conceptual artist, filmmaker and messaging strategist.” Over the past decade, he has remained consistent about seeing art and politics as two sides of the same coin.

“To sell a candidate is simply to sell a concept,” Mr. Taylor said during a 2018 lecture in which he compared politicians to ready-mades, manufactured objects like a urinal or bicycle wheel that Duchamp removed from their original context and redefined as artworks simply by calling them so.

“What we do is we communicate with the public that our guy (the proverbial toilet) is art in a way,” he said during the lecture for the American Association of Political Consultants. “We sell ideas by reassigning thoughts. We tap into our audiences’ hearts and their minds the exact same way you sell a ready-made.

“He or she is not a candidate or a cause but a set of conceptual principles elevated above all to be a pure belief.”

Mr. Taylor, 47, developed his interest in conceptual art as an undergraduate at Washington University in St. Louis, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in sculpture. But shortly after graduating in 2002, he entered political communications as part of the 2004 Bush-Cheney re-election campaign.

He then began working with the conservative nonprofit Citizens United while helping Republican candidates on their 2006 midterm campaigns. One of the documentaries he worked on with that group was called “Border War: The Battle Over Illegal Immigration” and was produced by Mr. Bannon.

Mr. Taylor worked on several projects with Mr. Bannon through the 2000s and 2010s, and had a breakout moment as editor of “Hillary: The Movie.” His 2016 directorial follow-up, “Clinton Cash,” was an adaptation of a book that accused the State Department under Mrs. Clinton of giving favors to foreign entities that made payments to the Clinton Foundation and her husband. (A spokesman for Mrs. Clinton’s presidential campaign told The New York Times then that no one “has ever produced a shred of evidence supporting the theory.”)

“Taylor merged his love of cinema with sculpture and fashion to develop a unique perspective on messaging to broad audiences,” Mr. Taylor’s biography says on the website of a consulting group he founded with his wife. On YouTube, he has uploaded short artistic films like “Droidica,” which demonstrates his conceptual approach to filmmaking.

Mr. Taylor also worked as a media strategist in the 2016 presidential election, as part of a PAC that supported Ted Cruz and, later, Mr. Trump. But instead of joining the new administration, Mr. Taylor continued to make documentaries with conservative talking points. The Verge described “The Creepy Line,” a 2018 movie directed by Mr. Taylor that accused internet companies like Facebook and Google of suppressing conservative voices, as a “conspiratorial playbook for right-wing tech backlash.”

He also spent years developing “Marcel Duchamp: Art of the Possible,” interviewing artists like Marina Abramovic, Jeff Koons and Carolee Schneemann. The 2020 film won some applause, with Mr. Taylor doing an interview for the Golden Globes’ digital publication, and ARTnews describing the documentary as “smart, searching and sophisticated.”

“It presented Duchamp with a lot of personality,” said David Piperni, whose distribution company handled sales of the film.

Mr. Taylor has continued to reinvent himself in the art world, producing a music video for a British rapper who he then interviewed under the pseudonym Dr. Bacon, a fictional podcaster in a wide-brimmed hat. The performance was part of an art collective that he and his wife created called Take Vienna — its motto: “The revolution is dead. Long live the revolution” — with plans to develop film and television series.

A White House spokesman called Mr. Taylor “a performance artist across many platforms and an avid Duchampian,” adding that “fun pseudonyms are historically a large part of performance art history.”

After his introductory conversation with Mr. Haley last year, Mr. Taylor landed a job in Washington at the National Endowment for the Humanities. By July 2025, Mr. Taylor was driving across the country to move into a brick townhouse.

A few weeks later, Mr. Taylor’s wife and business partner, Michelle Taylor, posted a screenshot on Instagram of a Wall Street Journal article headlined “White House to Vet Smithsonian Museums to Fit Trump’s Historical Vision.”

“The reason we moved from Austin to DC!” she wrote in the post, which included two American flags. “The storylines are all coming together.”

Last month, the Domestic Policy Council released a report about the Smithsonian that said the National Museum of American History was spreading “radical activist ideology” with programming that was “anti-white,” “pro-illegal alien” and “pro-abortion.” The leader of the Smithsonian pushed back against the report, saying it was “not a fair characterization” of the museum’s work, which he said was “driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story.”

The museum’s director was called before a House subcommittee this week and was questioned by Republican members about whether she should keep her job, given the report’s findings.

Two people with knowledge of Mr. Taylor’s work in Washington, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid blowback from the administration, said Mr. Taylor told them he was involved with the report. When asked about its authorship, the White House spokesman said Mr. Taylor “didn’t write a word.”

During Mr. Taylor’s time within the Trump administration, he has also found ways of increasing his artistic profile.

As the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts looked this year to fill programming gaps created by Mr. Trump’s takeover, it turned in part to Mr. Taylor and his documentaries.

He had screenings of his Duchamp documentary as well as “Gotham: The Fall and Rise of New York,” a 2023 film produced by a longtime president of the conservative Manhattan Institute that attributed New York’s improved reputation in the 1990s to Republican leaders like Mayor Rudy Giuliani.

The Kennedy Center labeled his films “Extraordinary Cinema.”

Zachary Small is a Times reporter writing about the art world’s relationship to money, politics and technology.

Why Lettuce Is Always Making People Sick

Wired July 22, 2026

Salad is usually synonymous with healthy eating. Except now, as the US grapples with an expanding outbreak of cyclosporiasis that’s sickened more than 7,100 people in Michigan alone, likely caused by iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.

In fact, leafy greens are frequently implicated in instances of foodborne illness. There was a 2022 multistate E. coli outbreak tied to romaine served on Wendy’s sandwiches and 173 cases of norovirus linked to Illinois eatery D. C. Cobb’s. In 2021, BrightFarms recalled packaged salad greens sold in several states after 31 people got salmonella. And in 2019, a total of 167 people were infected with E. coli after eating romaine harvested from the Salinas Valley region in California. This isn't even the first cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce: In 2020, Fresh Express salad kits were linked to more than 700 cases of people afflicted with the parasite.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that produce is responsible for almost half of the reported foodborne illness cases, with leafy vegetables topping the list. So what is it that makes lettuce a major source of America’s foodborne tummy troubles?

One big reason is simply because lots of people eat it. Lettuce is the second-most-consumed vegetable in the US behind potatoes. (The latest outbreak ensures potatoes will remain the king of US veggies. Plus, french fries.) Wraps, subs, tacos, you name a fast food sandwich and it’s almost certainly got lettuce on it. Salad-slinging chains are fixtures across the US. Grocery store coolers are stocked with salad kits, on top of the unadorned heads of iceberg lettuce and containers of spinach.

Those ready-to-eat salads and blends of spring mix pose a particularly acute risk because they contain multiple types of leafy greens, which can come from different farms and locations. If one type of lettuce in the mix is contaminated, it can contaminate the whole bag. And because that contaminated lettuce gets packaged into lots and lots of bagged salad, it has the potential to spread germs far and wide.

How lettuce is grown can also expose it to a wide array of pathogens. A 2025 study by researchers at Cornell University who studied E. coli outbreaks in romaine lettuce found that a lot of contamination originates from irrigation with untreated surface water applied through overhead spray irrigation systems. There are ways to lower that risk, including switching to irrigation systems that do not directly touch the leaves, but that would require upgrades and downtime.

Lettuce’s satisfying crunch is also what makes it prone to pesky pathogens. Since it’s eaten raw—really, who wants wilted lettuce?—there’s no opportunity to cook off any lingering contaminants. Like other raw fruit and produce, leafy greens don’t go through what’s known as a “kill step”—heating, pasteurization, or freezing—which is designed to eliminate pathogens during the food manufacturing process.

The texture of lettuce is an additional factor in its ability to spread disease.“Many lettuce types have a lot of crevices and folds,” says Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “It’s very easy for these tiny pathogens to get in there.”

Even prewashing procedures at manufacturing facilities don’t always remove microbes, which can cling tightly to leaves. In the case of cyclospora, the parasite has thick outer walls, making it highly resistant to most food sanitizers. Experts say vigorous washing that involves scrubbing is the best way to get rid of cyclospora.

“If you don't wash these products well, you're going to end up ingesting whatever is on the lettuce,” says Amira Roess, an epidemiologist at George Mason University.

The White House Is Trying to Figure Out What to Do About Chinese AI

Wired July 22, 2026

The Trump administration is split over how to respond to the rapid rise of China’s leading AI models, according to multiple people familiar with deliberations.

The debate is broadly divided between parts of the White House, which has pushed for stricter controls on Chinese AI that may soon rival the most powerful US models, and the Commerce Department, which has viewed those restrictions as unworkable.

The conundrum has become the latest flash point for the administration over AI, after China’s Moonshot AI lab last week released its Kimi K3 model that rivals the top US models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

In recent days, senior White House officials have discussed possible measures to stop China’s AI labs from developing their models by training them on US models, a practice known as distillation, the people say.

The White House is expected to take some sort of presidential action after Anthropic last month alleged the Chinese tech company Alibaba had carried out the “largest known distillation attack” against it to date. This action is not currently expected to take the form of an executive order, according to one of the people.

A White House spokesperson did not comment on the reporting in this story.

The White House has been taking distillation attacks especially seriously. It announced on Wednesday that Moonshot had developed Kimi K3 by distilling Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 model, and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent told Fox Business that covert distillation could lead to sanctions, describing it as “IP theft.”

While proposals have been making the rounds inside the White House, no formal request for input has been transmitted yet to the Commerce Department, which has its own ideas, according to two people familiar with deliberations.

The Commerce Department has increasingly emerged as an influential part of the intra-administration split over AI, in part because it oversees export controls through the Bureau of Industry and Security.

Lutnick has contemplated ways to create incentives for top US labs to create their own open weight models to counterbalance China, and has spoken with leaders at a number of AI labs in recent weeks, the people add.

Lutnick appears to be straddling a middle ground of regulation—he imposed export controls on Anthropic to bring them to heel—but has been more freewheeling than Cairncross, one of the people said.

Earlier this month, the biggest AI issue for the administration was Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and Fable 5 models, because of their ability to find vulnerabilities in government systems and critical infrastructure.

But policy headaches with AI have only escalated with the rise of so-called open weight models from China—models that have few to no safeguards to prevent hacking government systems and can be downloaded and used by anyone.

The Odyssey’s Success Is Inspiring Unprecedented Levels of Cope

Wired July 22, 2026

For months, Elon Musk and the right-wing cranks he caters to on X have whipped themselves into a raging froth over the supposed desecration of an ancient Greek poem by one of the most successful movie directors alive.

Now that their manufactured backlash has bombed, they’re searching for ways to cope with the reality that they are increasingly divorced from popular opinion.

Christopher Nolan’s artistic crimes in bringing The Odyssey to the screen, according to Musk and others in a furor, were instances of what they called “historical inaccuracy” in a lavish fantasy teeming with monsters, witches, and undead spirits—mainly the casting of Lupita Nyong'o, who is Black, as Helen of Troy, and Elliot Page, who is trans, as Sinon. The grand total of approximately 10 minutes of screen time between these actors in a three-hour saga, combined with the general hysteria over “wokeness” in Hollywood, a rejection of Americanized dialog, and lingering misogyny regarding scholar Emily Wilson’s 2017 translation of Homer’s epic (the first by a woman), resulted in countless teeth-gnashing posts and calls for a boycott that never materialized.

Instead, the mythic drama hauled in a staggering $264 million as it opened this past weekend, sailing toward continued box office dominance and, in all likelihood, a slew of awards. A few conservative commentators, including Ben Shapiro—no fan of DEI or “woke” values—acknowledged it as a landmark achievement. But while some who had predicted its doom knew enough to move on from this battle to other fronts in the culture war, many sank deeper into denial.

“BREAKING,” blared one anonymous X account on Monday. “The Odyssey is FAKING ticket sales by buying up theaters/seats (Fraud) to make the movie look like a success (already $400 million in the hole) moviegoers are reporting having to take terrible seats (because full) but when they show up the theaters are mostly empty.” The post included screenshots of unverifiable anecdotes from Reddit about quiet cinemas and no-show ticket holders.

What Universal Pictures, the studio behind the film, would stand to gain by spending millions beyond a $250 million production budget and $125 million in marketing costs to astroturf a flop was not exactly clear. Then again, these are the same conspiracists who find it suspicious that the critics’ reviews tend to all be published at the same time.

Musk, for his part, seemed to be inspired by an X user who posted three minutes of AI-generated scenes in which characters from The Odyssey are all white and speak in British accents. Commenting on the clip, which at best resembles a montage from a hokey 1970s adaptation, the richest man in the world declared: “Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

Those familiar with Musk know that when he vows to reach a milestone by year’s end, it basically never happens. The promise of a Grok-animated Odyssey, though minor compared to most of his ambitions—he even speculated in 2025 that the xAI model might “discover new technologies” within several months—is sure to fall by the wayside as well. Not only is it a tiresome idea with zero appeal to the mainstream moviegoer (who has or will soon see Nolan’s version), it’s also unoriginal: The AI studio Fountain 0 is planning the online release of an artificially generated feature titled Odyssey: The Fall this summer.

Moreover, both ill-conceived projects misunderstand the lesson that the entertainment industry seems to be taking from Nolan’s latest blockbuster. At a moment when executives imagine that AI is the key to cutting costs and turbocharging output, the director has shown once again that the practical craft of filmmaking beats out what he himself has disparaged as “slop.”

So, will this aggrieved little cadre of internet reactionaries ever be able to accept that they don’t understand what audiences want? Or that they have deluded themselves, thanks to skewed algorithms and bogus amplification, into thinking they possess an influence they never had? Please. They’re not capable of conceding a loss. And there’s always another outrage down the road.

China’s Open AI Models Are Challenging Silicon Valley’s Playbook

Wired July 22, 2026

The AI industry is not quite experiencing a DeepSeek 2.0 moment, but it feels very close. The leading Chinese AI labs have been on a roll lately, releasing a series of almost cutting-edge open-source models. Z. ai released GLM 5.2 in June, Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 last week, and Alibaba released Qwen 3.8 this Monday.

Silicon Valley and Washington started talking about the models immediately, especially K3, which is widely seen as the best of the bunch. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and AI adviser to President Donald Trump, called the performance of Moonshot’s model “concerning.” Earlier this week, Commerce Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the US might impose sanctions on Chinese AI companies.

On Wednesday, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, alleged that the Trump administration has “information that Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic’s Fable for the development of its K3 model,” which he said amounted to “stealing proprietary US technology and undermining American research” and was “unacceptable.” (Moonshot AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The new Chinese models have a few things in common: Third-party benchmarks show that they perform nearly as well as the best Western models; they are optimized for agentic coding tasks (the hottest thing in AI this year); and they are or will soon be released with open weights, making them accessible and transparent.

But perhaps the biggest parallel between the current moment and January 2025—when the world was shocked by DeepSeek’s R1 model—is that it reaffirms how American and Chinese AI labs are taking diverging paths when it comes to being open or closed.

When it first burst onto the scene, DeepSeek challenged the premise that only closed-source models built with billions of dollars of investment in compute infrastructure and training could achieve frontier performance. But since then, Western AI labs have continued developing AI the same way, and now American frontier models feel more roped-off than they were a year ago.

Anthropic said for months that its latest Mythos model was so dangerously good at hacking that only approved collaborators could use it. When it was finally released more widely, the White House responded by issuing broad export controls, which forced Anthropic to take Mythos and its less capable sister model, Fable 5, offline temporarily. OpenAI similarly delayed the release of GPT 5.6 after it received a request from the White House.

In China, meanwhile, the situation looks very different. Chinese startups and tech giants have doubled down on open source: Anyone with a good enough computer environment can now download an open-weight model, run it locally, add customizations, and overall enjoy a much greater degree of freedom than OpenAI and Anthropic would ever allow. In many ways, the open versus closed debate is more entangled with the US versus China debate than ever before.

There are a lot of reasons why Chinese labs have chosen a business strategy built atop open-source models. Being the newer, smaller fish in the AI field, making their models free and open can help Chinese firms attract more users, collaborators, and media spotlight. It also puts them in a separate lane of competition from the one that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, SpaceX, and other deep-pocketed giants are in.

Earlier this year, rumors spread that Alibaba might be considering joining the closed-source race after it rearranged its corporate AI model development teams. But the tech giant announced on Monday that it would again release the latest version of Qwen—its line of open-source models beloved by the global tech community—with open weights, signaling to customers and the public it is not pivoting away yet.

Perhaps the strongest validation of the Chinese approach is the models themselves. Chinese labs have produced what are widely considered the world's best open-source AI models, showing that American companies no longer have an exclusive hold on building the most capable systems.

Arena AI, a crowdsourced model evaluation platform, now ranks K3 as the best model when it comes to web development tasks and number four in agentic tasks, just below Anthropic’s Fable and Opus 4.8, as well as OpenAI’s GPT 5.6. Artificial Analysis, an independent AI benchmarking company, ranks K3 in the third spot in its intelligence index.

Shortly after Moonshot AI released a preview version of K3 on July 16, people around the world began rushing to try it out, consuming so much inference computing resources that the company is temporarily restricting new users from signing up.

As more people start using open-source Chinese models with capabilities nearly on par with that of their Western competitors, some have started questioning whether paying for OpenAI or Anthropic’s offerings is really worth it. The fact that multiple Chinese labs were able to create capable agentic models and were unafraid to release them to the public is poking holes in the popular understanding that OpenAI and Anthropic are miles ahead of the competition.

Just like with DeepSeek, K3 fans are now celebrating it as evidence that Western AI models are overhyped and overprotected. “It is absolutely wild how much love Kimi got,” Rui Ma, founder of the independent research firm Tech Buzz China, said in a social media post, referring to the company’s announcement that demand for K3 had overwhelmed its servers. “Only made possible by the poor comms and decisions from [Silicon Valley] labs in the past year,” she added.

“I think Anthropic has overhyped the risks, or described risks that are coming soon but do not currently proliferate,” says Nathan Lambert, an independent AI researcher in Seattle who recently visited Moonshot AI’s office in China. He admits, though, that just like the rest of the general public, he has little firsthand information about how Mythos really performs. “We rely on a few private companies and a federal government with depleted state capacity to make that judgment call,” he says.

In addition to challenging the mainstream Western narrative about AI, Chinese open-source models are also proving to be a practical commercial replacement for American closed models. They aren’t just talked about on X and benchmarked against other models—they have become a popular and readily usable option for a growing number of Western startups and individual users.

“There's a real shift toward actually using these newest models that started with GLM 5.2,” Lambert says, referring to Z. ai’s model. “​​Even weeks after the GLM 5.2 release, I hear from AI researchers in the Bay Area that they are still using it for a core part of their workflow. Kimi, being a stronger model, will only do more, especially in areas like cybersecurity, where Mythos, Fable, and GPT 5.6 are effectively unusable.”

In fact, this is already happening. On Tuesday, OpenAI disclosed a concerning incident in which its GPT-5.6 Sol model hacked into the production system of Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform. Hugging Face has said it resorted to using the open-source model GLM 5.2 to analyze the cyberattack because other frontier models were refusing to help due to built-in safety guardrails.

Chinese AI models also tend to be cheaper than Western alternatives, but that’s not necessarily their main selling point. While models like K3 charge less for tokens, early tests show that they may require more tokens than Western models to solve the same problems, thus making the cost gap smaller. “In my fairly limited use, [K3] also seemed very token-hungry. It's not obvious to me that this model is actually that cheap to run,” wrote Dean Ball, a former White House AI adviser who recently joined OpenAI as its head of strategic futures, in a social media post in which he also praised K3 as “a very good model.”

Even if they are relatively token-hungry, models like K3 do ultimately challenge a fundamental assumption that has driven OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s strategy for years: that AI labs need infinite funding to scale up their compute capabilities just to make better models. “In the end, open-weight models deter further AI capex,” Ball wrote.

Review: Dyson V10 Konical

Wired July 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

I’ve spent the past week living with Dyson’s newest vacuums, and a clear favorite has emerged. But it’s not the one I expected.

I was ready to love the V16 Piston Animal for all the capabilities and suction power it offers, but as I’ve been testing, it’s the the Dyson V10 Konical that has left me most impressed for its performance at this price. Funny enough, when thinking about Dyson’s new lineup. it’s the least flashy offering, and the one I always forget about. The V8 Cyclone revives a longtime favorite, while the V16 packs the highest suction we’ve seen yet, making both easy to remember and exciting to try.

It was easy to let the V10 Konical fade into the background. It has the same power level as the V8 but a slightly higher price tag thanks to the new All Floor Cones cleaner head instead of the older Motorbar style.

When placed side by side, though, the V10 Konical easily justifies its $100 higher price over the V8 Cyclone. It did better than the V8 in almost every test I ran when comparing Dyson’s vacuums side by side, and it did the best when vacuuming up sand on a rug (even better than more expensive Dyson vacuums like the V15 Detect and Gen5Detect). If you’re looking for a good Dyson vacuum that doesn’t cost the better part of a grand, this is the one to get.

The Dyson V10 Konical packs a solid range of features for its price. It packs 150 air watts of power, which is above average for lightweight stick vacs, though it is weaker than most of Dyson’s own stick vacs. Our favored V15 Detect has 240 air watts, for example, but the V10 Konical felt similar on carpet to the V15 Detect, even with the change in suction power. It even felt like it suctioned better when I used it in handheld mode.

Dyson V10 Konical

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

That’s because just suction power alone doesn’t make a vacuum great at sucking up dirt and debris. A great motor and vacuum head design are equally important, if not more so. Dyson says the V10 Konical’s engine has 15 cyclone chambers built into it for air to flow through and create efficient suction. So while the power is lower than the V15, the two vacuums feel much more similar than I expected, since it still has impressive suction for its power and price point.

The V10 also has a seven-cell lithium battery that lasts for 60 minutes, like the more expensive V15 before it. There are three power modes, but there’s no screen on this device—just a built-in light on the mode button that shows you which setting you’re on. There’s green for eco mode, blue for medium mode, and red for max mode. The mode changes the suction level, so eco is great for lighter cleans while max is best for bigger messes; each higher mode uses more battery. The lack of a screen also means you’ll fly blind on battery life, so beware how long you spend on more powerful modes.

The V10 comes with the new All Floor Cones cleaner head, which is similar to the head that comes with the new V16 Piston Animal (though that version can sense messes). The All Floor Cones head has cones on either side to suck up hair and debris; the cone design promises to detangle long hair instead of letting it get stuck around the vacuum head’s bar. So far, I haven’t seen any hair tangled around the cones, so it seems to be working as intended. There’s also a built-in illuminating light to spot dust and debris when you’re vacuuming hard floors, which is a nice bonus.

This vacuum comes with two attachments: a crevice tool and a mini motorized tool that’s designed for cleaning upholstery. Plus, unlike many older Dyson models, including the more expensive V15 or the cheaper (but equally new) V8, you’ll also get fully sealed, five-stage HEPA filters to keep allergens from circulating out of the vacuum and back into the air.

Dyson V10 Konical

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

It’ll also be compatible with Dyson’s new docking station, the Auto-empty Dok, hopefully out later this year. Only the V10 Konical and the V16 Piston Animal ($980) are currently slated to work with it.

What made me like the Dyson V10 Konical so much was how well it did in my testing rounds. I tested it with sand and cereal on rugs, followed by litter on hardwood, and then carpeted stairs and bedrooms. It did better than many Dysons in its overall score, beating the V15 Detect, V16 Piston Animal, and V8 Cyclone with its score.

My scoring criteria ran 1 through 4 on five tests—sand, cat litter, Cheerios, general vacuuming, and handheld mode—with 4 representing the best performance and 1 being the lowest. The V10 Konical walked away with a 14 out of 20, while the V15 came behind it with a 12 out of 20. The V10 came in second overall out of five Dyson vacuums, with only the Gen5Detect beating it with a score of 17. The V10 pulls ahead of the Gen5Detect if you’re looking for add-ons, though, as the V10 will be compatible with Dyson’s self-emptying docking station that will release later this year.

While testing, I was particularly impressed with how well it picked up sand for its lower suction power, and it did a great job sucking up an intentional mess of Cheerios I created. I was less impressed with the hard floor results, but since the V10 doesn’t work with the Fluffy Optic head like Dyson’s high-end vacuums, it was never going to be as effective as vacuums that can switch to a head made for that surface. Still, it’s not bad—it was still able to vacuum up the litter I scattered on hard floors as a test. It just needed a couple of passes instead of a single pass to get it all, and it didn’t shove it into a pile like the cheaper V8 Cyclone did. The V10 does well in handheld mode and on carpet and rugs, and it felt a little easier to push around on a low-pile rug than the V8 did with its Digital Motorbar head.

Overall, I’d recommend this vacuum if you’re set on a Dyson and have a home full of mostly carpets and rugs. It’s a better buy than going for the cheaper V8, and I found it a better all-around experience than some of the more expensive Dyson vacuums out there. I still wouldn’t call it better than the Shark PowerDetect, but if you’re set on a Dyson, this is the best buy on the affordable end of Dyson’s scale.

Which Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 or Flip8 Phone Should You Buy?

Wired July 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Samsung has steadily improved its foldables, but the eighth annual update includes a fresh face, the Z Fold8, which features the long-rumored wide form factor. It slots in between the flagship Z Fold8 Ultra, which is the successor to last year’s Fold7, and the smaller Flip8, which succeeds the Flip7. Is the newcomer an awkward middle child or the glue that holds Samsung's folding family together? Samsung also has a couple of new smartwatches, the Galaxy Watch Ultra2 and Watch9.

The new phones are available for preorder, but before you get yours, let’s dig into the details to help you decide which of Samsung’s folding phones to buy. I’ll break down the key differences and similarities, so you can make an informed choice. And remember, Samsung sells many other smartphones, and we highlight the ones worth looking at in our Best Samsung Phones guide.

Let’s take a quick peek at what the eighth-generation Samsung Galaxy Z foldables have in common this year.

Although Samsung’s foldables all feature exterior and foldout screens in completely different sizes, they all boast Samsung’s Dynamic AMOLED 2X technology, so you get a 120-Hz refresh rate, support for HDR, and higher peak brightness than ever before (up to 3,000 nits), making it easy to read your screen, even in direct sunlight. They also have features designed to filter blue light and reduce eye strain.

The Fold8 Ultra and Fold8 have a special Flex Titanium layer that reduces the visible crease and provides extra strength, flexibility, and resilience. The titanium-alloy film should help the displays last longer, but also means they are flatter and smoother than before, with an anti-reflective finish that reduces glare.

All three phones have Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor inside, with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB or 512 GB of storage. You can also get the Fold8 Ultra and Fold8 with 16 GB of RAM and 1 TB of storage. They are all IP48 water- and dust-resistant and feature Samsung’s Advanced Armor Aluminum frame, which is scratch-resistant and durable enough to survive minor drops. The Fold8 Ultra and Fold8 support fast charging at up to 45 watts and fast wireless charging at 20 watts; the Flip8 is slightly slower for both. All three support Wireless PowerShare to top up wireless earbuds and other devices. Connectivity includes Wi-Fi 7 and Ultra Wideband (UWB).

Aside from the sizes, the camera systems are very different, but here are all the specs, so you can see exactly where they diverge.

Samsung

Samsung

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra is the biggest and best foldable that Samsung offers. If you crave the largest screen available but want to fold it away and have something that feels close to a regular smartphone when closed, this is it. The 6.5-inch cover display and slimmed-down design are slick but won’t turn heads. Open it up and you get an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side.

Everything is smoother and stronger, with Samsung's usual raft of annual refinements. Both displays boast Samsung’s latest tech and a silky smooth adaptive refresh rate that also saves power. Speaking of which, the battery is significantly bigger than the Fold7 at 5,000 mAh, and it supports faster wired and wireless charging than its predecessor. The only slight disappointment is the lack of magnetic Qi2, which is such a handy feature for easy docking and perfect wireless charging alignment.

What truly makes the Fold8 Ultra “ultra” is the camera system. It’s a top-tier combo of a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Both the main and ultrawide can shoot 8K video, and you’ll find plenty of AI assistance in your photo and video editing options.

Who it’s for: The flagship fan who wants the best of the best and doesn’t mind spending to get it.

Samsung

Samsung

The Samsung Galaxy Fold8 is where things get interesting. So far, the best folding phones have all been either book-style like the Fold8 Ultra, or much smaller flip phones, like the Flip8 below, but the Fold8 strikes an interesting middle ground. It’s much shorter than the Fold8 Ultra at 124 mm compared to 158 mm, but it’s also wider at 161 mm compared to 143 mm unfolded (82 to 73 mm when folded).

This form factor gives you a 7.6-inch inner display with a 4:3 (landscape) or 3:4 (portrait) aspect ratio, a more natural format for some media. While the unfolded screen isn’t miles away from the Ultra’s, using the Fold8 when closed will take some getting used to; even though it’s only millimeters of difference, it looks short and squat. It’s also a little more pocket-friendly, and at 201 grams it’s the lightest large-screen foldable on the market.

Performance, display tech, and most of the rest of the spec sheet match the Fold8 Ultra, though the battery is slightly smaller at 4,800 mAh. The glaring difference is the camera system, which consists of a pair of 50-megapixel lenses (wide and ultrawide) and drops the telephoto lens altogether, though it does still offer 10X digital zoom. It can still record in 8K, and Samsung has included features such as dual recording and my FanCam, a post-video editing feature where you can tap a subject in footage and generate a reframed clip that keeps them centered for social-ready content without the need for manual cropping.

Who it’s for: Fun and adventurous folks seeking something a little bit different.

Samsung

Samsung

The Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world thanks to its redesigned chassis. It’s the perfect option for folks who miss smaller phones, as it flips shut to slide easily into any pocket or bag. You get a 4.1-inch cover screen, but it flips open to convert into a 6.9-inch candy bar, and the main screen has Samsung’s top display tech.

It’s tougher and more durable than ever, and it boasts the same excellent chipset and top-end performance as its two bigger siblings. The smaller, 4,300-mAh battery is likely enough for similar stamina, since the screens are so much smaller, though the wired and wireless charging are a touch slower. You also get a more basic camera system, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide, and video recording tops out at 4K, though that’s plenty for most folks.

Who it’s for: People who prize portability, but still want a fun, flip design that's satisfying to slam shut.

Life is easier when you buy your new phone unlocked, because you can jump carriers to find better deals and easily switch to international eSIMs when you travel. The Galaxy Z phones sold through Samsung’s website are always unlocked.

The best place to buy a Galaxy Z phone is Samsung. com, especially since some colors are exclusive to the storefront. Always check out the promotions to make sure you snag any deals and consider trading in your old model for a decent discount. You get a six-month trial of Google AI Pro with these phones.

Whichever Samsung Galaxy Z foldable you decide on, you might want to buy it with the Galaxy Card, because you can earn 5 percent cash rewards on all in-store or online purchases made directly from Samsung in the US. Other benefits include 3 percent cash rewards on purchases using Samsung Wallet, 2 percent cash rewards on streaming service subscriptions, and 1 percent cash rewards on everything else with the physical card.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 succeeds the Samsung Watch Ultra and promises to be more accurate, faster, and smoother, thanks to the Snapdragon Wear Elite chipset inside. It also has the brightest display in a smartwatch at up to 5,000 nits. It’s still titanium, but both the watch case and the band are thinner and lighter. Under the hood, there’s specialized pro-level sport tracking, hydration guidance, and depth measurement for divers.

The Watch9 boasts the same chipset, a 3,000-nit display, and a 20 percent battery bump over the Watch8 to 390 mAh. It tracks your vitals, warns about any deviation from your usual baseline, and gives you a personalized fitness score and recommendations to improve your health.

Why Samsung Gave Its Next Folding Phone a New Shape

Wired July 22, 2026

Think “folding phone,” and Samsung probably comes to mind. The company has led the charge in the category since it debuted the first Galaxy Fold in 2019. It has refined the hardware of its Fold and Flip devices ever since, making them thinner, lighter, and stronger.

So what’s next? A new shape, apparently. On Wednesday, at its second Galaxy Unpacked event of the year, Samsung revealed a brand-new design for the Galaxy Fold8—a passport-shaped, book-like fold—which sits between the now-rebranded Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra and the compact Galaxy Z Flip8.

Drew Blackard, Samsung’s senior vice president of Mobile Product Management, says it’s all about expanding the portfolio. The larger, heavier, big-screen Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra caters to productivity-oriented folks, the Flip8 satisfies anyone prioritizing portability, while the new Fold8 is all around consuming content.

The new passport-style Galaxy Z Fold8.

“One of the things we’re seeing, in the past few years is an explosive growth in mobile video watching,” Blackard tells WIRED. “Consumers watch 80 percent of their video on mobile devices now, not in front of a TV screen or tablet. The actual shape of the content has changed—you’ve gone from landscape view format for things like Netflix to vertical orientation for a lot of social media.”

The new Fold8 has a 10:16 aspect ratio for the front cover screen, and when opened, reveals a 4:3 inner display, both of which play well with all kinds of videos, whether that’s clips on YouTube or Instagram Reels. Also, the unfolded 7.6-inch inner screen is ideal for reading websites or ebooks when the phone is held in vertical orientation. That makes it more familiar and comfortable for consuming content, which is the lion’s share of what people use smartphones for these days, than the taller, narrower Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra.

It looks a lot like what Apple’s first folding device is rumored to look like, with a wider screen that’s much shorter than the traditional booklike fold we’ve come to know. It resembles the original Google Pixel Fold or even the poorly received Microsoft Surface Duo.

Blackard says that when its seventh-generation folding phones came out in 2025, the company thought it had reached an inflection point of a mainstream design—the phone was light enough and the hardware slim enough with few spec trade-offs when compared with candybar smartphones. Last year’s Galaxy Z Fold7, for example, shipped with the same 200-megapixel camera as the flagship Galaxy S25 Ultra. Blackard says he believes this hardware parity will only usher in a diversity of folding phone designs that meet “consumers’ different needs.”

The time for experimenting with new shapes is ripe. Earlier this year, Samsung released the Galaxy Z TriFold—an even bigger folding phone that expanded to tablet size, with an eye-watering price. The company has since stopped selling it, with Blackard saying it was always supposed to be a limited-run product; Samsung did roughly four drops in the US, and with each one, the $2,899 TriFold sold out in minutes.

The Galaxy Z Fold8, on the far left, is the latest folding-phone shape from Samsung, with the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra in the middle, and the Galaxy Z Flip8 on the far right.

Now there’s the new shape, at a still-expensive but more palatable $1,900. Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for data and analytics at IDC, says whether it’s reacting to Apple’s upcoming iPhone or just expanding the portfolio, the Fold8 is a good move for Samsung.

“When Apple launches the device, and it becomes popular, then they can also offer the same kind of format to their customers,” Jeronimo says. “They have nothing to lose in launching a new format because it’s just another offering. If someone says, ‘I don’t like the book style,’ then they have the passport style. We will probably see more form factors and devices coming next year.”

A part of what might also help to make these devices more mainstream is the much talked about crease. Folding phones have an unavoidable crease in the middle where the hinge sits, and many have voiced their disdain for it. Now, thanks to a new titanium display layer that Samsung calls Flex Titanium in the Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra, the crease isn’t as noticeable and feels “flatter” than the more obvious ridge in previous models. Apple has reportedly expended significant effort in trying to eliminate the crease. The lesser the crease, perhaps the more appealing the phone.

Samsung says this titanium plate and the titanium-alloy film also help improve durability. And overall, the phone is easier to open and close, though the Fold8 isn’t designed to sit half-open. Blackard expects most users will stick with the cover screen or inner display, and that “Flex Mode” behavior—with the screen open at a 90-degree angle—is something folks using the Fold8 Ultra or Flip8 are more likely to demonstrate.

Crucially, Samsung also claims the Fold8 is the lightest booklike folding phone on the market, weighing in at a mere 201 grams (32 grams less than the iPhone 17 Pro Max). Weight plays a big role in adoption, as many early folding phones were bulky, heavy, and cumbersome to use. Slimming them down and reducing weight makes them significantly more usable, and the value of having much more screen real estate is easy to appreciate.

Blackard isn’t worried about Apple’s foray into its territory. He says more competition brings visibility to the category—people may know what a folding phone is today, but many haven’t seen or actually used one.

“The more there is out there, the more people will be familiar with the form factor,” he says. “When it comes to their decision, we can rely on the fact that this is our eighth generation. Obviously, first generations tend to go through hiccups.” He also points out that Samsung has a portfolio of devices for consumers to choose from rather than just one.

While others—like Motorola and Huawei—have chipped away at Samsung’s foldable dominance, particularly in the US and China, Samsung’s biggest challenge will be the folding iPhone rumored to arrive as soon as this September. The device could swoop in and take nearly 30 percent of global foldable shipments in 2026, according to IDC forecasts, potentially catapulting Apple as the largest player in the category on the strength of that one device.

The Galaxy Z Fold8 (left), the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra (middle), and the Galaxy Z Flip8 (right).

All of these folding phones, however, are moving further into the “premium” market category. The Flip8 and Fold8 Ultra are seeing $100 price increases over last year, which Blackard attributes to the memory crisis and rising component costs. Motorola also recently jacked up the prices of its folding Razrs. (Apple’s iPhone Fold is also expected to cost north of $2,000.)

It’s unlikely that Samsung will offer a folding phone under $1,000 in the near term, even if the memory shortage were to resolve itself. Blackard says the $899 Galaxy Z Flip7 FE it introduced last year didn’t deliver “the experience consumers wanted.”

Jeronimo says Apple and Samsung are unique in that they can raise prices in this economic climate because most of their customers buy their devices on installment plans or on contract through carriers. “If it costs $200 more, but it means $3 to $5 more per month, of course no one will be happy, but it’s not something consumers will be saying, ‘No, I won’t buy it because it’s $200 more expensive,’’’ he says. “The impact of the price increase on premium devices is less significant than on midrange.”

Blackard did not address rumors that the company may axe the Flip8 series, which is less popular than the booklike fold among its consumers, but says that when people buy a folding phone, most don’t go back to traditional candybar smartphones.

“That’s the exciting part of the form factor innovation of foldables,” he says. “We’re still exploring what all of this can be, but at the same point in time we’ve learned a lot and have a lot of confidence in what we’re doing with this portfolio.”

Finally, Some Fans Worth Getting Excited About

Wired July 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

If you don’t think you need a new fan, you might want to reconsider. Even if the dusty old pedestal fan you've been carting around for 25 years is still kicking, modern fans can do a lot more than just blow air. They're smarter, quieter, and far more versatile than they've ever been, with new tech features that would have seemed like science fiction even five years ago.

The Dreo TurboPoly 707S, for instance, has radar that can track where someone is in the room and redirect airflow as they move about, while the company's 508S model can provide mood lighting in more than 1,000 hues. There are bladeless fans, fans just for fitness purposes, and ones that can mist or cool your skin with a cryo-inspired metal plate.

I've been covering fans at WIRED for almost two years, and I'm always on the lookout for the latest and most interesting fan technology. If you know of a cool fan you want me to check out, let me know in the comments.

If you're looking to take your fan on the go, be sure to check out WIRED's companion guide to the Best Handheld and Wearable Fans. For more ways to keep your indoor air quality cool and under control, check out our guides to the Best Indoor Air Quality Monitors, Best Air Purifiers, Best Humidifiers, Best Dehumidifiers, and Best Window ACs.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added the Dreo 513S ceiling fan as a pick; moved some previous picks to Others Tested based on longer-term testing; and overhauled the Others Tested section, adding fans from Elecom Nestout, Lasko, and Balmuda. I've also included new information about Matter compatibility for Dreo’s TurboPoly 765S and updated all links and prices.
